Title EN: Arts and Disability Program - DASH
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Cultural Domain: Design,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: British Council, Capaz Perú, Birds of Paradise Theatre Company
Main Feature: The overall goal of DASH is to strengthen the cultural sector in conjunction with artists with disabilities and institutions committed to ensuring full participation in the cultural life of the entire society. DASH is achieved through the creation of professional cultural connections between artists, agents, managers, cultural spaces and institutions, as well as the development of skills and abilities of artists and cultural managers, through workshops, tools and lessons learned in international good practices. The program was carried out between 2021 and 2024 thanks to the British Council's alliances with the Asociación Capaz Peru, Ministry of Culture, and Birds of Paradise Theatre Company of the United Kingdom, and with the support of UNESCO in Peru and Británico Cultural.  In the 4 training cycles, 120 cultural managers participated in sessions aimed at introducing them to the social model of disability, emphasizing the human rights approach, and learning about accessibility tools and considerations required to carry out cultural activities and events accessible to audiences with disabilities.  In parallel, the program included a mentoring opportunity for 03 collectives of artists with disabilities, which provided funding and mentoring sessions to support the development of artistic pieces that were staged at an event to commemorate National Day of Persons with Disabilities in 2022.  In 2023, the Accessible Culture Network was formed, made up of 5 cultural institutions graduated from the DASH program and motivated to continue developing and sharing their experience in the area of accessibility. In February 2024, the network developed an agenda of activities through which they would strengthen their commitment to inclusive practice.  In March 2024, the last stage of the program was presented, in which it sought to share knowledge about the social model of disability and accessibility tools with representatives of 05 General Directorates of the Ministry of Culture of Peru, with the aim of preparing them to elaborate, influence and implement proposals for change within current cultural policies. The projects developed by them in working groups were registered in a toolbox that seeks to serve as reference material and encourage compliance with these actions, in alignment with the Recovery Plan for Cultural Industries and the Arts at the same to 2030.
Results: The program has brought performing arts by artists with disabilities to an audience of 2,930 people in direct contact in Peru. It has also trained 156 people, 70 of whom have been beneficiaries of the DASH Scholarships that resulted from a collaboration with the Ministry of Culture and UNESCO. The mentoring program has resulted in three plays directed by and starring artists with disabilities that have reached 500 people and we have formed the Accessible Culture Network, which has 35 participants.  Below is the breakdown by activity: 2021 Digital exhibition of the piece Hijinx Theatre Metamorphosis at the Arts and Disability Meeting (EADIS), organized by the Capaz Peru Association (300 participants, virtual) 2022: Training for cultural institutions by Birds of Paradise Theatre Company, Mentoring Program with Birds of Paradise Theatre Company, Capable and supported by  British  Cultural (25 participants, hybrid) Creation program for emerging artists at the Sala de Parto Festival 2022-23 (01 Peruvian artist funded by the DASH program: Rosa Victoria Chauca) DASH delegation travels to the UNLIMITED festival in the United Kingdom (2 representatives from Peru, from Teatro La Plaza and Association Capaz Peru) Presentation of the 03 mentoring pieces at La Otra Vitrina, Festival of Arts and Disability (in collaboration with Asociación Capaz Peru,  British  Cultural: 500 people) DASH delegation travels to Festival Otros Territories in Mexico City. (01 representative of Peru, from the British Cultural) 2023: DASH Scholarships in collaboration with the Ministry of Culture and UNESCO Formation of the Network of Accessible Culture (35 participants, from Lima) Stand of the Accessible Culture Network at the International Book Fair (RCA formed by British Council, Association Capaz Peru, British Cultural, Cultural Center of Spain, Teatro La Plaza: 1630 people impacted) Show by Aby Watson, neurodivergent artist from the United Kingdom, at the Arts Meeting, participation of short actress, Sofía Olmos (MX) (500 people) Aby Watson provided training sessions to groups of artists selected for the Performing Arts Festival Incuba (in collaboration with  British Cultural, 30 participants).

Title EN: Arts and media activities that promote diversity of cultural expression
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Media diversity
Agency Implementation: Indonesian Journalists Association
Main Feature: THE Indonesian press media have some characters, like Indonesian people that we found in the country. They are easy to appreciate other nations, various believes, and cultures. Indonesian press also have special characters like those. Although some of them appreciate all kind of diversity, people have awareness to filter the news that come to them.  The Ministry of Communication and Telecommunication Republic of Indonesian always warns the people to be critical to get information from all kind of media platforms (print, online, radio, or TV). Even all journalists must be very aware about the contaminated information with fake news, misinformation and disinformation.  Furthermore recently Indonesian Journalists’ Association (Persatuan Wartawan Indonesia/PWI) led by Hendry Ch. Bangun as a Chairman of PWI launched the Anti Hoax Task Force to help people and the government to get true information based on the facts.  About two decades ago, when social media have started growing and bringing some fake news, Indonesian press faced the serious problem of the contamination of information environment. Such as the contaminated water, it needs to be purified, it needs lots of costs for purifying it when we want to use it for drinking. For treatment we should identify where the contamination come from, what’s kind of pollutant, and finally we should select what’s treatment will we do? For doing that, we must have knowledge and good strategy for purifying the contaminated water.  What about the contaminated information? The contaminated information will be dangerous for being consumed. It will mislead people, delude everyone who use it, and jeopardize the media which spread it, because people would not trust the media: printed media, electronic media, or online media. This is the reason why many mainstream media keep up the quality of their news, they must work hard to get pure of information, not fake news, not misleading news, not disinformation, and not misinformation.  Purifying the information to be real information is not easy to do, because it is the big project that cannot be finished for one month. It takes several years for doing it. It is a big job, and need to do seriously and continuously.  We have known that journalism has been surrounded by fake news, disinformation, and misinformation (false or inaccurate information). The cacophony of disinformation in social media often leak to the press media, and as soon as will drown the real information, and the media itself. So now, let’s fight against the roots of fake news.  Where should we start fighting the fake news? Do we want to fight it from inside or outside factors? From inside of the news media organization, we have to identify and check the capability, professionalism in many skills of journalism. A bad interview, sloppy verification, and unskilled journalist in surveying, will allow fake news and polluting information come into the news room.  The fake news in this context, conflate misinformation and disinformation. Without awareness of journalism competence, news room will be easy to be penetrated by malicious actors who spread fake news. The malicious actors who intent to disrupt the information become disorder, here then we call it as outside factor. They arrange communication strategy to create the disorder information for their special interests, not for public interest.  In the article Thinking About “Information Disorder”: Formats of Misinformation, Disinformation, and Mal Information, in the book of Journalism, “Fake News”& Disinformation (published in 2018 by United Nation Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization, Paris), Claire Wardle and Hossein Derachsan wrote: “…misinformation is information that is false, but the person who is disseminating it believes that is true. Disinformation is information that is false and the person who is disseminating it knows it is false. It is deliberate, intentional lie, and points to people being actively misinformed by malicious actors”. According to them, misinformation, included false connection (headlines, visual or caption do not support the content), and misleading content. While disinformation, included false context, imposter content, manipulated, and fabricated content.
Results: The education is the best answer to make all journalists strengthen their competence. The Press Council (of Indonesia) work together with Indonesian Journalists’ Association (Persatuan Wartawan Indonesia/ PWI) and some institute of test journalist competence (Lembaga Uji Kompetensi Wartawan) since 2011 launched the tests of journalist competency program (Uji Kompetensi Wartawan/UKW) for all over provinces in Indonesia.  Up to March, 2024, total amount of competent journalists as the result of UKW are about more than 20.000 people. Specially journalists who passed the UKW from PWI at the same time are about 18.321 people. “We are happy because some friends (journalist) are competent. It means, they did their job very well. Also the examiner or assessor did their duties well,” said Tri Agung Kristanto, a member of Press Council, and also the head of commission on education, training, and profession development of Press Council.  For strengthening capabilities of members of PWI, Chairman of PWI Hendry Ch. Bangun in 2023 has made grand design more than UKW. He erected the new Indonesian School of Journalism (Sekolah Jurnalisme Indonesia/SJI), a real mobile school that move from province to province all over Indonesia. The syllabus of SJI contain the newest media technology lesson, multitasking, integrity, nationalism, character building, and all aspect of journalism.

Title EN: Arts Capacity Building
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Agency Implementation: Ministry of Culture and Sport
Main Feature: Key Measures Implemented: Training Programs: Scope: These programs aim to raise general awareness about the cultural industry and cover various creative arts such as music, dance, theatre, and literature. Objectives: The primary goals are to develop professional skills among artists, promote artistic goods and services, and foster job creation within the sector. Target Audience: The training is designed for both talented individuals and amateurs interested in advancing their skills.  Training of Trainers: Program Structure: A critical part of this initiative is training government workers who will, in turn, become trainers themselves.  Partnerships: Ambo University and Laurate Thegaye G/Medhin Cultural Center hosted the initial training programs for trainers, helping to establish a strong training framework. Wachamo University hosted the first regional training for cultural officers, contributing to regional capacity building.  Sustainability and Implementation: Agreements: The Ministry has signed a two-year agreement with the participating universities to ensure the sustainability of these training programs.  Current Status: The Ministry remains actively involved in implementing these agreements, working closely with higher education institutions to achieve the program's objectives.  These initiatives are designed to enhance the capabilities of professionals in the cultural sector and contribute to the growth and sustainability of Ethiopia's cultural industries.
Results: After completing the Training of Trainers (TOT) program, several trainees have successfully begun conducting training sessions for students in schools. Among them, trainees from Laurate Thegaye G/Medhin Cultural Center have gone a step further by forming a legal business entity—an art group. This group not only generates income for the organization and the university but also uses the arts to provide valuable social services.  These initiatives have demonstrated the effectiveness of the TOT program, proving to be a valuable model for the Ministry of Culture and Sport. The success of the program with Laurate Thegaye G/Medhin Cultural Center has inspired the Ministry to explore similar collaborative efforts with other universities. This approach underscores the potential for university partnerships to enhance both educational and social outcomes in the cultural sector.

Title EN: Audiovisual Co-productions – Working Group of EU Member States’ experts
Goal: Achieve A Balanced Flow Of Cultural Goods And Services And Increase The Mobility Of Artists And Cultural Professionals
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 10 - Reduce inequality within and among countries,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Mobility of artists and cultural professionals
Agency Implementation: European Commission, EU Member State governments
Main Feature: The 2019-2022 Council Work Plan for Culture included a topic on co-productions in the audiovisual sector, for policy collaboration through a working group of EU Member States’ experts under the.  The task identified for this group was to develop ‘In order to stimulate co-productions, policy recommendations and incentives for co-productions in legal frameworks and audiovisual support schemes in order to stimulate co-productions will be developed.  The mandate of the working group (link above) called for it to take into account, inter alia: • the role of other European bodies such as Eurimages; • the role of legal frameworks, such as bilateral co-production agreements, the Council of Europe Convention on Cinematographic Co-production, and the European Convention on Transfrontier Television; • the contribution of private partners in financing and distribution; • the role of TV broadcasters, both public and private, and VOD, as well as the importance of the role of distribution in the value chain; • the emergence and the impact of new market players, in particular global video on demand (VOD) services and the new non-linear business models they have generated; • the impact of new digital technologies on audiovisual services, especially for the recommendation, personalisation and processing of audiovisual content; • the role of overseas or non-EU co-production partners; • changes in audience behaviour, especially in relation to how to engage young people.
Results: Recognising the potential of European co-productions to act as locomotives for the sector, the Council of the European Union in 2019 decided to create a Group of Member State experts to discuss how to stimulate European co-productions. Twenty-six Member States selected experts for this Group, which held six meetings between June 2019 and December 2021. The group produced a report, Co-productions that shine [https://op.europa.eu/en/publication-detail/-/publication/bc19a442-a01f-11ec-83e1-01aa75ed71a1/language-en], which pays attention not only to cinematographic works covered by the revised Council of Europe Convention on Cinematographic Co-production, but also to organic forms of cooperation among EU-27 producers, notably in the field of TV series, a format that is thriving. Whilst fully acknowledging the importance of co-productions with countries outside Europe, the Group decided to focus on co-productions among EU-27 Member States.

Title EN: Initiatives to enable sustainable creative careers
Goal: Promote Human Rights And Fundamental Freedoms
SDG: SDG 5 - Achieve gender equality and empower all women and girls,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels
Area of Monitoring: Artistic freedom
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: Ministry for Culture and Heritage Creative New Zealand  Ministry of Education Te Tāhuhu o te Mātauranga
Main Feature: The New Zealand Government has implemented a range of policies around the theme of sustainable careers. The policies implemented are mutually reinforcing to support the sustainability of the cultural sector more generally.  •	The Creative Careers Service Pilot (2020-2024) supported people in the creative sector to develop non-creative skills to build sustainable careers and income in their chosen creative field. The programmes delivered included a combination of one-on-one mentoring, online learning resources, and cohort-based professional development workshops and training. This supported the mobility of cultural professionals through skill development enabling them to better navigate and build their creative careers. •	The Creative in Schools programme (2020-now) was initially adopted as a short-term funding programme to provide opportunities for schools throughout New Zealand to apply for funding to deliver a creative project in partnership with professional artists and creative practitioners. This offered creative professionals new opportunities to work in the education sector. Creatives in Schools – Education in New Zealand •	Creative Spaces funding (2021-2024) invested NZ$17.1 million into 54 creative spaces: community arts organisations that provide access to art-making activities for people who face barriers to participation (e.g. neurodiversity, physical or intellectual disabilities).  •	Creative New Zealand has designed a Remuneration Policy for Artists and Arts Practitioners 2022 - Ko te Mahere Utu mā ngā Kaitoi, Kaiwaihanga Toi to support and promote the fair remuneration and employment practices for artists and arts practitioners. •	An Artist Resale Royalty Scheme is being established to ensure the creators of visual art are recognised and rewarded when their work is resold on the secondary art market. www.mch.govt.nz/our-work/arts-sector/artist-resale-royalty-scheme. This will add another ongoing source of income for visual artists to support their career sustainability and its reciprocity with other countries, as required in the UK and NZ free trade agreements will contribute to the flow of cultural services between New Zealand and countries overseas.  •	Under the Creative New Zealand Pacific Arts Strategy (Pacific Arts Strategy 2018 2023 | Creative New Zealand (creativenz.govt.nz)), there have been a number of vocational and training programmes supported including the Pasifika Conductors Masterclass developed in partnership with the New Zealand Symphony Orchestra to provide a foundational entry point to a professional creative career for Pasifika conductors.
Results: •	Creative Careers Service pilot programme: As of 31 October 2023, 1236 people have participated in the programme, including 426 Te Manatū Whakahiato Ora Ministry of Social Development (MSD) clients and 810 non-MSD clients. 59% of participants have increased their creative income since participating in the pilot.  •	Creatives in schools: Nearly half (45%) of creative practitioners engaged in the programme thought that Creatives in Schools helps them build a sustainable portfolio career to a high or very high degree. •	Creative Spaces: Funding enabled creative spaces to employ more staff and provided an employment pathway into the creative sector for creative spaces volunteers and participants, helping some of them become paid staff. The number of paid staff across all creative spaces increased by 44 percent (from 451 to 651) after just 18 months of funding. Most importantly it created additional job opportunities in the social sector for creative professionals.   •	The Artist Resale Royalty scheme is not yet active – the legislation comes into force on 1 December 2024.  •	Digital fellowship programme: the programme has provided five New Zealand participants with NZD $10,000 each to explore their digital practice through a mix of expert mentoring, workshops and collaboration.
Financial Ressources: •	Creatives Careers Service: $7.9 million NZD/$4.84 million USD over four years •	Creatives in Schools: $12 million NZD/$7.35 million USD over four years  •	Creative Spaces: $18 million NZD /$11.02 USD million over three years.  •	Artist Resale Royalty scheme: $0.954 million NZD/$0.58 million USD over four years.  •	Digital fellowship programme: $50,000 NZD/$30,613 USD.
Recommandations: •	An independent evaluation of the Creative Careers Service pilot programme found that the service is well-designed to meet the needs of creatives to professionally develop their creative careers. 59% of participants have increased their creative income since participating in the pilot.  o	https://www.msd.govt.nz/documents/about-msd-and-our-work/publications-resources/research/creative-careers-service-evaluation-report/creative-careers-service-evaluation-report.pdf) •	An evaluation carried out after the end of Round 3 of funding found that the programme continues to deliver important benefits to ākonga and students, schools, creatives and communities. The programme makes a worthwhile and valuable contribution and should be continued. It found that the programme supports: o	enhancing ākonga and student wellbeing, helping to engage and connect them in positive ways, in some instances re engaging them with schools. o	raising the confidence of kaiako and teachers in designing teaching and learning projects that engage the creativity of ākonga and students across the learning areas of the curriculum. o	developing more sustainable portfolio careers for many creative practitioners o	building better home school relationships with whānau and parents. o	https://www.educationcounts.govt.nz/__data/assets/pdf_file/0004/221539/Creatives-in-Schools-Evaluation-of-Round-3-2022-final.pdf •	An evaluation of Creative Spaces concluded that the NZD$18 million funding allowed the creative spaces sector to weather the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, and in some cases prevent spaces from having to close their doors permanently. However, the funding did more than just this. For the first time, many staff were not relying on additional jobs for income due to their role at the creative spaces alone not being sufficient. Staff also had more time and resources to develop new, or enhance existing programmes, providing better support to participants. The reach of the sector also increased through new programmes and locations for delivery, including an increase in Māori and Pacific participants. While the overall success of this was tempered by the disruption of COVID-19 restrictions, the funding has significantly enhanced the impact of the sector and benefits for its participant base. It has also helped us upskill and better connect creative spaces with one another, offering them ongoing opportunities to share knowledge and best practice and provide support.  o	https://www.mch.govt.nz/sites/default/files/2023-11/Creative-Spaces-Report-20230904.pdf •	The Resale Right for Visual Artists scheme will commence on 1 December 2024, and has not yet been implemented. There has not yet been an evaluation of the scheme.

Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Agency Implementation: Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment & the Ministry of Education and Culture
Main Feature: The Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment and the Ministry of Education and Culture launched the growth agreement process for the audiovisual sector at the beginning of 2022. The ministries tasked Business Finland and the Finnish Film Foundation, which are both within the ministries’ remit, with preparing the project. The steering group invited Audiovisual Producers Finland (APFI ry) to represent the industry. The industrial policy programme Film Tampere of the business development company Business Tampere Oy facilitated the practical development work with project funding from the Ministry of Education and Culture. Close to 200 persons representing all key operators in the sector participated in the growth agreement process. In total, the companies’ turnover amounts to more than EUR 600 million.    At the end of August 2022, representatives of the audiovisual sector submitted their views on the business objectives and necessary measures to the representatives of the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment and the Ministry of Education and Culture.   Based on this proposal, a public-private working group was established in autumn 2022. The objective of the working group was to create a common growth agreement based on open dialogue. This would be a new operating model aimed at the growth and internationalization of companies in the audiovisual sector. The report of the working group was published in May 2023 and it included concrete proposals for action.    The implementation of the growth agreement is driven by the global growth in the audiovisual market. Finland’s audiovisual sector aims to become part of a growing international market, which means that both the audiovisual field and the public sector must commit to a continuous, long-term development of the sector.   The creative economy has great potential for Finland’s national economy and culture. The Finnish audiovisual sector has been on the rise for a few years now, and it is important to identify measures to help those involved in the sector in the future too. Further work on the growth agreement will continue in the audiovisual sector, and based on good experiences, the agreement practice was also started in other creative sectors during 2023.   For more, see:   https://www.creativefinland.fi/julkaisut
Results: The report of the working group contains objectives and measures which have been agreed upon between the representatives of the audiovisual sector and public sector parties and which can be used to increase sustainably the business activities of the entire audiovisual ecosystem and to boost its significance for the Finnish economy. At the same time, companies can also carry out profitable business and offer their employees a good working environment.
Financial Ressources: 650 000 USD in three years

Title EN: Automatic Copyright Detection Research: An Inequality Tool
Goal: Promote Human Rights And Fundamental Freedoms

Area of Monitoring: Artistic freedom
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: Karisma Foundation
Main Feature: The Karisma Foundation conducted research in 2020 in Colombia that revealed how automated copyright infringement detection tools produce illegitimate notifications that harm the ability of small digital content producers in that country to attract new audiences and obtain economic benefits or digital interactions with your work. The investigation found multiple cases of unjustified notifications of alleged copyright infringements directed at public domain content, original content produced by the recipient of the notification, or content in which copyright law exceeds its limits.
Results: This investigation allowed the identification of specific cases in Colombia, in which access to information and cultural enjoyment was hindered or prevented due to the use of automatic copyright detection tools in the platform content moderation and curation processes, like Facebook or YouTube. The study provides arguments for the review of the regulatory and public policy frameworks of culture and copyright in digital environments and shows the need to protect the cultural rights of Colombian citizens following the principle of technological neutrality.

Title EN: Awareness campaign – Culture Objective 2030
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Partnering with civil society
Agency Implementation: NAME: International Federation of Coalitions for Cultural Diversity ( IFCCD ) EMAIL: coalition@CDCE-cdce.org PHONE: (+1) 514-277-2666
Main Feature: Over the past four years, the IFCCD has continued its involvement in the 2030 Campaign, an advocacy campaign bringing together numerous international cultural organizations and aimed at recognizing culture as the fourth pillar of sustainable development and integrating culture into the United Nations global development agenda. The campaign began in 2013 and aims to promote a stronger role for culture throughout the implementation of the current global development agenda (the United Nations 2030 Agenda), the adoption of culture as a distinct objective in the post-2030 development agenda, and the adoption of a global agenda for culture. Through its participation in the campaign, and, more concretely, by attending strategic meetings, contributing to common proposals and submitting others on its behalf, aligned with the overall objectives of the campaign, the IFCCD contributed to certain key gains. The Culture2030Goal campaign has long argued that culture has a key role to play, not only as a sector with the power to bring about change, but also as an overall dimension of sustainable development with a major effect on behavior and therefore on the effectiveness of policies. The IFCCD has therefore used its platforms to relay the informative materials produced by the campaign in the last four years, helping to promote the importance of diverse culture, such as the report “Culture in localizing the SDGs: an analysis of local reviews volunteers (ELV)”. #Culture2030Goal campaign published a Statement on Culture and the COVID-19 pandemic, which was officially launched on May 21, 2020, on the occasion of the World Day for Cultural Diversity, Dialogue and Development. This date illustrated the campaign's commitment to achieving the 2030 Agenda as well as the need to ensure that culture is placed at the heart of the Decade of Action to achieve the UN Global Goals. The IFCCD was represented by its president. In 2022, the IFCCD participated in the development and relayed the Declaration of the # Culture2030Goal campaign, a document which highlights that culture represents the fourth pillar of sustainable development and plays an indispensable role in supporting the well-being of individuals and communities, social cohesion, and the general effectiveness of policies. This document was submitted in view of MONDIACULT 2022, the UNESCO world conference on cultural policies and sustainable development which took place from September 28 to 30, 2022 and where the President of the Federation was invited to deliver a speech. In the numerous parallel and official events in which it took part, the Federation carried messages on the need to recognize the importance of culture in the United Nations' sustainable development goals, on the conditions necessary to put in place an " equitable culture” and on the need to involve all players, including private companies, in order to preserve the diversity of cultural expressions in the digital environment. “The diversity of cultural expressions can only flourish in a context of sustainable development where robust regional cultural ecosystems exist that strengthen the local value chain. Such ecosystems allow cultural content to be first produced and consumed at the local level, while ensuring creators and producers fair remuneration and good working conditions, and giving citizens access to the culture that interests them. To achieve this, we must address the serious inequalities that exist for coalitions outside of Europe and North America. », declared in particular the Secretary General of the Federation as part of the event A Culture Goal is essential for our common future, organized by the # Culture2030Goal campaign at Colegio San Ildefonso, on September 27, 2022. Finally, in December 2023, the FIDCD submitted an intervention to the UN in anticipation of the Future Summit, organized by the UN, which will be held in September 2024. The intervention aims to specifically draw attention to the importance of including the perspective of the diversity of cultural expressions in the SDGs. She also joined a collaborative intervention under the #Culture2030Goal campaign which calls for the addition of a dedicated culture goal to the 2030 agenda for sustainable development.
Results: Concretely, the most important gains from this campaign will occur in the coming years, since the closer 2030 gets, the more advocacy efforts will translate into concrete results.  However, the IFCCD welcomes the victory obtained during MONDIACULT 2022, during which 150 States adopted a historic declaration for culture. The latter, which uniquely recognizes culture as a global public good, echoes several requests put forward by the Federation, calling in particular to “integrate culture “as a specific objective in its own right” in the next United Nations Sustainable Development Goals" and "substantial regulation of the digital sector, in particular large platforms, for the benefit of online cultural diversity, the intellectual property of artists and equitable access for all to the contents”.

Title EN: Beyond Emerging Artists
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Agency Implementation: Abu Dhabi Department of Culture and Tourism
Main Feature: The "Beyond Emerging Artists" policy is designed to support and elevate the careers of artists who have moved beyond the initial stages of their artistic development and are poised for greater recognition and impact. This policy focuses on providing advanced opportunities for established artists to refine their craft, expand their professional networks, and gain exposure in broader, more prestigious platforms. Key features of the policy include funding for high-profile exhibitions and residencies, tailored mentorship programs with leading industry figures, and strategic partnerships with galleries and institutions that can help amplify the artists' visibility. Additionally, the policy encourages collaborations between seasoned and emerging artists, fostering an environment of knowledge sharing and innovation. By targeting artists who have already demonstrated significant talent and potential, "Beyond Emerging Artists" aims to propel their careers forward and ensure their contributions to the art world are acknowledged and celebrated on a larger scale.
Results: Some of its key achievements include providing a platform for emerging artists to showcase their talents and express their cultural diversity in an artistic format annually, which would further allow them to develop their practice and realize ambitious art projects. Additionally, selected artists participate in a year-long program of workshops and studio visits guided by a guest curator. This leads the artists to create new projects for the same program but with different artistic capabilities. The artists also experience exposure as their artworks are first showcased in Abu Dhabi and then in diverse location which provides them with recognition and the motivation they need to continue with their artwork. The program has fostered artistic growth and international exposure.
Recommandations: Emphasizes the importance of sustained support systems for mid-career artists, ensuring they have access to mentorship, funding, and resources to maintain their artistic momentum and achieve long-term success. It advocates for increased global exposure by providing access to international platforms, exhibitions, and residencies, fostering cross-cultural collaborations. Strengthening local art institutions and galleries is also essential to offer established artists opportunities to showcase their work, while public-private partnerships can create more exhibition spaces. Additionally, the measure highlights the need for cultural mobility and artistic freedom, enabling artists to work and move freely across borders, accessing global markets and contributing to international artistic dialogues. It also encourages artists to explore new mediums and interdisciplinary projects, ensuring they remain innovative and relevant as they continue to evolve in their careers. These recommendations collectively aim to provide artists who have moved beyond the emerging phase with the tools and platforms to thrive both locally and globally.

Agency Implementation: Ministry of Culture
Main Feature: Estonia has bilateral cultural cooperation agreements and joint programmes with nearly 50 countries from all over the world, more than half of these have been concluded with non-EU countries.   Usually, bilateral agreement shall remain in force indefenitely or for a certain period of time and thereafter shall be automatically renewed for successive period of equal duration, unless either of the Parties should express its opposition thereto, which must be notified in writing through diplomatic channels.   In addition to a bilateral agreement, Parties may agree upon and in accordance with the agreement a separate cultural cooperation programme for a certain time period. Such programmes can be prolonged by means of exchange of corresponding notes sent through diplomatic channels, unless either of the Parties should express its opposition.   Activities under cultural cooperation agreements/programmes are supported by both parties to the agreement/programme in finalizing projects within the agreement/programme (for example, usual practice is that the host country covers the costs of receiving guests and the visiting country takes care of the travel expenses). Within the frames of active bilateral cooperation agreements and programmes, different NGOs and private or state cooperation partners in the status of legal person registered in Estonia can apply for the support from the Estonian Ministry of Culture. Grants from the Ministry of Culture are combined with other Estonian sources of financing.   A five-year cultural cooperation programme between the Estonian and Ukrainian ministries of culture, based on a cultural cooperation agreement signed in 1996, is currently being renewed. The last cooperation programme was valid from 2017 to 2021. We plan to conclude a new cooperation programme in 2024.   Since 2022 some bilateral agreements have been terminated. Following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, Estonian Ministry of Culture withdrew from the cultural programme with Russia and Belarus.
Results: Development of cooperation in the field of culture by supporting (financially as well as the exchange of know-how) bilateral cooperation between creative persons and cultural institutions. Creation of a favourable environment for international cooperation, including exchange of know-how and activated cultural exchange. On a wider scale, enhancement of mutual understanding and friendship between the countries.
Financial Ressources: Financial resources correspond to the policy measure “Estonian Culture in the World”, e.g. ca 803625 USD yearly
Recommandations: Before prolonging the programme for the next period, both Parties evaluate the projects carried out within the previous period as well as the necessity to continue with the programme. So far, the general conclusion has been to continue with the agreements and programmes which have been active, effective and/or have been signed with our priority countries in international as well as development cooperation.

Title EN: Digital Creative Industries Roadmap 2024-2026
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture

Main Feature: Ireland’s Roadmap for the Digital Creative Industries was launched in January 2024. Developed by the Creative Ireland Programme within the Department of Tourism, Culture, Arts, Gaeltacht, Sport and Media (DTCAGSM) and the Department of Enterprise, Trade and Employment (DETE), the Roadmap seeks to leverage the clear potential of these sectors for sustainable and resilient employment, export growth and regional development. The Roadmap will focus on the specific digital creative industry sectors of: Commercial design sectors, Digital Games, immersive technologies and content creation.  The Creative Ireland Programme consulted extensively with industry bodies, business people, practitioners and academics in the fields of design-based, digital creative and content creation sub-sectors, and with other government departments, agencies and enterprise partners in order to develop the Roadmap. Its’ ambition is to “Enable new modes of learning in partnership with and for the digital creative industries, and embed creativity across further and higher education activities to future-proof our economy.” This includes advancement of apprenticeship/traineeship initiatives for digital creative industries and developing competency frameworks relevant to roles in specific sub-sectors.   Working across Government and in partnership with industry, the Roadmap will adopt an integrated approach, principally to address issues of fragmentation and efficiency through the following objectives: 1.	Enabling a collective industry voice to support sectoral engagement and to facilitate the perspectives of export potential digital creative industry sectors in the development of relevant policy and initiatives; 2.	Enhancing and driving stronger collaboration with relevant further and higher education partners to address education and training needs; 3	Strengthening our focus on supporting enterprises within the targeted digital creative industry sectors, particularly at microenterprise and SME levels;  4	Further leveraging the innovation and export potential of digital creative industries; 5	Continuing to build on the success of place based approaches to the development of the targeted digital creative industry sectors; and 6	Enhancing opportunities for trade, exports and MNC linkages for the targeted digital creative industry sectors  The Digital Creative Industries Forum has now been established on foot of the Roadmap published in January. The forum established will now facilitate collaborative dialogue and timely action on relevant issues for the sector, including AI as relevant. It is co-chaired by DETE and DTCAGSM to bring together relevant Departments and agencies to work with the industry bodies representing the 4 target areas: •	Design sectors including industrial design, product design, visual communications, Ui/Ux (User-interface/User-experience) and interaction design, service design and strategic design; •	Digital games sector;  •	Immersive technologies; and •	Content creation sectors including advertising and brand agencies, visual and audio-visual content for commercial social media and multimedia content for mobile applications For 2024 the focus is on workstreams covering: •	Data •	Enterprise supports and marketing opportunities •	Skills •	Regional Development  Roadmap Available Here: https://www.creativeireland.gov.ie/app/uploads/2024/01/CI_Creative_Industries_Roadmap_23_Screen_AW-3.pdf
Results: Implementation only began in January 2024.  First report to Government will be submitted by year end 2024.
Financial Ressources: The Department of Tourism, Culture, Arts, Gaeltacht, Sport and Media allocated €300,000 to this initiative in 2024.

Main Feature: The mission of the “Bioethics, Multiculturalism & Religion” project is to provide a forum in which representatives of diverse religions and traditions can: -	engage one another in a sustained scholarly dialogue about global bioethics; -	cultivate an amicable atmosphere so participants can learn about each other’s tradition or religion with discursive empathy; -	promote mutual understanding of global bioethics through respectful discussion and scholarship; -	strive to develop the linguistic and conceptual space in which common ground or convergence can emerge and be mutually recognized and appreciated; -	foster creative cooperation while respecting the dignity and uniqueness of each tradition. Nine International Conferences and workshops on “Bioethics, Multiculturalism and Religion” have been held in Jerusalem (2009), Rome (2011), Hong Kong (2013), Mexico City (2014), Houston (2016), Rome (2018), Casablanca (2019), Bangkok (2022), and Rome (2023). These academic conferences sought to foster the convergence and cooperation in global ethics among experts in bioethics coming from the world religions including Buddhism, Christianity, Confucianism, Hinduism, Islam, Judaism as well as the secular perspective. The 10th international workshop will take place in Madrid on December 17-19, 2024. The conferences are a first step in creating a permanent academic forum to promote dialogue and reflection about bioethical issues, considering the importance of human rights and the different features of each religion and cultural perspective actively-advancing medical, legal and technological environment. The academic conferences provide important benefits for the experts and institutions in the field of bioethics, as well as a media platform promoting recognition and visibility of the scientific commitment in the field of life sciences and medicine. Moreover the conferences aim to highlight the importance of dialogue in the globalized and diverse world.

Title EN: Brazilian Federal Constitution
Goal: Promote Human Rights And Fundamental Freedoms
SDG: SDG 5 - Achieve gender equality and empower all women and girls,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels
Area of Monitoring: Artistic freedom
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: Brazilian Judicial System
Main Feature: In Brazil, freedom of artistic and cultural expression is a fundamental right, guaranteed by the Federal Constitution, which establishes: a) the expression of intellectual, artistic, scientific and communication activity is free, regardless of censorship or license (art. 5, item IX);  b) any and all censorship of a political, ideological and artistic nature is prohibited (art. 220, paragraph 2). As artistic freedom is a corollary of freedom of expression, it is a fundamental right in Brazilian domestic law, which is why it cannot be subjected to restrictions that do not find constitutional support, being exceptional, necessary and considered. Therefore, it is not up to the State, through any of its bodies, including the Judiciary, to define, in advance, what can or cannot be created, produced, staged or published as art, and, in the event of infringement of any subjective right individual, that the constitutionally foreseen measure is, as a rule, compensation for moral damages (art. 5, item X), and not the prohibition of displaying the questioned work of art.
Results: Despite legal protection, artistic freedom has frequently been attacked in Brazil, with acts of censorship initiated by various levels of power and public authorities, as well as by private companies. The National Arts Foundation – Funarte, a public institution linked to the Ministry of Culture, participated in the “Workshop on the Construction of Inter-American Principles on Freedom of Artistic Expression and the Rights of Artists and Cultural Professionals”, held on November 6th and 7th, 2023, in Washington DC, USA. The event was organized by a group of partners: Article 19 Brazil and South America; Article 19 Mexico and Central America; Regional Alliance for Free Expression and Information; Brazilian Movement on Freedom of Artistic Expression (MOBILE); Special Rapporteur on Freedom of Expression (RELE); Special Rapporteurship on Economic, Social, Cultural and Environmental Rights (REDESCA); Washington Brazil Office (WBO); IFEX Global and Samambaia Philanthropies).

Main Feature: The British Columbia Arts Council (BCAC): is the primary grant funding body for the arts and culture sector in the province and offers funding programs for a range of arts and cultural activities. The BCAC was established in 1995 through the Arts Council Act for the purposes of: providing support for arts and culture in British Columbia; providing persons and organizations with the opportunity to participate in the arts and culture in British Columbia; and providing an open, accountable and neutrally administered process for managing funds for British Columbia arts and culture. In response to the challenges of the pandemic, the province provided resilience funding through the BCAC from 2020/21 to 2022/23 to support B.C. arts and culture sector in building back strong.   The New Foundations Strategic Plan: 2018-2022 committed to focusing on the diversity of both professional and community arts practices throughout the province, improving the accessibility and relevance of BC Arts Council funding programs. It also committed to deepening engagement with the processes of decolonization and reconciliation, taking a lead from Indigenous artists, organizations and communities and respecting the principle of self-determination.   The Extending Foundations Action Plan: 2022-2024 further committed to improving access to BC Arts Council programs, building principles of equity throughout the organization at every level to better support meaningful and genuine forms of diversity through collaboration and co-creation with underserved communities, and committed to bolstering support in much-needed funding areas to ensure that a diversity of artists and organizations are resilient, relevant and well supported to build capacity and create.
Results: BC Arts Council Funding Programs: In fiscal year 2020/21 BCAC provided 2,037 grants totaling CAD 35.8 million to individuals, organizations, and collectives - this includes CAD 4 million distributed through BCAC’s partner organization grant programs. BCAC also distributed CAD 35 million provided by the province in an additional one-time funding to support sector resiliency through the pandemic. This amount was broken up into CAD 29.7 million in resilience supplements and CAD5.3 million in funding for the Pivot Program (grants).   In fiscal year 2021/22, BCAC provided 1,702 grants totaling CAD 35 million to individuals, organizations, and collectives - this includes CAD 4.2 million distributed through BCAC’s partner organization grant programs. BCAC also distributed CAD 12.5 million in additional one-time funding to aid in the sector’s recovery and renewal from the pandemic. This amount was broken up into CAD 7.9 million in resilience supplements and CAD 4.5 million in additional funding for the Arts Impact Grant program.   In fiscal year 2022/23, BCAC provided 1,723 grants totaling CAD 36.9 million to individuals, organizations, and collectives - this includes CAD 4.2 million distributed through BCAC’s partner organization grant programs. BCAC also distributed CAD 34.5 million provided as one-time year-end funding from the province to continue to support the arts and culture sector as it worked towards recovery and renewal from the pandemic. This amount was broken up into CAD 30 million in resilience supplements and CAD 4.5 million to the Arts Infrastructure Program.  Strategic and Action Plan: The Action Plan supports the implementation of the vision, directions and commitments in the strategic plan including reviewing and revising peer assessment processes and program criteria to embed principles of reconciliation, equity, inclusion, diversity, and access.
Financial Ressources: FY 2021/22: CAD 47.475 million = USD 35.3 million FY 2022/23: CAD 71.372 million = USD 53 million
Recommandations: In 2022, significant work began on data collection and information management. Evaluation is continuous and Provincial funding for BCAC programs is ongoing.   Evaluation of the New Foundations Strategic Plan led to the recommendation to extend the plan and launch the Extending Foundations Action Plan, intended to support the arts and culture sector to navigate through a period of renewal and recovery as it emerged from the health, economic, social, and cultural impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic and address calls for social justice. A parallel third-party evaluation of progress made to inform the BC Arts Council’s next round of strategic visioning provided reflections on how progress has been perceived by the arts and culture community, where gaps remain and recommendations for addressing barriers.   For example, the need for safe, accessible and affordable cultural facilities continues to be a key issue for the sector. Amongst other concerns, places to gather to perform, present or exhibit in rural British Columbia are fewer in number when compared to other non-urban regions elsewhere in Canada, while urban centres face high costs and operational challenges. To help address these inequities, the BC Arts Council provided an increased Arts Infrastructure Program, bolstered by one-time funding from the province. Over CAD 8.5 million was provided for project planning, purchasing specialized equipment, building, and renovations.

Agency Implementation: Canada Council for the Arts
Main Feature: Launched in 2021, the Strategic Innovation Fund supports a broad range of activities undertaken by the arts sector to solve challenges and develop a stronger, more inclusive, equitable and sustainable sector. The fund offers different ways artists, arts groups and organizations can receive support to develop new ideas and business models, experiment and collaborate to advance digital transformation, contribute to a greener arts sector, or advance equity, diversity and inclusion according to the level of innovation readiness, scope, stage and budget requirements of each project. The fund has three main components:  •	The Seed component provides grants up to CAD 25,000 to fund innovative ideas, experiment, partner, and build capacity. It supports small-scale activities intended to explore and develop innovation projects that address systemic issues in the arts sector. Projects must respond to key strategic areas intended to rebuild a more resilient, sustainable, equitable, accessible, greener, healthier, and connected arts sector.  •	The Cultivate component provides grants of up to CAD 250,000 to implement, pilot, and protype innovation projects that address systemic issues and benefit and strengthen the broader arts sector. This component only supports collaborative projects that are undertaken in partnership with one or more organizations, collective or group of artists. Partnerships are not limited to the arts sector and cross sectoral collaborations with shared investment for shared benefit are encouraged.  •	The Grow component provides multi-year grants of up to CAD 1 million for longer-term, collaborative initiatives that propose sustainable solutions to issues within and beyond the arts sector and demonstrate strong potential to be scaled up for regional, national, or international impact.  In addition, partnerships and contributions across sectors are developed to help arts organizations, groups or collectives find creative solutions to complex social problems. For example:  •	The Council has partnered with the National Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada on the College and Community Social Innovation Fund to support projects that promote social innovation in communities and leverage the power and perspective of the arts sector in finding solutions to complex issues such as education, climate change, and health.  •	Availability and Affordability of Cultural Spaces: in 2023 the Council partnered with four major cities in Canada (Toronto, Vancouver, Calgary and Montréal) to explore and pilot potential solutions that address the availability and affordability of living and workspaces for artists and arts organizations, while actively sharing learnings with one another.
Results: •	Since launching in 2021, the SIF has provided support to over 600 organizations, groups, and individuals in their innovation journey whether they be at the very start, acquiring skills, knowledge and testing new business models, or leveraging their knowledge and skills with partners to implement or scale up innovation projects as they work towards building a more inclusive and sustainable arts sector. •	SIF projects have been supported in every province and territory across Canada, including projects from priority groups. Over 100 first-time applicants have received funding through the different Fund components. •	A mid-cycle informal analysis indicates that the SIF is building on the previous strategic initiatives and continues to support digital transformation of the arts sector, is stimulating the sector to explore new ideas, and is developing new partnerships and new ways of working. Through its grants and contributions, it has seeded over 200 cross-sectoral partnerships expanding arts networks to include health, tech, and academic sectors.

Title EN: Canada Council Arts Granting Programs
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture

Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: Canada Council for the Arts
Main Feature: The Canada Council Arts Granting programs are the primary way the Council helps individual artists, groups and arts organizations undertake activities that are integral across the arts sector. This includes, but not limited to, the creation, production and presentation of works as well as professional development, residencies, touring, travel and the development of the cultural sector, both in Canada and internationally.   Grants are available for Canadian citizens or permanent residents who have specialized training — though not necessarily in an academic setting — and are recognized as professionals by other artists and arts practitioners in the field of practice.   In line with the Council’s commitment to increase access to its funding by historically underserved and marginalized communities, the share of grant funding awarded to Indigenous People, Black and racialized people, deaf and disability arts, official language minority communities, and those at the intersections of these groups has increased notably since 2021.   While the Council doesn’t specifically target young people, two youth initiatives can be highlighted:   First, the Council created a New and Early Career Artists profile, as a three-year pilot, for artists at the start of their careers—including young artists as well as those who are new to Canada.  Second, since 2021, the Council has committed to allocating at least 20% of its project funding to first-time recipients. It has exceeded this commitment each year. This is another effort to ensure Council funding is open to young and emerging artists.
Results: 2020-21: -	CAD 372.1 million awarded in grants in Canada  -	CAD 5.1 million awarded in grants outside of Canada  -	2,592 arts organizations supported (CAD 269.1 million awarded)  -	682 arts groups supported (CAD 18.6 million awarded)  -	3,791 individual artists supported (CAD 89.6 million awarded)  -	550 New and Early Career Artists supported (CAD 10.4 million awarded)  -	855 communities with grants awarded  2022-22: -	CAD 450.1 million awarded in grants in Canada  -	CAD 5.6 million awarded in grants outside of Canada  -	2,332 arts organizations supported (CAD 281.9 million awarded)  -	809 arts groups supported (CAD 45.5 million awarded)  -	4,611 individual artists supported (CAD 128.3 million awarded)  -	914 New and Early Career Artists supported (CAD 22.7 million awarded)  -	922 communities with grants awarded   2022-23: -	CAD 359.7 million awarded in grants in Canada  -	CAD 4.2 million awarded in grants outside of Canada  -	2,177 arts organizations supported (CAD 228.6 million awarded)  -	568 arts groups supported (CAD 22.8 million awarded)  -	4,550 individual artists supported (CAD 112.4 million awarded)  -	903 New and Early Career Artists supported (CAD 23.4 million awarded)  -	850 communities with grants awarded  Over 2023, the Council expanded its reach to parts of the world where Canada’s arts sector has historically had limited reach. This is giving artists greater access to new and underexplored markets, often in places with strong ties to diasporic communities in Canada. Notably, the Council undertook several initiatives to build stronger relationships with countries in Africa. This included, for example, support to the Festival Afropolitain Nomade in Douala, Cameroon, held in June 2022. In 2023 the festival promoted women in the African music industry, and it brought together women musicians from both Canada and Africa.

Recommandations: In a review of first-time applicants as a whole, key findings concluded that: •	For many first-time recipients, a first Canada Council grant provides a sense of legitimacy and validation, increases confidence, brings greater financial security, and allows recipients to maintain or expand their practice. This is particularly important for recipients belonging to historically underserved and marginalized communities. •	A first Canada Council grant can also allow recipients to connect with mentors, peers, collaborators, and other key stakeholders in their artistic community. Through their first Canada Council project, many recipients expanded their network, initiated new partnerships, and shared their knowledge, skills, and experiences with others. •	Funded projects also have a positive impact on communities by offering representation and professional opportunities for members of their communities; increasing the visibility of underrepresented communities and practices; supporting advocacy; encouraging intercultural dialogues and contributing to discussions of social issues.

Agency Implementation: Canada Council for the Arts
Main Feature: The Council is committed to reaffirming and revitalizing its relationship with First Nations, Inuit and Métis peoples in Canada. The Council acknowledges the cultural sovereignty of Indigenous peoples and respects First Nations, Inuit and Métis self-determination, artistic expression, cultural protocols, Indigenous rights and Indigenous worldviews.  This program supports Indigenous individuals, groups, Indigenous-led arts organizations and arts/cultural sector development organizations that foster a vital and resilient Indigenous arts ecosystem. The program functions using a self-determined, Indigenous-centered approach. This means that it is guided by Indigenous values and worldviews, administered by staff of First Nations, Inuit and Métis heritage, and assessed by First Nations, Inuit and Métis individuals. Collaborations between Indigenous and non-Indigenous artists, that are led by Indigenous artists/organizations are encouraged and facilitated in Creating, Knowing and Sharing.

Recommandations: Though there has not been a formal evaluation of the program, it was one of the first of its kind, created by Indigenous people for Indigenous artists and communities, and has since been modeled after for similar programs elsewhere in Canada.   In 2022, The Canada Council for the Arts, in collaboration with Archipel Research and Consulting Inc., undertook a research project entitled: Research on the Value of Public Funding for Indigenous Arts and Cultures, a project grounded in Indigenous ways of knowing. This project was guided by Etuaptmumk, a Mi’kmaq methodology also known as Two-Eyed Seeing, which brings the strengths of both Indigenous and Western worldviews together to move forward in harmonious and sustainable relations.  Below are some of the conclusions of the Research on the Value of Public Funding for Indigenous Arts and Cultures, described above:  •	Arts and cultural practices are integral to Indigenous ways of being. Indigenous arts and cultures provide essential functions for cultural continuity and revitalization. •	Public funding is integral to the success of Indigenous artists, arts, and cultures. Funding through the Council has supported the meaningful work of Indigenous artists, that they might not have been able to do otherwise. •	Indigenous artists and organizations continue to face barriers to access the support they need.  Based on the research findings, Archipel prepared 26 recommendations for the Council and other arts funders to guide their path forward.

Main Feature: The Council advances its strategic engagement on the international stage for the benefit of the Canadian arts sector through the development and delivery of a robust and agile set of strategic international initiatives and partnerships, in line with Council’s strategic priorities.  Strategic international partnerships expand the scope of the Council’s international engagement, and both broaden and deepen the impact of its strategic initiatives. Furthermore, beyond sector development and cultural diplomacy objectives, partnership initiatives serve to advance the Council’s strategic priorities, with a focus on advancing equity and inclusion for youth, disabled and racialized artists, as well as contributing to decolonization and advancement of Indigenous arts and culture.  In the 2020-2023 period, the Council undertook 15 international partnerships with partners in 20 countries.    Two specific examples, highlighted here, are:  Arctic Arts Summit  The Council co-hosted the 2022 Arctic Arts Summit with the Government of Yukon (one of the three territories in Canada), in partnership with various national and international stakeholders. The Summit brought together representatives of Arctic countries and Indigenous nations from across the circumpolar region to discuss topics of shared interest as well as opportunities for future collaboration.   The Summit was successful in strengthening arts and culture in the North and to develop circumpolar cooperation that stimulates ongoing, sustainable collaboration in arts and creative industries throughout the region. The Summit created North-to-North opportunities, explored key questions, and advanced timely discussions. The focus was on Connection to the Land, exploring northern arts and culture in relation to:  •	Land: Language, Community, Heritage, Identity •	Indigenous Sovereignty: Self-determination, Indigenization and Decolonization •	Climate: Environmental Sustainability, Crisis and Action •	Creating: Makers, Making, and Sharing Artistic Production •	Representation: Institutions and Ethics, Engagements, Education, Policy, Protocol, Repatriation •	Circumpolar Collaboration: Cooperation and Mobility •	Technology: Digital Arts, Data, Access, New Media •	Activism: Artists, Movements and Social Change •	Possible Futures: New Directions, Youth Voices, Imaginings  Canada-Korea Partnership In 2023 and 2024, in the context of the 60th anniversary of diplomatic relations, the Council partnered with Arts Council Korea and Global Affairs Canada to support projects that will deepen and diversify collaborative relationships between Canadian and Korean artists around conversations on environmental sustainability and equity. The initiative advances these shared corporate priorities, while supporting increased opportunities for international engagement and post-COVID renewal of the arts sector. For example, the Year of Cultural Exchanges upcoming initiative in 2024-2025 will facilitate dialogue, enhance collaboration, and support projects in culture, arts, sports and creative industries. The participation of creative industries in the Team Canada Trade Mission to South Korea will take place in Seoul and will be one of the first key activities under the Year of Cultural Exchanges.
Results: Arctic Arts Summit In total, 130 Canadian and 120 international delegates representing 8 countries were brought together, including 84 artists and curators, and 95 organizations from public, private and civil society sectors (arts organizations, arts funders, First Nations, governments, embassies and universities).  A digital program facilitated broader audiences to participate in conversations and exchanges leading up to the in-person event.  Canada-Korea Partnership The funding for this partnership was delivered through two measures. The Canada-Korea Connection Fund was launched first in early 2023. It provided grants up to CAD 10,000 each for 22 projects. The strength and recent increase in popularity of artists from both Canada and Korea suggested this investment would be well received by artists in both countries and was evident in the over 140 applications received. The second measure, launched in late 2023 has seen the Council contribute up to CAD 25,000 each toward 10 co-creation projects initiated by Canadian artists and arts organizations.  Arts Council Korea provided a parallel fund for projects initiated by Korean artists and arts organizations in cooperation with Canadian counterparts.

Main Feature: An annual assembly convened on November 8 and 9, 2023, at the Hôtel-Musée Premières Nations de Wendake, focused on the transmission, expression, and preservation of Indigenous heritage, attracting nearly a hundred participants. The primary objective was to collectively explore the potential of the 2005 UNESCO Convention for the Protection and Promotion of the Diversity of Cultural Expressions, examining its role in providing financial support and promoting Indigenous creations, while acknowledging the significant influence of the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. Discussions centered on how the 2005 Convention could enhance the protection and promotion of Indigenous heritage, particularly within the digital sphere. Participants deliberated on whether the Convention could introduce additional levers beyond those outlined in the United Nations Declaration, and if so, how these levers could be implemented.
Results: In an attempt to raise awareness on the potential support of the 2005 Convention in addressing challenges faced by Indigenous communities, civil society representatives, UNESCO representatives, local artists, Indigenous experts and Chiefs, brought to light their insights.   As digital technology for the Expression of Indigenous Heritage is increasingly playing an important role among Indigenous artists and creators, and particularly in ways of representing traditions and contemporary realities, inspiring art projects using digital technologies have been carried out while others are currently under way.  These messages were warmly received by the participants on site. Building on this first step towards the Indigenous communities of Quebec, the Coalition for the Diversity of Cultural Expressions began to forge links with other Indigenous cultural actors in Canada to present the 2005 Convention to them.

Title EN: Cultura Legislations and Cultural Institutions Research (Tahalofat Alrass Project)
Goal: Integrate Culture In Sustainable Development Frameworks
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
