Results: -	5 ans au service de la collecte, le traitement et la diffusion de l’information culturelle   -	Formation et mobilisation d’une équipe de 10 jeunes spécialisées dans la production de contenus culturels -	Réalisation de 4 sessions de formation des acteurs des ICC au marketing digital  -	Promotion d’initiatives et d’événements culturels en ligne sur la plateforme -	Promotion du genre à travers la mise en place d’un projet de valorisation d’initiatives des femmes talentueuses du Bénin

Title EN: Mise en place du projet « la route cinématographique »
Goal: Integrate Culture In Sustainable Development Frameworks
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: International cooperation for sustainable development
Agency Implementation: Agence allemande de coopération internationale pour le développement (GIZ)
Main Feature: C’est un projet qui s’inscrit dans le cadre de la promotion du tourisme durable, composante fondamentale du programme « d’appui à la diversification du tourisme, au développement des chaines de valeur de l’artisanat et du design et à la valorisation du patrimoine culturel : tounes wejhatouna ».  Ce programme qui s’étale sur une période de 05 ans (2019-2024) est financé par l’Union européenne et se distingue par une gouvernance multilatérale menée conjointement par l’agence allemande de coopération internationale pour le développement (GIZ), expertise France et l’organisation des nations unis pour de développement (ONUD).  Son objectif global est de « contribuer au développement économique durable et inclusif de la Tunisie ». De ce fait, il implique un partenariat horizontal/ interministériel entre notamment, le Ministère des Affaires Culturelles (MAC) ; le Ministère du Tourisme et de l’Artisanat, le Ministère de l’économie et de la planification (MEP) ; le Ministère de l’Agriculture, des Ressources Hydrauliques et de la Pêche et un partenariat avec le secteur privé (PPP) avec notamment la fédération interprofessionnelle du tourisme tunisien (FITT), la fédération tunisienne de l’hôtellerie (FTH), la fédération tunisienne des agences de voyage (FTAV) ; ainsi qu’un partenariat avec la société civile locale. La création de « la route cinématographique » est fondée sur un constat qui fait du ciné-tourisme un outil de marketing qu’il faut intégrer dans la stratégie d’une destination touristique pour augmenter sa notoriété et sa visibilité. Mais au-delà de son apport comme simple facteur de repositionnement de l’image d’une destination, la mise en place de « la route cinématographique » se traduit par une certaine dynamique interrégionale dans la mesure où elle permet d’assurer une meilleure compréhension entre les cultures et renforcer les liens entre les populations locales. C’est aussi un facteur de création d’emploi surtout au profit des jeunes porteurs de projets innovants et des femmes qui peuvent en trouver un moyen pour créer leur propre business et nouer de nouveaux partenariats à travers la diversification de l’offre touristique et culturelle. C’est toute une dynamique culturelle économique et sociale qui se crée autour des lieux et sites de tournage.
Results: Un échange fructueux avec les différents partenaires a contribué à la sélection de 09 régions (Tunis- Monastir- Kairouan- Matmata- Djerba- Médenine- Tataouine- Nefta et Dgeuch) qui forment la trajectoire de « la route cinématographique » et ce en fonction des sites/ lieux de tournage des films (12 sites de tournage / 04 films : INDIANA JONES-PATIENT ANGLAIS-STAR WARS-MONTY PYTHON).  Résultats du développement de la route : •	Diversification de l’offre touristique •	Valorisation du patrimoine à travers les contenus culturels •	Promotion de l’image de la destination •	Création d’une dynamique inter-régionale •	Incitation à l’investissement et développement de l’entreprenariat culturel •	Création de l’emploi  Appui technique et financier lancé durant 2022- 2023  •	Un cycle de formation a été lancé aux profits des acteurs qui sont installés à proximité des sites de tournage (hôtels, maisons d’hôtes, cafés, restaurants, agences de voyages…) des régions cibles autour de 2 thématiques : technique d’accueil et marketing-commercialisation du produit. •	Une enveloppe de 100 M Euro a été allouée pour l’achat de matériel aux profits de 33 Opérateurs touristiques.   •	un appel à projets dans 3 zones de la route cinématographique est lancé afin de créer une dynamique autour des sites et diversifier le produit touristique :   Nefta Ong Jemal / Nefta chott el jerid – canyon bouhlel/ Tataouine Ksar Hdada   •	une candidature a été retenue de l’association ASPG pour développer des circuits pédestres et à vélo autour de ksar Hdada . Avec un budget de 60MDT ; Sur une durée de 1an et demi  •	une candidature retenue par wildyness pour redynamiser la région à Nefta (sur le canyon de Bouhlel) circuit de randonnée avec un budget de 45MDT sur une durée de 1 an).

Title EN: National Incentives Program
Goal: Achieve A Balanced Flow Of Cultural Goods And Services And Increase The Mobility Of Artists And Cultural Professionals
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 10 - Reduce inequality within and among countries,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Mobility of artists and cultural professionals
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: Ministry of Cultures, Arts, and Knowledge
Main Feature: The purpose of this program is to mobilize Colombian artists, creators, researchers, and cultural managers, whether at the national or international level, so that in the most diverse disciplines, they receive an incentive for their work, through scholarships, internships, national awards, recognitions or artistic residencies. It is aimed mainly at natural persons and operates through annual public calls for proposals, so that all actors in the cultural sector can participate in this range of opportunities.                  Starting in 2024, the Portfolio calls for proposals will no longer be organized thematically by directorates, dependencies, or units attached to this Ministry, but will be organized into four large fields: 1. Culture of peace, recognition and reconciliation; 2. Promotion of the arts, creative processes and practices; 3. Memories and heritage; and 4. Culture, good living and care for the common. Each call will appear in either of the fields depending on its content. With this new thematic distribution, the Portfolio goes hand in hand with some of the central objectives of the Government of Change, such as the promotion of the arts in all its forms, the consolidation of peace through them, the protection of heritage and memory, and the defense of the environment.                  The 2024 Portfolio proposes many more recognitions than in previous years, as it considers this a more direct way to promote arts and cultures.                   Types of incentives:                  •	National awards: they are the highest distinction awarded by the Ministry of Cultures, Arts, and Knowledge. They praise the work, career, dedication, processes, and contributions made by artists, creators, researchers, and managers whose work in the cultural field contributes in an outstanding way to the memory and cultural life of the country.          •	Recognitions: they highlight processes, projects, works, or trajectories of people and organizations that make an outstanding contribution to the cultural life of the country and are distinguished as references in the field in which they develop.          •	Scholarships: support the development of creation, training, circulation, or research processes through the execution of artistic and cultural projects. They are granted for the realization or completion of a particular proposal and not for an already completed project, work, or cultural product. Therefore, they require the completion of activities within a schedule and the execution of resources from a budget in accordance with the specific conditions of the call.         •	Residencies: these are short stays of immersion, research, or creation in a place other than the winner's home, which allow the development of projects, creative processes, or artistic or cultural explorations. Residencies can be made in Colombia or abroad. The total value of the stimulus will be awarded to the winners, who will decide how to use the money to cover the expenses involved in developing the residence.          •	Internships: allow the development of artistic and cultural activities or training processes in cultural institutions or entities defined in the calls. Internships can be held in Colombia or abroad. The total value of the incentive will be awarded to the winners, who will decide how to use the money to cover the expenses involved in carrying out the internship.
Results: Between 2020 and 2023, 4,303 incentives were granted, through the portfolio of calls for proposals of the National Incentives Program, broken down as follows:                  ●	Portfolio 2020. 1,144 incentives granted in 31 departments of the country, Bogotá D.C., and around 7 countries other than Colombia. These were distributed in 820 scholarships, 6 prizes, and 318 recognitions.                  ●	Portfolio 2021. 960 incentives granted in 31 departments of the country, Bogotá D.C., and in other regions of the country. These were distributed in 814 scholarships, 6 prizes, and 140 recognitions.         ●	Portfolio 2022. 929 incentives granted in 31 departments of the country, Bogotá D.C., other regions of the country, and some countries other than Colombia. These were distributed in 695 scholarships, 6 prizes, and 228 recognitions.                  ●	Portfolio 2023. 929 incentives granted in 31 departments of the country, Bogotá D.C., and some countries other than Colombia. These were distributed in 1,020 scholarships, 9 internships, 18 awards, 209 recognitions, and 14 residencies.                  ●	For the 2024 Portfolio, 14,239 proposals were received for 137 calls. To date they are in the final evaluation process. The results will be published on the website of the Ministry of Culture.

Title EN: Mobility Information Point (MIP) - Information and advisory support for international mobility in culture
Goal: Achieve A Balanced Flow Of Cultural Goods And Services And Increase The Mobility Of Artists And Cultural Professionals
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 10 - Reduce inequality within and among countries,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Mobility of artists and cultural professionals
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: Motovila
Main Feature: Motovila, an NGO based in Ljubljana, Slovenia, promotes transnational and cross-sectoral cooperation in the cultural and creative sectors. The institute implements information, advisory, training, networking, promotion, and research activities dedicated to empowering representatives of the cultural and creative sectors and facilitate their (inter)national connections. Motovila hosts Creative Europe Desk Slovenia, and is Culture Action Europe, On the Move and Mobility Information Point (MIP) member.  Since 2023, Motovila as MIP aims to establish a one stop shop in Slovenia to support artists and cultural professionals working internationally. MIPs are namely information centres who aim to tackle the administrative challenges artists and cultural professionals can face when working across borders. MIPs currently exist in Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Portugal, Slovenia, The Netherlands, United Kingdom, and the USA. The group cooperates to share resources in the European and international context, covering issues such as visas, social security, taxation, and customs rules. MIPs are members of the On the Move, the cultural mobility network that advocates for fairer and more responsible mobility in the arts and cultural sector.  Motovila with MIP provides free, accurate and reliable mobility-related information and services to individuals and organizations in all artistic and cultural disciplines, including the audio-visual field. Information is also free of charge accessible on our website. Besides, Motovila strengthens connections both with decision-makers and the cultural and creative sectors and raise awareness of their needs. Furthermore, Motovila contributes to the international exchange of resources and information, also by encouraging networking and the exchange of good (sustainable) practices between Slovene Artist in Residency programmes.  In 2023, Motovila cooperated on a project MIP’s Amplifier with the On the Move and touring artists (Germany) that aimed to facilitate and optimise the mobility in the EU of artists and culture professionals, by supporting, in a more documented and visible way, reliable, free and accessible tailor-made information. The project covered all arts and cultural sectors. MIP-Amplifier project was limited in time (6 months), though its outputs and learning will be further enriched and developed together with the MIPs and On the Move in the coming years. The project resulted in a MIP microsite, handbook to contribute to strengthening coherent and coordinated actions among existing and future MIPs, and a data report on MIP activities to inform further policies at EU and national levels.. The MIP-Amplifier project was supported by ECAS – European Citizen Action Service, as part of a financial support to third parties (re-granting) scheme under grant agreement 101104626, of which ECAS is the beneficiary for its EURECA 2023 project (European Citizenship Accelerator). This project receives funding by the Citizenship, Equality, Rights and Values programme of the European Union.
Results: In Slovenia, Motovila provides artists and culture professionals with information about international cultural mobility and cultural cooperation. As members of On the Move and Mobility Information Points, Motovila contributes to the development of information standards in this field.The creation of MIP website, , allows artists and culture professionals to have free access to information on administrative challenges when working cross borders. Besides Motovila offers free services in providing technical support to artists and culture professionals especially regarding mobility funding opportunities.  By cooperating in the MIP Amplifier project in 2023, Motovila organized professional training and public event presenting MIP services. Besides Motovila on a national level created a platform for exchange of information and cooperation between various public institutions and NGOs.   In the past 3 years, MIPs have been recognized at various levels as important organizations for tackling access to information providing direct and/or tailor-made information on administrative issues related to mobile artists and culture professionals (for example, see OMC Report on Status and working conditions of artists and cultural and creative professionals, Recommendation 8, page 64: “This existing network of MIPs has proven its efficiency but lacks support to operate more consistently at a European level through a stronger and larger group of information centres. It is recommended that the EU and Member States reinforce the capacity of the existing MIPs and establish new MIPs in all other EU countries”).  Furthermore, The European Parliament “encourages the Commission and the Member States to strengthen existing or, where not in place, set up new, adequately funded mobility information points as one-stop  shops that are easily accessible in all EU languages and will help CCS professionals gather all relevant sectoral information concerning their working conditions, mobility, fiscality and social protection benefits” (see European Parliament resolution with recommendations to the Commission on an EU framework for the social and professional situation of artists and workers in the cultural and creative sectors (2023/2051(INL)), Article 14).

Title EN: Mobility of Dominican artists and cultural professionals within the Transcultura UNESCO programme
Goal: Achieve A Balanced Flow Of Cultural Goods And Services And Increase The Mobility Of Artists And Cultural Professionals
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 10 - Reduce inequality within and among countries,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development

Main Feature: The UNESCO Transcultura Programme aims to deepen cultural integration and cooperation between Cuba, the Caribbean, and the European Union. Funded by the European Union, it focuses on empowering young professionals in the cultural and creative industries through education, capacity-building, and entrepreneurship.  Key features of the Transcultura Programme include:  1.Capacity Building and Education 2.Entrepreneurship Support 3.Grants and Scholarships  Through dissemination in the official media of the Ministry of Culture and the support of the Dominican National Commission for UNESCO as liaison with the Havana Regional Office, Dominican artists have actively participated in the programme, benefiting from the various training and capacity-building opportunities offered. These activities have help them enhance their skills, gain new knowledge, and access broader markets and networks within the cultural and creative industries.   Within the Transcultura program funded by UNESCO, a group from the Taimascaros of Puerto Plata troupe was able to participate in the Nice Carnival in France, being one of the most significant initiatives of outward mobility of this period. Results: More than 150 Dominican artists have benefited from the initiatives of this program, they have  participate in online and in person workshops, capacity building courses, activities and masterclasses; including the participation of the Taimascaros carnival troupe in Nice Carnival (20 participants).

Title EN: Model for Sustainable Regional Cultural Development (since 2018)
Goal: Integrate Culture In Sustainable Development Frameworks
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: National sustainable development policies and plans
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: Lithuanian Council for Culture
Main Feature: The Model for Sustainable Regional Cultural Development was approved in July 2018. The aim of this model is to empower local communities by devolving decision making powers on culture policy priorities and distribution of funds for art and culture to the regional level.  According to this model, 10 Regional Culture Councils (one for each county in the country) were established. Every Council includes one representative of the corresponding municipality, i.e. one expert from the municipality. There are from 2 to 4 elected experts from the local art/culture community in every Regional Culture Council.  This initiative is expected to increase the democratization of culture by bringing the decision-making process closer to local communities and creating a coordinated network of expertise and knowledge. It also encourages cultural project managers and communities to reconsider the identity of their region, the ways they collaborate with each other or internationally and the need to ensure accessibility to variety of cultural activities.  The first achievement of this initiative remains – the increase in communication activities: various conferences and meetings between Regional Arts Councils and their communities have been organized yearly. It has resulted in growing activity of project managers from the regions and the increased trust in the Lithuanian Council for Culture as the main funding institution in the country for cultural projects.  The second achievement – democratization of the distribution of the funds. The representatives of the Regional Culture Councils are being consulted when the changes for the model are being planned and implemented. This way the local experience and expertise from the Regions, the recommendations from the Lithuanian Council for Culture and the political programme of the Ministry of Culture are used to improve the Programme "Model for Sustainable Regional Cultural Development".
Results: In addition to the evaluation of cultural projects, the Regional Art Councils are also responsible for the provision of consultations to cultural communities, analysis of cultural processes and provision of recommendations to the Lithuanian Council for Culture. In 2019, regional development priorities for the period of 2020-2023 were identified and presented to the public. In 2024 new development priorities were developed while some remain active from 2020. These development priorities are expected to enable the Regional Art Councils to participate in the regional policy making process more systematic and independent.  An internal analysis by Lithuanian Council for Culture which was conducted and presented in Compendium conference "Right to Culture" in 2023.  Main findings:  The funding for the programme accounts for 24–27 percent of programme funding in Lithuanian Council for Culture in 2020–2023 and it is the primary financing tool for the cultural projects in the regional municipalities in 8 out of 10 counties compared to other Lithuanian Council for Culture programmes. Since the beginning of the Regional model (2019), organizations started experimenting with artforms and events, for example: art residencies, local history literature, digital projects, outdoor painting, art camps. But the most common artforms remain the same — festivals, educational events and workshops.  Since the start of the programme the representation of folk culture increased from 10% in 2019 to 18% in 2023. Local cultural identity is integrated in 93% of the projects.
Financial Ressources: In 2020, a total of more than USD  3,2 million (EUR 2 887 016) was allocated to finance 615 regional cultural activities. In 2021, a total of more than USD 3,7 million (EUR 3 297 229) was allocated to finance 668 regional cultural activities. In 2022, a total of more than USD 3,7 million (EUR 3 309 996) was allocated to finance 613 regional cultural activities. In 2023, a total of more than USD 3,6 million (EUR 3 290 000) was allocated to finance 548 regional cultural activities.

Title EN: Multilingualism and translation – Working Group of EU Member States’ experts
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Agency Implementation: European Commission, EU Member State governments
Main Feature: The 2019-2022 Council Work Plan for Culture included the topic of multilingualism and translation, for policy collaboration through a working group of EU Member States’ experts. The group of EU Member States’ experts published the “translators on the Cover” report on the role of public policies and funding schemes at national and European level in helping  1) the circulation of translated books and  2) the development of a vibrant translation sector able to cover all cultural sectors.
Results: This group of EU Member States’ experts met regularly in 2021 and decided to divide its tasks among 3 subgroups: initial and continuous training of translators; professionalisation, status and remuneration of translators; and cross-border circulation and promotion of translated books.   Key issues discussed included the offer of language and translation studies at secondary and high-education level; the quality of book translations and film subtitling in a context of automatisation of translation and pressure on translators to keep prices low; fair remuneration, copyright issues and the transposition of the EU directive; European cooperation between national promotion and translation agencies in Europe and beyond; support to sales and market access.   The proposed recommendations focused on improving the translators’ working conditions and professional developments, as well on as how public institutions can stimulate the translation and promotion of European books.  The report recommends making the translation profession more attractive by providing more training opportunities for translators, reinforcing translators’ (professional) associations and improving remuneration and working conditions through the opportunities offered by the Digital Single Market Directive.  The report advocates for more public funding for translation projects so publishers can take on a higher number of translation projects and can fairly remunerate the translators working on them.  Reading promotion actions should also have a strong European dimension and promote openness to diversity and books from abroad.  Finally, the report encourages national public institutions to engage in more cooperation at a European level, for instance through multi-country book promotion activities and a harmonized approach to data collection.

Title EN: Multiple programmes
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Agency Implementation: SANGEET NATAK AKADEMI
Main Feature: Sangeet Natak Akademi (SNA) plays a pivotal role in nurturing and promoting India's diverse performing arts heritage through its esteemed institutions and wide-ranging initiatives across the country. At its heart are two prominent dance-teaching units: Jawaharlal Nehru Manipur Dance Academy (JNMDA) in Imphal and Kathak Kendra in Delhi. JNMDA stands as a leading institution in Manipuri dance education, offering comprehensive courses encompassing Manipuri dance forms, music, and cultural traditions such as Lai Haraoba and Thang-ta. These programs are meticulously designed to provide a robust foundation for aspiring professional artists. Similarly, Kathak Kendra in Delhi is renowned for its excellence in Kathak dance education, offering courses across various levels in Kathak dance, vocal music, and the Pakhawaj, a traditional percussion instrument.   Complementing these institutions, SNA oversees four centers dedicated to preserving and promoting distinct Indian performing arts traditions: Kutiyattam Kendra in Thiruvananthapuram, Sattriya Kendra in Guwahati, Chhau Kendra, and the North East Centre. These centers serve as hubs for conducting festivals, workshops, and training programs that ensure the continuity and vitality of Kutiyattam, Sattriya, Chhau, and traditional folk performing arts from the northeastern regions.   SNA's commitment extends beyond education to fostering employment opportunities within the cultural sector through three primary programs:   1. Training Programs and Workshops: These initiatives aim to develop the skills of emerging artists and provide employment opportunities for seasoned practitioners. Currently, SNA conducts diverse training programs covering music, folk and tribal arts, Chhau dance, mask making, Kutiyattam theater, and various instrument-making techniques such as Tabla, Rabab, and Sarod. These efforts not only preserve traditional arts but also ensure their transmission to future generations.   2. Festivals: SNA is instrumental in hosting and sponsoring numerous festivals nationwide, celebrating music, dance, drama, folk and tribal arts, and puppetry. These festivals serve as vital platforms for emerging artists to showcase their talents while also providing significant financial support. They play a crucial role in safeguarding and promoting India's rich cultural heritage.   3. Sangeet Natak Akademi Awards and Fellowships: These prestigious awards recognize outstanding practitioners in music, dance, and drama, serving as the highest national honors in these fields. The Akademi Awards, including the Akademi Ratna and Akademi Puraskar, carry substantial monetary awards, underscoring SNA's commitment to honoring excellence in the performing arts. Additionally, the Ustad Bismillah Khan Yuva Puraskar supports young artists with grants aimed at nurturing their talents and encouraging their contributions to the arts.   Under the visionary leadership of Chairman of Sangeet Natak Akademi, several transformative initiatives have been launched. Among these, the "Kala Dharohar" series stands out for its focus on enhancing cultural education among school students in alignment with the National Education Policy (NEP). Through interactive sessions, workshops, and performances conducted across schools nationwide, Kala Dharohar invites SNA awardees, eminent artists, gurus, and scholars to engage directly with students. This initiative not only enriches students' understanding of Indian performing arts but also fosters a deeper appreciation for the country's cultural heritage. In 2023-2024, Sangeet Natak Akademi's Kala Dharohar series, chaired by Dr. Sandhya Purecha, aims to educate school students across India about performing arts. Events include folk songs in Assam by Shri Dulal Manki, patriotic songs in Sikkim by Shri Pawan Rai, Kathak dance in Jharkhand by Ms. Gauri Diwakar, and acting in Chandigarh by Deep Mandeep Kaur. Artists like Glory Baba and Gopal Singh Habbi also showcase folk music and dance in Jammu & Kashmir. Tripura hosts Kuchipudi dance and puppetry by Boby Chakraborty and Prabitangshu Das, respectively, while Odisha and Madhya Pradesh feature vocal music and Odissi dance.   Another significant initiative, "Kala Deeksha," exemplifies SNA's dedication to preserving rare and endangered performing arts forms. Launched under the Guru-Shishya parampara scheme, Kala Deeksha aims to transmit invaluable cultural treasures through training programs led by eminent Gurus and experts. This initiative is pivotal in fulfilling the government's commitment to safeguarding India's intangible cultural heritage, ensuring its continuation across generations. The Ministry of Culture, Government of India, has expressed full support for reviving endangered art forms, encouraging artists to contribute ideas for the advancement of these cultural legacies.   Amrit Kala Utsav and Kala Srijan are other initiatives taken by SNA which is conducted across India from 2022 focusing on celebrating and commemorating the rich cultural heritage of India. It includes organizing festivals, events, and performances that highlight various classical and folk traditions of music, dance, and theatre. The aim is to preserve, promote, and propagate these art forms among a wider audience, ensuring their continuity and appreciation for future generations; and the program is geared towards fostering creativity and innovation within the realm of performing arts. It supports the creation of new works, productions, and collaborations across different genres of music, dance, and theatre. Kala Srijan encourages artists to explore contemporary themes and techniques while maintaining a connection to traditional roots, thus contributing to the evolution and dynamism of Indian performing arts respectively.   Sangeet Natak Akademi has aimed to promote the publication of books and periodicals on music, dance, and drama in all Indian languages, including English. Recognizing that such publications often lack commercial viability, the scheme covers printing costs to enable authors and publishers to share their work with the public. Financial support is granted following expert evaluation of manuscripts for books and published issues for periodicals. This initiative has facilitated the publication of numerous works in diverse Indian languages over the past fifty years.   In conclusion, Sangeet Natak Akademi remains at the forefront of preserving, propagating, and celebrating India's diverse performing arts traditions. Through its educational institutions, cultural centers, supportive programs, and visionary initiatives like Kala Dharohar and Kala Deeksha, SNA continues to nurture creativity, honor excellence, and safeguard India's rich cultural tapestry for future generations. By bridging the past with the present, SNA not only ensures the survival of these invaluable cultural traditions but also enriches the cultural fabric of the nation as a whole.
Results: The Sangeet Natak Akademi (SNA) does play a role in supporting a sustainable system of governance for culture, although it is primarily an advisory and promotional body for the performing arts in India. Its efforts align with broader cultural governance by preserving, promoting, and documenting diverse cultural expressions, which contribute to a sustainable cultural ecosystem. Here's an overview of how SNA contributes to cultural governance and the results achieved so far:    - Advisory Committees: SNA has various expert committees that advise the government on policy matters related to the performing arts. This input helps shape policies that ensure the sustainability of cultural practices.    - Collaborations: The Akademi collaborates with other cultural institutions and government bodies to implement policies and programs that promote cultural sustainability.    - Archival Projects: SNA has undertaken extensive documentation and archival projects to preserve traditional and contemporary performing arts. This ensures that cultural heritage is maintained for future generations.    - Publication Initiatives: The Akademi publishes research and books on various aspects of Indian performing arts, contributing to the academic and cultural repository.    - Workshops and Seminars: SNA regularly organises workshops, seminars, and training programs to enhance the skills of artists and cultural practitioners. This helps in building a robust framework for cultural governance by empowering individuals and institutions.    - Scholarships and Fellowship: The Akademi offers scholarships and fellowships to young artists and researchers, promoting sustained cultural development and innovation.    - Grants and Financial Assistance: SNA provides financial assistance to artists and cultural organisations, ensuring they have the resources needed to continue their work. This financial support is crucial for the sustainability of the cultural sector.    - Awards and Recognitions: By recognizing excellence in the performing arts through various awards, SNA incentivizes high standards and continuous improvement in the cultural sector.    - Festivals and Performances: The Akademi organises national and international festivals and performances, providing a platform for artists to showcase their work and reach wider audiences.    - Digital Initiatives: SNA has been increasingly leveraging digital platforms to promote and disseminate cultural content, especially in response to the COVID-19 pandemic through live streaming of performances.   Results Achieved      - Increased Recognition: Artists and cultural practices supported by SNA have gained national and international recognition, contributing to the prestige and sustainability of India's cultural heritage.    - Cultural Exchange: SNA's festivals and collaborations have facilitated cultural exchange, promoting a better understanding of Indian performing arts globally.    - Comprehensive Archives: SNA's documentation and archival efforts have resulted in a comprehensive repository of Indian performing arts, which serves as a valuable resource for researchers, artists, and the public.    - Published Works: The publications by SNA have contributed significantly to the knowledge and understanding of India's diverse cultural traditions.    - Skill Development: Through its training and capacity-building programs, SNA has empowered artists and cultural practitioners with the skills needed to sustain and innovate within their fields.    - Financial Stability: Grants and financial assistance have provided a degree of financial stability to artists and cultural organisations, enabling them to continue their work without financial duress.    - Policy Impact: SNA’s advisory role has influenced cultural policies that support the sustainability of cultural practices and institutions.    - Community Engagement: The Akademi’s initiatives have increased community engagement with the performing arts, fostering a culture of appreciation and support for cultural heritage.     While the Sangeet Natak Akademi is not the primary body responsible for cultural governance, its initiatives significantly contribute to a sustainable cultural ecosystem. The results achieved through its various programs and initiatives reflect its commitment to preserving and promoting India's rich cultural heritage. Moving forward, continuing and expanding these efforts will be crucial for sustaining a vibrant and diverse cultural landscape.

Title EN: Modernized Official Languages Act
Goal: Integrate Culture In Sustainable Development Frameworks
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: National sustainable development policies and plans
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: Department of Canadian Heritage
Main Feature: The federal government is committed to enhancing the vitality of the English and French linguistic minority communities in Canada, as members of both official language communities, and supporting and assisting their development in recognition of their unique and diverse character, and their cultural and historical contributions to Canadian society, as well as fostering the full recognition and use of both English and French in Canadian society. The modernized Act recognizes arts and culture as sectors essential to the vitality of official language minority communities.  To enhance the vitality of Canada's French-speaking minorities and support their development, the Department of Canadian Heritage has been working for several years to strengthen cooperation between federal institutions that implement positive measures for Canada's French-speaking artistic and cultural communities.  Section 43 (1) of the modernized Act states that the Minister of Canadian Heritage shall foster and promote the equality of status and use of English and French in Canadian society, and to that end may, among other things: • support the development and promotion of francophone culture in Canada, in particular through the activities of the organizations for which it is responsible and by ensuring that the cultural policies of the federal government reflect the purpose of this Act; • subject to the approval of the Governor in Council, to enter into agreements or arrangements with foreign governments that recognize and reinforce Canada's bilingual identity.  Section 42.1 of the Modernized Act states that the Government of Canada recognizes that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, in carrying out its objects under the Broadcasting Act in accordance with the licences granted to it under that Act by the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission and subject to the regulations of that Commission, contributes through its activities to the vitality of the English and French linguistic minority communities in Canada and to the protection and promotion of both official languages. This recognition respects the freedom of expression and journalistic, creative and programming independence enjoyed by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
Results: • The Action Plan for Official Languages 2023-2028: Protect - Promote - Collaborate (hereinafter Action Plan), announced by the federal government on April 26, 2023, reiterates the federal government's commitment to putting in place the conditions to ensure true equality between English and French in Canada. The federal government is committed to fostering the development and promotion of Francophone culture through all Canadian Heritage organizations involved in supporting culture and media in Canada, particularly in terms of Francophone cultural production and support for artists. • Some of the initiatives in the Action Plan that will have an impact on arts and culture include the following new or enhanced initiatives: o CAD 5 million over 5 years to enhance the PassepART program, providing micro-grants to francophone artists so they can present their work and artistic careers in French first-language and immersion schools; o CAD 2.5 million over 5 years for the Development of Quebec's English-speaking communities through the arts, heritage and civic participation; o CAD 5 million over 5 years for the Canada Music Fund to support francophone music artists and entrepreneurs in official language minority communities; o an additional CAD 5 million over 5 years to modify and extend the Media Internship initiative to all sectors of activity related to the arts, culture, heritage and civic participation. • Then the following permanent initiatives, all renewed for the 2023-2028 period and on an ongoing basis beyond 2028: o CAD 28.2 million over 5 years for the Community Cultural Action Fund; o CAD 2.75 million over five years for the Market Access Strategy for artists from official-language minority communities; o CAD 5.75 million over five years for the Vitrines musicales program for artists from official-language minority communities; o CAD 4 million over five years for the National Translation Program for Book Publishing, to increase the number of Canadian-authored books translated from one official language to another, and thus broaden Canadians' access to our culture.
Financial Ressources: For the period 2023-2028 and on an ongoing basis beyond 2028: USD 29.7 million (CAD 40.7 million).
Recommandations: The expected results of the bill are as follows: •	Canadians have better access to opportunities to learn the official languages. •	Federal institutions better understand their official languages obligations and fulfill those obligations to the benefit of all Canadians. •	Certain discretionary powers of the Treasury Board become mandatory, resulting in increased monitoring by the Board and stronger official languages accountability and compliance across the federal government. •	The Commissioner of Official Languages is able to intervene more effectively thanks to new powers over and above those he previously wielded. For example, he has the power to impose administrative monetary penalties on certain privatized entities and Crown corporations that currently have obligations under the Official Languages Act in the transportation sector serving the travelling public, allowing him to play a stronger role. •	Official language minority communities see benefits and the official languages are better promoted thanks to new clarifications on positive measures to be taken by federal institutions. •	The institutions of official language minority communities are better protected across Canada. •	The French language is better supported across Canada, including in Quebec, and on the international scene. •	The introduction of a new statute distinct from the Official Languages Act ushering in new rights to work and to receive service in French in federally regulated private businesses in Quebec and in regions with a strong Francophone presence. •	The modernized Act requires Canada to adopt a Francophone immigration policy with objectives, targets and indicators to increase Francophone immigration to Francophone minority communities. •	Amend the OLA by removing the existing exception so that the Supreme Court would have the same duty as other federal courts to ensure that judges who hear proceedings can do so directly, in the official language or languages chosen by the parties, without the assistance of an interpreter. •	The OLA would be amended to support a body independent of the Government of Canada that would be responsible for administering a program, such as the Court Challenges Program, whose purpose would be to provide funding for test cases of national importance relating to language rights to be brought before the courts •	The modernized OLA would be more specific about the key sectors linked to the development of official language minority communities (for example, immigration, education from early childhood to post-secondary studies, health, culture and justice) and would explicitly seek to protect and promote the presence of strong institutions serving these communities.

Main Feature: The Momentum international delegate programme brings together policy makers, festival organisers, curators, creative entrepreneurs, funders, officials, producers and programmers from all over the world to immerse themselves in this unrivalled showcase of global cultural excellence.    Each delegate is provided with a specially tailored schedule of activities, briefings and meetings to help foster collaboration and exchange. Results: Since 2011, Momentum has brought over 700 international delegates to Edinburgh. Title EN: Multiple programmes
Goal: Integrate Culture In Sustainable Development Frameworks
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: National sustainable development policies and plans
Agency Implementation: Indian National Trust for Art and Cultural Heritage (INTACH)
Main Feature: 1.     Member of the Arts and Culture Committee of the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) contributed to suggestions for sustaining communities during COVID, apart from regular contribution and recommendations for the cultural sector. 2.     As a Member of the Executive Committee of AIMA, the International Association of Agricultural Museums, organised the CIMA 23 Conference in India, to raise awareness about ICH in agricultural traditions in India and the wealth of knowledge found in agricultural activities, practices and food heritage. 3.     Workshops, Dialogue, and Conferences: ·         Workshop on Rice Cultures in Assam was organised in collaboration with local colleges, village representatives and Leiden and Ambedkar Universities, focussing on the rich cultural significance of rice. ·         A joint workshop with Rajiv Gandhi University, Arunachal Pradesh, engaging in dialogues with diverse communities in Arunachal Pradesh to understand the challenges faced in preserving intangible heritage. ·         In ajoint projectwith Ambedkar University, the Shillong International Conference on “Oral Traditions: Continuity and Transformations in Northeast and Southeast Asia” was conducted. ·         The Agricultural Heritage MuseumsConference (CIMA 23) – was organised to explore and engage on educating the public through Agriculture Museums on the significance of agriculture to human society, and to explain the many ways that agriculture has evolved. It was meant to facilitate dialogue between museums across the globe about agricultural heritage topics and discoveries. ·         Manjusha Art Workshop – A workshop on Manjusha craft was organisedwhere students were taught the art form; the workshop was aimed at promoting the art form and its learning and transmission process. ·         A collaborative Himalayan Heritage National Conference with the UNESCO C2C at the Wildlife Institute of India, Dehradun, was organized on the intangible culture of the Himalayan regions. The aim is to establish links between scholars, communities, and government/non-government bodies, to further the efforts of safeguarding intangible andlived heritage, and to explore itsconnections with economic regeneration. ·         “This is Dahanu”, a locally conducted project by the INTACH Dahanu chapter created an E-Newsletter and a video project. The initiative encouraged students from diverse backgrounds, languages, and educational levels to contribute articles, artwork, and essays focusing on their local heritage. This mentorship aimed to help students achieve a satisfactory standard in their work, fostering a deeper understanding and appreciation of Dahanu's cultural heritage. ·         A Patna Kalam workshop organised by the INTACH Patna Chapter, was an initiative to promote and preserve the unique Patna Kalam style of painting. The hands-on training by skilled artists included lectures, demonstrations, and interactive sessions. The goal was to encourage new generations to appreciate and continue this traditional art form.   4.     Films and Audio- Visual documentation: ·         Award-winning film made on the Kumbh mela, KUMBH – THE NECTAR OF FAITH, looks at the ethos of the Maha Parv Kumbh. Inscribed by UNESCO on the Representative List of Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, this event witnesses the largest peaceful gathering of devotees in the world, embodying the true spirit of inclusiveness. They congregate at four locations in India in the designated six-year cycle (Ardh Kumbh) or the twelve-year cycle (Maha Kumbh) with a single purpose – a dip in the nectar of faith. The film explores its deep significance for the people of the sub-continent. ·         The Ramayana Project: VIGNETTES OF RAMAYANA To review the transmission, mobility, adaptation and concrete expressions of the Rama theme among different communities and regions in India, and to study at close quarters the power of the ‘oral word’, a series of films have been made under the Ramayana Project. The 34 short films were made to understand and capture the ethos of the Ramayana. They portray how the story in the epic has changed to include local flavour without losing the central theme and message. The films, through experts, bring out the nuances of the distinct forms of the Ramayana as performed in different parts of India.                                                                                                                                                                                            ·         Film on the River Ganga: A LOVE BEYOND REASON The documentary film highlights the lesser-known ICH elements, including Indigenous knowledge systems, folklore, performing arts, oral history, fairs, festivals, crafts, and culinary traditions of communities and regions along the river Ganga. The documentary showcases the above-mentioned living cultural treasures, and how the people of the country engage with the river and get impacted by it. ·         Documentary on the RAAS (RAAX) MAHOTSAV OF MAJULI, Assam, outlines aspects of the Raas festival held at Majuli in Assam and its significance in the life of the people of the world’s largest river island. The film looks at four Satras—Uttar Kamalabari Satra, Dakshinpat Satra, Samaguri Satra and Garamur Satra—and the Missing Community’s celebration of this festival. ·         Film on Gaya Pitrapaksha traditions: GAYA: STRINGS OF FAITH. 5.     Social Media and YouTube ·         The Instagram handle of the ICH Division @intach_myheritage has been active in spreading awareness of Indian cultural and artistic traditions. The team has employed the approach of creating visual articles to educate and introduce the complex intangible processes underlining Indian art and culture to a general audience. As a result, the newly started Instagram handle has seen consistent growth in followers and visibility. ·         The documentary films and audio-visual documentation have been uploaded on the INTACH YouTube platform for wider dissemination. 6.     Museum Work ·         RSSM – The Museum has been set up at Jabalpur with building restoration, design, development of content, and creation of AV documentaries on the life of great Gond Raja Shankar Shah and his son Raghunath Shah depicting their heroic life and death during the Mutiny of 1857. ·         Virtual Experiential Museum at Man Mahal (an ASI Building), Dashashwamedha Ghat, Varanasi, was set up by INTACH to showcase the rich cultural heritage of Kashi. 7.     INTACH’s Heritage Craft and Community Division Work ·         HCCD and the INTACH Aurangabad Chapter has restarted the tradition of handmade paper-making in Kagzipura, Maharashtra, to revitalise its paper-making craft, combating extinction with workshops, making it into a craft village and successfully creating sustainable livelihoods for the Kagzi Community there. Also recognized at G-20 – W20, Kagzipura paper products are gaining international acclaim. Future plans include a Paper Museum, Kagzipura Lake rejuvenation, and global handmade product promotion. ·         The Kerang fabric (made from the bark of a tree) revival project was executed with the INTACH Orissa-Koraput Chapter. Through skill-upgradation and design implementation workshops and awareness campaigns, the project aims to revitalize the demand for Kerang fabrics both locally and globally. INTACH is in the process of applying for the GI Tag for Kerang. Recognizing the significance of preserving indigenous crafts and empowering local communities, the Government of Orissa is in discussions to formalize a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with INTACH for the phase 2 of promotion and revival of Kerang fabrics.   ·         The Sacred Waste Training Programme – a pan India project - provides training for converting flower waste into incense sticks and cones. The project, besides providing a sustainable solution for tackling pollution, also provides a livelihood for the marginalized sector (especially women). The first Scared Waste training programme was held in Maihar, MP, and adopted by various INTACH Chapters like Jammu, Ayodhya, Sekhawati, Vishakhapatnam and Shivpuri.
Results: The activities conducted by INTACH are deeply researched and are backed by in depth, comprehensive fieldwork, which is why they lend credibility to the organisation and its work in this sphere. INTACH’s activities have been widely appreciated. The dissemination programmes and workshops have effectively raised awareness about lived and practiced heritage, provided exposure to heritage under threat and to the livelihoods of communities engaged in cultural activities or creative economies. The use of social media has further amplified the impact by reaching a wider audience. Additionally, the successful screening of numerous films at various locations, resulting in National and International Awards, is a testament to the success of the initiatives. Collaborationson ongoing discourse and dialogues with government bodies, scholars, universities, and cultural organizations have been instrumental in establishing valuable connections that help in safeguarding the living cultural traditions.

Agency Implementation: The Museum Council of Iceland
Main Feature: The Museum Council of Iceland is an advisory board for the Ministry of Culture. The Council  deals with various tasks regarding museums, whether cultural, artistic or natural history. The Museum Council assesses applications from museums that seek accreditation and prepares a proposal for the Minister of  Culture that issues the accreditation. In 2024, 47 accredited museums exist in Iceland. Among the Museum Council’s duties is overall supervision of museum activities in Iceland, drafting policies in collaboration with the central museums and designating standards in relation to matters such as accessibility and safety. The Council also establishes the rules for allocation from the Museum Fund and evaluates applications to the Fund. Allocations from the Fund are granted to accredited museums for particular projects. Accredited museums which are not publicly owned are able to apply for operating grants and non-accredited museums are able to apply for support in particular projects that they engage in in collaboration with accredited museums. International projects are also supported by the Fund. Three principal, or central, museums in Iceland form strategies for other museums in their respective fields: The National Gallery; The Museum of Natural History; and the National Museum of Iceland. Title EN: NIKE – 30ème Journées européennes du patrimoine - Réparation et Réutilisation
Goal: Integrate Culture In Sustainable Development Frameworks
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: National sustainable development policies and plans
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: NIKE Centre national d’information sur le patrimoine culturel
Main Feature: Pour l'année culturelle 2023, la 30e édition des Journées européennes du patrimoine avait pour thème « Réemploi et Recyclage » et s'est déroulée les 9 et 10 septembre 2023 dans toute la Suisse.  427 manifestations ont eu lieu dans les 26 cantons suisses ainsi qu’au Liechtenstein. L'offre allait des visites guidées et expositions aux projections de films, concerts et événements innovants comme les marchés aux puces et les événements de quartier, en passant par des promenades, des tables rondes et des ateliers. Le programme couvrait des stations reconnues et moins connues et s'adressait à un public varié de tous les âges.
Results: Lors des Journées européennes du patrimoine, près de 45 000 visiteuses et visiteurs ont franchi les frontières linguistiques et cantonales pour jeter un coup d'œil dans les coulisses de bâtiments, de paysages et de traditions de grande valeur en Suisse. C'est ainsi que l'on parvient à ancrer durablement la connaissance de l'importance et de la diversité du patrimoine culturel bâti dans différentes couches de la population suisse.   Un design pour toute la Suisse : les Journées européennes du patrimoine se sont présentées avec l’identité visuelle nationale élaborée par les organismes responsables. Pour la première fois, toutes les actrices et tous les acteurs de la campagne se sont présentées et présentés sous un design national commun, avec l’ajout de la marque « Découvrir le patrimoine ». La marque ombrelle définit le cadre visuel et laisse aux cantons, grâce à sa structure modulaire, la liberté de créer leurs propres brochures et affiches régionales.  Nouvelle plateforme web : le 1er juin 2023, le Centre NIKE a publié le site www.découvrir-le-patrimoine.ch.  Outre une interface utilisateur moderne, le site offre d’une part un nouveau masque de saisie, qui donne plus de droits aux services spécialisés dans la conservation des monuments historiques et l’archéologie, en leur permettant de gérer les inscriptions d’autres organisateurs. D’autre part, il présente l’ensemble du programme dans un calendrier numérique des manifestations. Les retours adressés au Centre NIKE montrent que les personnes utilisatrices sont majoritairement favorables au calendrier des manifestations disponible de manière mobile. Sur la base des premières expériences, le Centre NIKE évalue le site et optimise l’interface utilisateur pour l’édition 2024, notamment l’aperçu du programme.  Le nouveau site web a entraîné une augmentation significative du nombre de personnes utilisatrices. Entre le 1er juinet le 17 septembre 2023, il a enregistré un total de 53 207 visites. La page manifestations a été vue 127 202 fois, soit presque dix fois plus que les années précédentes. Avec 4 minutes 11 secondes, la visite moyenne a duré deux fois plus longtemps qu’en 2022. 53 % des visites étaient directes, 24 % depuis d’autres sites internet, 16 % depuis des moteurs de recherche, et 6 % des réseaux sociaux.  Réseaux sociaux : le Centre NIKE a développé la présence des Journées du patrimoine sur les réseaux sociaux. En juin 2023, il a ouvert un compte en allemand « kulturbeentdecken » et un autre en français « découvrirlepatrimoine » sur Facebook et Instagram. Pour la promotion des événements et le dialogue avec la communauté des Journées du patrimoine, il a utilisé les hashtags #KulturerbeEntdecken, #DecouvrirLePatrimoine et #ScoprireIlPatrimonio. Les publications ont mis en valeur chaque manifestation, le thème annuel et les contributions des organisations participantes. En peu de temps, le Centre NIKE a réussi à créer une première communauté.

Title EN: National Cultural, Artistic and Heritage Agent Register (RAC).
Goal: Promote Human Rights And Fundamental Freedoms
SDG: SDG 5 - Achieve gender equality and empower all women and girls,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels
Area of Monitoring: Artistic freedom
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: Undersecretariat of Cultures and Arts, Ministry of Cultures, Arts and Heritage.
Main Feature: The RAC is a measure from the Ministry of Cultures, Arts and Heritage for gauging and characterising cultural agents (individuals and organisations) who work in the artistic, cultural and heritage areas in Chile. The implementation of this initiative is a response to a historical and broad-based demand from the artistic, cultural and heritage field, identified the need across the board for information, records and updated registers, that have stable continuity; provide knowledge about the situation and characteristics of cultural workers, associations and organisations throughout the national territory and, lets us know the cultural reality of the country, in its various dimensions.   In the heritage area, the RAC "Patrimoniales" emerges in 2021 as a survey that sought to diagnose the state of cultural, artistic and heritage agents, during the pandemic.   The form was available for the last time in 2022 for the process of Bono Cultura, cultural benefit applications, which exponentially increased the number of registered individuals. Currently, the tool has almost 5,000 organisations and almost 72,300 individuals registered. In particular, the RAC contains information about cultural and heritage agents in Chile and their education, territory, economic, work and social characteristics.   Lastly, regarding monitoring framework of the 2005 Convention, this measure is part of the indicator on "measures that strengthen the skills and capacities of civil society".
Results: The main reports derived from working with the information in the RAC, are the document on "Cultural, Artistic and Heritage Agents. Approaching measure and characterisation" (free translation) which was published in 2021 by the Department of Studies, part of the Undersecretariat of Cultures and Arts of MINCAP, and the “Study and analysis on the dynamics of the work of cultural, artistic and heritage agents” (free translation), prepared by the Cultural Policy Observatory (CPO) in 2022.   These studies, among other results, show that currently the main characteristics of cultural work are their interdisciplinary nature (almost two thirds of the agents in the Register), multiple jobs, flexibility, informality, seasonality and intermittency. Work as an independent contractor is the predominant work relationship in the culture sector in Chile, and is consistent with what the literature.  With these results in mind, this measure supports equitable distribution of cultural resources and inclusive access to them, as not only does it provide information about cultural work for public policy-making regarding the sector in Chile, it was also used in 2022 for the Bono Cultura (economic benefit provided by MINCAP in the context of the COVID public health emergency) application process.   Lastly, work is in progress for the use of the RAC as an identification tool, helping with applications, monitoring, characterisation and reporting on the cultural agents benefitted by MINCAP's different programmes.

Title EN: National Theatre and Dance Policy
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Agency Implementation: Department of Sport, Arts and Culture
Main Feature: The national Theatre and Dance policy was approved in August 2023 and was developed to address the following sector focus areas: •	Transformation of the sector: The need to facilitate transformed access for all theatre and dance practitioners, including physical spaces, training and festivals, and ensure that all who seek to make their livelihoods in the theatre and dance sector have access to the resources that will allow them to do so in the dance and theatre ecosystems. •	Education and training: Ensuring that theatre and dance practitioners in all provinces have access to accredited qualifications through formal and non-formal training sectors in liaison with the Culture, Arts, Tourism, Hospitality, Sports Sector Education Training Authority (CATHSSETA) so that accredited training is available and accessible in all provinces and previously disadvantaged communities. •	Business development: Liaison with the departments responsible for trade and industry, and small and medium enterprises to inculcate a collaborative approach towards theatre and dance business development. Facilitating access to production capital, resources and supporting entrepreneurship for theatre and dance practitioners. •	Infrastructure and facilities: Liaison across all three tiers of government to innovate infrastructure and public space use to ensure that theatre and dance are housed and accessible across the country. Community arts centres are to become key vehicles through which cultural infrastructure and access to the arts themselves will be made available to previously disadvantaged communities. •	Research and documentation: Public-funded Cultural Institutions and other funded strategic programmes within theatre and dance sector should ensure there is documentation, research and knowledge development in various forms of texts. Here, texts cover written work, audio-visual and other forms of documentation. •	Market and audience development: To grow the sustainability of the theatre and dance sector by increasing national and international markets for South African productions. The established theatre and dance task team/committee, by any other name, to go beyond policy review and draw up nuanced national and international theatre and dance marketing and audience development trends in liaison with the sector stakeholders. •	Rights and social benefits: Liaison with the department responsible for labour to ensure that theatre and dance practitioners are protected as per the Labour Relations Act, 1995 (Act No. 66 of 1995). A medical aid and pension scheme/provident fund that take into account the itinerant nature of theatre and dance work. Create a relief fund for practitioners who have fallen on hard times or who have grown too old or frail to work. •	Networking and representation: The National Theatre and Dance Policy acknowledges that networking and representation is driven by the sector; therefore, the Department will offer support to facilitate meeting this policy's objectives. The theatre and dance sector to build relationships with like-minded partners in Africa and across the globe to provide its members with opportunities for collaboration, advocacy, residencies, joint ventures and exchanges. •	Awards and recognition: The theatre and dance sector curates and run awards and recognition initiatives that go beyond artistic excellence to the intangible values which theatre and dance create. Once the theatre and dance sector has curated and/or is running awards and recognition initiatives, an invitation will be extended to the relevant tiers of government, based on the reach and impact of the awards and/or recognition initiatives. The relevant public offices will give appropriate support and delegate representatives to attend such events. •	Funding and resource mobilisation: Theatre and dance will be considered as a specific line item when considering public funding for arts and culture through the strategic arts and culture implementation plans of all three tiers of government. Levelling the playing field and distributing services and material support to the majority of theatre and dance practitioners in the country requires far greater synergy between national, provincial and local levels of government. If arts and culture structures at the provincial and local level of government do not operate effectively, it is virtually impossible to create a vibrant and dynamic theatre and dance sector.
Results: the policy has been translated into South African languages by the DSAC language Services, University of Pretoria is using the approved policy as part of its Arts Management Curriculum for 3rd year students. South African School of Motion Picture Medium and Live Performance - Durban Campus, commonly known as AFDA Durban is drafting a policy research journal based on the approved policy. Title EN: National Film Board of Canada’s Equity, Diversion and Inclusion Measures, Activities and Commitments Initiatives
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Media diversity
Agency Implementation: National Film Board of Canada (NFB)
Main Feature: As a public producer and distributor with a mandate to reflect the lives, experiences, and perspectives of all Canadians in its works, the NFB is firmly committed to specific engagements and best practices that ensure equitable representation of underrepresented demographic groups behind the camera, in key craft positions, in the stories the NFB produces and in how those stories are told. This measure aims to support the contribution of creation of Canadian audiovisual content, in particular by promoting greater participation of underrepresented communities in the creative process.   In February 2021, the NFB published its plan for equity, diversity and inclusion (EDI), complete with 24 goals and commitments to transformational change. The plan includes concrete actions within four key areas: organizational structure, production and distribution, staffing, and governance. The plan values diversity, as diversity brings together memories of the past and visions for the future and expands horizons. The NFB wants to ensure equity for Indigenous people and underrepresented linguistic, racialized and cultural communities, and people of all sexual identities and gender expressions, as well as those with disabilities—reflecting the full richness of humanity. By carrying through on these commitments, the NFB can contribute to eliminating decades of injustice that have arisen not only in Canadian society, but also within the institution. The plan was developed in conjunction with the NFB’s ongoing Indigenous Action Plan and its plan for gender parity, both of which are continuing commitments.  Within the identified 24 objectives, the NFB’s EDI plan emphasizes the need for:  •	equitable programming that includes, promotes, and highlights works by artists from underrepresented and racialized groups;  •	a respectful, clear, convenient and transparent method of data collection to measure progress; and  •	NFB films to be accessible to everyone, by ensuring each new film includes described video and subtitles.   As a federal employer, the NFB also has a five-year employment equity plan to ensure the NFB workforce is more diverse and reflective of Canadian society.   From this EDI plan, the NFB made a firm commitment that by March 31, 2025, at least 30% of its current productions and co-productions will be made by filmmakers/artists who identify as Black and People of Colour (BPOC). This figure represents a minimum: the NFB is aiming for more but certainly not less than this objective. The NFB will prioritize skill development and career acceleration for a diverse pool of artists, with the aim of supporting a creative ecosystem that’s not just inclusive, but sustainable as well. The NFB has experience in reaching targets, having set them for both gender equity (in 2016) and Indigenous production spending (in 2017), and anticipates positive results when its EDI action plans are finalized.
Results: The implementation of an EDI plan has led to the achievement of several milestones at the NFB.   In April 2023, the NFB implemented a confidential, non-mandatory self-identification questionnaire sent to filmmakers, artists, and production team members. Respectful, responsible and confidential self-identification is an evidence-based approach that measures and tracks the NFB’s progress towards equitable programming. Since its implementation, the self-identification form received a response rate of 88%. The NFB commits to publishing the results of the self-identification questionnaire annually, with the first report to be released in fiscal 2024–25. The publication of this data will offer insight into its action plans’ progress towards racial, Indigenous and gender equity across all of its productions. Progress towards equity is meant to be evolutive and responsive to feedback from the community.   A similar self-identification survey addressed to NFB staff revealed that, as of March 31, 2023, 58.3% of the NFB workforce is made up of women, 17.6% belong to visible minorities, 3.7% identify as disabled and 2.5% are Indigenous. Two key new positions were created in support of institutional change. The NFB welcomed its inaugural Director of Indigenous Relations and Community Engagement in addition to a Senior Equity, Diversity and Inclusion Advisor. In 2022, the NFB also introduced a subsidized Indigenous trainee position: Coordinator of Indigenous Relations and Community Engagement. The NFB further provided unconscious bias and anti-racism workshops to all staff to address discriminatory behaviour, microaggressions, allyship and privilege, thereby fostering awareness and attitudinal change. The NFB’s Director of Indigenous Relations and Community Engagement facilitated a foundational, mandatory training session for all employees (entitled “Truth Before Reconciliation”), educating them on Indigenous cultures, histories, and current issues. In 2023, all employees were asked to continue their learning by focusing on the realities of Inuit communities by taking mandatory Canada School of Public Service courses. In 2022–2023, a Community of Care for Indigenous hires was introduced. The program has created a culture of inclusivity and support for new Indigenous staff. Furthermore, the NFB actively organized events and internal communications to promote understanding of ethnocultural and racial diversity and the challenges faced by diverse groups. Notably, it held panels and discussions, during Black History Month for example, which celebrated Black filmmakers and facilitated learning. It further continued prioritizing recruitment of NFB directors general, directors, executive producers and producers from underrepresented groups (Black, racialized and 2SLGBTQI+ communities, people with disabilities, and Indigenous People). These and other initiatives contributed to creating an inclusive and informed workplace culture.  NFB has continued efforts to identifying and removing barriers for members of equity-seeking groups beyond the NFB workplace. The NFB is looking forward to continuing in these endeavours, and more, in keeping with the commitments in its 2023–25 Accessibility Plan, published earlier this year.
