Title EN: Policies and Measures that Protect the Economic Rights of Artists
Goal: Promote Human Rights And Fundamental Freedoms
SDG: SDG 5 - Achieve gender equality and empower all women and girls,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels
Area of Monitoring: Artistic freedom
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: 1. Ministry of Tourism and Creative Economy/Tourism and Creative Economy Agency   2. Ministry of Law and Human Rights  3. Ministry of Finance  4. Ministry of Education, Culture, Research, and Technology  5. National Collective Management Institution
Main Feature: In the past four years, policies and measures that protect the economic rights of artists include: 1. Law 17 of 2006 on Amendments to Law 10 of 1995 on Customs;   2. Law 28 of 2014 on Copyrights (Law on Copyrights);  3. Draft Law on Communal Intellectual Property;  4. Government Regulation 20 of 2017 on Controlling the Import or Export of Goods Suspected of Constituting or Originating from Violations of Intellectual Property Rights;  5. Government Regulation 56 of 2021 on the Management of Song and/or Music Copyright Royalties;   6. Government Regulation 24 of 2022 on the Implementation Regulation of Law 24 of 2019 on Creative Economy;   7. Government Regulation 56 of 2022 on Communal Intellectual Property;  8. Head of Creative Economy Agency Regulation 9 of 2017 on Marketing of National Creative Economy Products;  9. Minister of Finance Regulation 40/PMK.04/2018 on Recording, Restrainment, Guarantee, Temporary Suspension, Monitoring and Evaluation in the context of Controlling the Import or Export of Goods Alleged as or Originating from the Proceeds of Intellectual Property Violations;  10. Minister of Tourism and Creative Economy Regulation 11 of 2022 on the 2020-2024 Ministry of Tourism and Creative Economy/Tourism and Creative Economy Agency Strategic Plan (2020-2024 Kemparekraf Strategic Plan);  11. Minister of Law and Human Rights Regulation 9 of 2022 on Implementation of Government Regulation 56 of 2021 on Management of Song and/or Music Copyright Royalties;   12. Draft Minister of Education, Culture, Research, and Technology Regulation on Permits to Utilize Culture Advancement Objects for Commercial Purposes for Large Industries and Foreign Parties; and  13. Minister of Law and Human Rights Decree HKI.2.OT.03.01-02 of 2016 on the Ratification of Royalty Rates for Users Who Make Commercial Use of Works and/or Rights Products related to Music and Songs.  Most of the policies reported in the 2020 QPR, namely (1) Law 17 of 2006 on Amendments to Law 10 of 1995 on Customs; (2) Law 28 of 2014 on Copyrights; (3) Government Regulation 20 of 2017 on Controlling the Import or Export of Goods Suspected of Constituting or Originating from Violations of Intellectual Property Rights; (4) Head of Creative Economy Agency Regulation 9 of 2017 on Marketing of National Creative Economy Products; (5) Minister of Finance Regulation 40/PMK.04/2018 on Recording, Restrainment, Guarantee, Temporary Suspension, Monitoring and Evaluation in the context of Controlling the Import or Export of Goods Alleged as or Originating from the Proceeds of Intellectual Property Violations; and (6) Minister of Law and Human Rights Decree HKI.2.OT.03.01-02 of 2016 on the Ratification of Royalty Rates for Users Who Make Commercial Use of Works and/or Rights Products related to Music and Songs, are still valid while drafting this report.  Then, one of the policies reported in the 2020 QPR, namely the Head of the Creative Economy Agency Regulation 8 of 2017 on the 2015-2019 Creative Economy Agency Strategic Plan, has expired and been replaced by the 2020-2024 Kemparekraf Strategic Plan. Meanwhile, another policy reported in the 2020 QPR, Law 20 of 2016 on Trademarks and Geographical Indications, has been revoked. The regulations contained therein, including those related to guaranteeing recognition and protection of artistic freedom, are included in Law 6 of 2023 on the Stipulation of Government Regulation in Lieu of Law 2 of 2022 on Job Creation to into Law (see Goal 1, Policies and Measures that Encourage Job Creation and Entrepreneurship in Culture and Creative Economy Sectors). Finally, one measure reported in the 2020 QPR, Indonesia Creative Incorporated, has not run since 2019.   Apart from the policies and measures reported in the 2020 QPR, several new policies have been published in the past four years. In 2021, the Central Government issued Government Regulation 56 of 2021 on the Management of Song and/or Music Copyright Royalties. This regulation has at least two main contents. First, the scope of activities required to pay royalties is expanded; not only does the direct use of songs, such as concerts and karaoke but now includes playing recorded songs and broadcasting recorded musical performances via various media, including the internet. Second, regarding the establishment of a Song and Music Data Center (Pusat Data Lagu dan Musik, PDLM), which will be built by the Directorate General of Intellectual Property, Kemenhukham, as well as a Song and Music Information System (Sistem Informasi Lagu dan Musik, SILM) which LMKN will build. It is hoped that PDLM and SILM can increase transparency and accountability in royalty management in Indonesia. To speed up the implementation of this policy, Kemenhukham has issued Minister of Law and Human Rights Regulation 9 of 2022 on Implementation of Government Regulation 56 of 2021 on Management of Song and/or Music Copyright Royalties.  The government is also drafting regulations for implementing the mandate of the Law on Copyrights and Government Regulation 24 of 2022 on the Implementation Regulation of Law 24 of 2019 on Creative Economy (see Goal 1, Specific Policies that Regulate Culture and/or Creative Economy Sectors) regarding the possible use of wealth intellectual property as fiduciary collateral. It is hoped that artists and creative economy actors will soon be able to use their work to obtain funding support from financial institutions by pledging the work they own. It is hoped that soon, Kemenhukham and Kemenparekraf can formulate a mechanism for utilizing intellectual property as fiduciary collateral.  Another new policy is Government Regulation 56 of 2022 on Communal Intellectual Property. This GR aims to consolidate protection guarantees for artists and cultural arts workers whose expressions are closely related to traditional culture. Some of the regulations referred to by this GR are the Law on Copyrights and Law 5 of 2017 on Culture Advancement (see Goal 1, Specific Policies that Regulate Culture and/or Creative Economy Sectors). Specifically, regarding the use of cultural expressions by large industries and foreign parties, Kemendikbudristek is currently preparing a Draft Minister of Education, Culture, Research, and Technology Regulation on Permits to Utilize Culture Advancement Objects for Commercial Purposes for Large Industries and Foreign Parties. The main aim of this policy is to protect arts and culture actors from exploitation by large industries. At the time of drafting this report, other related developments needed attention, namely the registration of the Draft Law on Communal Intellectual Property in the National Legislation Program. However, it has not yet received priority for completion in 2024.   In general, policies and measures that protect the economic rights of artists are aimed at contributing to achieving the following agenda(s) of the National Strategy for Culture: 1. Utilize objects of culture advancement to improve people’s welfare (Agenda 4); and  2. Strengthen the role of the government as a facilitator of culture advancement (Agenda 7).
Results: Distribution of royalties by LMKN: 2019: Total IDR 76,239,143,277 /4.645.197,63 USD  (IDR 54,678,398,587 / 3.330.800,26 USD for creators, IDR 10,848,221,732 / 660.832,44 USD for performers, and IDR 10,712,522,958/ 652.605,83 USD for recording producers).  2020: Total IDR 51,288,196,757 / 3.123.471,82 USD (IDR 37,692,289,633 / 2.296.210,52 USDfor creators, IDR 6,826,335,375 / 415.859,67 USD  for performers, and IDR 6,769,571,750 / 412.401,63 USD for recording producers).
Recommandations: An evaluation of digital music copyright protection carried out in 2022 by Koalisi Seni, supported by the UNESCO Jakarta Office and Korea Funds-In-Trust, resulted in the following conclusions/recommendations. 1. The three main problems that prevent musicians from getting proper remuneration for their work in the digital era are as follows. a. Indonesia does not yet have a domestic music-listening platform that can compete with foreign platforms. This weakens the country's bargaining power with foreign platforms. b.The development of digital platforms as the primary vehicle for music distribution presents new stakeholders, such as aggregators and the expanding role of music publishers. Unfortunately, involving musicians does not determine this change, which affects how royalties are calculated and divided. c. The growing practices of the digital music industry mean that musicians are increasingly losing their bargaining power.  2. The situation as described in point 1 continues because of the Law on Copyrights and its derivatives: a. are not yet able to accommodate changes in music distribution patterns in the digital era; b. have not yet identified parties that have emerged in the digital platform era, such as aggregators and publishers; and c. still focuses on piracy, not the new economic relations created between musicians and other actors in the ecosystem that have emerged due to technological developments.  3. It is recommended for the Central Government to: a. make changes to the Law on Copyrights to be able to accommodate various changes that arise from the presence of digital platforms as a vehicle for distributing works; b. accelerate the establishment of a digital royalty distribution mechanism that is transparent, accountable, and openly accessible to musicians; c. prepare standard licensing agreements that favor musicians; d. support the development of domestic digital platforms and e. involve a broader range of musicians in the formation of copyright policy.  Government Regulation 56 of 2021 on the Management of Song and/or Music Copyright Royalties: The evaluation by Muthmainnah et al. (2022) on GR 56 of 2021 resulted in the following conclusions/recommendations. 1. The subject of royalties for copyrights in the field of songs and/or music is every person who uses songs and/or music in the form of commercial public services based on a license agreement that can be excluded when used for performances. Meanwhile, the object of royalties is commercial, public services, which are contained in the provisions of Article 3 paragraph (2).  2. The GR 56 of 2021 as a lex specialist gives LMKN authority as the royalty management coordinator who receives payments, withdraws, collects, and distributes royalties for the economic interests of creators and owners of related rights in the field of songs and/or music, assisted by LMK, especially in determining tariff quantities, basis of estimates, payment structures, and royalty payment control systems.  3. Procedures for withdrawing, collecting, and distributing royalties aim to protect the economic rights of creators or copyright holders and owners of related rights. This procedure is initiated by the user or users who make payments based on a predetermined basic royalty rate. After knowing the royalty rate, users make payments to LMKN, the institution authorized to manage royalties, especially when receiving payments from users. This royalty management is based on data integrated into the song and/or music data center through the SILM system. Furthermore, these royalties are distributed to the creator/copyright holder and related rights owners. It is known that the GR 56 of 2021 has not fully accommodated the protection and regulation for micro, small, and medium enterprises regarding the amount of royalty rates that must be paid.  4. GR 56 of 2021 has positively impacted the royalty management process aimed at creators or copyright holders and owners of related rights to their work so that they are fair, transparent, and accountable. However, realizing that these regulations do not yet accommodate complete clarity regarding royalty management is essential because the latest follow-up regulations do not yet support them. The provisions of the GR, which only cover micro businesses, result in the need to create a new, clear, and specific regulatory basis to optimize and emphasize the imposition of royalties.  5. The royalty withdrawal mechanism needs to be more widely disseminated to provide understanding to the public, especially for users who use songs and/or music commercially.  6. LMKN is still pioneering the formation of an accurate song and/or music data center. Due to the long development process, which requires considerable costs, it is recommended that the development be accelerated through collaboration with the private sector.  7. The recommended system to be built for charging royalties is an online-based system on the LMKN website. This system can use a license calculator whose object has been updated to determine rates according to the object of royalty imposition. An online-based payment feature connected directly to LMKN that sends proof of payment to the user's email can also be built to avoid double charges. In line with this, royalties must be distributed online to creators, copyright holders, and related rights owners. Finally, LMKN can create a live chat feature with users to provide users with understanding and answer questions related to royalties.  References: Muthmainnah, N., Pradita, P.A., and Bakar, C.A.P.A. (2022). Perlindungan hukum terhadap hak cipta bidang lagu dan/atau musik berdasarkan PP Nomor 56 Tahun 2021 tentang pengelolaan royalti hak cipta lagu dan/atau musik. Title EN: Policies and Measures that Support the Digital Transformation of Cultural and Creative Industries
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Digital environment
Agency Implementation: 1. Ministry of Education, Culture, Research and Technology 2. Ministry of Tourism and Creative Economy 3. National Library of Indonesia
Main Feature: In the past four years, policies and measures that support the digital transformation of cultural and creative industries include: 1. Minister of Communication and Informatics Regulation 2 of 2021 on the 2020-2024 Ministry of Communication and Informatics Strategic Plan (2020-2024 Kemenkominfo Strategic Plan); 2. Indonesia Creative Cities Network (ICCN); 3. Creative City Index (Indeks Kota/Kabupaten Kreatif, IKK); 4. National Library Collection Digitalization;  5. Indonesian Cultural Digital Library (Perpustakaan Digital Budaya Indonesia, PDBI); 6. Archipelago Rhythm (Irama Nusantara);  7. Media Arts Community Festival (Festival Komunitas Seni Media, FKSM); 8. Kiranamaya (Indonesia Bertutur Festival); and  9. Light Festival (Gaung Sakala Bhumi Majapahit).   Several measures, namely ICCN, IKK, National Library Collection Digitization, and PDBI were reported in the 2020 QPR and are still ongoing while drafting this report. In recent developments, the number of creative cities and regencies in Indonesia that have joined the ICCN has increased. ICCN has also linked cross-community forums and initiatives in cities/regencies. Creative actors can use the Creative City application to view profiles and access various news and activities about various creative cities/regencies in Indonesia.  Meanwhile, IKK is just starting to be realized, with cities and regencies in the West Java Province being the first to have IKK scores after previously reported in the 2020 QPR 2020 that it was still in development. Preparation of the West Java IKK had been carried out from 2019 to 2023. The process of compiling the 2023 IKK was carried out by distributing surveys in 27 cities/regencies, one of which was measured by the Digitalization and Information Communication Technology factor with eight indicators such as ownership of networking sites and social media accounts, digital competence, to the ability to manage local markets (marketplaces). From a qualitative perspective, what is highlighted is that training on using digital platforms and social media to support the creative economy is essential to help creative economy actors in marketing and branding.  Several policies have been reported in the 2020 QPR, but in the past four years have been revoked. The first is Presidential Regulation 74 of 2017 on the 2017-2019 National Electronic Trading System Roadmap and its annexes. Next is the Minister of Communication and Informatics Regulation 15 of 2018 on the Indonesian Telecommunications Regulatory Body which was revoked following the enactment of Presidential Regulation 112 of 2020 on the Dissolution of the National Research Council, Food Security Council, Surabaya-Madura Regional Development Agency, National Sports Standardization and Accreditation Agency, Indonesian Hajj Supervisory Commission, National Economic and Industrial Committee, Telecommunications Advisory Board, National Commission for the Elderly, Indonesian Professional Sports Agency, and the Indonesian Telecommunications Regulatory Body.  One of the new relevant policies in the past four years is the 2020-2024 Ministry of Communication and Informatics Strategic Plan. One of the targeted programs, namely the migration of terrestrial television to digital through the Analog Switch Off (ASO) program, will be completed in 2020-2024 and will produce a digital dividend that will have an impact on the digital economy, such as the addition of 181,000 new MSMEs, the addition of 232,000 jobs, and others. The Ministry of Communication and Informatics also has an 8 million MSME Go Online program, which aims to increase the MSMEs’ ability to sell in marketplaces. Until 2024, the Ministry of Communication and Informatics will hold 1,000 Digital Startup programs, implement the One Data Indonesia program, and carry out the 150 smart cities program and digital literacy program for 50 million Indonesian citizens.  In the past four years, there have also been several measures that have not been reported in the 2020 QPR. Established in 2011, Irama Nusantara is a digital archiving effort that has succeeded in providing free access to various archives of Indonesian popular music releases from the 1920s to the 2000s, as well as various mass media and other related literature. This digital archiving effort began in 2020 through a collaborative initiative from the Directorate of Film, Music and Media, Kemendikbudristek. This collaboration program has succeeded in digitizing 1000 releases of Indonesian popular music per year.  There is FKSM, an annual media art exhibition from Kemendikbudristek that highlights junior artists. This festival was previously called Media Arts Week, and the first event was held in 2015. In the past four years, FKSM has been held three times, namely (1) in 2021 at City Gallery, South Tangerang, with the theme "Artidentity: Food Culture"; (2) in 2022 at the Technical Implementation Unit of the Bengkulu Province Cultural Parks Service with the theme "Medi(t)ation Rites/Routes"; and (3) in 2023 at the Mataram Cultural Park with the theme "Land of Dialectics."   Then, there is the Indonesia Bertutur Festival, held for the first time in 2022 to maintain sustainable culture and cultural heritage as a source of knowledge. To advance the cultural ecosystem, this festival was held in the Borobudur Temple Area, Magelang, Central Java, from September 7 to 11, 2022. One of the popular activities in this festival is Kiranamaya, which presents various light art installations by artists whose works use lighting, interactive, and architectural technology.  Finally, the first Light Festival was held in November 2023 in the Trowulan (Majapahit) cultural heritage area, East Java. This activity showed the re-enactment or bringing back the situation of Majapahit in its heyday using the medium of light art. This Light Festival is just one of the new activities of the annual Gaung Sakala Bhumi Majapahit event, but it gained high appreciation from the participants.  In general, policies and measures that support the digital transformation of cultural and creative industries are aimed at contributing to achieving the following agenda(s) of the National Strategy for Culture: 1. Develop and utilize cultural resources to strengthen the position of Indonesia internationally (Agenda 3); 2. Utilize objects of culture advancement to improve people’s welfare (Agenda 4); 3. Culture advancement that protects biodiversity and strengthens ecosystems (Agenda 5); and 4. Strengthen the role of the government as a facilitator of culture advancement (Agenda 7).
Results: ICCN: ICCN has covered 361 cities and regencies throughout the country and connects cross-community forums and initiatives from 260 cities and regencies in 37 Indonesian provinces.  The 2023 West Java IKK: There is an increase of more than 10% compared to the IKK assessment in 2022.  National Library Collections Digitization: Until 2023, there were 12,652,551 unique entries from 3,187 institutions, 4,355 libraries, and 11,725 ​​repositories, including governments, schools, universities, publishers, foundations/institutions, and the general public. FKSM: In 2023, it involved around 50 artists, curators, and event organizers with around 5,000 visitors.  Indonesia Bertutur Festival: In 2022, around 900 cultural actors displayed more than 100 works.
Recommandations: The 2023 West Java IKK: Evaluations carried out by Disparbud Jabar (2023) have produced several conclusions as follows.  1. Quantitative assessment results show that there is an increasing trend in several factors, namely (a) culture, recreation, and tourism; (b) output and creative work; (c) cultural capital and participation; (d) government and regulation; and (e) digitalization and ICT. However, there has also been a decreasing trend in human resources, talent, and education.  2. Based on quantitative and qualitative analysis results, the 2023 West Java IKK is proven to be mature (robust). This means that it can describe the level of creative cities/regencies according to real conditions and is not sensitive or does not change easily.  3. Although several areas have experienced significant increases, others have remained stable or experienced smaller increases. Meanwhile, seven cities/regencies in West Java experienced a decrease in total scores and several categories when updating the city/regency index. Identify cities/regencies in West Java that meet the requirements for being a Creative City/Regency in West Java.  2. It is a basis for sound planning to encourage cities to be more attractive and to optimize the potential in developing the creative economy towards a Creative City/Regency.  3. Title EN: Policies and Measures that Support the Inward Mobility of Foreign Artists and Cultural Professionals to Indonesia
Goal: Achieve A Balanced Flow Of Cultural Goods And Services And Increase The Mobility Of Artists And Cultural Professionals
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 10 - Reduce inequality within and among countries,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Mobility of artists and cultural professionals
Cultural Domain: Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: 1. Ministry of Manpower  2. Ministry of Tourism and Creative Economy/Tourism and Creative Economy Agency 3. Provincial Government of DKI Jakarta
Main Feature: In the past four years, policies and measures that support the inward mobility of foreign artists and cultural professionals to Indonesia include: 1. Law 13 of 2003 on Manpower (Law on Manpower); 2. Law 10 of 2009 on Tourism (Law on Tourism); 3. Law 6 of 2023 on the Stipulation of Government Regulation in Lieu of Law 2 of 2022 on Job Creation into Law (Law on Job Creation); 4. Draft Law on Amendments to Law 13 of 2003 on Manpower (Draft Law on Manpower); 5. Draft Law on Amendments to Law 10 of 2009 on Tourism (Draft Law on Tourism); 6. Government Regulation 34 of 2021 on the Use of Foreign Workers (GR on Foreign Workers);  7. Minister of Tourism and Creative Economy Regulation 4 of 2021 on the Business Activity Standards in the Operations of Risk-Based Business Licensing in the Tourism Sector; 8. Minister of Manpower Regulation 8 of 2021 on the Implementation Regulation of Government Regulation 34 of 2021 on the Use of Foreign Workers;  9. Minister of Manpower Decree 228 of 2019 on Certain Positions Which Foreign Workers May hold in the Arts, Entertainment, and Recreation Category;  10. DKI Jakarta Regional Regulation 3 of 2015 on Amendments to Regional Regulation 13 of 2010 on Entertainment Taxes (DKI Jakarta Entertainment Taxes); and 11. Kharisma Event Nusantara.   Two policies, namely (1) Minister of Manpower Decree 228 of 2019 on Certain Positions Which Foreign Workers May Hold in the Arts, Entertainment, and Recreation Category and (2) DKI Jakarta Entertainment Taxes, were reported in the 2020 QPR and are still valid at the time of drafting this report.  Policies regarding foreign workers largely influence the inward mobility of foreign artists and cultural professionals to Indonesia. Several policies specifically regulate foreign workers, including the Law on Manpower and the Law on Job Creation (see Goal 1, Policies and Measures that Encourage Job Creation and Entrepreneurship in the Culture and Creative Economy Sectors). The Law on Job Creation stipulates that every employer who employs foreign workers must have a Plan for the Use of Foreign Workers (Rencana Penggunaan Tenaga Kerja Asing, RPTKA), which the Central Government approves. Individuals cannot employ foreign workers; only companies/institutions with legal entities are permitted.  The types of RPTKA are regulated through the GR on Foreign Workers. This GR replaces Presidential Regulation 20 of 2018 on the Use of Foreign Workers, which was reported in the 2020 QPR. In this GR, the following are the articles that are relevant to the arts, entertainment, and recreation: (1) RPTKA for temporary types of work with a period of up to 6 months and cannot be extended, for example, for commercial film making purposes; and (2) RPTKA for types of work with a period of more than six months shall be granted up to 2 years and can be extended. This GR has no changes regarding the impresario services reported in the 2020 QPR. The only relevant additional new arrangement is that social, religious, educational, and cultural institutions, as well as impresario service businesses, can become employers of foreign workers after prioritizing the use of Indonesian workers in all types of available positions.  One of the impacts of the issuance of this GR on Foreign Workers is the revocation of Minister of Manpower Regulation 10 of 2018 on Procedures for the Use of Foreign Workers and the issuance of Minister of Manpower Regulation 8 of 2021 on the Implementing Regulation of Government Regulation 34 of 2021 on the Use of Foreign Workers. The Minister of Manpower Regulation 8 of 2021 stipulates the use of foreign workers in impresario services and filmmaking businesses as follows: (1) impresario services businesses can be employers of foreign workers, and (2) applications for RPTKA approval for temporary work can be granted for impresario service businesses as well as filmmaking activities that are commercial and have received permission from the competent authority.  Furthermore, another policy reported in the 2020 QPR, namely the Minister of Tourism and Creative Economy Regulation 26 of 2014 on Business Standards for Impresario Services, has been revoked and replaced with Minister of Tourism and Creative Economy Regulation 4 of 2021 on the Business Activity Standards in the Operations of Risk-Based Business Licensing in the Tourism Sector. Regarding the mobility of foreign artists and cultural professionals to Indonesia, this regulation stipulates (1) Business Standards for Theme Park/Other Amusement Park Activities with Medium-Low Risk and (2) Business Standards for Other Man-Made/Man-Built Tourist Attractions with Medium-Low Risk.  Business Standards for Theme Park/Other Amusement Park Activities with medium-low risk contain provisions for business product requirements for theme park/other amusement park activities regarding the theme of the amusement and recreational park – which may include adventure, water activity themes, nature, culture and arts, educational themes, flora and fauna themes, environmental themes, fantasy themes, and/or horror themes – and/or the presence of traditional, modern and/or contemporary performances which include art, music, entertainment, recreation, showcase, and/or comedy.  Business Standards for Other Man-Made/Man-Built Tourist Attractions with medium-low risk contain the requirements for other man-made/man-built tourist attraction business products, which may include the presence of (1) cultural artworks, cultural heritage buildings and objects, cultural art events, historical objects, daily activities and lifestyle (way of life) of the society; (2) artificial tourist attractions for recreation, learning or education about cultural artworks, for performing cultural activities such as dancing, singing, painting, and also enjoying local and global culinary delights as well as purchasing cultural arts products as souvenirs; (3) an information and interpretation center for cultural artworks and man-made/man-built tourist attraction business products; and (4) a certified or licensed (issued by an authorized institution) guide and who has knowledge and insight into man-made/man-built tourist attraction.  Apart from the Law on Manpower and the Law on Job Creation, one of the other central policies related to the inward mobility of foreign artists and cultural professionals to Indonesia and which has not been reported in the 2016 and 2020 QPRs is the Law on Tourism (see Goal 1, Policies and Measures that Encourage Job Creation and Entrepreneurship in the Culture and Creative Economy Sectors). Contrary to the Law on Manpower and the Law on Job Creation, which focus more on workers, especially foreign workers, the Law on Tourism focuses more on activities and areas that become the destination of artists and cultural professionals’ mobility and tourism manpower. In recent developments, stakeholders have identified the need to update the Law on Manpower and the Law on Tourism to respond to current developments, challenges, and opportunities. Even though both laws have been registered in the National Legislation Program, only the Draft Law on Tourism has become one of the priorities for completion in 2024. At the time of drafting this report, it was already at the final draft stage.  One of the new measures reported in the past four years is Kharisma Event Nusantara. This program was initiated by Kemenparekraf in 2021. This program aims to stimulate the economy by presenting quality regional activity events that can improve Indonesia's economic and tourism sectors. These events are spread across almost all provinces in Indonesia, such as the Samosir Music Festival, Semarang Old Town Festival, Jember Fashion Carnaval, Ubud Village Jazz Festival, and Numbay Creative Festival.  In general, policies and measures that support the inward mobility of foreign artists and cultural professionals to Indonesia are aimed at contributing to achieving the following agenda(s) of the National Strategy for Culture: 1. Provide space for the diversity of cultural expressions and encourage cultural interaction to strengthen the inclusiveness of culture (Agenda 1); 2. Develop and utilize cultural resources to strengthen the position of Indonesia internationally (Agenda 3); 3. Institutional reform and culture budgeting to support the culture advancement agenda (Agenda 6); and 4. Strengthen the role of the government as a facilitator of culture advancement (Agenda 7).
Results: DKI Jakarta Entertainment Taxes: DKI Jakarta's income from entertainment taxes decreased drastically in 2020-2021 due to the COVID-19 pandemic but gradually increased afterward.  Kharisma Event Nusantara: In its third year of implementation in 2023, 110 selected events were strictly curated from 291 events proposed by Provincial Tourism Offices across Indonesia.

Title EN: Policies and Measures that Support the Supply of Data and Information Trends in the Digital Environment
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Digital environment
Agency Implementation: Ministry of Communication and Information Technology
Main Feature: In the past four years, policies and measures that support the supply of data and information trends in the digital environment include:  1. Law 16 of 1997 on Statistics (Law on Statistics); 2. Law 14 of 2008 on Open Public Information (Keterbukaan Informasi Publik) (Law on KIP); 3. Draft Law on Amendments to Law 16 of 1997 on Statistics (Draft Law on Statistics); 4. Draft Law on the Integration of Development Data (Draft Law on the Integration of Development Data); 5. Presidential Regulation 39 of 2019 on One Indonesian Data (Satu Data Indonesia); 6. Minister of Communication and Informatics Regulation 2 of 2021 on the 2020-2024 Ministry of Communication and Informatics Strategic Plan; 7. Ministry of Communication and Informatics One Data Portal (Satu Data Kominfo); and  8. Indonesian Digital Society Index (Indeks Masyarakat Digital Indonesia, IMDI).  The Law on Statistics and the Law on KIP are two fundamental policies related to the provision of data and information trends that have not been reported in the 2016 and 2020 QPRs. For more detailed information on both policies, see Goal 1, Policies and Measures on Information Systems and Cultural Statistics Used in Policy Development.   Moreover, while observing the Minister of Communication and Informatics Regulation 2 of 2021 on the 2020-2024 Ministry of Communication and Informatics Strategic Plan (see Goal 1, Policies and Measures that Support the Digital Transformation of Cultural and Creative Industries), relevant stakeholders regarding Digital TV migration, digital literacy activists, MSME employers and employees, and private sectors that focus on the market can synergize activities that respond to real needs in the field. The needs mentioned include implementing the Law on KIP and the Satu Data Indonesia policy (see Goal 1, Policies and Measures on Information Systems and Cultural Statistics Used in Policy Development). Based on the Strategic Plan, Kemenkominfo built Satu Data Kominfo, which presents data from all units and work units in Kemenkominfo. Two types of available data related to digital data trends are the number of digital MSMEs and the number of internet users.  Meanwhile, IMDI ​​measures people's competence and skills in using digital technology in daily life and work. The IMDI ​​survey has been conducted since 2022 and will be performed again in 2023. The objectives of the IMDI ​​measurement are: (1) to determine the level of digital competence of the community; (2) the importance of having measurements down to the city/regency level; (3) to encourage inclusivity in the digital economy; and (4) as a reference in planning digital human resource development programs in Indonesia. The four pillars of IMDI ​​consist of infrastructure and ecosystem, digital skills, empowerment, and employment.  In general, policies and measures that support the supply of data and information trends in the digital environment are aimed at contributing to achieving the following agenda(s) of the National Strategy for Culture: 1. Provide space for the diversity of cultural expressions and encourage cultural interaction to strengthen the inclusiveness of culture (Agenda 1); 2. Protect and develop values, expressions, and practices of traditional culture to enrich national culture (Agenda 2); and 3. Strengthen the role of the government as a facilitator of culture advancement (Agenda 7).

Main Feature: To promote the inward mobility of professionals, including those in the cultural field, the UAE has implemented policies, regulations, and programs to remove barriers to employment and entrepreneurship. These measures have increased flexibility of movement and reduced the costs associated with obtaining work permits. MoHRE issues 12 types of work permit which allow establishments registered with MoHRE to recruit employees, depending on the nature of the job. The types of permits are: 1. a work permit to recruit a worker from outside the UAE 2. a work permit to transfer a foreign worker from one establishment to another 3. a work permit for a resident on a family sponsorship 4. a temporary work permit to hire a worker to complete a job within a specific period 5. one-mission work permit to recruit a worker from abroad to complete a temporary job, or a particular project for a specific period 6. a part-time work permit to recruit a worker under a part-time contract where his working hours or days are less than his full-time contract 7. a juvenile permit to recruit a juvenile between 15 and 18 years 8. a student training and employment permit to employ a 15-year-old student who is already in the UAE 9. UAE/GCC national permit to employ a UAE or a GCC national 10. a golden visa holder permit to employ a worker holding the UAE�s Golden Residence visa 11. national trainee permit to train a UAE national 12. a freelance permit issued to self-sponsored foreigners in the UAE, who provide services or perform tasks to individuals or companies (without being sponsored by a specific employer in the UAE and without having an employment contract). 13. Private teacher work permit
Results: The policies, regulations and programs outlined above have encouraged the private sector to hire skilled professionals, resulting increasing in skilled workers, which also included creatives and professionals in the cultural sector.

Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Agency Implementation: 1. Coordinating Ministry for Human Development and Cultural Affairs   2. Coordinating Ministry for Maritime and Investment Affairs   3. Ministry of Education, Culture, Research, and Technology
Main Feature: In the past four years, policies on cooperation among government institutions include: 1. Presidential Regulation 92 of 2019 on the Coordinating Ministry for Maritime and Investment Affairs (Kementerian Koordinator Bidang Kemaritiman and Investasi) (PR on Kemenkomarves);  2. Presidential Regulation 35 of 2020 on the Coordinating Ministry for Human Development and Cultural Affairs (Kementerian Koordinator Bidang Pembangunan Manusia and Kebudayaan) (PR on Kemenko PMK); and 3. Draft Presidential Regulation on the 2025-2045 Culture Advancement Master Plan (Rencana Induk Pemajuan Kebudayaan 2025-2045) (2025-2045 RIPK).       In the 2020 QPR, it was reported that based on Presidential Regulation 9 of 2015 on the Coordinating Ministry for Human Development and Cultural Affairs, Kemenko PMK facilitates cooperation between government institutions in the field of culture, including the creative economy. Following the replacement of Presidential Regulation 9 of 2015 with the new PR on Kemenko PMK, the scope of coordination authority mandated to Kemenko PMK has changed. In recent developments, Kemenko PMK only facilitates the coordination of inter-agency cooperation in the field of culture, excluding the creative economy. Ministries under the coordination of Kemenko PMK include (1) Ministry of Religious Affairs, (2) Kemendikbudristek, (3) Ministry of Health, (4) Ministry of Social Affairs, (5) Ministry of Villages, Development of Disadvantaged Regions, and Transmigration; (6) Ministry of Women Empowerment and Child Protection; and (7) Ministry of Youth and Sports.  Meanwhile, the coordination of government inter-agency cooperation in the field of the creative economy when drafting this report falls under the responsibility of Kemenkomarves. This new arrangement is based on provisions in the PR on Kemenkomarves which stipulate that ministries under the coordination of Kemenkomarves include: (1) Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources; (2) Ministry of Public Works and Housing; (3) Ministry of Transportation; (4) Ministry of Environment and Forestry; (5) Ministry of Marine Affairs and Fisheries; (6) Ministry of Tourism and Creative Economy; and (7) Ministry of Investment/Investment Coordinating Agency. In the master plan, 29 ministries/agencies will be involved in culture advancement efforts. The roles and responsibilities of each ministry/agency will be regulated in more detail in the National Action Plan for Culture Advancement, which will be prepared for five years. Kemendikbudristek will coordinate the entire RIPK implementation process. The list of ministries/agencies to be involved is as follows.  1. Title EN: Policies that Underlie the Creation of an Environment that Empowers CSOs
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development

Agency Implementation: Ministry of Home Affairs (Kementerian Dalam Negeri, Kemendagri)
Main Feature: In the past four years, policies that underlie the creation of an environment that empowers CSOs include:  1. Law 28 of 2004 on Amendments to Law 16 of 2001 on Foundations (Law on Foundations);  2. Government Regulation in Lieu of Law 2 of 2017 on Amendments to Law 17 of 2013 on Community-based Organizations (GRiLL on Community-based Organizations);  3. Draft Law on Second Amendments to Law 17 of 2013 on Community-based Organizations (Draft Law on Community-based Organizations);  4. Draft Law on Associations; and  5. Draft Law on Public Participation.  Law on Foundations and GRiLL on Community-based Organizations have been reported in the 2020 QPR and are still valid when drafting this report. In recent developments, stakeholders have identified a real need to update GRiLL on Community-based Organizations to be more responsive to current developments and all challenges and opportunities. Title EN: Policy for the diversity of audiovisual content through the Televisión Metropolitana S.A. signal. Of  C.V. Channel 22

Title EN: POLITIQUE GENRE DE L'ENSEIGNEMENT TECHNIQUE ET PROFESSIONNEL

Par ses diverses initiatives et collaborations, elle œuvre pour une participation accrue des femmes et des filles dans les filières techniques, contribuant ainsi à un développement plus inclusif et équitable. Elle vise également à promouvoir l'égalité des genres dans les programmes de formation et d'apprentissage. Elle développe des initiatives pour encourager la participation des femmes dans les secteurs traditionnellement dominés par les hommes et lutte contre les stéréotypes de genre dans l'éducation. La Cellule Genre du Ministère de l'Enseignement Technique et la Formation Professionnelle a pour mission de : -de veiller au respect de l’équité et de l’égalité entre les sexes ; -d’élaborer le plan triennal et le budget d’activités de la cellule en matière d’égalité et de genre ; - de suivre et d’évaluer l’intégration de l’approche genre dans les activités du Ministère de l’Enseignement Technique, de la Formation Professionnelle et de l’Apprentissage ; - d’informer, de sensibiliser et de former le personnel des Directions et autres structures du Ministère sur l’approche Genre ; - d’identifier les besoins en formation en genre et développement du personnel du ministère ; - de veiller à la prise en compte des besoins pratiques et stratégiques des femmes et des hommes dans l’élaboration, la mise en œuvre, le suivi et l’évaluation des programmes et/ou projets du Ministère.

Il a été recommandé de renforcer les partenariats avec les ONG locales pour étendre la sensibilisation et d'introduire des programmes de mentorat pour les jeunes filles.

Title EN: Policy to disseminate literature and make Armenian literature more recognizable and perceptible abroad
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Agency Implementation: Ministry of Education, Science, Culture and Sport of the Republic of Armenia
Main Feature: The policy of the Ministry of Education, Science, Culture and Sport of the Republic of Armenia to disseminate literature and make Armenian literature more recognisable and perceptiable abroad is aimed at ensuring proportionate development of all circuits of the literary field; preserving, developing, disseminating and raising awareness of literary-cultural heritage through literary products; civil society formation; creating conditions for reproduction and enhancement of the creative potential of society and creating favourable conditions for international cooperation in the sector of dissemination of literature. This policy is also implemented with the participation of Armenia in international book fairs. During the book fairs, the “Armenian Literature in Translations” grant programme is presented with special emphasis; the grant programme supports the publishing houses of foreign countries that wish to publish books by classic and contemporary Armenian authors in foreign languages in their respective countries. The aim of the programme is to make Armenian literature popular beyond Armenia. It not only contributes to the popularisation of Armenian writers, but also to increase in the level of recognisability of Armenia. Over the past 4 years, more than 67 books have been published under this program in 20 foreign languages.
Results: For the period 2022-2023, through the "Literature Publishing" grants program were published 11 foreign language books (including: "The Endangered Armenian Christian Heritage of Artsakh" in English, "Historical and Cultural Heritage of Armenia" in English, "Handwritten Heritage of Artsakh and Utik" in French, "Historical and cultural heritage of Yerevan" in English, "Armenian rugs and carpets: the collection of the Folk Art Museum" in English). Through the grants program “Armenian Literature in Translations” 54 books of Armenian classical and modern literature were translated into more than 20 languages and published in foreign countries.
Recommandations: Participation in international book fairs in Bologna, Tehran, Moscow and Frankfurt has been ensured. Armenia has participated in the aforementioned international book fairs with separate pavilions. In general, international book fairs serve as a best platform for presenting classic and contemporary literature and gather a large number of publishers, writers, translators, literary agents and readers. International book fairs serve as a major opportunity to present Armenian literature published in foreign languages, establish contacts with foreign publishing houses and literary agents and reach agreements over the publication of classic and contemporary Armenian literature in foreign languages abroad. In recent years, there has been interest in the format of participation of the main museums of Armenia in book fairs, which present albums published in foreign languages. Among these museums are the Matenadaran, the Komitas museum-institute. Armenian publishers, who participate in the fairs, have more than 20 meetings and discussions every day. As a result of these meetings, every year in Armenia we publish approximately 2486 books, as well as literary cooperation projects. The best result of participation in book festivals is also the memorandum of cooperation signed with China in the field of book publishing, as a result of which an agreement was reached to translate and publish 20 books in Armenian and Chinese during the 5 years.

Main Feature: According to the Citizenship Act of the Republic of Slovenia, a person of full age may acquire citizenship of the Republic of Slovenia by naturalisation if this is done for the benefit of the state for scientific, economic, cultural, national or similar reasons, provided that the person has actually lived in Slovenia for at least one year without interruption prior to the application and has the legal status of a foreigner and meets the following conditions: - he/she has secure means of subsistence to ensure his/her material and social security and the material and social security of the persons to whom he/she is obliged to provide maintenance; - the person has not been sentenced by final judgement to imprisonment without parole for more than three months, or the person has not been sentenced to imprisonment without parole for more than one year; - the naturalisation of the person does not pose a threat to public order or the security or defence of the state - the person has fulfilled all tax obligations - the person swears to respect the free democratic order enshrined in the Constitution of the Republic of Slovenia. However, a person may exceptionally obtain Slovenian citizenship even if they do not fulfil the condition of uninterrupted one-year residence in Slovenia and do not have a regulated foreigner status. In such cases, their exceptional contribution to the development and international reputation or recognition of Slovenia is taken into account.  According to the Foreigners Act, certain categories of foreigners, including artists and cultural workers, can obtain a long-stay visa (a so-called D visa, which is valid for more than 90 days and up to one year) if in the opinion of the Ministry of Culture, the Republic of Slovenia is interested in them. A foreigner staying in the Republic of Slovenia on a long-stay visa may subsequently be issued the first uniform residence and work permit (a temporary permit valid for one year and renewable after one year). This means that such a foreigner can apply for a residence permit in the country before the visa D expires. Consequently, the foreigner does not have to leave the country, but can apply for a residence permit while remaining in Slovenia. Certain categories of foreigners who are already legally residing in Slovenia (either on the basis of a visa, as EU citizens or as citizens of certain other countries) can also apply for the issuance of the first uniform residence and work permit. This is an exception to the general principle that foreigners must obtain a residence and work permit before entering the country. These exceptions include: - Foreign correspondents or foreign journalists who are already accredited in the Republic of Slovenia or whose accreditation is in the process of being renewed, - Persons who, on the basis of a declaration by a specialised ministry, demonstrate an interest of the Republic of Slovenia in the fields of education, science and culture.

Numerous associations, organizations and entities take part in the event, including artists' associations, critics, historians and academics; universities with art degrees or their faculties, institutes and institutes of art. The National Exhibition of Visual Arts respects equal participation of men and women, with the juries, the pre-selection of works and the prizes established in the National Exhibition of Visual Arts being assigned a proportion no lower than the CINCU, and the prizes established in the National Exhibition of Visual Arts being awarded to women. In the Salón Nacional De Artes Visuales, equal participation in terms of gender is respected, assigning in the integration of the juries, the pre-selection of the works and the prizes established in a proportion of not less than FIFTY PERCENT (50%) to women and not less than FIVE PERCENT (5%) to non-binary, transvestite and trans persons, and federal participation is respected, assigning to persons residing outside the Autonomous City of Buenos Aires, a proportion of not less than FIFTY PERCENT (50%).
Results: The first edition of the SNAV, in 1911, signified a strong push for the development of the visual arts in Argentina. The first editions of the Salon (1911 and 1912) only included works in the categories of Painting and Sculpture. Subsequently, other sections were added to the Salón Nacional de Artes Visuales: Architecture in 1913 (until 1925). Decorative arts in 1913 (until 1919). Recorded in 1948 (from 2022 Gráfica). Drawing in 1951, as "Salón Nacional de Grabado y Dibujo". Visual Research in 1968 (until 1971). Arte Fotográfico in 1974, as "Salón Nacional de Arte Fotográfico" (since 1986 Photography). Ceramic Art in 1976, as "National Exhibition of Ceramic Art" (from 2015 to 2020/21 Ceramics, from 2022 Arts of Fire). Tapestries in 1978, as "Salón Nacional de Tapices" (in 1982 it was renamed Textile Art, and since 2015 it has been called Textile). Electronic Arts in 2000 (in 2001 it was called Installations, from 2002 to 2014 New Media and Installations, since 2015 Installations and Alternative Media; as a whole, the section could be seen as a continuation and reorientation of Visual Investigations). Non-Disciplinary Space in 2022. Financial resources allocated to the policy/measure in US dollars. Title EN: Producing handcrafted products from fabric remnants in Van Phuc craft village, Ha Dong district, creating livelihoods and facilitating community integration for individuals with disabilities
Goal: Integrate Culture In Sustainable Development Frameworks
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: National sustainable development policies and plans
Agency Implementation: Vụn Art
Main Feature: Vụn Art is a collective economic model, established in 2017 by Mr. Le Viet Cuong, an individual with mobility impairments. Vụn Art was founded with the desire to preserve and promote traditional culture, create employment opportunities for people with disabilities, and utilize surplus materials from the production process to protect the environment. Vụn Art produces a diverse and innovative range of handcrafted products designed from fabric remnants and crafted by individuals with disabilities at Vụn Art. These products reflect continuous creativity, based on the materials from the traditional silk village and the combination of elements of folk culture with contemporary influences.
Results: After 5 years of establishment and development, with creative thinking and unceasing efforts, Vụn Art's products have been widely recognized by tourists and are gradually asserting their position in the market. Vụn Art has produced and sold tens of thousands of products, including bags, shirts, puzzle game sets, postcards, and pictures made from fabric remnants - utilizing the discarded raw materials in Van Phuc Silk Village, contributing to reducing environmental pollution and avoiding resource waste. The products have been selected as gifts to many individual customers as well as large enterprises and organizations such as the US Embassy in Viet Nam, the Foreign Trade University, the World Coffee Museum, travel companies, agencies, and businesses. Vụn Art has also exported products to England, the United States, Japan, etc. Additionally, Vụn Art has created jobs, providing social integration opportunities for over 30 workers (mostly women), while actively participating in vocational training for people with disabilities. Vụn Art, in particular, has also operated a creative space, developing cultural experience tours, and attracting students, young people, and tourists to visit, learn, and practice making fabric collage paintings. Visitors, especially international ones, are very interested in these products and their production method. Vụn Art's social enterprise model, addressing the issue of employment for people with disabilities on the basis of preserving and promoting the cultural values of Viet Nam, has been recognized and highly appreciated. Notably, Vụn Art allocates part of its profits to create a fund for disabled people and to continue vocational training to further expand the model.  Vụn Art is also proud to have won prestigious awards for sustainable social enterprise models. In 2019, the cooperative had four products, including fabric collage paintings, handbags, T-shirts, and puzzle painting kits, appraised by Hanoi City to achieve 4-star OCOP - handicrafts with export quality, representing the national brand. In 2020, Vụn Arts won the second prize in the SDG Challenge 2019: Entrepreneurship competition for solutions for people with disabilities in Viet Nam. In 2020, Mr. Le Viet Cuong - founder of the cooperative "Vun Art", was honored as one of 23 authors of a startup project for disabled people, awarded the Golden Swallow Award and Prospects Award at the 3rd Women's Entrepreneurship Competition. TNI King Coffee also sponsored and supported the startup project. In 2021, Vụn Art won the Global Tenacity Award at the Global Competition on Social Business Creation (SBC). According to the United Nations criteria, Vn Art has also been evaluated as a sustainable creative model, introducing culture while creating jobs for vulnerable groups.

Agency Implementation: Ministry of Cultures, Arts, and Knowledge
Main Feature: In the context of the activities carried out by UNESCO to comply with the 2005 Convention, it was agreed to carry out a pilot project for the creation of national Roadmaps for the protection and promotion of cultural and creative industries with a focus on digital and a work process that led to the holding of a capacity-building workshop in June 2021 with a UNESCO expert began.NA
Results: The workshop brought together 14 national-level entities and involved an awareness-raising day about the 2005 Convention and the objective of developing the Digital Environment Roadmap for Colombia. After the workshop, an information collection exercise was carried out with the entities on the status of initiatives in the country for each UNESCO goal and recommendations to be implemented in Colombia to guarantee compliance with the Convention in the digital environment.                  The previous information mapping exercise provided important inputs for the preparation of the Roadmap for Colombia, which was part of the commitments of the CONPES 4090 document of Orange Economy: Strategies to Promote the Economy of Culture and Creativity of 2022 However, as a first exercise, it also served to identify that it was necessary to carry out a complementary mapping that involved more entities and that allowed those that had already participated in the workshop to delve deeper into some aspects requested by UNESCO.                  For this purpose, a work schedule was proposed to continue with the process of preparing the Roadmap, proposing as main milestones the sending of a matrix to the relevant entities in the process to strengthen the information baseline, the formation of a working group between MinCulturas, MINTIC and DNP all in Spanish, the convening of an inter-institutional working group for the construction of the roadmap with the relevant entities and the preparation of a first draft of the roadmap to be presented in February 2023 to UNESCO in the framework of the Intergovernmental Committee of the 2005 Convention.
