Every January, it presents the newest and most significant short films from all around the world, while also gathering together filmmakers, industry representatives, and film lovers.  Established in 2006, the Festival has become a unique platform in Lithuania, screening global short films made by both emerging and established talents. Each year, the Vilnius Short Film Festival holds the International Competition, which features approximately 30-40 of the most acclaimed short films from the past two years. In addition to the International Competition, the Festival hosts a National Competition showcasing a carefully chosen selection of the newest Lithuanian short films. The festival’s programmers team consists of five international competition film selection assistants and International and National Competitions' selection and programming team of three.  The International and National competitions are judged by an International Jury, which awards three short films with three prizes: the Festival Grand Prix, Best International Short Film, and Best National Short Film. Moreover, the Festival features special non-competition programs such as retrospectives, programs for kids, youth, and seniors, as well as theme or country-based short film selections. For these programmes external film professionals are invited to contribute, ensuring a more diverse selection. Additionally, the festival includes non-professionals – such as children, young adults, and seniors – in the film selection process for specific programs. Complementing the Festival screenings, there are numerous events for both the public and film industry professionals. Every year, the Festival offers a tailored Industry Day program for filmmakers and other industry professionals, which includes networking opportunities, workshops, and seminars. Moreover, the Festival invites its fans to various music and interactive events, as well as workshops for families and late-night screenings. The Festival is a member of the Short Film Conference association, the European Film Festival Network “Young4Film!”, the European Network for Film Discourse “The END” and the Nordic-Baltic Short Film Festivals Network.  In last edition, the Festival has made significant strides in inclusivity and gender equality. This included rebranding its visual identity to attract a wider audience and enhance name recognition while adhering to trends in sustainability and diversity. The Festival's National programmes included SDH and audio descriptions, and one screening venue was selected for its full accessibility to individuals with disabilities. Key events were translated into Lithuanian Sign Language, and both staff and volunteers were informed about how to assist attendees with disabilities. An accessibility guide provided information on the Festival’s accessibility features and offered advice on interacting with people with disabilities. In 2024, the Vilnius Short Film Festival received prestigious recognition from the Vilnius City Municipality, being granted the esteemed status of Vilnius City Festival. This honour was bestowed upon the Festival in acknowledgement of its active representation of the city on an international stage through cinema. After the festival ends, it organizes additional events and screenings to broaden the reach of short films and introduce Lithuanian creators to a wider audience. These events aim to familiarize people with the short film format, promote the tradition of high-quality film viewing, and provide a platform for dialogue between creators and audiences. Screenings are held in cinemas, public spaces, and cultural institutions across Vilnius and other Lithuanian cities. Examples include "Culture Night", "Kino kelionės" for seniors, screenings at Lukiškės Vol. 2, and participation in the "Gilios upės tyliai plaukia" project. Throughout the year, the festival also actively engages in international film industry events. It is presented at prominent festivals and markets such as Clermont-Ferrand (France), Cannes "Short Film Corner" (France), and "Talents and Short Film Market" (Italy). Additionally, the festival participates in major European short film festivals including Tampere (Finland), Oberhausen (Germany), Uppsala (Sweden), interfilm Berlin (Germany), Odense (Denmark), Winterthur (Switzerland), Hamburg (Germany), Nordisk Panorama (Sweden), Black Nights (Estonia), Short Waves (Poland), Concorto (Italy), Encounters (United Kingdom), Kyiv (Ukraine), and others. Since 2013, Vilnius SFF has been organized by Lithuanian Short Film Agency “Lithuanian Shorts”.
Results: Each year, the Vilnius Short Film Festival receives around 1,500 to 2,000 submissions for its International and National Competition programs, with the number of submissions increasing annually. Each edition features two National Competition programs, six International Competition programs, and approximately ten special non-competition programs, totaling around 100 short films per year. Festival films are screened in major Lithuanian cities and on the VoD platform “ŽMONĖS Cinema.” Over the past three years, the festival has averaged 70-80 screenings per edition, attracting more than 16,000 spectators and 1,500 event visitors. The festival has established itself as a significant platform for showcasing Lithuanian short films, with a growing number of film applications for its National Competition programs and an increasing number of national premieres each year. Since 2022, the festival has participated in the "Kino kelionės" initiative by "Lithuanian Shorts," which aims to promote access to professional cinema for seniors, provide quality leisure time, disseminate professional culture, and foster critical thinking. Moreover, the Festival is a part of is "Young4Film Film Festival Network," a European network of seven film festivals focused on innovative film education methods to enhance children's and young people's openness and attentiveness to their world, community, and country. The Festival organized workshops for both – young adults and kids. The fact that the festival belongs to more than one international festival network and also hosts other international and national projects, such as "Baltic Women in Film Industry", "European Network for Film Discourse (The END)", “Shorts Critics”, demonstrate the importance and relevance of the festival and its potential to bring together the communities of both the audiovisual industry and film lovers. Beginning in 2023, the festival has placed significant emphasis on improving accessibility for people with various disabilities (deaf and hard of hearing, visually impaired and blind, and those with physical disabilities). This includes efforts to increase their participation in cultural life and enhance their visibility in society. The festival collaborates with organizations representing these communities to understand their needs and expectations better, implementing inclusive communication strategies for the project.

Main Feature: The ProChile sectoral plans are a set of activities that follow an internationalisation strategy of Chilean culture, which includes participation in international fairs, for which there are public calls for the selection of beneficiaries. The arts and creative sectors include animation, audiovisual, performing arts, visual arts, design, publishing, fashion, music,  graphic narrative, illustration and video games.   The international fair are events that take place around the world, as annual meeting points for different, including the creative, sectors. At these events, international buyers and chilean export companies come together to create high-impact and long-lasting commercial relationships with different countries. The fairs also serve as a showcase to the world, showing Chilean goods and services exports, as well as a showcase for our diversity of cultural expressions, transforming them into an excellent means to promote growth and internationalisation.   Today, Chile has a presence at the following fairs and/or international festivals in the creative sector: Berlinale â"European Film Market (Germany), Marche du Film â" Cannes Film Festival (France), Guadalajara International Film Festival (Mexico), Game Developer Conference (U.S.), Big Festival (Brazil), Gamescom (Germany), Tokyo Game Show (Japan), Bologna Book Fair (Italy), International Book Fair of Bogota (Colombia), Buenos Aires Book Fair (Argentina), Frankfurt Book Fair (Germany) and Guadalajara International Book Fair (Mexico). Results: In recent years, ProChile's sectoral plans and international fairs has have incorporated more than 700 new beneficiaries from the creative sector, increasing exports and contribution to the Chilean economy in the cultural and creative sectors, strengthening the economic dimension of culture. Furthermore, inter institutional alliances have been built in order to strengthen the value chain of each sub-sector and participation models in the main cultural and creative industry markets world-wide.   Lastly, the ProChile's strategies have been incorporated into different current cultural and regional policies, namely, the National Policy on Reading and Books (2015 - 2020), the National Policy for the Audiovisual Sector (2017 - 2022), the National Music Policy (2017 - 2022), the National Visual Arts Policy (2017 - 2022), the National Performing Arts Policy (2017 - 2022) and the National Plan for the Promotion of the Creative Economy.

Agency Implementation: Planning Institute of Jamaica (PIOJ)
Main Feature: Vision 2030 Jamaica is the country’s first long-term strategic development plan and covers the 21-year period, 2009-2030.  It embodies the plans and processes for the realization of a collective vision, encapsulated in the statement: “Jamaica, the place of choice to live, work, raise families and do business.” Vision 2030 Jamaica is geared towards engaging all Jamaicans and development partners in the process to achieve and benefit from sustainable and inclusive development. The achievement of the 4 Goals and 15 National Outcomes will result in a vibrant and internationally competitive economy; a secure and cohesive society;  a healthy natural environment; a high level of human capital development; and greater opportunities for social and economic mobility and prosperity. The Creative Industries is listed as one of the National Outcomes, which is to achieve an internationally competitive structure status by 2030.
Recommandations: Vision 2030 Jamaica – National Development Plan (NDP) is built on an integrated evidence- and results-based management (IERBM) framework.  The IERBM Framework underpins an approach that integrates performance management with evidence-based management.  It promotes coherence between Monitoring and Evaluation (M&E) and other evidence-based processes in informing the implementation of Vision 2030 Jamaica.  In other words, it is geared  at continuously improving the strategies and systems applied in the coordination of Plan implementation and the strategic programming employed to advance the achievement of the national goals and outcome The approach to reporting on development performance under Vision 2030 Jamaica includes reporting on both development gains and gaps in the achievement of planned development outcomes and explanations for the performance. Gaps in development are usually demonstrated in performance that shows: no improvement, improvement that falls short of targets, and development losses. Performance measurement and reporting include focus on indicators of inclusion or “leaving no one behind” such as poverty prevalence and disaggregation to determine group-specific experiences of development and vulnerability, such as disaggregation by age, sex, and locale.  Reports on National Development Results, based on monitoring of  1.	the National Outcome Indicators, are due quarterly which is informed by annual data (calendar year).  2.	An Annual Progress Report is completed at the end of each Fiscal Year based on the data available up to March of that year.  3.	A 3-year Performance Report on the MTF is also completed which includes quasi-evaluation data and information and provides more in-depth details on implementation, programme performance and the factors that have contributed to performance regarding the national outcomes and goals.

Title EN: WEDDING MARKET (Marché Africain du Mariage et des Accessoires)
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture

Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Agency Implementation: BOJOUR EVENT
Main Feature: BOJOUR EVENT est une  structure spécialisée en décoration, organisation de cérémonies,  mariages et autres, et de formation.  Le dernier événement  organisé avait pour  thème général «MARIAGE INTER-ETHNIQUE, SOURCE DE COHESION SOCIALE». Il avait pour but non seulement d’éduquer ‘’culturellement’’ les populations mais également de promouvoir toutes les industries créatives qui gravitent autour du mariage et qui pourraient être des débouchés pour certaines jeunes femmes qui ont un talent de décoratrices, et de permettre à certaines d’entre elles d'être des  entrepreneuses ou d'avoir des emplois directs.  Le WEDDING MARKET est un véritable espace d’expression, de visibilité et de création de richesses locales et artisanales car il met un choix particulier sur toutes les créations locales afin de les valoriser.  Cet événement a pour contexte le fait que quelques soient les origines et les traditions, le mariage reste l’un des moments les plus importants de la vie d’un être humain.  Pour l’honneur et l’image des familles représentées, tous les moyens matériels et financiers sont mis en œuvre aux fins d’assurer la réussite de cet événement majeur.  Ce, en mettant un point d’honneur à la prise en charge des différents axes liés à  l’organisation pratique. Comme toutes activités nécessitant des investissements, une industrie s’est peu à peu développée autour du mariage. Ainsi, tous les contours du domaine sont à ce jour couverts par des professionnels qui, se sont adaptés aux us et coutumes des pays, des régions dont ils dépendent:  la restauration, les cérémonies traditionnelles  et occidentales, les tenues, la logistique, la salle de réception, la décoration, les conseillers… En Afrique et plus précisément en Côte d’Ivoire, cet événement revêt une dimension toute particulière. Il ne s’agit plus seulement de l’organisation d’une cérémonie visant à unir deux personnes, mais il s’agit pour les familles réunies de prouver aux amis, alliés et connaissances leur capacité de réception. Ainsi, tous rivalisent d’ingéniosité pour offrir la meilleure organisation du moment. A ce titre,  il a été convenu d’organiser une plate- forme de formation, d’instruction, de découvertes et d’affaires autour du mariage qui prendrait en compte, ici, les spécificités liées au mariage africain intercommunautaires.
Results: Après cinq années de réalisation du WEDDING MARKET, Marché Africain du Mariage et des Accessoires nous avons atteint divers résultats tant directs qu’indirects. A savoir : - la promotion des mariages traditionnels à travers la valorisation des tractations familiales qui font ressortir tout le patrimoine culturel de chaque région selon les appartenances ethniques des futurs mariés; - la vulgarisation des alliances culturelles, source de cohésion sociale; - le développement des 24 corps de métiers qui gravitent autour du mariage tradi-moderne; - la création du Réseau des Professionnels de Événementiel en Côte d’Ivoire (REPECI) qui regroupe plus d’une cinquantaine de professionnels du domaine de Evénementiel.

Title EN: White Paper on Art and Culture for, with and by Children and Youth. Report no. 18 (2020-2021) to the Storting  (Meld. St. 18 (2020-2021) Oppleve, skape, dele. Kunst og kultur for, med og av barn og unge.)
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Agency Implementation: Norwegian Ministry of Culture and Equality
Main Feature: The white paper presents a comprehensive policy focus on arts and culture for, with and by children and young people. This is the first time that the field of children’s and youth culture in Norway is presented as a unified political focus area at the national level. The report provides an overview of the responsibilities of the public sector in the field, as well as a historical review of developments in the policy area. The report also discusses children and young people’s cultural habits, including digital culture. The main political goal is to provide all children and young people, regardless of their background, with access to high-quality arts and culture.   The white paper's primary objectives are:  1.	Access to Arts and Culture for Children and young people: o	The report emphasizes the importance of ensuring that all children and young people have access to high-quality art and cultural experiences. This includes promoting cultural activities in schools, cultural schools, community centres, and other relevant spaces. o	Strategies involve collaboration between cultural institutions, schools, and local communities to create accessible and engaging cultural programs. o	The Cultural Schoolbag (Den kulturelle skolesekken) plays a central role in achieving these goals. This program offers free arts and cultural activities during school hours, aiming to avoid geographical and economic disparities. The white paper establishes new national goals for the program and confirms that the implementation of the program must occur in close collaboration and interaction with municipalities, regional authorities, the cultural sector, and the education sector.   2.	Participation and Involvement: o	The document highlights the need to actively involve children and young people in cultural policy decisions. Their perspectives and voices should shape cultural offerings and policies. o	Initiatives include youth councils, workshops, and consultations to gather input and engage young people in shaping cultural experiences.  3.	Artistic Standards: o	Maintaining high artistic standards for content created specifically for children and youth is crucial. This applies to literature, theatre, music, visual arts, and other forms of expression. o	The report encourages artists, creators, and cultural institutions to produce content that is both artistically excellent and age-appropriate
Results: The government’s focus on children’s and youth culture aims to enhance access to art and cultural programs for all young individuals, regardless of their background. By prioritizing quality and inclusivity, they intend to ensure that children and young people can actively participate in arts and cultural activities that interest them.   The government allocated 15,7 mill. NOK as a direct follow-up to the white paper in 2021, including :  -	Strenghtening The Cultural Schoolbag and encourage more new productions within this program (4 mill. NOK) -	Initiating a pilot project to integrate child and youth culture into municipal planning (4 mill. NOK) -	Support to digital initiatives within the field of child and youth culture (4 mill. NOK) -	Support to various organization for targeted child and youth initiatives  (2,7 mill. NOK) -	Initiating and supporting the work on a strategy for children and media, led by the Norwegian Media Authority (Medietilsynet) (1 mill. NOK)  Following the white paper, an external assessment of The Cultural Schoolbag and an evaluation of Kulturtanken (the national agency responsible for the program) were conducted. Based on recommendations from the evaluation, the ministry expanded Kulturtanken’s responsibilities to enhance task execution and goal achievement in the field of children’s and youth culture. Kulturtanken’s mandate was updated in 2024, designating it as the state administrative body for children’s and youth culture. Key tasks include advising the government on matters related to children’s and youth culture, facilitating collaboration, coordinating efforts with relevant stakeholders, maintaining knowledge in the field, and managing various grant programs to support specific goals or activities.

Title EN: White Paper on Museums - Report no. 23 to the Storting (2020–2021) about museums in society ‘Musea i samfunnet: Tillit, ting og tid’ [Museums in Society: Trust, Artefacts and Time] - regjeringen.no (only in Norwegian)
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Agency Implementation: Norwegian Ministry of Culture and Equality
Main Feature: The White Paper was presented to the Parliament in March, 2021. It points out the main priorities for the Government’s museum policy towards 2050 and formulates key areas for the further development of the museum sector in Norway. It underlines the role of museums as parts of the infrastructure for democracy and the freedom of expression. Museums play a key role in promoting democratic values.    Five policy objectives have been formulated to ensure delivery of this development:  •	Robust knowledge production •	Relevant dissemination •	Holistic collection development •	Preventive conservation •	Active engagement This recommendation to the Storting demonstrates broad parliamentary consensus about the general thrust of museum policies for the time ahead. Their objective is to facilitate a professionally based museum sector that is proficient, explorative and actively targeted at the community. It is also essential that museums actively seek partnerships that will support a robust economy by involving a variety of funding sources It is a fundamental principle of Norwegian cultural policy that our cultural institutions must be independent of government. Museums are professionally autonomous institutions. Museum policies should facilitate positive development within the sector rather than laying down rules that interfere with their curatorial independence and priorities.
Results: The White Paper and the related political process has stimulated public debate and give given an updated base for the annual budgetary priorities for governmental spending on museums.

Title EN: Women Empowerment Programs, Cultural Exchange Programs, Festivals and Exhibitions, Networking and Collaboration, Community Development Projects, Educational Initiatives, Research and Documentation, Workshops and Seminars, Cultural Rights Advocacy, Cultura
Goal: Promote Human Rights And Fundamental Freedoms
SDG: SDG 5 - Achieve gender equality and empower all women and girls,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels
Area of Monitoring: Gender equality
Agency Implementation: Folkland International Centre for Folklore and Culture
Main Feature: Women Empowerment Programs Folkland and Women Empowerment Programs are designed to harness the potential of women in the cultural sector. These programs provide training in traditional crafts and arts, which not only help preserve cultural practices but also offer economic opportunities. By focusing on skill development, these programs enable women to achieve financial independence and enhance their social status. Workshops and training sessions often include business skills, such as marketing and entrepreneurship, ensuring that women can successfully manage and grow their cultural enterprises. Additionally, theseprograms foster a sense of community and support networks among participants, promoting gender equality and empowerment.  Cultural Exchange Programs Folkland organizes Cultural Exchange Programs to facilitate the sharing of cultural knowledge and practices across borders. These programs enable artists and cultural professionals to travel and participate in international festivals, workshops, and residencies. Through these exchanges, participants gain exposure to diverse cultural expressions, which enhances their creativity and broadens their perspectives. These programs also promote mutual understanding and cooperation between different cultures, fostering global cultural harmony. By providing opportunities for artists to collaborate and learn from each other, Folkland helps to sustain and innovate traditional cultural practices.  Festivals and Exhibitions Festivals and Exhibitions hosted by Folkland are vibrant celebrations of cultural heritage.Festivals and exhibitions serve as platforms for artists to gain visibility and recognition, and for the public to engage with and appreciate cultural diversity. They also provide opportunities for cultural exchange and networking among artists, fostering a sense of community and collaboration. These events are meticulously organized to highlight the richness of traditional arts and crafts, promoting their preservation and appreciation.  Networking and Collaboration Folkland places a strong emphasis on Networking and Collaboration to enhance the impact of its initiatives. By partnering with local, national, and international cultural organizations, educational institutions, and government bodies, Folkland expands its reach and resources. These collaborations result in joint projects, co-hosted events, and shared expertise, which amplify the effectiveness of cultural preservation and promotion efforts. Networking also facilitates the exchange of best practices and innovative ideas, which can be implemented to improve programs and initiatives. These partnerships ensure that Folkland’s initiatives are well-supported and integrated into broader cultural and developmental strategies.  Community Development Projects Community Development Projects by Folkland integrate cultural activities into sustainable development initiatives. These projects often involve training community members in traditional crafts and arts, which helps preserve cultural heritage while creating economic opportunities. By empowering local communities with skills and resources, these projects contribute to poverty alleviation and sustainable livelihoods. Folkland’s approach ensures that cultural heritage is not only preserved but also utilized as a catalyst for economic and social development. These projects often include infrastructure development, such as establishing cultural centers and workshops, which provide spaces for community engagement and cultural activities.  Educational Initiatives Educational Initiatives at Folkland aim to instill an appreciation of cultural heritage among younger generations. By incorporating folklore and traditional arts into school curricula, Folkland ensures that students learn about their cultural roots. These initiatives include organizing cultural camps, storytelling sessions, and traditional music and dance classes. By engaging students in hands-on activities,Folkland makes learning about culture interactive and enjoyable. Educational programs also involve teacher training, ensuring that educators are well-equipped to teach cultural subjects. These initiatives foster a sense of identity and pride among students, encouraging them to value and preserve their cultural heritage.  Research and Documentation Research and Documentation are critical components of Folkland’s efforts to preserve cultural heritage.The Folkland Research Centre conducts extensive studies on traditional cultural practices, rituals, and folklore. This research involves fieldwork, interviews with cultural practitioners, and the collection of artefacts and oral histories. The documented knowledge is compiled into publications, databases, and archives, making it accessible for future generations, researchers, and the public. By systematically recording and analysing cultural practices, Folkland ensures that valuable cultural knowledge is preserved and can be used to inform cultural policies and educational programs. This research also highlights the dynamic and evolving nature of cultural traditions.  Workshops and Seminars Workshops and Seminars organized by Folkland provide platforms for knowledge sharing and capacity building. These events cover a wide range of topics, including traditional arts, cultural rights, sustainable development, and entrepreneurial skills. By bringing together experts, practitioners, and community members, these workshops facilitate the exchange of ideas and experiences. Participants gain new skills, knowledge, and perspectives, which they can apply in their cultural practices and communities. These events also serve as forums for discussing challenges and opportunities in the cultural sector, fostering collaborative solutions and innovations.  Cultural Rights Advocacy Cultural Rights Advocacy is a cornerstone of Folkland’s mission. The organization actively promotes the cultural rights of marginalized and indigenous communities, ensuring that their traditions and expressions are recognized and respected. Advocacy efforts include campaigns, policy recommendations, facing discrimination or censorship. By raising awareness about cultural rights, Folkland helps to create an environment where cultural diversity is valued and protected. These efforts are crucial in promoting freedom of expression and safeguarding the cultural heritage of vulnerable communities.  Cultural Training Programs Cultural Training Programs at Folkland focus on skill development in traditional arts and crafts. These programs are designed to preserve cultural practices while providing economic opportunities. Training sessions cover various crafts, including weaving, pottery, and folk music, and often include business skills like marketing and entrepreneurship. By equipping participants with these skills, Folkland ensures that they can sustain their cultural practices and contribute to the local economy. These programs also foster a sense of pride and identity among participants, strengthening their connection to their cultural heritage. The training programs are tailored to meet the needs of different communities, ensuring that they are relevant and effective.
Results: Folkland - International Centre for Folklore and Culture has achieved significant results through its diverse range of initiatives aimed at promoting cultural heritage and fostering community development. Women Empowerment Programs have empowered women by providing training in traditional crafts and arts, leading to increased economic independence and social empowerment. Many participants have successfully launched their own cultural enterprises, contributing to local economies and preserving cultural traditions. Cultural Exchange Programs have facilitated cross-cultural dialogue and artistic collaboration, resulting in enhanced global visibility for Indian folklore. Artists and cultural professionals have gained exposure to diverse cultural practices, enriching their creative work and broadening their perspectives. Festivals and Exhibitions organized by Folkland have not only showcased traditional arts and crafts to large audiences but also boosted tourism and local economies. These events have strengthened cultural identity and community pride while fostering appreciation for cultural diversity. Networking and Collaboration initiatives have expanded Folkland's reach and impact by partnering with local, national, and international organizations. These partnerships have facilitated joint projects and shared resources, amplifying the effectiveness of cultural preservation efforts and promoting sustainable development. Community Development Projects integrating cultural activities have created economic opportunities through skill development in traditional crafts. These projects have improved livelihoods in local communities while safeguarding cultural heritage. Educational Initiatives have successfully integrated cultural education into school curricula, fostering a deeper appreciation of folklore among younger generations. Research and Documentation efforts have significantly enriched the understanding and preservation of traditional cultural practices. The Folkland Research Centre work has resulted in comprehensive documentation of cultural heritage, providing valuable resources for researchers, educators, and policymakers. Workshops and Seminars organized by Folkland have provided platforms for knowledge exchange and capacity building in the cultural sector. Participants have gained new skills and insights into cultural rights, sustainable development, and entrepreneurial practices, enhancing their abilities to contribute meaningfully to their communities. Cultural Rights Advocacy by Folkland has raised awareness and promoted the rights of cultural practitioners, ensuring their freedom of expression and protection from discrimination. These advocacy efforts have influenced policy changes and improved legal frameworks for cultural rights protection. Cultural Training Programs have equipped participants with skills in traditional arts and crafts, enabling them to preserve and transmit cultural heritage while generating income. These programs have fostered a sense of pride and identity among participants, strengthening their connection to their cultural roots and promoting cultural diversity.

Créée en 1984, cette émission est un concours de talents destiné aux jeunes ivoiriens pendant les vacances scolaires.  L'objectif principal de "Wozo Vacances" est de promouvoir la culture ivoirienne, de découvrir et de mettre en avant les talents des jeunes dans des domaines variés tels que le chant, la danse, le théâtre, et d'autres activités artistiques et culturelles. L'émission encourage également les valeurs de solidarité, de discipline et de respect entre les participants.  L'objectif principal de "Wozo Vacances" est de promouvoir la culture ivoirienne, de découvrir et de mettre en avant les talents des jeunes dans des domaines variés tels que le chant, la danse, le théâtre, et d'autres activités artistiques et culturelles. L'émission encourage également les valeurs de solidarité, de discipline et de respect entre les participants Chaque année, de nombreux jeunes se présentent aux auditions pour tenter de participer au concours, et les meilleurs talents sont sélectionnés pour concourir dans différentes catégories. "Wozo Vacances" est très populaire et suivie par un large public en Côte d'Ivoire, contribuant à la découverte de nombreuses stars locales. WOZO Vacances est une émission culturelle de jeux et de distraction destinée aux enfants de trois (03) à quinze (15) ans, issus des différentes communes, qui vise à promouvoir la diversité culturelle en Côte d’Ivoire. Elle se déroule pendant la période des grandes vacances scolaires
Results: Depuis sa création, "Wozo Vacances" a atteint plusieurs résultats significatifs en Côte d'Ivoire : - Découverte et promotion de jeunes talents : - Émergence de stars locales : de nombreux artistes ivoiriens aujourd'hui célèbres ont été découverts grâce à l'émission. Elle a servi de tremplin pour leur carrière artistique. -Promotion de la culture ivoirienne : l'émission a largement contribué à la promotion des diverses formes d'expressions culturelles ivoiriennes, telles que la danse traditionnelle, le théâtre, et la musique. Impact éducatif et social : -Encouragement des valeurs positives : "Wozo Vacances" promeut des valeurs telles que la discipline, le respect, et la solidarité parmi les jeunes participants. -Sensibilisation et éducation : par le biais de divers segments éducatifs, l'émission sensibilise les jeunes à des enjeux sociaux importants comme la santé, l'environnement, et la citoyenneté. Renforcement de la cohésion sociale : -Promotion de la diversité culturelle : En réunissant des participants de différentes régions et groupes ethniques  de Côte d'ivoire y compris les étranger vivants sur ce territoire, l'émission contribue à renforcer l'unité nationale et la compréhension interculturelle. -Interaction positive entre les jeunes : Les compétitions et activités en groupe encouragent les interactions positives et le travail d'équipe entre les jeunes. Développement des compétences : Amélioration des compétences artistiques : Les participants bénéficient de formations et de conseils de professionnels, ce qui améliore leurs compétences artistiques. Opportunités professionnelles : Les meilleurs talents se voient offrir des opportunités pour des collaborations et des contrats professionnels dans le secteur culturel. Impact économique : - Création d'emplois : L'émission génère des emplois pour les techniciens, les producteurs, les animateurs et autres professionnels du secteur audiovisuel. - Dynamisation du secteur culturel : "Wozo Vacances" stimule l'industrie culturelle et de divertissement en Côte d'Ivoire, contribuant ainsi à son développement économique. En somme, "Wozo Vacances" a non seulement révélé de nombreux talents artistiques mais a aussi joué un rôle crucial dans la promotion de la culture ivoirienne, l'éducation des jeunes, le renforcement de la cohésion sociale et le développement économique du pays.
Recommandations: Les principales recommandations sont:  -Soutien Accru aux Initiatives Culturelles : - Il est recommandé de continuer à soutenir et à financer des initiatives similaires qui valorisent la culture et les traditions locales, afin de préserver le patrimoine culturel ivoirien. - Expansion du Programme : -Étendre le programme à d'autres régions et inclure des jeunes de divers horizons socio-économiques pour garantir une représentation plus large et équitable. 3.	Renforcement des Capacités des Participants : o	Offrir des formations supplémentaires et des ateliers pour aider les participants à développer leurs talents et compétences, ce qui pourrait avoir un impact positif sur leur future carrière professionnelle. Partenariats Stratégiques : Établir des partenariats avec des institutions éducatives, des entreprises et des organisations culturelles pour fournir un soutien supplémentaire et des opportunités de développement aux jeunes participants. Suivi et Évaluation : Mettre en place un système de suivi et d'évaluation pour mesurer l'impact du programme sur les participants et les communautés locales, et pour identifier les domaines nécessitant des améliorations. En appliquant ces recommandations, Wozo Vacances peut continuer à jouer un rôle crucial dans le développement culturel et éducatif des jeunes en Côte d'Ivoire.

Title EN: Audiovisual Media Services Directive (Directive (EU) 2018/1808 amending Directive 2010/13/EU
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Media diversity
Agency Implementation: EU Member State governments; European Commission
Main Feature: The revised AVMSD creates a regulatory framework fit for the digital age, leading to a safer, fairer and more diverse audiovisual landscape. It lays down essential rules to create a level playing field for audiovisual media services, preserve cultural diversity, protect children and consumers, combat racial and religious hatred and guarantee the independence of national media regulators.  It coordinates EU-wide legislation on all audiovisual media, including both traditional TV broadcasters and on-demand video services, and lays down essential protection measures with regard to content shared on video-sharing platforms.  The revised AVMSD strengthens also the promotion of cultural diversity, by introducing clear obligations for on-demand services to have at least a 30% share of European content in their catalogue and to ensure the prominence of this content. These rules will contribute to a broader and more diverse offer of AV content for Europeans and will have a positive impact on cultural diversity and create more opportunities for European creators and AV industry. The Commission has produced guidelines to facilitate the implementation of this obligation.  The AVMSD includes specific measures to protect minors. In order to protect them from harmful content online, the Directive requires video-sharing platforms to put in place certain measures, including establishing and operating age verification systems, with respect to content which may impair the physical, mental or moral development of minors. The Directive also includes measures to reduce the exposure of children to certain advertising.  The revised AVMSD has set out specific measures to help improve citizensâ€™ media literacy skills. The Directive provides that Member States should promote and take measures for the development of media literacy skills and report on such measures to the Commission. The Commission has adopted (in February 2023) guidelines for Member States to report on,and share best practices regarding media literacy. Furthermore, the Directive provides that video-sharing platforms should put in place effective media literacy measures and tools and raise users' awareness of those measures and tools. These initiatives will be particularly beneficial for younger users.
Results: The Commission has issued a report on the application of the AVMSD in January 2024, covering  the period between 2019 and 2022.   The report focuses on the main changes brought by the revised Directive and looks at a wide range of important areas of the AVSMD, in particular: the scope of application, the country-of-origin principle and the cooperation between national regulators and the European Regulators Group for Audiovisual Media Services (ERGA), the protection of minors, the accessibility of audiovisual media services to persons with visual or hearing disabilities, the rules on prominence of audiovisual media services of general interest, the rules on signal integrity, the audiovisual commercial communications, the co-/self-regulatory initiatives, the rules on video-sharing platforms and the independence of media regulators.  The report confirms that the AVMSD remains an essential instrument to govern the Union-wide coordination of national legislation for all audiovisual media. Its revision has proved useful for addressing developments in the audiovisual market, such as the growing importance of digital services..
Recommandations: The Commission is currently assessing whether the Member States' national transposing measures are in line with the AVMSD provisions.

Main Feature: In 2020, the Government, in its fourth supplementary budget for the year, proposed a 5 million EUR (ca. 5 435 000 USD allocation to support the media in financial difficulties due to the covid-19 pandemic and its effects on the media and journalistic fields. An additional 2.5 million EUR (ca. 2 717 000 USD) was allocated for the same purpose in the Governments seventh supplementary budget for the same year. The purpose of the grant is to support the content production media that has been affected by the COVID 19 epidemic. The aim is to increase versatile journalistic content and its supply as well as to promote and develop journalism at local, regional and national levels. A total of 7.5 million EUR (ca. 8 153 000 USD) was granted to 97 businesses and 237 media outlets.  In 2023 the Government issued a decree on discretionary government grants for supporting communications and news media in the same year. The government grant is used to support media sector operators that have suffered from major changes in the operating environment. The grant may be awarded for the payroll costs of persons engaged in journalistic work and for freelancers’ fees.  Media subsidies granted on a one-off basis last year and targeted at journalistic work and the recruitment of journalists can be considered a more effective means. A total of EUR 7 million (ca. 7 610 000 USD) was distributed among 69 applicants and 188 media outlets engaged in news broadcasting so that one group could not receive more than EUR 200,000 and enterprises employing at most four persons received a grant 1.3-fold. In this way, the support specifically favoured small media at the expense of the big ones.  The grant can be admitted to national, regional or local news-producing papers, online publications, radio and telvision channels. The news media has to cover a wide array of different topics and serve a wider public. Publications targeted to specific professions, hobbies or political parties are exluded.
Results: The government granted a total of circa 8 153 000 USD as support to media and journalism outlets to tackle the effects of the covid-19 pandemic in the field. The grants are awarded by the Government Grants and Guaranteed Income for Artists Committee, which has five members appointed by the Norwegian Ministry of Culture for a period of four years at a time. The grant committees perform a professional assessment of the applications and submit recommendations for a decision by the Government Grants and Guaranteed Income for Artists Committee. The only factors accorded weight in the award of grants are artistic quality and activity. A separate guide has been drawn up for the grant committees’ work. In part, this is intended to ensure that the committees comply with the Public Administration Act’s provisions concerning impartiality, confidentiality and duty to offer guidance. All told, the grant committees have approximately 195 members. The Government Grants for Artists scheme normally has six different grants that are awarded annually. These are: – Work grant: 1-5 years – Work grant for younger and newly established artists: 1–3 years  - Grant for established artists: 10 years (or until the recipient reaches 67 years)  - Grant for senior artists: 10 years (or until the recipient reaches 67 years)  – Miscellaneous grant and Miscellaneous grant for recently graduated artists: One-time payment of a maximum of   NOK 100,000 for artistic activity.  The work grants are NOK 318 352 per year disbursed in monthly payments.  In 2020, as a result of the pandemic, 679 extraordinary grants were awarded. In 2021, a further 100 temporary one-year grants were awarded. The purpose of this initiative was to maintain the continuity of artistic production, safeguard employment and help boost demand for art during the Covid-19 pandemic.  In the past two years, the Government Grants for Artists’ various schemes have been significantly reinforced. In 2022, 120 permanent new work grants were established. In 2023, this was expanded with the addition of a further 44 new grants. In 2023, a total of 402 artists were awarded one-year or multi-year work grants.
Results: Norway has a strong financial commitment to the support of practising artists. The grants help further develop established artists and support new artistic endeavours. The various grant schemes are therefore designed to help develop artists at various stages in their careers. This includes grants for newly qualified artists as well as seniors.  In 2024, 693 work grants and 497 grants for established artists, senior artists and guaranteed incomes are available, a total of 1,190 work grants. In 2023, 59 per cent of the grants were awarded to women, while 41 per cent were awarded to men.

Agency Implementation: Ministry of Culture and Communications (MCC) Cultural Business Development Corporation (SODEC)
Main Feature: The Fund for Young Francophone Creation (“Fund”) Created in 2017, the Fund is an initiative of several French-speaking partners who are members of the Organisation internationale of la Francophonie (OIF), notably from France, Wallonia-Brussels, Quebec, Belgium, and Canada.   It aims to support, mainly via a residency, the emergence of new authors, directors and producers from French-speaking sub-Saharan Africa, the Indian Ocean and Haiti and to support them in their projects, whether at the stages of development, production or post-production.   The countries targeted by this fund are: Benin, Burkina Faso, Burundi, Cameroon, Congo Brazzaville, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Ivory Coast, Djibouti, Gabon, Guinea, Comoros Islands and Mauritius, Madagascar, Mali, Niger, Central African Republic, Rwanda, Senegal, Seychelles, Chad, Togo and Haiti.   The objectives of the Fund for Young Francophone Creation are also to develop innovative strategies and new mechanisms in the countries concerned; to support authors and producers in their international efforts and familiarize them with the different contracts; to support the progress of projects at all stages of the production chain; and to promote the development of an international network of young filmmakers, producers and their teams, in particular through the monitoring of projects supported by the Fund, through the organization of events or meetings within festivals, the implementation network of film teams, and more.  Quebec's participation  Since 2018, the Society for the Development of Cultural Enterprises of Quebec (SODEC) and the Ministry of Culture and Communications of Quebec (MCC), in collaboration with other partners, have ensured full coverage of transport costs, accommodation, catering and personalized support linked to the residency offered at the National Institute of Image and Sound (L’Inis). From 2018 to 2023, 13 participants were welcomed to L'inis thanks to this support.  L’Inis is a professional training center in cinema, television and interactive media based in Montreal (Canada). The L'inis residency is open to authors, as well as screenwriters of feature-length fiction and documentaries. It offers a complete training program around the development of their project. The screenwriters benefit from four weeks of personalized support, development workshops and meetings with Quebec professionals (producers, screenwriters, directors). The screenwriters will also have the opportunity to be accredited to a Montreal film festival - if the dates match those of the residency (e.g. Montreal International Documentary Meetings, New Cinema Festival, Les Rendez-vous Québec Cinéma, etc.)  The Fund constitutes a direct response to Quebec's commitments regarding preferential treatment with developing countries (article 16 of the 2005 Convention).
Results: Over the course of the different editions of the Fund, much positive feedback was received from authors, directors, producers and institutional representatives from several French-speaking countries. This demonstrates the importance of the Fund for the promotion and development of an international network of young filmmakers, producers, and their teams. Also, this feedback is significant and reflects the fact that the profile and promotion of Quebec expertise in film and audiovisual production, at all stages of the process of creating a work, is fundamental.
Financial Ressources: The MCC paid an amount of CAD 20,000 (approximately USD 14,630) annually for the financial years 2019-2020 to 2023-2024.

Main Feature: We are a network platform for music, carried out jointly in various cities and countries in Latin America, Europe and Africa. It takes place in the period close to the celebrations related to Carnival, the birthplace of Brazil, and is presented as an option to complement the traditional celebrations of these dates. Produced collaboratively since 2007, the Grito Rock Festival was created as an alternative to the Carnival of Cuiabá, capital of Mato Grosso (central-western Brazil). Its open and participatory format has allowed edition after edition, more and more producers to share their experiences and strengthen the local musical production network, reaching more than 300 cities around the world in its latest edition. This year cities such as Potosí, Sucre and Tarija, Santa Cruz, Pando joined in the organization of the festival with Cochabamba and La Paz, which, like the year before last, held this event. Pioneering in its integrated, collaborative and decentralized logic, the festival has an unprecedented track record of expansion. It promotes its sustainability through collaborative economies and the hacking of systems integrated into state and private structures. El Grito has been characterized since its beginnings by being a festival connected to its time and the changes of the planet, articulating campaigns and joint actions for transformations and new activist expressions. We promote and strengthen logics and practices based on Barter and Ayni (reciprocity), as collective, collaborative and community dynamics.

Title EN: Icelandic Literature Center
Goal: Achieve A Balanced Flow Of Cultural Goods And Services And Increase The Mobility Of Artists And Cultural Professionals

Area of Monitoring: Mobility of artists and cultural professionals
Agency Implementation: Icelandic Literature Center
Main Feature: The Icelandic Literature Center is a public body. The role of the Center is to raise awareness of Icelandic literary culture, both in Iceland and abroad, as well as promoting its distribution through translation and travel grants. The objective is to ensure a wide range of high-quality publishing in Iceland, the international advancement of Icelandic literature, and the translation of literature from foreign languages into Icelandic. Grant allocations are made annually to domestic publishing of Icelandic literature and translation subsidies for Icelandic literature abroad. The Center cooperates with many local entities in particular campaigns to raise awareness of Icelandic literature domestically. The promotional work that the Icelandic Literature Center engages in abroad mainly involves participation in literary exhibitions. Among other things, the Center promotes various Icelandic literary works, awards received by Icelandic authors, as well as consulting with foreign publishers and translators. Authors, publishers and organizers of literary events can apply for support in the promotion of literary works written by Icelanders. The Center also supports the publication of Icelandic works of literature and the publication of literary works translated into Icelandic,as well as the advancement of literary culture in Iceland. The Center always strives to allocate support to diverse activities in the literary field on both national and international levels. The Center allocates grants each year to publishers and authors in Iceland and abroad: publication grants, grants for books for children and young readers, translation grants, innovation grants, travel grants for authors, residential grants for translators, sample translation grants and reader's report grants. The Center supports and promotes Icelandic literature internationally and assists Icelandic authors and publishers in various ways with promotional activities abroad. The Center annually publishes a brochure of books published in Iceland over the course of the previous year, deemed promising for publication abroad. The Center assists Icelandic publishers in strengthening their bonds with colleagues abroad through publisher exchanges between Iceland and other countries. In order to ensure professionalism in the allocation of grants, the Center commissions external literary advisers, appointed for one year at a time, to make proposals for allocations of grants. The board also monitor grants, as well as holding ultimate responsibility for compliance with the law. Gender equality is pursued in all the work the Center engages in, such as allocations of grants, authors' participation in events and selection of literary advisers. The Center engages in targeted measures to encourage reading, in collaboration with a broad-based group in the literary field, with the objective of increasing interest in reading and deepening the relationship between authors and readers. One aspect of this is visits by authors to upper secondary schools, which commence in 2020 in collaboration with educational authorities and other partners. The Center also conducts annual reading surveys in Iceland, in collaboration with professional organizations and bodies within the literary sector. The Center takes the initiative in active collaboration with as many professional and stakeholder organizations as possible in the fields relating to its activities, including authors, publishers, translators, universities, libraries, literary festivals, institutes, Icelandic embassies and the Reykjavík Literary Festival, Reykjavík UNESCO City of Literature, the Árni Magnússon Institute for Icelandic Studies, Icelandic embassies abroad and Promote Iceland. A Translators' Seminar is held in alternate years for translators of Icelandic literature into foreign languages, in collaboration with leading bodies in the literary field. A literary award to translators of Icelandic literature, Orðstír, is presented at the Seminar. Work is to continue on the development, promotion and use of the Translators page on the Center's website.
Results: The Icelandic Literature Center’s continuous work in promoting Icelandic literature has been of great assistance in terms of general awareness raising of Icelandic authors and literature, both nationally and internationally. The International Translators’ Seminar in Reykjavík and Orðstír award, briefly mentioned previously, is an example of a project established and conducted by the Center that supports diversity within the Icelandic literary field and promotes Icelandic literary works to a broader audience. The Icelandic Literature Center equally promotes Icelandic literature nationally. The Center has engaged in some projects in this endeavor, such the launching of a reading website in association with Reykjavik UNESCO City of Literature.
Financial Ressources: In 2024 598.585 USD was allocated to the Icelandic Literature Center (82.700.000 ISK)

Title EN: Green Film
Goal: Integrate Culture In Sustainable Development Frameworks
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: National sustainable development policies and plans
Agency Implementation: Trentino Sviluppo Spa
Main Feature: Green Film is a label that certifies environmental sustainability for audiovisual productions conferred for projects conducted in an environmentally respectful manner.         MANDATORY PREREQUISITES         Planning sustainability         Plan beforehand in order to reduce environmental impact to a minimum and to optimise transportation and therefore reduce its environmental and economic impact.         CRITERION A:         Energy saving.         Ensure an efficient reduction of environmental impact, limiting as much as possible polluting emissions and wastage of energy resources, rationalise use of resources favouring economic savings.         CRITERION B         Transport and accommodation         Reduce polluting emissions and fuel consumption costs deriving from motorised transport, through a rational organisation of movements.         CRITERION C         Catering         Guarantee healthy and good quality nutrition, that respects the environment by reducing the production of waste and CO2 from catering operations.         CRITERION D         Material selection         Encourage use of materials that respect the environment and avoid wasting materials by efficient reuse solutions.         CRITERION E         Waste management         Correct management and recycling of waste thereby reducing the production’s impact on the environment.                  CRITERION F         Communication         Communication of good practices linked to sustainability, development public’s awareness regarding sustainability.
Results: Hundreds of films have been certified over the years.          A research project (Green Film Research Lab) coordinated by the Trentino Film Commission in collaboration with APPA - Provincial Agency for the Protection of the Environment of the Autonomous Province of Trento and with the support of the Ministry of Cultural Heritage and Activities was undertaken, which consisted of several phases:         1. Scientific study                   The research, carried out in collaboration with APPA Trento, and with the critical review of ARPAE Emilia-Romagna to ensure the validity of the scientific approach used, is intended to serve as a starting point for companies and entities in the film industry supply chain that are now called upon to make their contribution to support the fight against climate change.                   The study was designed with the objective of quantifying the environmental benefits in terms of reducing climate-altering emissions associated with the application of each criterion of the Green Film specification and the additional economic commitment required to meet them, through a comparative analysis of certified productions versus “business as usual” productions, carried out by means of the Life Cycle Assessment.                  The key aspects that emerged from the study are two:                   - the confirmation that the application of the criteria of the Green Film specification makes it possible to reduce environmental impacts in terms of climate-changing emissions;                   - the fact that the application of the specification most often also results in economic savings.          2. Dissemination of results to stakeholders                   The event “Green Filming: towards a common approach” held on February 19, 2023 at the European Film Market in Berlin garnered a great deal of interest: over 120 people attended the presentation.         The meeting was opened by Charlotte Appelgren of CineRegio, who has been involved in coordinating the association's Green subgroup for 10 years, and Luca Ferrario, founder of Green Film, to talk about the goals and evolution of the project.         3. Producer Involvement.         To collect and analyze producers' expectations and needs related to environmental sustainability and, in parallel, the real or perceived factors that currently hinder the adoption of sustainable practices, we developed a quick and easy questionnaire.         4. Revision of the specification and new declinations                  Documentaries have different production methods than feature films or TV series and a reduced impact on the environment.         For this reason, the need was felt to study special measures and thus provide producers with tools that can finally be right for their needs.         Thanks to the collaboration with Doc/it, Associazione Documentaristi Italiani, and APPA, a specification dedicated to the production of documentaries has been developed that, in addition to helping in the management of sustainability on the set, proves to be a functional tool for the certification of documentary productions and co-productions.

Title EN: Holding of the 3rd Edition of the Brazilian Creative Industries Market – MICBR 2023
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture

Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: Secretariat of Creative Economy and Cultural Promotion of the Ministry of Culture
Main Feature: Between the 8th and 12th of November 2023, the Ministry of Culture, in partnership with the Organization of Ibero-American States for Education, Science and Culture (OEI), held the 3rd edition of the Brazilian Creative Industries Market - MICBR 2023, at the Hangar Centro de Convenções e Feiras da Amazônia, in Belém-PA, which had a general audience of 8 thousand visitors over the four days of the event. The market program included business rounds, showcases , mentoring, workshops, market panels, keynote conferences and various cultural activities. All programming was free and open to the interested public. In the 2023 edition, MICBR expanded the creative sectors of its programming from 9 to 15: Crafts, Visual Arts, Audiovisual & Animation, Design, Editorial, Gastronomy, Electronic Games, Music, Fashion and Museums & Heritage, in addition to Technical and Hip Hop, debut sectors. Theatre, Dance and Circus were included in the MICBR as separate independent creative sectors (until then, the MinC worked with the performing arts as an integrated sector) and complete the list of sectors covered. To guarantee the selection of professionals for the business rounds and other activities of MICBR 2023, a Public Call Notice was launched on July 17th, which selected 261 Brazilian entrepreneurs, including buyers and sellers, from the five regions of the country, of which 259 participated. To pay support to those selected, the Ministry of Culture allocated resources in the order of US$225,605.2706 ( R$1,118,054.60) to the notice. Additionally, registrations were opened for participants interested in participating in business rounds without financial support from MinC, totaling 40 registrants. Finally, a delegation made up of 60 Argentine entrepreneurs and a Chilean delegation with 7 members also participated in the rounds. In total, 17 countries, in addition to Brazil, were represented in the business rounds, namely: South Africa, Germany, Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Congo, Ecuador, Spain, USA, France, England, Mexico, Mozambique, Norway, Poland, Portugal and Uruguay.  During the event, more than 2,500 business rounds were held with the 424 participating companies, including invited buyers and representatives of prominent national and foreign companies in their sectors. The business rounds are the heart of the event, with the main objective of creating networking and collaboration opportunities to drive business growth. In addition, 24 showcases (short artistic presentations for commercial purposes) were held from six creative sectors, with groups from all Brazilian regions. In partnership with Sebrae, six kitchen shows were also held, with the participation of a Colombian Chef. The MICBR program consisted of 94 free training activities, such as mentoring, workshops, market panels and major conferences. The event also featured important activities parallel to its programming, made possible by the Ministry of Culture and the OEI, such as the Workshop of the National Creative Economy Program, the Extraordinary Meeting of the Forum of State Secretaries of Culture and the State Final of the MCs Duel National. It should be noted that holding major events in the North aims, in addition to the commercial potential of the region, to give greater projection to the cultural diversity of the Amazonian people and the entire country, while encouraging regional deconcentration in the holding of these major events in Brazil.
Results: » 2,508 business rounds were held between entrepreneurs selected via notice, commercial delegations from Argentina and Chile, spontaneously registered entrepreneurs and national and international buyers; » General audience of 8 thousand people in the activities carried out over the four days of the event; » 424 participating companies, 259 of which were selected through a public notice, 58 national and specialized buyers, 60 from the Argentine delegation, 7 from the Chilean delegation and 40 entrepreneurs registered spontaneously; » 94 free training activities, such as mentoring, workshops, market panels and keynote conferences; » 3 Keynote Lectures: Diversity and Inclusion in the Brazilian Creative Economy – Challenges and Advances; Amazons , Technology and Youth: the Future we want; Voice of Change: Partially Brazilian Music x Brazilian Popular Music; » 14 artistic presentations in the opening and closing shows of the event, which featured the participation of individual artists and bands, national and international, connecting exponents from different origins and regions and promoting diversity and inclusion through music, with emphasis on Amazonian representatives; » 24 showcases from the fashion, circus, hip hop, music, theater and dance sectors and 6 Kitchen-Show exhibitions; » US$ 14,124,863.796 (R$ 70 million) expected to close closed deals after the event (based on data collected in the Public Notice's accountability form).
Financial Ressources: US$2,340,691.7148 (R$11.6 million), of which US$909,469.84 (R$4,449,308.35) invested by the Ministry of Culture

Title EN: GT Funarte Accessibility
Goal: Integrate Culture In Sustainable Development Frameworks
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: National sustainable development policies and plans
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: National Arts Foundation
Main Feature: The National Arts Foundation – Funarte, an entity linked to the Ministry of Culture, created, through an ordinance published in the Official Gazette of the Union, a Working Group whose main objective is to debate and ensure access and accessibility for people with disabilities in activities and artistic institutions. The Group has an equal composition between members of Civil Society and Public Power, related to the articulation and implementation of the National Arts Policy through Funarte and the Ministry of Culture. Collectively constituted, based on provocations from cultural agents with disabilities from the arts production network (artists, technicians, producers, researchers, among others), the Working Group will discuss, plan, propose, articulate, monitor, enhance and promote accessibility . It is made up of 20 agents from different segments of the arts production network, from the five regions of Brazil, 85% of whom have some disability, who are divided between ten Holders and ten Substitutes, and who are integrated with 20 other agents of Power Public, also between Members and Substitutes, being: 12 representatives of the transversal boards and artistic languages of Funarte and 8 representatives of the Audiovisual Secretariats; Book and Reading Training; and the Citizenship and Cultural Diversity Department of the Ministry of Culture, as well as the Social Participation and Diversity Advisory Department of the Minister's Office. One of the Working Group's strategies for promoting access and accessibility is the reservation of vacancies and/or resources in development mechanisms and other selection processes. The notices released by Funarte's new management have already included reservation of vacancies and/or resources for arts and culture agents with disabilities. In addition to proposing, monitoring and implementing access and accessibility policies in art promotion notices, the Working Group's duties are to map the different agents with disabilities in the arts production network and their demands for public cultural policies; claim financial and budgetary resources and monitor the implementation of public policies on cultural accessibility with Funarte and other transversal bodies.
Results: The Working Group is still working on mapping artists with disabilities throughout Brazil, with the expectation of giving visibility to the work of several artists with disabilities who make up the cultural scene, which will also benefit the development of specific public policies for the segment. According to the Labor Inspection Portal, an initiative by the Ministry of Labor that monitors the right to work of minority groups , 2,166 people with disabilities occupied formal jobs related to culture in 2021. This is only 65% of the vacancies legally provided for this group. The basic legislation is the Law of Quotas for People with Disabilities (8,213/91), which determines that companies with 100 employees or more reserve 5% of vacancies for People with Disabilities. This may be one of the explanations for the low number of positions in the cultural area, which has a sector made up of small and medium-sized companies, but with almost no reserved vacancies. To date, one of the few mappings with this content carried out in the country is the Art and Access Platform, from Fundação Itaú Cultural, which presents the work of around 250 artists. This work found that, in the first quarter of 2023, there were five million cultural workers in formal jobs, more than half of them – 3 million people – in informal jobs.
Financial Ressources: Not applicable.

Main Feature: The IDAVA Foundation's mission is to make full access and involvement in art, culture and the sciences possible for people with disabilities. In turn, it seeks to ensure involvement of people with disabilities as artists and creators, with the corresponding reasonable adjustments, so that they can perform under the same conditions and to ensure sensory accesibility at performances so that they can access information on the works.   Within its actions, it stands out as a pioneering organisation in the implementation of Braille music in Chile. This tool enables people with visual impairment to access written music. In terms of training, the IDAVA foundation, provides specialised support in music theory for students with visual impairment, Braille music courses for students and music teachers, musical instrument workshops, singing, music theory and stage presence for people with visual impairment.   This organisation relates to the indicator on "policies and measures that promote and protect social and economic rights of artists" within the monitoring framework of the 2005 Convention.
Results: The IDAVA Foundation has succeded in having an impact on the applications for competitive funding from the Ministry of Cultures, Arts and Heritage (MINCAP), as a question in the application form was added regarding the presence of people with disabilities in the project teams.   This is a specific action that has an impact on cultural policies in Chile, favouring diversity and access to artistic expression. Furthermore, the IDAVA foundation has been able to reach 500 people with disabilities as an audience of our activities that feature sensory accesibility and 50 artists with disabilities throughout the national territory.

Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
