Cultural Domain: Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: Federation of Icelandic Artists
Main Feature: The Federation of Icelandic Artists (BÍL) has not had a formal involvement in this agreement, which the Icelandic National Commission for UNESCO is in charge of in Iceland, and therefore, the agreement has not been a guiding light in the Icelandic government’s dealings with BÍL as the general organisation of artists in Iceland. Nevertheless, BÍL and the Ministry of Cultural Affairs have a current agreement on collaboration in culture, art and consultancy regarding the working environment of artists. On the basis of this agreement, the UNESCO office turns to BÍL, as a representative of non-governmental organisations, to provide their views on the status of the art forms. Although BÍL is not a direct party to this convention of the Icelandic National Commission for UNESCO, their partnership agreement with the Ministry of Cultural Affairs is based on the same principles as UNESCO’s approach. This agreement is meant to ensure that communication channels between working artists and the government are kept short and effective. The agreement springs from over 30 years of collaboration between BÍL and the ministry and was last renewed at the start of 2022. The public policy in culture in Iceland was set and agreed in Parliament in 2013 and is still valid. Most public decisions regarding culture are based on this document, which is, content wise, not very different from The UN Convention on the Protection of the Diversity of Cultural Expressions. The spirit of the 2013 public policy largely echoes UNESCO’s focus. The follow-up of public cultural policy is most demonstrable in the government’s budget proposals each year, and every year BÍL issues a public statement on cultural funding and appears before the budget committee to air artists’ views on the emphasis apparent in appropriation towards the field. In the last two years, there have also been public policies set in single art forms and fields regarding culture and art, such as a children’s culture operation plan, agreed in Parliament in 2023, but the plan was created in collaboration between the government, an artist representative and advocates of children’s culture. The visual arts policy, https://www.stjornarradid.is/library/04-Raduneytin/Menningar--og-vidskiptaraduneytid/Myndlistarstefna%20til% 202030.pdf, the music policy, https://www.althingi.is/altext/153/s/1060.html and a revamped design policy were agreed in Parliament in 2023. Each of this policies is created in collaboration between ministry officials and respective artists’ organisations. Work is ongoing on similar policies for performing arts and literature. It is important to emphasise that all these policies have been agreed and certified in Parliament, so it is the government’s responsibility that they be carried out. The joint emphasis of these policies is to strenghten the arts as a line of work and open up possibly larger markets or basis of operations with increased international focus. Diversity is not heavily highlighted, but there is increased focus on education and on supporting the art funds. Sustainability is a key term in everything, mostly regarding the environmental consequences, rather than the social aspect of the sustainability concept.
Results: The most important feature that has been achieved through the enactment of the 2013 culture policy is the institutions’ growing understanding of numerical information. Statistics Iceland has systematically gathered more information and the statistics of culture and art are gradually taking shape. Concurrently, a research centre of the creative arts has been established, initiated by people from the culture sector with the participation of universities, but financed by the Ministry of Cultural Affairs. The situation created during COVID hastened the gathering of this data in a more effective manner than before. Institutions like Statistics Iceland and the universities bear the brunt of this work, with the participation of artists and organisations in the creative sector. Concurrently to the strategic planning of single art forms, those same art forms have reorganised their centres and funding systems. The art centres are private foundations, run by artists’ professional associations. The reorganisation has been carried out in collaboration with the government, as the government donates most of the centres’ working capital. These art centres are then in charge of their respective funds. This creates an arms’ length distance between political influence and the direct distribution of grants to artists and culture companies. This is meant to improve the operating conditions of individuals and smaller companies within the arts sector. From the authorities, there is no call for increased diversity, nor in their partnership agreements with the art centres, but most of them have established procedural rules regarding diversity and inclusion in their operations and allocations. Another measurable result is that, at the time when this is written, there is a bill in Parliament regarding the furtherance of the artists’ stipend. In Iceland, the artists’ stipend is in a fund that artists can apply to once a year. The allocation is based on peer assessment. This is emphasised in the 2013 culture policy and it has been one of the key factors in BÍL’s culture politics to strengthen this route, in order to create at least a temporary financial certainty for artists so they can carry out their creative work.

The use of the code ensures interoperability and compatibility between the usage reports processed by different platforms, allowing them to align their catalogues with data from external sources such as descriptive metadata provided by third parties. Among its goals is connecting the São Tomé and Príncipe community with artists, designers, and curators from across the African continent. It aims to expand the diversity of perceptions surrounding Africa, drawing inspiration from history and global issues, and focusing on creating alternative and positive future narratives.  The Biennial highlights the power of African arts and culture and how African artists and designers contribute to the future of society. It serves as a platform where art and inspiring dialogues foster a more connected humanity, bridging the gap between the North and South of the world and the rest of the African continent. This enables sharing, collaboration, inspiration, and mutual learning. It provides a democratic space for Africa's creative spirits, dedicated to understanding and valuing contemporary African art and culture.  In 2022, the General Directorate for the Arts (DGARTES) supported the São Tomé and Príncipe Biennial of Art and Culture for the first time. This edition emphasized performing arts and prioritized the participation of artists from Portuguese-speaking countries. The program featured a diverse range of artists known for their strong connection to Portugal and their cultural and artistic expression in the Portuguese language. They are highly regarded by their peers, the public, and Portuguese institutions for their artistic and cultural production in Portugal and Portuguese-speaking countries.
Results: The Biennial aims to assert the archipelago of São Tomé and Príncipe in the international cultural community, with a particular emphasis on collaboration with Portuguese-speaking countries. It has a significant impact and projection internationally, enhancing its presence in the professional landscape of contemporary art.  In 2022, under the theme "Discovering Ourselves and the Peoples of the Portuguese-Speaking World," special attention was given to performing arts and priority was given to the participation of artists from Portuguese-speaking countries (Angola, Mozambique, Cape Verde, Guinea-Bissau, Portugal, Brazil). Title EN: Community Culture Programme
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Agency Implementation: Directorate General for Cultural Liaison / Dirección General de Vinculación Cultural. Ministry of Culture.
Main Feature: The ‘Community Culture Program,’ implemented by the Ministry of Culture through the General Directorate of Cultural Liaison, was launched in 2019. Its primary objective is to promote the effective exercise of cultural rights for individuals, groups, and communities facing social vulnerability, including migrant populations. The program achieves this through strategic initiatives that foster culture for peace, social transformation, participation in cultural life, community cultural development, and local capacity-building. The program has nationwide coverage with localized implementation in coordination with local governments. It prioritizes specific populations in municipalities marked by vulnerability due to inequality or violence, where cultural participation has historically been limited. By doing so, the program aims to enhance social cohesion.  Underpinning the program are principles of interculturality, inclusion, participation, and non-discrimination. It primarily serves individuals who encounter challenges in exercising their cultural rights within their communities—whether due to inequality, discrimination, or violence. Through artistic and cultural training experiences, participants can reshape their life narratives and contribute to new cultural dialogues.  The program operates through three cyclically recurring methodological moments: ‘Collect Ideas,’ ‘Sembrar Processes,’ and ‘Harvesting Alternatives.’ Active community participation is fundamental to its success.  Among the program’s activities, the ‘Creative Seedbeds’ and ‘Permanent Cultural Days’ stand out. The Creative Seed Workshops provide community-focused artistic training for vulnerable children and youth. These seedbeds cover various artistic languages, including performing arts (dance, community theater, social circus), visual arts (engraving, plastic arts, illustration, painting, and photography), creative writing, musical training (community orchestras, traditional ensembles, instrumental bands, traditional and symphonic bands, and mobile choirs), and audiovisual production (radio and cinematography). Additionally, they embrace cultural expressions rooted in tradition, such as textiles, lutherie, embroidery, pottery, and traditional toys, as well as artistic creations based on indigenous languages.  The ‘Cultural Days’ represent another ongoing initiative. These events reclaim public spaces for cultural purposes by featuring community-oriented cultural billboards. They cater to audiences of all ages, particularly in municipalities where violence has previously restricted the use of these spaces
Results: During the reporting period, the Community Culture Programme conducted over 23,000 community-oriented activities to promote cultural rights. These activities engaged more than two million people across 701 municipalities nationwide, representing 28.4% of the country’s total municipalities.  These initiatives were specifically targeted at municipalities where the local population faced challenges in fully exercising their cultural rights due to marginalization or violence.  The Community Culture Program also bolstered local cultural capacities by collaborating with cultural agents in the region. This approach allowed for work within local social contexts and emphasized cultural expressions that define the identity of the communities where cultural actions were implemented.  To date, 693 cultural events have taken place, most of which are permanent, featuring over 7,900 sessions and involving more than 695,000 participants.  Additionally, the Creative Seedbeds played a crucial role in promoting cultural rights for girls, boys, and young people. By the end of 2023, 443 Creative Seedbeds operated continuously across all 32 entities of the country, spanning 302 municipalities and engaging over 15,000 young individuals.
Recommandations: The Design Evaluation of the Community Culture Program with Field Work 2019-2020, coordinated by the National Council for Evaluation of Social Development Policy (CONEVAL) was positive in considering that Community Culture strengthened local culture, social interaction and, possibly , helped restore the social fabric of some communities afflicted by violence and lack of economic opportunities.  The evaluation suggestions focused on the need to improve the inter-institutional coordination process with local cultural agencies and to improve internal coordination to develop a process of planning and execution of activities that facilitates their implementation and the comprehensive use of human resources. , financial and information generated by the program.

Title EN: Community engagement within Performing Gender – Dance in Your Shoes

Main Feature: Performing Gender – Dancing in your shoes was a three-year audience development project designed to establish a firm bond between cultural professionals, artists and their local communities in the field of dance and performing arts through exploration of gender and sexuality. The challenge consisted of bringing marginalised voices to the foreground and sharing new stories on gender, with relevance to new dance audiences.  The communities were the core of a co-design process, bringing together 16 dancemakers, 9 artistic directors, 8 audience developers, 11 project managers, 3 academic researchers and 1 artistic advisor and local communities in 9 cities accros Europe.  They engaged in a series of activities, such as training, workshops and co-creation. Link to the website of the project In addition to these activities, the conducted research contributed to the experimentation, sedimentation and dissemination of new practices, methodologies and tools of audience engagement. It was focused on three main levels of analysis: 	cultural organizations and their capacity building process in relation to the role of audience developer;  	practices of audience engagement, co-design and co-creation processes, and how they challenge hierarchies, dominant narratives, power relations; and  	value of the cultural experience of communities engaged in the artistic process.   Nobody Whistles Anymore is a performance created as part of the international project Performing Gender. The intergenerational community that has trained and formed itself over a three-year creative period, has completed its final phase with theatre director Brina Klampfer Merčnik and choreographer Vita Osojnik. The central theme of all participating countries was the question of how to perform gender. A group from Slovenia, with participants aged 27 to 74, explored the theme of performing gender in different ways: in the form of workshops, conversations, homework tasks, improvisations and through dance. They explored the common movement of an intergenerational group and tried to focus on what intrigues us all, regardless of gender and age. The result is an author-based performance, a collage of scenes and of our reflections on the given theme. This performance has already been on tour in Sweden (Umea), England (Leeds). They have also run a workshop in the Netherlands (Hertogensbosch).
Results: •	Engaged community and audience development; •	Intergenerational exchange; •	Active participation in professional artistic production; •	Development of new production models in contemporary arts; •	Raised awareness about gender equality and gender related stereotypes within the targeted community; •	Improved social inclusion of elderly; •	Positive impact on mental well-being and health participants of extended dance engagement od targeted community;

Title EN: Conduct Researchs and Dissemination
Goal: Promote Human Rights And Fundamental Freedoms
SDG: SDG 5 - Achieve gender equality and empower all women and girls,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels
Area of Monitoring: Artistic freedom
Agency Implementation: Selam Ethiopia
Main Feature: Research: Selam Ethiopia through its project called Culture Leads the Way, has planned and carried out various activities aimed at creating platforms and channels for the distribution of music, research findings, and culture. Culture fora has been established to provide spaces for cultural expression, and Selam has undertaken four research projects to assess the potential and challenges of the sector. The research projects aimed to evaluate artistic freedom in Ethiopia, the role of arts and culture in peacebuilding in Ethiopia, the role of art in promoting human rights and democracy, and the potential of culture/art in creating employment opportunities in Ethiopia. These research projects were conducted to assess the current status and potential of the cultural sector in Ethiopia. After having the final drafts of the research, Selam has organized various workshops to receive expert feedback from concerned bodies and validate the findings of the studies. So far, all research are published and disseminated in hardcopies and available on Selam Ethiopia’s webpage. An Assessment of Artistic Freedom in Ethiopia: The study found that there is no legal censorship or restriction on artistic expression in Ethiopia, but challenges to artistic freedom remain. Recommendations include comprehensive government support, policy measures, involvement of practitioners, addressing economic problems, privatization of theater houses, support from fund providers, attention to practicing artistic freedom in law institutions and updating the Copyright Act The Role of Arts and Culture in Peacebuilding in Ethiopia: The study found challenges facing the arts and culture sector in Ethiopia that hinder its ability to contribute to peacebuilding and national unity. Recommendations include building institutional synergy, creating platforms that bring together artists and peace actors, co-designing projects that use arts and culture for peacebuilding, engaging the arts and peace sectors in sustainable peace efforts, and sensitizing the arts and culture community about their roles in peacebuilding. The Role of Art in Promoting Human Rights and Democracy: The study found that the arts and culture sector in Ethiopia needs to integrate humanist principles and human rights values into artistic practice. Recommendations include designing an art critique training project, initiating and leading an art for dialogue project, supporting the establishment of an association of art communities, encouraging participatory applied theatre, creating a network of artists and human rights activists, using ongoing recreational and beautification projects, developing a platform for TikTokers and bloggers, designing a generic quality assurance mechanism, enhancing art education courses, and promoting dialogue and collaboration within the arts and culture community. Assessment of the Potentials of culture/art in creating employment opportunities in Ethiopia: The study identified challenges facing the cultural industries sector in Ethiopia and recommended creating a statistical database, establishing cultural standard statistical methods, improving policy ideas, adjusting organizational structures, encouraging professional artists and cultural workers, conducting capacity-building training, integrating the arts with education, building collaboration with key partners, providing investment incentives, establishing legal frameworks, and putting into effect government-supportive legal measures and financial assistance. Market Survey Research  Selam Ethiopia initiated a comprehensive market survey to explore the potential of the music and film sectors in Addis Ababa, aiming to enhance job creation and economic growth. Conducted by MATH Consulting PLC from February to March 2024, this survey was part of Selam’s commitment to strengthening the creative sector's systems and infrastructure in Ethiopia. The survey aimed to analyze trends and opportunities within Addis Ababa’s music and film industries, identifying areas for investment and development, while showcasing the sectors' true potential to attract stakeholders and investors. A multifaceted approach was employed, focusing on demand, supply, and market dynamics within both the music and film sectors. The survey incorporated industry and consumer analyses, emphasizing the interconnections with leisure activities and traditional events, as well as exploring educational links. The study revealed significant untapped potential within the creative sector, alongside challenges such as infrastructure limitations and regulatory barriers. It highlighted the cultural significance of music and film in Ethiopian society and their role in economic development through job creation and cultural exports. Based on the survey, recommendations were made for short-term, medium-term, and long-term strategies to address the identified challenges against key actors in the sectors such as for government, professional associations, artists, producers, and others in both industries.   The findings and recommendations from the market survey were presented at Selam’s CCI summit, offering valuable insights into the music and film sectors' capacity for innovation and economic contribution. The initiative underscores Selam Ethiopia's role in empowering the creative industry, paving the way for sustainable growth and cultural enrichment in Ethiopia and beyond.
Results: The researches are conducted, published, and disseminated. Four separate discussion forums were also held on each topic at a national level.

Title EN: Continuing education and pedagogical resources for teachers. Arts Education Collection.
Goal: Integrate Culture In Sustainable Development Frameworks
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: National sustainable development policies and plans
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: Ministry of Cultures, Arts and Heritage (MINCAP).
Main Feature: Arts education is fundamental for integral education of children and youth, reason why in Chile it is part of the curriculum from the first levels os education, with higher concentration of hours in primary education. Nevertheless, in most of the country's educational establishments, mainly in public system, arts subjects are taught by generalist teachers who do not have disciplinary training that would allow them to properly address these teaching processes.  In this context, and following the recommendations of the UNESCO world conferences on arts education, in 2015, the National Programme for Arts Development in Education was created, with the purpose of strengthening the quality of the educational offer of institutions that organise arts education programmes for school-aged children and youth, based on various strategies, including development of teaching materials for teacher support.  The purpose of the initiative is to enrich teaching practice in arts education and to contribute to the continuous training of educators, through a collection of pedagogical resources that produce contents and didactic tools oriented towards promoting the central role of the arts in learning processes, considering it as an activator of critical thinking, creativity, socio-affective skills and aesthetic sensibility.  Arts Education Collection has four lines: (1) teaching workbooks, (2) reflection on arts education, (3) mediation and (4) promotion. With the included contents and the pedagogical proposals of each of the lines, contemporary art education is promoted, focused on learning processes, which create knowledge away from the arts and crafts paradigm, the technique and/or the mere reproduction without an underlying meaning, positioning the arts as a motor of knowledge and a driving force for creativity.  Additionally, the materials incorporate three cross-curricular approaches: legal, intercultural and gender.
Results: The main results of this measure, reported in evaluations conducted by MINCAP, show a high ranking of the materials, given by teachers, who recognise their contribution to development of pedagogical practices in arts education. The aforementioned is echoed by the demand for participation in the self-training courses taught by the Centre for Improvement, Experimentation and Pedagogical Research (CPEIP), using the developed materials.  On the other hand, the Art Education Collection currently has more than 40 didactic resources available as a free download. Finally, more than 150,000 copies have been printed and distributed, through an alliance with MINEDUC, to public and subsidised school libraries, as well as to the Chilean public library network.
Recommandations: A study conducted in 2019, to assess perception of the Teaching Workbooks, a pedagogical tool for teachers, shows that these are positively evaluated by the teaching teams. A series of recommendations are also identified, the most important one being the need to encompass references close to the children and youth and introduce fun methodologies to bridge the generational gap and motivate students.   On the other hand, it is perceived that these resources strengthen the teaching art methods and creative processes in schools, serving as support for teachers who do not necessarily have training in this matter. In the same way, priority topics to be addressed in the period 2021-2024 were identified: youth, urban and street art, new media, contemporary art and indigenous peoples.   To date, there is a resource collection that can be strongly boosted by strengthening new alliances, however, a new study is needed to monitor usability more closely and to research new trends that artificial intelligences can provide for this type of project.

They encompass various areas and include the Education, Training, and Culture axis among the priority intervention sectors. They aim to achieve new levels in bilateral relations within the framework of cooperation for development, and the planned interventions in each of the identified sectors contribute to the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals.  The intervention sectors of the PECs are organized according to the five Pillars and five Thematic Axes of the Portuguese Cooperation Strategy 2030:  People (Thematic Axis 1 - Promote human development: Education, Science, and Culture; Health Thematic Axis 2 - Promote just and inclusive societies: Social Affairs; Youth and Sports);  Peace (Thematic Axis 3 - Promote peace and the link between security and development: Justice, Security, and Defense);  Prosperity (Thematic Axis 4 - Ensure sustainable and inclusive economic growth: Quality Employment/Decent Work; Public Finance and Economy; Infrastructure; Public Administration and Territorial Cohesion; Digital Transformation; Tourism; Private Sector);  Planet (Thematic Axis 5 - Strengthen sustainability and resilience: Environment, Biodiversity, Water and Energy; Agriculture, Maritime Affairs, and Blue Economy);  Partnerships - The implementation of thematic priorities involves actively promoting partnerships with all relevant public and private actors, particularly sectoral stakeholders, favoring an integrated and cross-cutting approach in this regard. In addition to a cross-cutting approach to human rights, PECs also adopt Gender Equality and Women's Empowerment as a cross-cutting axis, with all PECs expected to contribute to this goal.
Results: Cooperation Strategic Programs embody the Portuguese Cooperation Strategy 2030, which serves as the framework for implementing the public policy on international cooperation for development. This strategy is based on the interaction between human development and sustainable development. The PCS 2030 defines the mission of Portuguese cooperation policy as the eradication of poverty, the fight against inequalities, and the promotion of sustainable, equitable, and inclusive global development, grounded in respect for human dignity and ensuring that no one is left behind. It establishes gender equality and women's empowerment as a cross-cutting priority. SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Digital environment
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: The Member States of the European Union; their relevant national authorities
Main Feature: The Directive sets out various provisions aiming to modernize the EU copyright framework. One set of measures aims in particular at creating a fairer marketplace for online content, especially as regards press publications, online content sharing service providers and the remuneration of authors and performers.   Reference is made to the provisions that deal with fair remuneration for authors and perfomers (Arts.18-22) as well as the rules governing the use of content by online content sharing service providers (Art. 17).    The first set of rules (Arts. 18-22) aim at increasing the transparency and balance in the contractual relations between content creators (authors and performers) and their producers and publishers. These rules aim ultimately at strengthening the position of authors and performers.   The objective of Article 17 is to reinforce the position of creators and right holders to negotiate and be remunerated for the online use of their content by certain user-uploaded content platforms. Article 17 also provides certainty to uploaders of content on these services: when acting on a non-commercial basis or when they do not generate significant revenues, they are covered by the licences service providers conclude with rightholders; they can also able to benefit from the fact that certain exceptions (e.g. parody, quotation) are made mandatory across the European Union.    Apart from these provisions, the Directive also sets out specific rules to facilitate the licensing of out-of-commerce works (Arts. 8-11). These new rules will make it easier for cultural heritage institutions to obtain the necessary licences to digitise and make available, notably online and across borders, the out-of-commerce works in their collections.    Finally, the Directive introduces new exceptions to copyright to facilitate digital uses of copyright-protected content for research, innovation, teaching and preservation of cultural heritage. The exceptions for Text and Data Mining (TDM) sets out provisions which are relevant to the use of copyrighted-protected material for the training of artificial intelligence (AI) models and applications. The first exception applies to TDM carried out for scientific research purpose, while the second one applies to TDM more broadly, including for commercial purposes. The broader TDM exception applies under the condition that the rights over the content used have not been expressly reserved by rightsholders. The reservation represents a balancing mechanism, allowing rightsholders to opt-out from the TDM exception and keep control over the use of their works.
Results: Following the adoption of the DSM Directive, the Commission issued guidance on the application of Article 17, which applies to online content sharing service providers.   To date, 26 EU Member States have transposed the DSM Directive into their national laws and they are responsible for its proper implementation. The Commission currently monitors the conformity of the transpositions and will assess the results achieved in the context of the review which will take place no sooner than 7 June 2026 (Article 30).

Male and Female Artists in Poland.'  According to this report, the artistic community in Poland numbers around 60 thousand people. This is not a large professional group. In the common imagination there seem to be more. This is influenced by the phenomenon of multi-professions, which is common in this group, the coefficient of which 2.5 means that this group is estimated to be about 2.5 times larger, even 150 thousand people. Results: As a result of the conducted research, estimated data on the number of artistic communities in Poland were obtained. In addition to estimating the total number of artists, creators and performers, the research also allowed for estimating the number of individual cultural industries by profession. The research was also used to obtain information from respondents on, among others: their metric data, the distribution of respondents in industries by gender, professional experience, the share of income from creative work in total income, forms of work, membership in industry organizations, conditions of performing the profession, as well as respondents' opinions on the introduction of systemic solutions dedicated to artists and creators. The research report was published in the form of a book in 2020.

Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: Društvo Asociacija
Main Feature: Asociacija aims to secure sustainable conditions and systematic support for professional non-governmental producers and independent creators in Slovenia. The network started as informal activities in 1992 and has grown into a professionally coordinated organization providing advocacy and support services to its members and others in the field of independent culture.   We are a democratic network of creators in the field of independent culture, who share experiences and continuously build strong advocacy together. The network is based on professional competencies, in-depth acquittance with the field and building partnership relations with decision makers in order to improve the conditions in culture sphere, while also offering support to its members with a widespread peer-to-peer network.  Our vision is to be a strong and stable partner when it comes to the mutual efforts of identifying culture as a driver of development thorough our advocacy and support activities. We strive for a cultural policy system that encourages diversity of artistic expression and creates equal possibilities for access to cultural contents for all. The values we embody in our work are: inclusive democracy, solidarity, equality, transparency, structured social dialogue, sustainable development.  We are fulfilling this mission through: (1) connecting, articulating and advocating for common interests of our members in relation to various decision-making structures; (2) continuous and structured advocacy activities and policy formation proposals (at the local, national, Western Balkans and European level); (3) cultural sector promotion by informing, organizing events and researching cultural policies; (4) networking at the local, national and European level; (5) connecting with strategic partners and internationalization of our activities; (6) encouraging partnerships within and outside of the NGO cultural sector; (7) capacity building for NGOs through counselling, educating, mentoring etc.
Results: What are the results achieved so far through the implementation of the measure/initiative? (400 words)  Association Asociacija, in line with its operational strategy, focuses on advocacy, service activity, strengthening operation of the network, getting involved in implementation of partner projects and other activities.  As part of the regular activities of the service and as one of our central activitieswe work on strengthening  competences, individual assistance and service services. Through all this, we aim to give access to a set of skills important for career and organizational development. We have a database in which we collect answers to various questions from a wide field of activity and business individuals who work in the field of culture. Approximately 30 artist and cultural workers a month seek our support, advice and expertise via e-mail, phone calls or live meetings.  In terms of ensuring sustainable conditions for professionals in NGOs and/or independent creators we are preparing RESPONSES TO PROPOSED LAWS, REGULATIONS, AND OTHER ACTS AND FUNDING MECHANISMS in culture that were later adjusted and changed due to our involvement. We are successful in our advocacy activities where we are a part of different working groups and bodies, consultative bodies, part of expert bodies, where we are part of developing different national and local strategies. For instance, representatives of the association attended meetings of the Working group for permanent dialogue with the self-employed and other workers in culture, Dialogue groups of Municipality of Ljubljana with NGOs, consultation meetings of the Ministry of Culture on the topic of a cultural model tailored to the future, National session of the Council for Culture etc. We regularly publish our electronic newsletter Kulturosfera, where monthly information about key movements and activities in the field of cultural policy (events, research, legislative changes, initiatives, etc.) is available. At the same time we introduce the work and thinking of the members Asociacija. We are publishing Kulturosfera's podcast, in which it is possible to listen to contributions about key movements, activities and practices in the field of independent culture in local, national and international environments.  The association has important ties in the international environment and is a member of regional networks in the Western Balkans Kooperativa; Culture Action Europe at the level of the European Union and EAIPA – European Association of Independent Performing Arts and is part of differenct project consortiums.

Title EN: CPLP Audiovisual Program - Community of Portuguese-Speaking Countries Audiovisual Production and Diffusion Program
Goal: Achieve A Balanced Flow Of Cultural Goods And Services And Increase The Mobility Of Artists And Cultural Professionals
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 10 - Reduce inequality within and among countries,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Flow of cultural goods and services
Agency Implementation: Community of Portuguese-Speaking Countries (CPLP) and respective Member States
Main Feature: The CPLP Audiovisual Program (PAV) is a joint initiative of the audiovisual authorities of Portugal and Brazil, proposed by the Audiovisual Secretariat of the Ministry of Culture of Brazil and the Portuguese Institute of Cinema and Audiovisual, launched in 2015. It aims at capacity building, co-production, and television broadcasting of audiovisual content, using a network operation model where each participating State/Region simultaneously co-produces audiovisual works and ensures their broadcasting through public television broadcasters.  The objective of PAV is to promote the production and broadcasting of audiovisual content in the member states of the Community of Portuguese-Speaking Countries, through National Selection Contests for documentary and fiction TV films in all Member States of the Community and the launch of the Nossa Língua program. The CPLP Audiovisual Program seeks to:  Produce audiovisual content that presents a contemporary vision of the member countries of the Portuguese-speaking community; Promote the exchange of experiences among audiovisual creators and producers from Portuguese-speaking countries; Consolidate the CPLP Audiovisual Network as a platform for the production and circulation of content; Stimulate cultural exchange among the peoples of CPLP countries; Contribute to the implementation of integrated public policies to foster audiovisual production in CPLP member countries; Promote the broadcasting of audiovisual production from CPLP in the global market; Generate business environments and dynamics conducive to the production and circulation of Portuguese-language audiovisual content in various national and international markets.
Results: The success of the first edition of the Program led to the realization of a second edition, with plans for a third currently in development.  This Program was preceded by another successful project: the CPLP Documentary Production and Broadcasting Program - DOCTV CPLP, which started in 2008 and focused solely on documentaries.  The 1st edition took place between 2014 and 2016, producing nine documentaries (one per country) and four TV films (Angola, Brazil, Mozambique, and Portugal).  The 2nd edition took place between 2017 and 2019, focusing only on the DOCTV module, resulting in nine documentaries, one from each Member State.
Financial Ressources: The initial budget of PAV, when launched in 2015, was approximately $3.24 million. Financial resources projected for the implementation of the 3rd edition include approximately $270,000 from Angola and $1.08 million from Portugal/ICA. Additionally, there is a remaining amount from previous PAV editions of approximately $36,353.04. Confirmation of co-financing from Brazil, amounting to approximately $1.08 million, is awaited. Therefore, the total budget allocated for the future Program will be approximately $2.46 million.
Recommandations: The CPLP Audiovisual Program (PAV) has been establishing itself over the years as a flagship project of CPLP, with its continuity unquestioned by Member States, including within the scope of the Meeting of Ministers of Culture.  Based on past experience, it is concluded that there should be increased investment in fostering audiovisual production, strengthening the legal and policy framework in the cultural and creative industries sector, and supporting new talents and advocating for gender non-discrimination measures.  The main recommendations for the future of the program are:  Increase impact by expanding the number of beneficiaries, both in terms of training and production funding (directly dependent on co-financing amounts); Diversify content by introducing a short film category; Enhance training and capacity-building by replacing the Creative Project Design Workshop (which only benefited winning projects) with national seminars for a broader range of beneficiaries (winners of a pre-selection phase); Develop a marketing plan for PAV content, aiming for financial returns that diversify funding sources for future PAV editions, while promoting the diffusion of Portuguese-language audiovisual content and the visibility of CPLP, its Member States, and their cultural diversity; Prepare a report on the audiovisual landscape in CPLP Member States, with contributions from academics and Culture Focal Points and other relevant authorities in Member States, to be released at a conference on the subject; Host a CPLP Audiovisual Showcase, including a roundtable discussion on public audiovisual policies in Member States, concurrent with the Planning and Distribution Meeting (in 2024).

Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Agency Implementation: CYENS Research and Innovation Centre of Excellence
Main Feature: CYENS Thinker Maker Space is a multifunctional creative space that supports local entrepreneurs, designers, artists and researchers. TMS promotes technology led innovation by encouraging the local creative community to develop projects that utilise digital fabrication techniques and rapid prototyping.  The space is open to the public under a membership program, offering easy and free access to cutting edge equipment and professional technical support. TMS organises various exhibitions and delivers numerous talks and workshops. These initiatives provide an important milestone and a point of reference for creatives, not only for Cyprus and the eastern Mediterranean but also internationally.  CYENS Thinker Maker Space was designed to meet the standards of a creative innovation hub within Nicosia’s historic centre. The project is co-funded from the European Structural Investment Funds E.S.I.F, allocated to Nicosia Municipality for the implementation of its Sustainable Urban Development Strategy “SUDS”.  The Research and Innovation Centre on Interactive Media, Smart System and Emerging Technologies – CYENS Centre of Excellence (formerly known as RISE), empowers knowledge and technology transfer in the region. CYENS CoE is supported by the European Commission, the Republic of Cyprus and its founding Partners, the Municipality of Nicosia, the Max Planck Institute for Informatics (MPI), University College London, the University of Cyprus, the Cyprus University of Technology and the Open University of Cyprus.   CYENS, as a Centre of Excellence, cultivates a culture of innovation and creativity in an inspiring environment filled with academics, researchers, creative and onward-looking people, innovators, entrepreneurs, and practitioners. The Centre operates under the moto “Inspired by Humans Designed for Humans” with the vision to produce world class research that drives innovation towards social and economic benefit while conducting excellent, internationally competitive scientific research in the areas of visual sciences, human factors and design, communication, and artificial intelligence. It sets out to meet the challenge with a total potential funding of more than 30 million Euros for the first 7 years, from a Horizon 2020 Teaming Action and multiple other sources, and a business plan for long-term sustainability and growth.  Hosting CYENS at the heart of the designated Creative Industries and Technology Quarter is part of the Municipality’s strategy to foster the development of an inclusive innovation hub and vibrant creativity ecosystem.  CYENS, through its Maker Space, a multifunction creative space open to the public; with cutting edge equipment and knowledgeable tutors and mentors, deploys scientific methodologies and state-of-the-art techniques into the research and product development pipelines of entities in Cyprus while minimising their risks and costs. The CYENS Maker Space aims to offer researchers, entrepreneurs, students and self-made makers, opportunities to transform, share, test and perfect their ideas. The Co-working space is a space where start-ups and spin-offs; created by the researchers at CYENS or by collaborating groups will have a place to work. Collaborating groups or diverse groups of independent creative professionals and individuals will be able to work in a shared setting. The CYENS Co-working space aims to help those with common values develop potential synergies. Finally, CYENS aims to appeal to local youth, our next generation of innovators, and cultivate their interest in emerging technologies and STEAM-led education and equip them with skills, ambitions and networks to exploit opportunities that can transform the economy.

Title EN: création de l'agence nationale  pour la promotion d ela culture

Agency Implementation: agence nationale pou la promotion de la culture
Main Feature: Mesure 1 : Création de la Direction du Cinéma  En 2021, le président de la République de Djibouti a créé une Direction dédiée au cinéma, marquant une étape décisive pour le secteur.  En 2023, cette direction a été intégrée aux départements culturels fusionnés, formant la nouvelle Agence Nationale pour la Promotion de la Culture (ANPC) sous la tutelle du Ministère de la Jeunesse et de la Culture. Cette mesure a offert une structure organisationnelle spécialisée pour soutenir et promouvoir le cinéma djiboutien, facilitant ainsi la coordination et la mise en œuvre des politiques culturelles.  Mesure 2 : Politique de Professionnalisation de la Création Cinématographique.   La professionnalisation de la création cinématographique djiboutienne est une priorité stratégique. Un programme annuel, constamment ajusté aux réalités du secteur, a été mis en place. Ce programme commence par une formation intensive dispensée par le département de la cinématographie de l'ANPC à une vingtaine de jeunes. Les meilleurs d'entre eux reçoivent ensuite un soutien technique, logistique et financier pour la concrétisation de leurs projets de film. Cette politique vise non seulement à développer les compétences locales mais aussi à créer une dynamique durable dans la production cinématographique de qualité à Djibouti.  Mesure 3 : Festival du Film de Djibouti La première édition du Festival du film de Djibouti a eu lieu en février 2023, avec pour objectif principal de promouvoir les créations cinématographiques djiboutiennes. Ouvert à tous, le festival met particulièrement en avant les jeunes bénéficiaires de la politique de professionnalisation du secteur, leur offrant une plateforme pour démarrer et développer une carrière durable dans l'industrie cinématographique. Ce festival joue un rôle crucial en termes de visibilité et de reconnaissance des talents locaux, contribuant ainsi à l'essor du cinéma djiboutien.  Mesure 4 : Développement d'un Cadre Légal pour l'Industrie Cinématographique.   Le département de la cinématographie a entrepris, avec l'aide d'une experte juridique djiboutienne, la rédaction d'une loi visant à réglementer l'industrie cinématographique djiboutienne. L'objectif est de créer un cadre légal solide qui soutienne le développement du secteur et encourage les investissements. La mise en place de cette législation est essentielle pour structurer et pérenniser l'industrie cinématographique locale.  Mesure 5 : Bureau d'Accueil des Productions Étrangères.   Le département de la cinématographie a créé un Bureau d'accueil des productions étrangères à Djibouti. Ce bureau a déjà accueilli un projet de long métrage de fiction réalisé par un jeune réalisateur américain en janvier 2024, ainsi qu'un projet de film documentaire russe en février 2024. L'objectif de ce bureau est d'attirer des productions internationales à Djibouti, facilitant ainsi un transfert de compétences précieuses et contribuant à la lutte contre le chômage des jeunes Djiboutiens. Cette initiative vise également à positionner Djibouti comme une destination attrayante pour les cinéastes étranger
Results: réalisation du 1er festival du cinéma de djibouti

Dans cette optique,  le  gouvernement marocain  a  mis en place  une panoplie  de  mesures pour améliorer la culture entrepreneuriale et encourager la création de l’entreprise. La politique du gouvernement à cet égard est essentiellement marquée par le soutien de l’auto-initiative d’emploi, l’accompagnement des entrepreneurs, l’encouragement de l’esprit de créativité et d’innovation et l’accroissement de la promotion des initiatives de l’emploi. Intelaka est un dispositif lancé le 3 février 2020 par le Ministère de l'Économie, des Finances et de la Réforme de l'Administration en collaboration avec la Caisse Centrale de Garantie (CCG). Il vise à encourager l’entrepreneuriat et à faciliter l’insertion professionnelle des jeunes grâce à un mécanisme de financement amélioré et adapté. Doté d’un fonds de 8 milliards de dirhams financé par l'État, le secteur bancaire et la Fondation Hassan II pour le développement économique et social, Intelaka facilite l'accès au financement pour les jeunes porteurs de projets, les auto-entrepreneurs, les micro-entreprises et les TPE informelles, aussi bien en milieu urbain qu'en milieu rural. Ce programme s'étend à plusieurs domaines, y compris les industries culturelles et créatives numériques.  Afin de soutenir les jeunes porteurs de projets culturels et artistiques, le Département de la culture a mis en place une cellule dédiée spécifiquement à leur accompagnement. Cette cellule a pour mission de doter les jeunes entrepreneurs des techniques nécessaires pour mieux élaborer leurs projets culturels et bénéficier du financement sollicité. Composée d'experts dans les métiers des arts et de la culture, cette cellule offre un soutien spécialisé pour maximiser les chances de réussite des projets soumis.
Results: La création de la cellule d’accompagnement des jeunes acteurs culturels s’inscrit dans une perspective globale de développement d’une offre culturelle numérique nationale. Parmi les résultats phares, on note une augmentation significative du nombre de projets culturels financés. De nombreux jeunes porteurs de projets dans les domaines des arts et de la culture ont ainsi réussi à obtenir des financements, leur permettant de concrétiser leurs idées et de lancer leurs initiatives. En outre, les programmes de formation administrés par la cellule ont eu un impact notable sur le renforcement des compétences. Grâce à l'accompagnement personnalisé par des experts, les jeunes entrepreneurs ont acquis des compétences précieuses en gestion de projets culturels, ce qui a amélioré la qualité et la viabilité de leurs projets.
Financial Ressources: Étant donné que la politique de culture numérique est une politique horizontale intégrée dans la politique culturelle globale du Ministère, il est difficile de fournir un chiffre des ressources financières allouées à cette mesure.

Main Feature: The Creative Ireland Programme is an all-of-government initiative based in the Department of Tourism, Culture, Arts, Gaeltacht, Sports and Media, running from 2017 to 2027. It aims to place creativity at the centre of public policy and to promote individual, community and national wellbeing through culture-based programmes.   One of the pillars of its work is Creative Climate Action and Sustainability. The goal is to place culture at the vanguard of climate change. The programme seeks to harness the power of the arts, culture, and wider creative sectors to communicate the impact of the climate crisis in imaginative and engaging ways.   The Creative Ireland Programme led on the delivery of the first Creative Climate Action Fund which was launched in March 2021. 166 applications were received from a diverse range of organisations and consortiums across the country, of which 15 projects were selected to receive funding. These projects engaged multiple diverse audiences around the country including farming communities, rural communities, and inner-city communities. They used a variety of creative mediums and approaches including co-creation and embedded artists.  Following the success of the inaugural Creative Climate Action Fund in 2021; the Department of Tourism, Culture, Arts, Gaeltacht, Sport and Media in collaboration with the Department of the Environment, Climate and Communications and the Department of the Taoiseach launched Creative Climate Action Fund II – Agents for Change.  The Creative Climate Action Fund II: Agents of Change is unique in that it pairs creative minds with experts in climate science, sustainability and biodiversity, all with the aim of connecting the public to the profound changes that are happening in our environment, society and economy arising from climate change and can transform that connection into behaviour change or climate action. The fund received 239 applications from an array of disciplines and industries  In July 2023, Creative Ireland announced 42 successful recipients of the €5.8 million Creative Climate Action Fund II – Agents for Change. Title EN: Creative Youth Plan 2023-2027
Goal: Integrate Culture In Sustainable Development Frameworks
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: National sustainable development policies and plans
Agency Implementation: Creative Ireland Programme (within the Department of Tourism, Culture, Arts, Gaeltacht, Sport and Media)
Main Feature: The Creative Ireland Programme (led by the Department of Tourism, Culture, Arts, Gaeltacht, Sport and Media) was set up to enable the creative potential of all people living in Ireland, to enhance their wellbeing and the collective wellbeing across all areas of our society. We focus on encouraging and supporting new ways and opportunities to participate in creative and cultural activities. The Creative Ireland Programme is an all-of- government culture and wellbeing programme running until 2027. More information is available at www.creativeireland.gov.ie. The Plan has five pillars, one of which is Creative Youth.  The Creative Youth Plan 2023-2027 provides access to children and young people, from birth to 24 years, to creative, cultural and artistic engagement across all aspects of their lives. Prioritising those that are seldom heard, the Plan supports engagement in activities such as creative writing, youth theatre and creative technology. Programmes such as Creative Schools put arts and creativity at the heart of school life, strengthening links between schools and the broader cultural and community infrastructure. Funding is allocated to all 31 local authorities to deliver Cruinniú na nÓg annually, the national day of free creative and cultural activities for children and young people.     Guiding principles of the Creative Youth Plan 2023-2027 •	All children and young people must have opportunities to be creative and develop their creative skills.  •	Both the intrinsic, and instrumental or transferable value of creative pursuits can be supported and developed simultaneously.  •	Parents & caregivers, educators, artists, and creative practitioners need to be supported to recognise the centrality and value of creativity to children and young people. •	Children and young people must have agency and a voice in decision-making on the implementation of the plan The Plan has seven strategic objectives •	Facilitate and provide creative opportunities for children and young people •	Strengthen equity of access to creative activities for the most seldom heard children and young people. •	Supporting the implementation of Aistear, the Early Childhood Curriculum Framework •	Promoting the value of creativity across the Education system and supporting Curriculum Frameworks in schools. •	Further promote and nurture the development of creative skills in Further and Higher Education, including apprenticeships •	Supporting the enhanced wellbeing of children and young people •	Establish a programme of research The strategic framework encompasses a series of expanded and new initiatives that will be implemented between 2023 and 2027, designed to empower children and young people, spanning from birth to 24 years old. Its primary focus lies in promoting creativity within both formal education settings and out-of-school contexts. By nurturing artistic and creative expression, the plan seeks to enrich young lives and contribute to a vibrant cultural landscape.   The Creative Youth Nurture Fund was announced in April 2023. The pilot fund is the first of its kind in Ireland and aims to provide children and young people with a voice in the planning and implementation of their creative activity. It focuses on specific groups of young people that have the least access to creative opportunities and supports organisations and individuals that can reach specific groups of young people that are seldom heard. Support has been provided to organisations that support young refugees, young members of the Traveller community, those in youth detention and young people leaving the care system amongst others.  https://www.creativeireland.gov.ie/en/news/announcement-of-the-creative-youth-nurture-fund/   Cruinniú na nÓg Cruinniú na nÓg, a key commitment in the Creative Youth Plan, is the national day of free creativity for children and young people under 18. Ireland is the first, and only, country in the world to have such a day. Celebrated annually in June, young people are invited to participate in a programme of free, creative activities, demonstrate their creative skills, try a new creative activity, and above all have fun. Within the programming of Cruinniú na nÓg the fundamental principle of allowing the Voice of the Child to be heard bears practical effect with many of the events devised by young people.  https://www.creativeireland.gov.ie/en/creative-youth/cruinniu-na-nog/  https://www.creativeireland.gov.ie/app/uploads/2023/03/Creative-Youth-Plan-2023-2027.pdf   The Department of Education is committed to ensuring that all learners have access to creative opportunities across the curriculum. In particular, they include:  BLAST (Bringing Live Arts to Students and Teachers) BLAST aims to provide pupils in primary and post-primary schools throughout Ireland with the time and space to collaborate with professional artists, by providing in-school arts education residencies for Primary, Post-Primary, Special Education Settings and Youth Reach Centres.   In 2023, BLAST enabled 425 new arts in education residencies in schools, ensuring thousands of students could benefit from this experience along with teachers and schools. Some of the trained artists/creative practitioners available to schools covered topics such as  •	multimedia,  •	fine art,  •	mosaics,  •	stained glass  •	sculpture/animation  •	performance art. https://www.gov.ie/en/service/69096-blast-arts-in-education/  Creative Clusters Creative Clusters is an initiative whereby clusters of between three and five schools engage in collaborative, professional learning communities on any kind of creative challenge or theme over a two-year period. The schools work together over two years on building capacity in creativity with the support of a specialist facilitator and benefiting from partnerships with artists and cultural organisations.   https://www.creativeireland.gov.ie/en/news/creative-clusters-scheme-brings-schools-a-new-kind-of-lesson/   Local Creative Youth Partnerships (LCYP) Local Creative Youth Partnerships are centred in local Education and Training Boards (ETBs). LCYPs are community-based collaborations that bring together schools, artists, and cultural entities. They are specifically focused on reaching the more marginalised and disadvantaged groups.  https://www.creativeireland.gov.ie/en/creative-youth/creative-youth-partnerships/   TAP (Teacher Artist Partnership) The Teacher-Artist Partnership (TAP) initiative brings teachers and artists together in training to support the delivery of artist residencies in schools, ensuring that there is a shared understanding of creativity within the school setting. The overall aim is to empower teachers and artists to enhance the creative potential of every child through collaborative practice.   https://www.creativeireland.gov.ie/en/creative-youth-guide/tap/#:~:text=TAP%2B%20(Teacher%20Artist%20Partnership%2B),in%20primary%20and%20special%20schools.   I Am Creative I Am Creative was piloted in 2023. This brings together teachers, artists, Special Needs Assistants and school leaders to train together to support the delivery of artist residency in special educational settings.

Title EN: Creativity and Innovation Awards
Goal: Integrate Culture In Sustainable Development Frameworks
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: International cooperation for sustainable development
Agency Implementation: Culture and Development East Africa (CDEA)
Main Feature: The NOW-Us Awards, initiated by Culture and Development East Africa (CDEA) in collaboration with Voice in Tanzania/ Hivos East Africa, to recognize organizations in Tanzania and the wider East African region for their use of creativity and innovation in driving sustainable development. Rooted in the principle of "Nothing About Us Without Us," borrowed from the disability rights movement, the awards aim to promote inclusivity by spotlighting champions within organizations who directly engage in decision-making processes affecting their communities.  In 2022, the NOW-Us Awards focused on inclusion, facilitating a boot camp for 10 organizations responding to Voice Global's call on "Faith, Freedom, and Feminism," emphasizing artistic expression as a tool for social transformation. Three winners received seed funding for project implementation, supported by mentorship from CDEA in financial management and best practice documentation.  Building on this success, the NOW-Us Awards 2024 emphasized creativity and innovation in sustainable development. Guided by CDEA's mission to leverage culture, creativity, and ICTs for social justice and environmental balance, the awards celebrate organizations excelling in artistic expression, media, and immersive technologies for development impact.  The NOW-Us Awards serve as a platform for showcasing best practices and inspiring others to adopt innovative approaches to societal challenges. By spotlighting organizations championing creativity and innovation, CDEA fosters collaboration and learning within the development community.
Results: In 2022, the focus on celebrating inclusion resulted in the successful facilitation of a week-long boot camp for 10 organizations. These organizations, responding to Voice Global's call on "Faith, Freedom, and Feminism," were empowered to utilize artistic expression as a catalyst for social transformation towards achieving freedom.  As a result of CDEA's support, including pitch deck preparation and mentorship in financial management and best practices documentation, three winning organizations received substantial seed funding totalling TZS 50,000,000. This funding enabled them to implement projects aimed at addressing societal challenges through creative and innovative means. Main Feature: The International Cultural Relations (ICR) Division of the Ministry of Culture aims to propagate Indian culture in new territories and enhance cultural relations between India and other countries worldwide. One of its primary mandates is to establish bilateral cultural agreements that strengthen cultural ties and foster friendship between India and partner countries. These agreements encompass various cultural domains, facilitating cultural exchange programs between the parties: Music and Dance: Exchange of music and dance ensembles, including classical and folk troupes, for agreed periods. Details are mutually determined through diplomatic channels. Theatre: Facilitation of theatre performance exchanges and participation in local and international theatre festivals on mutually agreed terms. Educational materials on theatre are also exchanged. Exhibitions, Seminars, and Conferences: Reciprocal exchange of contemporary and modern art exhibitions. Participation in international seminars, symposiums, conferences, camps, residencies, etc., is encouraged. Archaeology: Collaboration in the protection, conservation, and promotion of cultural heritage through training programs, workshops, and exchange of experts. Archives: Exchange of information and digital preservation practices. Training courses offered by the National Archives of India and counterpart institutions are promoted. Library: Reciprocal exchange of publications and visits by library experts to enhance library sciences in both countries. Museums: Exchange of exhibitions, museum exhibits, and personnel. Joint organization of exhibitions and exchange of museum professionals to share expertise. Literature: Exchange of writer delegations, promotion of literary translations, and collaborations on literary works. Research and Documentation: Collaboration on cultural heritage studies, folklore, creative activities for cognitive development, and production of educational materials. Science Museums/Centres: Exchange of senior-level science communication professionals to study and strengthen interactive science centres and non-formal science education. Anthropology: Exchange visits of anthropology experts from respective institutes. Festivals: Mutual organization of festivals including tours of performing arts groups from both sides. Mass Media: Exchange of programs depicting cultural facets through radio and TV organizations. Collaboration in international film festivals and training exchanges. Youth Programs: Encouragement of youth exchange programs, participation in youth festivals, and sharing of experiences and knowledge in youth-related seminars and conferences. These initiatives are developed on the basis of reciprocity, aiming to enhance mutual understanding and cultural cooperation between India and its international partners.
Results: Bilateral Cultural Agreements and Cultural Exchange Programs (CEP): The ICR Division has facilitated several Cultural Exchange Programs and signed Bilateral Cultural Agreements with countries like Uzbekistan, Serbia, and the Russian Federation. These agreements aim to strengthen cultural cooperation and deepen cultural ties between India and partner countries. These events serve as tools of cultural diplomacy, enhancing India's soft power and cultural influence globally. These grants facilitate programs and activities such as discussions on Indian culture, seminars, performances of Indian troupes, exhibitions, and courses in yoga and Indian music/dance. In FY 2022-23, Rs. 666.72 lakhs were sanctioned to support 229 Cultural Societies across 35 Indian Missions abroad. Participation in Multilateral Cultural Platforms: India actively engages in cultural cooperation on multilateral platforms such as BRICS, SCO, G20, BIMSTEC, SAARC, ASEAN, etc. These engagements foster cultural dialogue and collaboration among member countries, promoting mutual understanding and cooperation in cultural affairs. Cultural Diplomacy and Soft Power Projection: Through these initiatives, India integrates its soft power dimensions into external relations, focusing on spiritual, cultural, and philosophical aspects. The exchange of cultural programs and exhibitions enhances India's image abroad and promotes cultural tourism and economic ties.

Title EN: Cultural Cities Enquiry and Recovery Reports
Goal: Integrate Culture In Sustainable Development Frameworks
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: National sustainable development policies and plans
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: Arts Council England
Main Feature: The Cultural Cities Enquiry was an independent enquiry supported by Arts Council England that was convened in 2019 to propose recommendations to radically improve the ability of towns and cities across the country to use culture to drive inclusive growth. In September 2020, the Enquiry was reconvened and expanded as the Cultural Cities Recovery, which looks at how culture can help the nation to recover from the Covid-19 pandemic.
Results: The Arts Council convened two roundtables with 21 stakeholders from a range of sectors including property, business, local government, education, urban regeneration, hospitality, culture, civil society, among others. The group put forward independent policy recommendations for consideration by the Arts Council, local and national government and partners that might help the cultural sector recover from the impact of the pandemic, and to contribute to the social and economic recovery of places across the UK.
Recommandations: Cities and towns can benefit from increased strategic leadership and coordinated action to enhance culture’s contribution to recovery and renewal post Covid-19 and its role in ‘levelling up’ opportunities across places. Strategic investment in culture and a more efficient use of existing assets can increase places’ ability to stimulate and capture future economic growth opportunities.     Sources of investment into the cultural sector and early stage creative enterprises are narrow, and use of loan finance remains limited. Depressed commercial revenue due to Covid-19, along with strains on local public investment, threaten the sustainability of the cultural sector, and cultural assets (property, data, brand value, content) are often under-utilised.    The ability of a place to grow, attract and retain talent is key to its prosperity. Career pathways into the cultural and wider creative industries are often narrow, and the small scale of enterprises within the sector makes it difficult for them to benefit from and contribute to national training schemes and structured training programmes.     Covid-19 is restricting local opportunities for young people, especially in places with lower economic resilience and communities already at risk of exclusion. At the same time, the cultural sector doesn’t always reflect the diversity of local communities – especially young people.    The pandemic has intensified pressures on local high streets, with a reduction in footfall heightened by the closure of retail and hospitality venues and an absence of office workers. Cultural venues are suffering depressed demand from audiences and face capacity limits due to Covid-secure regulations.     Covid-19 has struck already left-behind towns, city centres, and post-industrial areas. Cities and towns have an untapped wealth of cultural assets to support regeneration; however, places often lack capacity and resources to optimise their value. Planning policy must support the optimization of cultural activity to fully realise its benefits for places.
