Title EN: Lithuanian Film Tax Incentive
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Agency Implementation: Lithuanian Film Centre under the Ministry of Culture
Main Feature: Lithuanian Film Tax Incentive came into effect in January 2014 as a new policy measure to foster local and foreign film production in Lithuania.  The main purpose of the Lithuanian film tax incentive is to create favourable conditions for film production in Lithuania for domestic and foreign film producers and to allow Lithuanian companies willing to support film production to reduce their corporate income tax.   From 1 January 2019 until 2023 the total eligible support granted to Lithuanian or foreign filmmakers was up to 30% of the total production costs of the film. (In 2014-2018 Lithuanian Film Tax Incentive offered an opportunity to save up to 20% of the film production budget through private investment scheme).  At the end of 2023, the Parliament of Lithuania (Seimas) approved the proposal to extend the Film Tax Incentive scheme for another five years period until 31 December 2028. The updated provisions entered into force on 1 January 2024. It is significant to note that the eligible support remained the same – 30% of the total production costs of the film. (For more detail look: https://e-seimas.lrs.lt/portal/legalAct/lt/TAD/TAIS.157066/asr).   Film production companies get a financial aid for filmmaking in Lithuania if their production meets eligibility requirements and they comply with the formal procedure approved by the Lithuanian Film Centre.  Private donors in return can deduct the amount granted for filmmaking process from their taxable income. The estimated net profit for the donor participating in the scheme is up to 11,25%.  The incentive is available for the production of feature films, TV dramas, documentaries and animated films. It includes domestically produced, co-produced or commissioned films (produced under the service agreement). At least 80% of eligible film production costs must be incurred in Lithuania and the total amount of eligible spend in Lithuania must be no less than 43,000 EUR.  Once a company has chosen which project it wants to invest in, it signs a contract with the production company and transfers the desired amount, which cannot exceed 30% of the film's budget in Lithuania. The investment certificate issued by the Lithuanian Film Centre becomes the basis for declaring the reduced corporate income tax.  Updated version of Description of the Evaluation Procedure of Cultural Content and Production of the Film Produced in the Republic of Lithuania has been agreed with Ministry of Culture and Ministry of Finance. The updated Description should enter into force October 2024. In updated version film producers will have more freedom to apply with series projects, as duration per episode restrictions will be removed. This could lead to even greater success of Lithuanian Film Tax Incentive scheme. In new version there are also many small changes that will give producers more freedom.   Benefits for investors:  The tax relief is available to any business operating in Lithuania that has provided funds to a Lithuanian film producer free of charge. The benefit is:  A reduction in taxable income due to the amount granted for the production of the film or part of it; a reduction in corporate income tax on the amount granted for the production of the film or part thereof.  A Lithuanian film producer producing a national, co-produced or commissioned film or part of a film may apply for the Tax Incentive support. The following categories of film production are eligible to apply:  Feature, documentary and animated feature-length or short film production; Animated multi-part film production (where the total duration of the film is at least 24 minutes); Production of a television drama film (where the duration of a series is at least 30 minutes per series and the number of series per season does not exceed 25); Television fiction documentary film production (where the total duration of all the instalments is not less than 50 minutes). Applications are not accepted for the production of promotional films, promotional videos, television programmes, music videos, computer games, soap operas, situation comedies or other similar series of no artistic merit.
Results: Domestic and foreign film production projects in Lithuania not only increase the professionalism of the Lithuanian film industry, but also have a direct impact on the country's economy, through the taxes paid and the growing employment of in sectors not directly related to the cinema, such as hotels, catering, transport, retail, entertainment and others. This has been supported by a study on the economic impact of the Lithuanian Film Tax Incentive commissioned by the Lithuanian Film Centre: KEA_Evaluation of the fiscal incentive scheme for film production in lithuania.pdf (lkc.lt)  Since 2014, 472 productions have benefited from the Lithuanian Film Tax Incentive by getting a total of approx. USD 99,5 million (EUR 89,72 million) in investment for film production.   The scheme was used by: 99 foreign films; 96 co-productions; 277 national films.  Investments for film production were granted by 325 local companies in amounts ranging from approx. USD 1108 (EUR 1000) to over USD 1.7 million (EUR 1.6 million). Evaluating the results of several years, thanks to Lithuanian Film Tax Incentive, the capabilities of the Lithuanian film industry have increased several times. In 2019, film production costs in Lithuania amounted to about USD 24 million (EUR 22 million). In the following year 2020, this amount reached approx. USD 43 million (EUR 39 million). After that, the annual cost of film production never dropped and kept growing until it reached more than USD 77,6 million (EUR 70 million) in 2023.
Financial Ressources: Since year 2014 until year 2023 approx. USD 99 560 774 (EUR 89 718 640) have been allocated for this purpose.  In 2020 	approx. USD 12 526 700 (EUR 11 288 300)  In 2021	approx. USD 16 848 200  (EUR 15 182 700) In 2022	approx.  USD 19 822 300 (EUR 17 862 700) In 2023	approx. USD 23 392 300 (EUR 21 079 904)  Each year the investment received through the Lithuanian Film Tax Incentive scheme  cannot exceed approx.  USD 61 million (EUR 55 million).
Recommandations: In 2018 evaluation of the fiscal incentive scheme for film production (period 2014-2017) in Lithuania was concluded: KEA_Evaluation of the fiscal incentive scheme for film production in lithuania.pdf (lkc.lt)  The report shows a clear positive impact of the Lithuanian Film Tax Incentive on the production sector for a minimum cost to Lithuanian taxpayers. The Tax Incentive enables Lithuania to position itself in the fast growing international audiovisual sector that is expanding significantly with the explosion of digital distribution platforms and new formats for story telling (notably virtual reality).

Main Feature: Celebrating UAE sports and cultural heritage in Abu Dhabi, the Liwa International Festival features motorsport, falconry, horse and camel competitions, live music, and family entertainment. This hallmark collaboration with the Department of Culture and Tourism, Abu Dhabi, is an annual event scheduled from the first week of December to early January. The festival is renowned for its thrilling motorsport competitions, including drag racing and hill climbs on the Moreeb Dune, one of the tallest sand dunes in the world. These events attract both professional and amateur racers, offering a unique and challenging experience. The festival also hosts traditional Emirati competitions such as falconry, horse racing, and camel racing, celebrating the rich cultural heritage of the UAE and providing visitors with an authentic glimpse into traditional sports and practices. Cultural performances are a key aspect of the festival, with live music and traditional dance showcases providing entertainment and cultural enrichment. These performances highlight the diverse musical and dance traditions of the region, adding to the festival's vibrant atmosphere. Family entertainment is an essential component of the festival, offering a variety of activities for all ages. Games, workshops, and food stalls cater to families seeking fun and entertainment, making the festival a popular destination for family outings.
Results: The Liwa International Festival has promoted and preserved UAE's cultural heritage through its diverse range of traditional sports and cultural activities. The festival has enhanced tourism in the Al Dhafra region, attracting thousands of visitors both locally and internationally. This has led to increased economic benefits for the local community. Additionally, the festival has fostered community engagement and cultural exchange, providing a platform for showcasing Emirati traditions and fostering a sense of national pride.
Recommandations: The evaluation of the Liwa International Festival has highlighted its substantial impact on sports and tourism in the region. Since its inception in 2004, the festival has grown significantly, attracting motorsport enthusiasts and showcasing traditional camel and horse sports. By January 2023, the festival had attracted 283,988 participants, including both local residents and international tourists, and 114,442 cars, in addition to achieving 271.5 million views on various social media platforms.

Area of Monitoring: Media diversity
Agency Implementation: Ofcom
Main Feature: There are 34 local television services broadcasting across the UK with each service covering a town, city or metropolitan area.    A number of local TV services offer training, learning and development initiatives that aim to provide pathways into the sector for those with protected characteristics. A number of local TV services have also developed programming around equality and diversity, which has benefited communities and is aimed at particular protected characteristic groups within the area or locality in which those services broadcast.    The legislative framework for local TV is the Local Digital Television Programme Services Order 2012, which was made under section 244 of the Communications Act 2003. The statutory objectives for local TV are set out in the 2012 Order and set out the criteria for local TV services. Whilst local TV services must specifically broadcast only within a particular geographic area, they must also meet the needs of the locality their service is received in, bring social or economic benefits to that locality, cater for the tastes and interests of those living or working in the locality, broaden the range of programmes available, increase the number and range of programmes about the locality and those made in the locality.
Results: Local TV services are an important part of the wider broadcasting ecosystem and deliver a number of benefits, which include contributing to media plurality and diversity of programming with the provision of local news and content (particularly to those audiences who may be digitally excluded), engaging local communities, preserving a shared ‘local voice’ in communities and providing training and learning opportunities for those seeking industry experience.
Recommandations: Ofcom, as the regulator responsible for local TV,monitors and reports on matters related to local TV licence holders and sector stakeholders more broadly. Licence holders report to Ofcom annually and Ofcom continues to review the performance of licence holders on an ad hoc basis alongside standard monitoring of compliance with licence conditions. This monitoring includes whether licence holders are meeting their programming commitments, which are built upon the statutory objectives for local TV.

Title EN: Longitudinal research (April 2020 – May 2022): Slovenian Cultural and Creative Worker in Times of COVID-19
Goal: Promote Human Rights And Fundamental Freedoms
SDG: SDG 5 - Achieve gender equality and empower all women and girls,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels
Area of Monitoring: Artistic freedom
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: Poligon, Institute for development of creative industries
Main Feature: The cultural and creative sectors (CCS) were among those hardest-hit by the COVID-19 crisis. This prompted the team of Poligon to immediately take on longitudinal tracking of its effect on cultural and creative workers in Slovenia. Based on the research, which included four surveys  (spring and autumn 2020, spring 2021 and spring 2022)  with 4.459 respondents from the ranks of Slovenian cultural and creative workers, focused on the analysis of the characteristics of non-work and business during the time of the epidemic, the views and coping mechanisms of the workers and their chances of getting through it. This study, funded by the Slovenian Centre for Creativity, is unique, as the cultural and creative sectors are the only ones in Slovenia with such detailed data on the impact of the epidemic. Moreover, no other country in Europe has carried out a comparable longitudinal study for the cultural and creative sectors. The four surveys conducted thus far included over 10% of the total active population of creative and cultural workers.  The initial purpose of the now three-year long study was to carry out diagnostics to see the extent of damage caused by the COVID-19 epidemic in our two sectors. In the course of the four surveys, numerous interim debates and deep reflection, it was becoming clear that focusing merely on the impact of the epidemic on the work and life of workers in the cultural and creative sectors would not suffice. The wounds in the two sectors run much deeper and were not inflicted by the epidemic alone. This last crisis merely accentuated them further. The chronic precariousness of the two sectors, the grinding poverty and – discussed here for the first time – the disturbing practices of public cultural institutions are all problems predating the virus. And yes, everyone in the two sectors knows practically everything about all these issues. But what is new in this study is that, for the first time, these problems were being translated into numbers so that someone who is not in sectors circles and has the (political) power to tackle these problematic practices can put themselves in the shoes of workers in the cultural and creative sectors.  A chain is as strong as its weakest link. Statistics show that every other link in the chain of workers in the cultural and creative sectors in Slovenia is weak. Every other link could notafford to replace their work equipment if it broke. Every other link earns up to 1,000 euros per month, which is only just above or even below the poverty line. Every other link cannot live a decent life without the help of their loved ones, particularly in a time of growing inflation and energy crisis. Most of these weakest links are precarious workers in the private, independent part of the industry.   However, their contribution in content is essential to the industry’s operation. It is a paradox that many stronger links in the chain are highly dependent on their production, yet they are often their biggest exploiters. Unethical collaboration practices are the industry’s original sin. This sin was not caused by the COVID-19 crisis, nor the right-wing government; these exploitation practices are ingrained in the very essence of how public cultural institutions work. Public institutions provide poor or zero payment for 40% of their outsourced work performed by artists and other profiles. The issues of poverty and labor exploitation in the two sectors cannot be resolved without also identifying the (in)formal power cliques. While the unlimited terms of management positions in the public part of the cultural and creative sectors can enable a stable and continuous operation at a high level, it may also promote only certain collaborations and the exposure of only certain topics. Relying on the responsible self-limitation of managers is not producing the desired effects; a systemic regulation is needed in order to open public cultural institutions.   Furthermore, only two out of ten private entities in the two sectors have predominantly public funding, which debunks the myth about the artists being dependent on the state and points to the inaccessibility of funding. The generation-based analysis shows that the economic situation of most cultural workers has not improved over time, which is quite discouraging and disconcerting. Even though administration likes to classify them into specific fields, our data shows that cultural workers are clear hybrids, most of whom work in more than one subfield, many even in three or more.
Results: The longitudinal research Slovenian Cultural and Creative Worker in Times of COVID-19 is the most widely recognized and cited CCS study in Slovenian media since independence. The study developed an arsenal of measures to be introduced to correct economic, generational, social and other inequalities in the two sectors, to free the two sectors from the grip of poverty and provide the workers with decent working conditions and fair payment.  Given the aforementioned turbulent political atmosphere in Slovenia described by The New York Times in 2021 as »a cultural war«, which led many cultural workers to occupy the streets in protest since April 2020, the effect of the first three studies was to equip the right-wing government opposition and experts with extensive data to demand the implementation of the measures to save the impoverished Slovenian CCS. In 2022 when appointed by the National Assembly, newly elected Minister of Culture, Asta Vrečko, cited the study among the documents to direct the future cultural politics in Slovenia.  In October 2022 a new trade union representing freelance workers in the cultural sector called ZASUK has been officially founded to improve the social security of freelancers and achieve fundamental change in how such workers are treated. The union which is now already in the process of negotiating a collective contract with the Ministry of Culture was co-funded by Poligon as a direct consequence of the research findings and workers organizing.

Title EN: Maihi Karauna – The Crown’s Strategy for Māori Language Revitalisation 2019–2023
Goal: Integrate Culture In Sustainable Development Frameworks
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: National sustainable development policies and plans
Cultural Domain: Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music
Agency Implementation: Te Puni Kōkiri Ministry of Māori Development  Te Taura Whiri i te Reo Māori (Māori Language Commission)
Main Feature: Describe the main features of the policy/measure:  Te Whare o Te Reo Mauriora, the House of the Living Language, is an active partnership between the Government, iwi and Māori. The intent of this partnership is established through Te Ture mō Te Reo Māori 2016, the Māori Language Act 2016, (s6(2)) to support the revitalisation of te reo Māori (s3). The vision for Te Whare o Te Reo Mauriora is Kia mauri ora te reo Māori – May the Māori language survive/thrive.  The features of Te Whare o Te Reo Mauriora are modelled on a traditional wharenui (meeting house) and represent important members and aspects of the partnership model.  There are two maihi (gables of the meeting house) that represent each side of the whare for the partners of te reo Māori revitalisation – the Maihi Māori strategy and the Maihi Karauna strategy.   Te Ture mō Te Reo Māori 2016 requires the Government to issue a Māori language strategy, the Maihi Karauna. This strategy sets out the Government’s objectives and policies relevant to the revitalisation of the Māori language, as well as the long-term strategic direction. The Maihi Karauna Strategy focuses on a macro-level approach with the aim to create the societal conditions for te reo Māori to thrive in Aotearoa New Zealand. After its launch in 2019, a draft of the first Maihi Karauna implementation plan was developed and released by Te Puni Kōkiri Ministry of Māori Development. Te Taura Whiri i te Reo Māori (the Māori Language Commission) have led the coordination of the Maihi Karauna implementation.  The Maihi Karauna sets out three audacious goals to achieve by 2040: •	85% of New Zealanders (or more) will value te reo Māori as a key part of national identity. •	One million New Zealanders (or more) will have the ability and confidence to talk about at least basic things in te reo Māori. •	150,000 Māori aged 15 and over will use te reo Māori as much as English. The Crown has three key outcomes: •	Aotearoatanga - te reo Māori is valued by Aotearoa whānui as a central part of national identity. •	Mātauranga - Aotearoa whānui has increased levels of knowledge, skill and proficiency in te reo Māori. •	Hononga - Aotearoa whānui is able to engage with te reo Māori.  Te Ture mō Te Reo Māori 2016 requires Te Mātāwai to lead the development of a Maihi Māori strategy. The Maihi Māori is complimentary to the Maihi Karauna strategy and focusses on the micro-level goals and activities for community, whānau (family), hapū (sub-tribes), and iwi (tribes). The Maihi Māori is convened by Te Mātāwai, in accordance with Te Ture mō Te Reo Māori 2016 Māori Language Act 2016.
Results: The Maihi Karauna Annual Report 2022/23 shows that agencies are increasingly contributing to implementation of the Maihi Karauna strategy. Key findings are: •	Te reo Māori lessons, signage and use is normalised across the agencies •	Māori staff are not always relied on (unless in a specific role), and non-Māori take the lead •	There is a growing number of agencies that push te reo Māori in all business activities, for example all staff karakia each week, or twice a week.  •	31 of 33 agencies have Māori language plans and language plans are often included in plans to increase Māori-Crown relations capability •	Almost every agency celebrated Te Wiki o te Reo Māori, Māori language week •	Monitoring of language plans is still not consistent across the agencies and there is a need to address capacity and capability in te reo Māori teaching/training to meet increasing demand and maintain momentum and motivation.
Financial Ressources: Investment in initiatives that contribute to Maihi Karauna, The Crown’s Strategy for Māori Language Revitalisation, is spread across agencies and is not directly reported.
Recommandations: The Formative Evaluation of the Maihi Karauna 2021/2022 found that agencies faced challenges in implementing the strategy – there was confusion about roles and who was leading and agencies were required to do a lot of work within their current baselines. New funding through Budget 2019 and Budget 2021 meant that Te Taura Whiri i te Reo Māori (the Māori Language Commission) is now able to better fulfil its coordination role to implement the Maihi Karauna strategy.   Despite the challenges, the evaluation found that agencies were improving their understanding of the Maihi Karauna strategy and how they can contribute to it. There was also increasing collaboration between agencies and 31 of the 33 agencies have a Māori language plan. Agencies are also regularly attending Chief Executive forums.  The Formative Evaluation recommended the following improvements: •	The next Maihi Karauna strategy (2023-2027) should be developed with active participation from all key agencies, with consideration for the broader vision, the Maihi Māori and the different priorities of agencies  •	Commence cross-agency meetings to revisit the strategic direction and buy-in from the governance level   •	Revise the implementation plan and approach, so that there is an overarching implementation plan  •	Restrict the Maihi Karauna implementation plan activities to deliberate and targeted ones for agencies rather than core business ones •	Consider the inclusion of other priority groups outside the public sector •	Ensure Maihi Karauna implementation plan activities encourage active and meaningful collaboration between agencies on a common purpose  •	Ensure agencies routinely report on activities  •	Ensure that core agencies have adequate resourcing to be able to implement the strategy.

It articulates the enablers that will propel the country towards achieving economic independence, inclusive wealth creation, self-reliance and a high quality of life for all its citizens. Title EN: MARCHE DES ARTS DU SPECTACLE D'ABIDJAN(MASA)

Area of Monitoring: Flow of cultural goods and services
Agency Implementation: MASA
Main Feature: Le Marché des Arts du Spectacle d'Abidjan (MASA) est un événement culturel biennal qui vise à promouvoir les arts du spectacle en  Côte d’Ivoire et en Afrique et à renforcer les échanges culturels internationaux. Il offre une plateforme pour les artistes, les producteurs, et les professionnels de l'industrie culturelle pour se rencontrer, échanger et collaborer. Le MASA comprend des spectacles, des ateliers, des conférences et des rencontres professionnelles, favorisant ainsi la mobilité des artistes et l'exportation des biens et services culturels africains. Les principales caractéristiques de la politique sont fondées sur l’aide à la création, à la promotion, à la mobilité et à la création de réseau de travail et de développement culturel. Le MASA allie bourse d’échanges, plateforme de réseautage, espace d’expression artistique et professionnel et cadre de formation aux métiers des arts de la scène. Le MASA dédie à la jeunesse deux programmes spécifiques que sont les activités Jeunes publics (programmation de spectacles crées et dédiés à ce public, création de Village artistiques pour enfants) et le MASA Zone Street Arts exécuté par les jeunes acteurs et promoteurs culturels africains. Ce projet vise à fédérer et valoriser en réseau les créations des jeunes artistes du domaine des cultures urbaines. La sélection des artistes est fondée sur les propositions artistiques des jeunes artistes émergents.  La 13 ème édition du MASA d’Abidjan s'est déroulé du 13 au 20 avril 2024 à Abidjan autour du thème : « jeunesse, innovation et entreprenariat : des leviers pour le développement des industries des arts du spectacle africain ». Son lancement a eu lieu le jeudi 04 avril 2024 en présence de membres du corps diplomatique, d’acteurs du secteur des Arts et de la Culture et de la presse nationale et internationale. Pour cette édition, le Rwanda et la République de Corée du Sud étaient respectivement  les  pays à l’honneur et  invité spécial.
Results: Le MASA a réussi à attirer des milliers de participants internationaux, renforçant ainsi la visibilité des artistes africains sur la scène mondiale. Il a facilité de nombreux partenariats et contrats internationaux pour les artistes et les professionnels de la culture, contribuant à la croissance économique et culturelle du continent africain. il a également contribuer au développement des créations artistiques, plus de mobilités des artistes africains programmés au MASA, plus de collaboration artistique, plus d’acteurs des métiers des arts ivoiriens, africains formés aux métiers des arts de la scène. En 2024 : 300 spectacles présentés/2000 artistes programmés/150 contrats signés/ 600 artistes et opérateurs formés.
Financial Ressources: 2 milliard de francs CFA soit  environ 3267974 USD
Recommandations: L'évaluation a montré que le MASA est un événement important pour la promotion des arts du spectacle en  Côte d'Ivoire et en Afrique. Les recommandations incluent l'augmentation des financements pour les artistes émergents, l'amélioration des infrastructures de spectacle, et le renforcement des programmes de formation pour les professionnels de l'industrie culturelle. L’impact économique du MASA tant pour les acteurs culturels que pour le secteur économique classique (transport, hôtellerie, restauration,…) est établi. Son rôle dans le développement de carrière et le renforcement des capacités des opérateurs culturels est primordial. Le MASA est également un acteur de structuration du spectacle vivant en Afrique.

Title EN: Measures that Monitor Women Participation in Cultural/Creative Economy Life
Goal: Promote Human Rights And Fundamental Freedoms
SDG: SDG 5 - Achieve gender equality and empower all women and girls,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels
Area of Monitoring: Gender equality
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: 1. Ministry of Tourism and Creative Economy/Tourism and Creative Economy Agency 2. Ministry of Women Empowerment and Child Protection  3. Statistics Indonesia
Main Feature: In the past four years, measures that monitor women participation in cultural/creative economy life include: 1. Social Cultural Statistics; 2. Tourism and Creative Economy Manpower Statistics; 3. Creative Economy Statistics; 4. Gender Development Index; 5. Gender Empowerment Index; 6. Gender Inequality Index; 7. Human Development Index; 8. Culture Development Index (Indeks Pembangunan Kebudayaan, IPK); and 9. Gender-based Human Development Books.  Almost all measures to monitor women participation in cultural/creative economy life reported in the 2020 QPR, apart from the Creative Economy Book, are still ongoing while drafting this report. The Creative Economy Book itself was last published in 2016. The Creative Economy Statistics was then published in 2020 as a replacement. Then, in the latest development, the 2018-2022 Tourism and Creative Economy Manpower Statistics was published (see Goal 1, Policies and Measures on Information Systems and Cultural Statistics Used in Policy Development). These three books resulted from the collaboration between Kemenparekraf and BPS, presenting categories of data and information similar to the results from BPS processing of the National Work Force Survey.  This measure provides additional information to the Data on Women's Participation in Cultural Life reported in the 2020 QPR. It summarizes data related to the women workforce in the creative economy sector from the publication of the Tourism and Creative Economy Manpower Statistics.  A critical step in monitoring women participation in cultural/creative economy life is through the 2021 Social Cultural Statistics (see Goal 1, Policies and Measures on Information Systems and Cultural Statistics Used in Policy Development). This book includes data on women participation in various aspects of culture, such as access to information, social interaction, and involvement in culture advancement objects.  The 2020 Creative Economy Statistics combined data from various sources to provide a complete picture of Indonesia's creative economy development, including women's contribution. This book states that in 2020, the creative economy sector absorbed many women workers, especially in the fashion, culinary, and craft subsectors. Title EN: Measures that Provide Funds for CSO Capacity Development
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Partnering with civil society
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: 1. Ministry of Education, Culture, Research, and Technology 2. Ministry of Finance  3. Education Fund Management Institution  4. State Film Productions
Main Feature: In the past four years, measures that provide funds for CSO capacity development include: 1. Dana Indonesiana;  2. Innovative Productive Research Funding Program (Program Pendanaan Riset Inovatif Produktif, RISPRO); and 3. Indonesia Film Financing (IFF).  Dana Indonesiana, or the Endowment Fund for Culture, is a mandate of Law 5 of 2017 on Culture Advancement (see Goal 1, Specific Policies that Regulate Culture and/or Creative Economy Sectors). In the 2020 QPR, Indonesia reported plans to create a cultural endowment fund to facilitate cultural advancement initiatives from the community. The endowment fund mechanism was chosen so that government assistance in the cultural sector no longer has to depend on budget availability in the National and/or Regional Revenue and Expenditure Budget and can use financial mechanisms that are not as rigid as the typical state financial management.  Dana Indonesiana itself was launched by Kemendikbudristek together with Kemenkeu on March 23, 2022, as an integrated grant service program in the culture sector for: (1) facilitation in the culture sector; (2) facilitation in the cultural field of cultural interaction; (3) institutional support for cultural organizations; (4) utilization of public space; (5) stimulant of cultural expression activities; (6) documentation of the maestro's work/knowledge; (7) creation of innovative creative works; (8) work assistance funds for international distribution; (9) study of culture advancement objects; (10) microcinema; and (11) scholarships for cultural actors. This program, which Kemendikbudristek jointly manages through the Museum and Cultural Heritage Public Service Institution and Kemenkeu through the LPDP Public Service Institution, integrates three sources of funds for grants for cultural activities, namely: (1) Facilitation in the Field of Culture (2) Endowment Fund for Culture, and (3) Endowment Fund for Education. To ensure fair access for all, Dana Indonesia has a particular affirmation policy for female cultural actors and cultural actors from disadvantaged, frontier, and outermost areas when selecting beneficiaries.  Furthermore, regarding LPDP, as the manager of endowment funds to fund scholarships, this institution has a RISPRO funding program with the themes "Tourism and Creative Economy Development" and "Social Humanities - Arts and Culture - Education." LPDP financial management is guided by the policies established by the LPDP Board of Trustees consisting of the Minister of Education, Culture, Research and Technology, the Minister of Finance, and the Minister of Religious Affairs.  Lastly, IFF is a program organized by PFN to provide funding solutions for film producers in Indonesia. This program offers more accessible and flexible funding for film producers and potential profits for investors interested in investing in the film industry. PFN prioritizes films whose contents fit cultural and national values ​​in the four pillars of Indonesian nationality: NKRI, UUD 1945, Pancasila, and Bhinneka Tunggal Ika. Films that receive funding are expected to enlighten, educate, and entertain the Indonesian people and have global influence.  In general, measures that provide funds for CSO capacity development are aimed at contributing to achieving the following agenda(s) of the National Strategy for Culture: 1. Utilize objects of culture advancement to improve people's welfare (Agenda 4);  2. Institutional reform and culture budgeting to support the culture advancement agenda (Agenda 6); and 3. Strengthen the role of the government as a facilitator of culture advancement (Agenda 7).
Results: Dana Indonesiana: 1. In 2020, 63 recipients of funds were involved in public space utilization, 80 in creating innovative, creative works, and 45 in documenting the maestros' work/knowledge. 2. In 2021, 82 recipients of funds were involved in public space utilization, 30 in creating innovative, creative works, and 16 in documenting the maestro's work/knowledge. 3. In 2022, 30 recipients of funds were involved in public space utilization and 9 in documenting the maestro's work/knowledge.  IFF: In 2023, of the 37 production houses that applied, two of them received approval from PFN.
Financial Ressources: Dana Indonesiana:  1. Total funds for 2022 were IDR 3 trillion / 182.723.400,00 USD; 2. Total funds for 2023 were IDR 5 trillion / 304.539.000,00 , with a maximum utilization of around IDR 200 billion/12.180.980,00; 3. Projected funds for 2024 are IDR 7trillion / 426.334.300,00 USD .  IFF: Total funds for 2023 were IDR 4.75 billion / 289.228,45 USD
Recommandations: Dana Indonesiana:  Evaluations by Koalisi Seni on establishing the cultural endowment fund and managing Dana Indonesiana resulted in the following conclusions/recommendations.  1. According to Gumay (2022): a. Based on discussions between stakeholders and the President while participating in the Indonesian Culture Congress, the President stated that he would allocate a budget of IDR 5 trillion / 306,498,500,00 USD as initial capital to establish the Cultural Endowment Fund. However, the 2020 National Revenue and Expenditure Budget (Anggaran Pendapatan dan Belanja Negara, APBN) only budgeted IDR 1 trillion / 61,299,700,00 USD  and then only increased to IDR 2 trillion / 122,599,400,00 USD  in the 2021 APBN. b. Another problem is that the Central Government has not yet established an institution to manage the Cultural Endowment Fund. Without this institution, artists and arts and culture activists cannot feel the benefits of the allocated funds in the APBN. c. Koalisi Seni proposes an endowment fund as the most appropriate management method to ensure the Cultural Endowment Fund's sustainability. d. Koalisi Seni proposes a Public Service Institution as an institutional form for managing these funds, free from rigid bureaucratic and financial mechanisms like ordinary work units in ministries. e. Koalisi Seni suggests forming a board of trustees consisting of elements of arts and culture activists as a form of benefit-sharing mechanism to select funding application proposals objectively.  2. According to Putri (2023): a. The main problems with arts and culture funding from public funds are the small availability of funds, the rigid government budget cycle for dynamic arts and culture activities, the low transparency of recipient selection mechanisms, and the lack of funding allocation for activities other than exhibitions. b. To advance culture optimally, a stable, sustainable public fund management system that is not tied to the government budget cycle and is transparent and accommodating to the needs of arts and culture actors is very much needed. c. In 2023, Kemenkeu plans to increase the budget for Dana Indonesiana to reach IDR 5 trillion /  306,501,000,00 USD  according to the President's initial commitment. d. Before the Endowment Fund for Culture was established, Kemendikbudristek had begun testing the distribution mechanism through the Facilitation in the Field of Culture from 2020 to 2021 using grant allocations from the APBN. e. In 2022, funds distributed to arts and cultural actors through Dana Indonesiana were estimated to reach IDR 200 billion/12,260,040,00 USD , with more than 300 individual and institutional recipients in 34 provinces in Indonesia. Most of them were cultural arts practitioners in Java. f. The first main problem is the management of information, awareness-raising, and workshops which were less transparent, accurate, and effective in helping arts and cultural actors through all stages of Dana Indonesiana. Important information that had not been adequately disseminated were: (1) funding sources, (2) preparation of Cost Budget Plans, (3) technical instructions, (4) use of eRISPRO in preparing reports, and (5) list of annual fund recipients from each category along with the resulting knowledge products. g. The second main problem was inadequate human resources at the central and regional government levels. Institutional adjustments at LPDP and Kemendikbudristek are essential to optimize services by establishing new directorates at LPDP and a Public Service Institution with dedicated staff for Dana Indonesiana at Kemendikbudristek. Meanwhile, at the regional level, verifiers from the Cultural Preservation Center in each work area need training and increased personnel to equalize service quality.  References: Gumay, H. Title EN: Mise en place du programme « Tfanen » : appui au secteur culturel et créatif en Tunisie
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: Le Ministère des affaires culturelles (MAC): structure hôte du programme. - Le British Council
Main Feature: Le programme Tfanen (« Sois créatif » en tunisien) est un programme d’appui au secteur culturel et créatif en Tunisie entre 2016 et 2022 financé par l’UE avec un budget de 9.7 millions d’euros et mené par le British Council au nom du pôle EUNIC (réseau des instituts culturels de l’UE établis en Tunisie). Il a pour objectif principal d’accompagner les dynamiques culturelles et démocratiques de la société tunisienne à travers :  •	Le financement direct des opérateurs associatifs et privés. •	La consolidation des compétences et la professionnalisation des praticiens. (nes) de la culture. •	La modernisation des politiques culturelles nationales tout en prenant en considération la diversité des expressions culturelles qui se manifeste, au sens de l’article 4 de la convention de 2005 notamment, à travers « divers modes de création artistique, de production, de diffusion, de distribution et de jouissance des expressions culturelles, quelques soient les moyens et les technologies utilisés... ». Tfanen a ciblé l’équilibre entre les priorités socioculturelles des territoires et la professionnalisation du secteur culturel tunisien, ainsi que la promotion de la richesse des territoires, d’identification, de compréhension et de proximité avec les acteurs culturels régionaux, ce qui a  permis,  toujours dans l’esprit de la convention 2005 et conformément à ses principes directeurs (article 2), la découverte de plusieurs pépites culturelles et donné naissance à des projets prometteurs dans des zones vulnérables selon des critères de développement.  Le programme de subventions de Tfanen a ciblé des catégories distinctes de bénéficiaires : les organisations de la société civile, les organisations artistiques indépendantes, les entreprises culturelles et les établissements publics opérant dans les secteurs de la culture. Les opérateurs ont divers niveaux de maturité, la plupart d’entre eux ayant une existence relativement récente (maximum une dizaine d’années), une identité, positionnement ou vision stratégique encore dans ses débuts, et des expériences d’envergure très différentes.  Tfanen a déployé, dans sa première phase essentiellement une activité de subvention de projets par appels à propositions couplé d’un accompagnement technique des bénéficiaires. A partir de la deuxième phase du programme, commencée en 2019 et concrétisée sur les années 2020, 2021, 2022, le projet s’est enrichi de nouvelles activités, qui ont permis de répondre d’une façon plus équilibrée à certains besoins spécifiques du secteur. Les grands axes d’intervention de Tfanen dans sa deuxième phase sont : 1.	Renforcement des opérateurs (Soutien financier direct : Subventions) 2.	Professionnalisation (Programme de professionnalisation Tfanen Takwin) 3.	Renforcement institutionnel (Initiative Services Publics- ISP) 4.	Renforcement de compétences et réseautage (Labs) 5.	Appui au financement de projets et partenariats internationaux (Europe créative) •	Le projet « Tfanen Takwin » est un cycle d’une année de formation pour les professionnels du secteur culturel en Tunisie, articulé autour d’enseignements théoriques et pratiques, se concluant par un stage dans une structure culturelle tunisienne et un autre dans une structure européenne. Il est mis en œuvre par l’Institut Goethe en coordination avec le pôle EUNIC. Il s’adresse à des professionnels du secteur culturel. Il comporte des modules de formation dans différents domaines touchant la gestion culturelle, le patrimoine, les technologies digitales, etc., ainsi que des stages obligatoires, où chaque apprenant a passé un mois d’immersion dans une structure culturelle européenne et un mois dans une structure tunisienne. Le bilan de « Tfanen Takwin » totalise 20 apprenants, tous des professionnels travaillant dans le secteur culturel, ayant suivi le cycle de formation.  •	L’initiative Services Publics a été conçue et menée en étroite collaboration avec le MAC. Elle s’adresse principalement aux acteurs et opérateurs culturels publics afin d’instaurer de nouveaux modes de gouvernance, indispensables pour renforcer le secteur et le réformer. 13 projets ont été soutenus, tous répondant à des demandes issues d’un appel à projets interne au MAC, au bénéfice du ministère et de ses structures dépendantes (les établissements sectoriels sous tutelle). •	Les laboratoires de consolidation de compétences, d’apprentissage et partage (Labs) ont été conçus comme des cycles d’échange, réunissant chacun une trentaine d’opérateurs provenant de structures publiques, associations, monde artistique/culturel ou secteur privé, au niveau d’une région ou bien autour d’une thématique spécifique. Ces Labs intégraient des activités de renforcement de compétences en programmation et gestion de projets, avec des travaux en groupe, développement des échanges et réseautage de participants, avec une vision de pré-incubation de projets concrets.
Results: Les résultats atteints à travers la mise en place de cette mesure cadrent parfaitement avec les objectifs et les principes directeurs véhiculés par la convention 2005 sur la protection et la promotion de la diversité des expressions culturelles : •	Les organisations de la société civile (OSC) impliquées dans le projet, ont créé des collaborations productives, durables et créatives avec des opérateurs culturels publics et privés, et amélioré leur capacité à proposer et à gérer des subventions pour offrir des produits culturels innovants ;  •	Les organismes publics décentralisés, culturels ou autres, ont renforcé leur collaboration avec les opérateurs culturels et leur compréhension/appréhension de leurs besoins, menant à des partenariats, à un soutien renforcé et à une valorisation par la culture des infrastructures publiques locales ;  •	Un nombre accru de citoyens, notamment des filles/femmes et des jeunes, et particulièrement dans les zones prioritaires, ont participé ou assisté à des initiatives culturelles locales, en raison de l'amélioration de l'accès à la culture et à l'information culturelle ;  •	Les jeunes artistes impliqués dans le projet ont vu leurs niveaux d’information, capacités, savoir-faire et réseaux renforcés suite à leur participation au projet ;  •	Les entreprises privées – à vocation culturelle – impliquées dans le projet, ont établi des collaborations durables avec des opérateurs culturels publics et de la société civile, et ont renforcé leur capacité et la pérennité de leurs actions ;  •	Des plateformes numériques culturelles existantes ont amélioré la qualité et la portée de leurs produits, soutenant ainsi l'accès à l’information sur la culture tunisienne à destination d'un public national et international ;  •	Le patrimoine et le tourisme culturel en Tunisie sont mieux valorisés grâce à l'amélioration de l'expérience des visiteurs et à l'amélioration de l'accessibilité et des collaborations productives sont établies entre les sites cibles et les acteurs locaux. Les statistiques tirées du système de monitoring et suivi de "Tfanen" sont largement positives et confirment des impacts avérés dans la démocratisation de l’accès à la culture et la décentralisation/délocalisation des activités culturelles : Sur le plan du développement culturel et social local :  •	"Tfanen" a permis, à travers les projets financés, l’organisation de 428 évènements culturels publics répartis sur tout le territoire national et adressés en particulier au public cible du programme (59% enfants et jeunes et 52% femmes) ;  •	47 projets (54%) menés par les organismes financés par "Tfanen" sont réalisés dans des régions défavorisées (selon des critères de développement) ;  •	Plus de 150.000 personnes ont participé à ces différents évènements culturels publics, avec un niveau de satisfaction sur leur qualité très élevée exprimé par les participants dans les sondages post-évènement ;  •	32,1% des participants aux évènements culturels publics proviennent des régions défavorisées, et seulement 12,1% du grand Tunis;  •	Les projets bénéficiaires d’une subvention "Tfanen" ont permis l’organisation de 426 ateliers éducatifs et culturels couvrant plusieurs domaines, notamment le théâtre, le cinéma, la musique, les arts plastiques, les débats, les marionnettes, le leadership et la gestion culturels, le chant et la création de caricatures ;  •	Plus de 13.000 participants (principalement des enfants et des jeunes) ont bénéficié de ces ateliers d’éducation artistique ; •	50 projets (57%) impliquent des jeunes artistes à travers une ou plusieurs activités. Au total 897 jeunes artistes ont été impliqués directement (travail rémunérant) ou indirectement (volontariat) dans les projets soutenus. Les femmes représentent 49% des participants aux différents ateliers culturels et éducatifs organisés et 52% des participants aux évènements culturels ;  Sur le plan de professionnalisation des opérateurs : •	"Tfanen" a organisé 29 séminaires et ateliers de formation en faveur de 211 organisations culturelles (avec la participation de 680 personnes) sur des sujets pertinents (encadrement en préparation de dossiers de candidature complète, formation en protection des enfants, workshops de suivi et évaluation).  •	85,7% des participants jugent qu’un savoir-faire a été acquis et 92,3% recommanderaient une formation de "Tfanen" à un professionnel de la culture. Sur le plan de la structuration sectorielle :  •	Établissement de nouvelles collaborations et partenariats (environ 400) dans le cadre des projets, jugés stratégiques et de bonne qualité avec des indices de maturité et durabilité intéressants. •	La professionnalisation des opérateurs culturels et des artistes et particien.(nes) de la culture est renforcée, plus adaptée à leurs besoins concrets, •	Les capacités opérationnelles et institutionnelles du MAC sont renforcées et mieux adaptées aux exigences nouvelles imposées par la transformation numérique et les enjeux liés aux nouvelles technologies de communication, •	L’accès à la culture dans ses expressions diverses est relancé et amélioré à travers notamment l’appropriation de l’action culturelle par les populations locales surtout par les enfants, les jeunes et les femmes dans les zones les plus défavorisées.
Financial Ressources: 9.7 millions d’euros
Recommandations: -	En 2021, "Tfanen" est considéré, au terme d’une sélection parmi 700 projets, comme une bonne pratique par les nations unis pour sa contribution aux objectifs de développement durable (ODD). (Voir le lien suivant:https://sdgs.un.org/partnerships/tfanen-tunisie-creative-strengthening-cultural-sector-tunisia).  -	La clôture de "Tfanen" a été célébrée les 9 et 10 Mai 2022 à la cité de la culture dans le cadre de la semaine de l’Europe dans un format inédit «Tfanen Days » alliant débats, ateliers d’échange, rencontres et réseautage grâce à des sessions d’entreprenariat créatif et ce, en présence des partenaires tunisiens et européens ayant conjointement admis que l’objectif principal de "Tfanen" a été atteint dans le sens où il a été possible de créer un écosystème vivant et viable dans le secteur créatif et de promouvoir la diversité culturelle et l’accès à la culture à l’échelle nationale régionale et internationale.  -	D’après le rapport d’évaluation finale du programme d'appui au secteur de la culture en Tunisie (PACT), les principales conclusions sont :  Sur le plan de professionnalisation des opérateurs du secteur : •	Les méthodes de travail et les exigences contractuelles de "Tfanen" ont permis de soutenir et renforcer des opérateurs de toute taille (émergents et plus structurés), contribuant à leur développement de compétences organisationnelles et opérationnelles de façon concrète. Le développement des compétences en matière de gestion et planification stratégique, de suivi-évaluation des résultats, problématique permanente dans le secteur créatif et culturel de beaucoup des pays de la région, a été largement couvert et réussi avec l’approche "Tfanen".  Sur le plan du développement culturel et social local : •	A travers les projets subventionnés, "Tfanen" a largement dynamisé le secteur culturel au niveau local et régional, en développant des activités culturelles de proximité et diversifiant l’offre culturelle, notamment dans les régions défavorisées et reculées, et en faveur de publics plus vulnérables. "Tfanen" a contribué d’une manière directe et à court terme à l’employabilité des jeunes.  •	Les projets ont facilité la création de 546 emplois à temps partiel ou à temps plein rémunérés par les associations et de 207 emplois rémunérés par les entreprises. Pour ce qui est du public cible prioritaire, Tfanen a facilité une action positive envers les jeunes et les femmes. Pour des groupes plus vulnérables (handicapés, jeunes en difficulté etc.), "Tfanen" a accompagné quelques projets remarquables adressés à des collectifs à besoins spécifiques (ex : Massart, Théâtre pour la tolérance, etc....). Sur le plan de la structuration sectorielle :  L’impact au niveau plus structurel a été fortement ralenti par la crise covid-19, qui a minimisé considérablement les nouvelles orientations et actions programmées par "Tfanen". Cependant, des dynamiques très positives sont visibles et à capitaliser. "Tfanen" a encouragé et contribué à l’établissement de nouvelles collaborations culturelles efficaces comme moteur d’une structuration durable du secteur au niveau local : •	La majorité des projets "Tfanen" ont travaillé en partenariat ou construit des collaborations avec des partenaires assez diverses (institutions publiques et secteur associatif et privé confondu). Les associations confirment l’établissement de nouvelles collaborations et partenariats (environ 400) dans le cadre de leurs projets, jugés stratégiques et de bonne qualité pour le succès du projet ;  •	Une consultation post-projet menée par "Tfanen" sur 21 projets montre que sur les 81 partenariats développés, 76 ont été maintenus dans d’autres projets culturels (94% des partenariats), affichent des indices de maturité et durabilité intéressants. Pour ce qui est plus concrètement des partenariats public-privé dans la culture, la collaboration avec des partenaires publics décentralisés encouragée par "Tfanen" représente un moteur de structuration de l’action culturelle, plus active et durable, au niveau local. Un nombre important de projets ont passé des conventions de partenariat avec les autorités ou intégré les organismes publics de manière cohérente lors de la mise en œuvre des projets. Les établissements publics se sont engagés progressivement de façon plus rapprochée dans l’accompagnent des projets Tfanen, avec des appuis variables, allant de la simple facilitation des actions, la mise à disposition d’espaces de travail ou des apports en nature, a l’appui technique et financier dans certains cas. 39 associations et entreprises culturelles bénéficiaires (44% du total des bénéficiaires) ont utilisé des espaces publics décentralisés pour l’organisation de leurs évènements culturels et 10 espaces publics existants ont été réaménagés et renouvelés afin d’en faire des points d’accès à la culture pour le public local. Cette forte implication des projets dans l’animation des maisons des jeunes, des bibliothèques, des théâtres communaux, de centres culturels et musées, ont certainement contribué à améliorer qualitativement et quantitativement la programmation de ces établissements.  •	Une enquête réalisée auprès des structures ayant terminé les projets subventionnés révèle que ces structures sont toujours opérationnelles. Toutes les structures ayant été contactées étaient encore en vie. Il est difficile de quantifier la place des subventions et du soutien technique de "Tfanen" dans cette résilience en période de crise, mais les bénéficiaires consultés ont été très nombreux à attribuer au moins partiellement cette dynamique et leur survie même à l’intervention du Programme. Sur la base de l’enquête réalisée :  -	100% des structures sont toujours en activités de 3 et 5 ans après la fin du projet (projets financés en 2017 et 2018) ;  -	81% des structures ont acquis des éléments structurants durant le projet "Tfanen" qui ont servi à renforcer la structure; -	69% des structures bénéficiaires de "Tfanen" ont obtenu des nouveaux financements auprès d’autres institutions/bailleurs de fonds, après la fin du projet financé par "Tfanen".

Title EN: Measuring cultures, the arts and heritage. Annual Report of Cultural Statistics.
Goal: Integrate Culture In Sustainable Development Frameworks
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: National sustainable development policies and plans
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: Ministry of Cultures, Arts and Heritage, National Statistics Institute (INE)
Main Feature: The Cultural Statistics Report is an annual statistical compilation jointly developed by the National Statistics Institute (INE) and the Ministry of Culture, Arts and Heritage (MINCAP), whose purpose is to measure the artistic, cultural and heritage sector in Chile. This annual report presents a summary of important information regarding the artistic, cultural and heritage sector, which is obtained from administrative records of 38 public and private institutions that participate by providing their annual management data to be systematised.   The increasing publication coverage, topic diversity and the comparability over time, constitute a valuable resource for the multidimensional understanding of the sector and for design of evidence-based public policies. The systematisation of annual cultural data and statistics includes different cultural domains (heritage, performing arts, musical arts, visual arts, crafts, among others) and the phases of creation, production, dissemination, value enhancement and use, commercialisation, exhibition, conservation and restoration, and appropriation.   Among them, there are statistics on employment, foreign trade, public budget, competitive funds, art and heritage education, attendance, copyright, among  others. This considers a total of 340 tables and one annual publication. To date, nineteen versions have been published, and the twentieth edition is at the planning stage. Finally, from the 2005 Convention monitoring framework, this strategy is part of the indicator on “policies and measures that support equity in the distribution of cultural resources and inclusive access to such resources”.
Results: The value of this measure to support equity in the distribution of cultural resources and inclusive access to such resources lies, first of all, in the fact that this is the oldest statistic series in the cultural, artistic and heritage field, covering almost 20 years of information. In this way, the instrument makes the relationship between culture and development and its impact on national level, visible.   Regarding the 2005 Convention, it provides information on the diversity of cultural expressions in Chile. In addition, the instrument generates inputs for measuring and assessing cultural public policies and facilitates international comparability. In particular, it is used by civil servants of the Ministry of Cultures, Arts and Heritage (MINCAP) who are in charge of justifying designed plans, programmes, projects and cultural policies; Similarly, by academics, students and those interested in cultural sector knowledge and intellectual observation; Finally, by cultural managers and artists interested in practice and project implementation.   Considering different quantitative data provided by this report, and according to the figures of its latest edition from 2021 (published in 2023), we can highlight that the public budget set aside for culture, corresponded to 0.29% of the total central government budget. On the other hand, creative companies represented 8% of the total number of the national companies in 2021, while workers in the cultural sector make up1.7% of national total.   Finally, regarding the Culture Funds awarded by MINCAP, we can highlight that 78,985 projects applied, for example, in the years 2017-2021, of which 15,651 were selected, covering the requests of 19.8% of total initiative applications.
Recommandations: Year after year, the teams from the National Statistics Institute (INE) and from the Department of Studies of the Undersecretariat of Cultures and the Arts prepare an internal evaluation of the recently published instrument. The recommendations go hand in hand with improving report presentation formats and standardising them, with increasing the number of included informants and statistics, with noting lower quality information, with improving methodology documentation, among others.   However, there is a need to establish a feedback system with the units that use the information from Annual Report in order to incorporate their recommendations and requirements. It is worth mentioning that this quantitative information adds significant value for the formulation and/or reformulation of data-based public policies on culture.

Title EN: Media literacy
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Media diversity
Agency Implementation: Ministry of Culture
Main Feature: The measure aims to develop skills and knowledge that enable citizens to: make informed choices about media content and media services; use media services and media content safely; create media content and participate responsibly, ethically and effectively in different forms of communication.
Results: The amendments to the Law on Radio and Television (in force since 22.12.2020) have introduced specific norms regarding the development of media literacy in Bulgaria. A new competence of the Council for Electronic Media is provided for: to undertake and promote measures and activities aimed at the development of media literacy in society. The Minister of Culture shall initiate and lead the development of a national media literacy policy, which should contain concrete measures for the development of skills and knowledge that enable citizens to make informed choices about media content and media services; to use media services and media content safely; to create media content and to participate responsibly, ethically and effectively in different forms of communication.  The Council for Electronic Media works to develop media literacy in collaboration with a wide range of stakeholders, including the Ministry of Culture, the Ministry of Education and Science and other public authorities, media service providers, academics, civil society organisations and consumers. A Standing Council of Experts on Media Literacy under the Minister of Culture was established by Order of the Minister of Culture in mid-2021, comprising representatives of various institutions and NGOs, including CEM.   In 2022. The Council gathered information on media literacy activities of media service providers:  National public providers BNT and BNR  Bulgarian National Television has launched its own podcast on the topic of media literacy in 2020 - "MeGra". BNT is also taking other measures and developing initiatives in the field of media literacy as part of the ability to think critically and the culture of communication and the ability to show the viewer the true value of media content. BNT has structured a content verification team to monitor for misinformation in on-air and internet news content. Journalists are trained by representatives of the France-Press Agency. The topic of media literacy is also covered as part of the BNT Academy project, which annually trains students from various universities. The media team shows the students the mechanisms for checking news content, how fact-checkers work, how to weed out fake news, what the global experience is and the importance of avoiding hate speech. The BNT plans to produce additional video tutorials on topical issues for young people on the topic of media literacy. It is also planned to strengthen the role of the Youtube channel through talks with experts on the subject. BNT also creates user-generated content on the topic, which is often featured in news programmes and in the news in the form of reports on cyber security, the difference between different types of messages, including commercial, political, etc.  Bulgarian National Radio also has initiatives and actions in the direction of increasing media literacy. BNR has had its own independent fact-checking team since November 2021, which is trained and prepared by fact-checkers from https://factcheck.bg/. The BNR maintains a separate section for this, and professional fact checking of facts and allegations is carried out. The fact-checking team (FET) is made up of journalists working at BNR whose status is regulated by the Broadcasting Act. Members of the EPF receive no funding for their activities other than through their employment with the broadcaster. The guiding principles in the work of the EPF are respect for professional journalistic standards, impartiality, including with regard to political and economic interests, independence from all forms of external influence, honesty, transparency. The EPF adheres to high standards in the verification of allegations and news stories, both in the application of evidence and assessment, without taking sides. The selection of claims and materials for verification is made on the basis of their public relevance and dissemination, regardless of who makes them. The BNR makes efforts to discuss the topic of media literacy not only in its linear programmes, but also in its official digital channels for disseminating information and direct contact with young people - mainly school and university students. Many off-screen initiatives are being implemented, one of them being the collaboration with the See website and their News in Children's Language project. It is planned to expand this project in two directions - increasing the content and the number of programmes included in it. The topic of increasing media literacy is often discussed not only in the main news programme HORIZONT, but also in the cultural and educational programme HRISTO BOTEV - most often in the The Network media programme, but also in programmes such as ArtEfir, What is Happening? and The Voice of the Times. As a programme aimed at a youth audience, RADIO SOFIA seeks to inform adolescents and young people how to safely use different communication channels and the importance of developing their skills and knowledge to be able to make informed choices about media content. Every Saturday morning the programme broadcasts "News in Children's Language" and the team works in collaboration with the Young Journalist Club in Sofia. For more than a year, the Radio Sofia's Little Commentators column has also been broadcast by children members of the club. BNR also implements initiatives in other regional programmes.   The Association of Bulgarian Broadcasters - ABBRO informs that its members individually undertake and further develop measures aimed at the development of knowledge and skills of citizens for informed media choices. In order for citizens to feel involved and actively participate, opportunities are provided by providers to participate in the creation of media content through various forms of communication. A range of online channels and mobile applications are maintained and enriched, allowing audience feedback, comments and recommendations, sending alerts and news about events from anywhere in the country. These are the My News platforms of Nova Broadcasting Group Ltd. and I, the Reporter of BTV Media Group Ltd. ABRBO envisages the creation of a dedicated section on its website to explain in an accessible way media-related topics such as: media ownership, funding, advertising policy, editorial content creation, regulation and the limits of regulation, self-regulation, copyright and related rights.  Actions and initiatives taken by CEM  CEM should work to develop media literacy in collaboration with a wide range of stakeholders, including the Ministry of Culture, the Ministry of Education and Science and other public authorities, media service providers, academics, civil society organisations and consumers. In November 2022, the European Commission will launch a European Media Forum. The Council for Electronic Media organised a large-scale meeting with representatives of the Bulgarian Media Literacy Coalition and other institutions specifically mentioned in the provisions of the Media Literacy Act, as well as organisations working in the field of media literacy, to inform and exchange good practices. Various views were expressed at the meeting on the level of media literacy in Bulgaria and ways to improve it, including through education in school settings.   The CEM report on the implementation of the media literacy measures is available on the Council's website at: https://www.cem.bg/activitybg/2252.  In 2023, the need to increase media literacy in society, even more so in the context of a military conflict taking place nearby and the methods of manipulation and propaganda being used, remains paramount. Media literacy plays a critical role in protecting society from manipulation and disinformation by promoting critical thinking, the ability to analyse sources and distinguish truth from falsehood, and it is therefore essential to promote training and education in this area. The problem of misinformation is becoming increasingly relevant and challenging for the media sector, with greater responsibility and filtering of content required. So-called 'deepfake' videos are becoming increasingly common, raising serious concerns about the possible negative effects, given the advancement of technology and the difficulty of distinguishing the false from the true. The use of famous screen faces in such videos to mislead audiences is on the rise. CEM continued to work actively in cooperation with a wide range of stakeholders, including the Ministry of Culture, the Ministry of Education and Science and other public authorities, media service providers, academics, civil society organisations and consumers. In early 2023, CEM members met with the project leaders of the Bulgarian-Romanian Digital Media Observatory - BROD. The aim of the project is to create a multidisciplinary and multifaceted, multinational hub for detecting, analysing and combating misinformation in Bulgaria and Romania. CEM members and project representatives agreed on the need for joint cooperation in the fight against disinformation and fake news.  The Council for Electronic Media and organized a round table on Media Literacy. Representatives of the CEM, the Ministry of Culture, the Ministry of Education and Science, media service providers, self-regulatory bodies, media associations and journalists discussed the policy and development of media literacy in Bulgaria. Event information and video: https://www.cem.bg/displaynewsbg/925.  In the Programme for Governance of the Republic of Bulgaria June 2023 - December 2024 of the Council of Ministers (item 13.2.26. Combating disinformation - a priority given its direct and immediate significance for national security), it is envisaged to start work on introducing workable mechanisms for combating fake and hybrid news; a mechanism balancing responsibility for published fake news with the need to protect freedom of speech; a ban on directing EU and budget funds to media used for disinformation. Competent institutions: MC; CEM; BNR; BNT; Association of Bulgarian Broadcasters; Media Literacy Coalition, etc. Signed Memorandum of Cooperation between the main institutions and organisations involved in the implementation of media literacy measures.  In implementation of the above measure, a Memorandum of Partnership has been developed between the parties for the implementation of a media literacy campaign, with the aim of achieving a broad awareness of citizens regarding media regulation and self-regulation, the rules and principles of good journalistic practice and ethical journalism according to the Code of Ethics of the Bulgarian Media; the rules for honest and truthful advertising in the sense of the National Ethical Rules for Advertising and Commercial Communication. The Memorandum was signed on 5 February by the Minister of Culture, the Chairman of the CEM, the Directors General of BNT and BNR, the Chairman of the Media Literacy Coalition and the Executive Director of the Association of Bulgarian Broadcasters - ABBRO.  The Council for Electronic Media undertook in 2023 the development of audio and audiovisual clips. The aim is to raise awareness and engagement of Bulgarian citizens on the need for critical insight and informed choices about media content.  A Bulgarian Coalition against Disinformation was established in Bulgaria in 2022 to strengthen cooperation at operational and expert level between the European institutions, Bulgarian national institutions, fact-checkers and the media. It was established on the initiative of the Representation of the European Commission in Bulgaria, CEM was invited to participate with a proposal for joint cooperation to fight disinformation. Representatives of CEM participate in round tables and meetings with experts organised by the Representation and the Coalition, and information on disinformation narratives is also submitted to colleagues from the Coalition and fact-checkers.   CEM has also been holding periodic open days since 2022. Members of the Council and experts inform students and citizens about the specifics of supervision and the challenges facing the regulator. In 2023, a separate Media Literacy section has been created on the Council's website, and CEM aims to gradually develop and enrich it with relevant information and materials.
