Title EN: Plateforme « Rhizome »
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Agency Implementation: G.Rhizome
Main Feature: Rhizome est une plateforme d'art contemporain et une résidence d'artistes située à Alger, dans l'ancien atelier et la maison de l’artiste moderne « Mohammed Khadda », avec une présence locale et une visibilité internationale pour les artistes émergents et établis. Elle joue également le rôle de centre de recherche, mettant en avant la diversité des pratiques artistiques et visant à développer un environnement artistique et culturel dynamique inclusif et non exclusif.  Dans son espace à Alger, Rhizome organise environ quatre (4) expositions annuelles, notamment les expositions personnelles, avec des programmes publics tels que les conférences, les débats, les tables rondes et les séminaires accessibles en ligne afin de toucher un plus large public. Parmi les artistes exposés figurent Mehdi Djelil, Sonia Merabet, Abdo Shanan, Maya Benchikh El Fegoun, Lydia Ourahmane, Hichem Merouche, Massinissa Selmani et Fella Tamzali.  Outre ses projets d'exposition et de promotion des artistes, Rhizome organise des sessions de formation régulières pour professionnaliser le secteur des arts en collaboration avec l'Association Internationale des Critiques d'Art, pour traiter des thèmes tels que le commissariat aux expositions, la médiation culturelle et l'écriture critique dans l'art. Grace à sa dimension internationale, Rhizome a également développé des programmes de résidence jumelés, notamment avec Triangle-Astéride à Marseille et l'Abri à Genève, pour permettre aux artistes algériens de mener des recherches dans des contextes internationaux et les artistes internationaux de se confronter à la scène algérienne. La politique/mesure cible-t-elle spécifiquement la jeunesse ? Oui
Results: Les principaux résultats atteints jusqu’à présent grâce à cette politique mesure sont :  En plus des expositions organisées à Alger, Rhizome a encouragé la visibilité des artistes algériens sur les plateformes internationales de l'art contemporain, notamment Art Dubai, Paris Internationale, Cape Town Art Fair, Liste Basel, SWAB Barcelona Art Fair, etc. Elle co-produit des projets d'exposition avec des institutions muséales internationales, tel que l'exposition « Tassili » de l'artiste Lydia Ourahmane avec Sculpture Center, New York ; la Fondation Louis Vuitton, Paris ; Kamel Lazaar Foundation, Tunis ; Mercer Union, Toronto ; et Nottingham Contemporary, ainsi que l'exposition « 1000 Villages Socialistes » de l'artiste Massinissa Selmani en partenariat avec Index Foundation à Stockholm, soutenue par Arab Fund for Arts and Culture. En tant que plateforme internationale de résidence, Rhizome joue également un rôle essentiel pour accueillir chaque année environ 15 artistes dans l'ancienne maison et l’atelier de l'artiste Mohammed Khadda, dont les artistes de la diaspora et des artistes internationaux. Elle permet aussi de soutenir la recherche, la collaboration et les échanges entre artistes et différents professionnels de l'art toutes disciplines confondues. Parmi les artistes accueillis en résidence figurent, entre-autres, Carmen Amengual (Argentine), Ludovic Hadjeras (binational algéro-français), Fatou Dravé (binational camerounaise et malienne), Éloi Calame (Chili), Nabil Djedouani (binational algéro-français), Giulia Crisci (Italie), etc. D’autres résultats ont été atteints, à savoir :  •	la promotion des artistes algériens à l'échelle internationale grâce à la co-production, les foires d’art et les résidences de recherche ou de création,  •	la création de partenariats stratégiques avec des institutions de renom, pour améliorer la visibilité des artistes algériens,  •	la mise en place de programmes de résidence internationale pour que les artistes algériens aient des opportunités d'exposition et de collaboration à l'étranger  •	la formation de professionnels et le renforcement des compétences dans le secteur artistique en Algérie, •	l’amélioration de la visibilité internationale de l'art algérien, grâce aux collaborations et la présence affirmée sur la scène mondiale.

Title EN: Plateforme Filmexport
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Agency Implementation: Fondation Hiba
Main Feature: Créée en 2016, FilmExport est l’unique plateforme au Maroc visant à promouvoir le cinéma Marocain à l’échelle internationale. Un projet inédit qui se veut une solution efficace pour donner de la visibilité aux productions nationales qui ont connu depuis quelques années un développement remarquable tant en termes de quantité que de qualité.  FilmExport compte parmi les projets ambitieux et prometteurs incubés par la Fondation HIBA. Une fondation royale qui a vu le jour en 2006, à l’initiative de Sa Majesté le Roi Mohammed VI. Une organisation non gouvernementale œuvrant pour le développement et la promotion de l’art sous toutes ses formes : Cinéma, Musique, Photographie, Mode et Design, Arts de la rue, Danse et Théâtre.  FilmExport soutient les réalisateurs et producteurs Marocains, en intégrant leurs productions dans son catalogue et son site web, qui ont été mis en place spécialement pour participer aux marchés de droits audiovisuels autant en Afrique que dans le monde comme Le Discop, Le Marché internationale du cinéma et de la télévision africaine (MICA), Asian film Market, Berlinale, Cannes, Londres et Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF). Le but est d’avoir plus de visibilité et donc plus de chance pour vendre les diverses productions marocaines.  Pour la première fois au Maroc, les détenteurs de droits jouissent de la présence d’un intermédiaire confiant et facilitateur de communication, qui leur permettra de présenter leurs productions aux acheteurs de droits audiovisuels. En effet, la particularité de ce projet innovateur, c’est qu’il s’inscrit dans une stratégie de communication notamment digitale, en se basant sur une plateforme numérique « www.filmexport.ma » ainsi que les différents réseaux sociaux.
Results: Afin de rendre accessible en ligne le patrimoine cinématographique marocain, il y a eu lieu le lancement de la plateforme de référencement et de promotion du cinéma marocain Filmexport, une plateforme qui constitue une base de données en ligne présentant les informations générales sur les films. Cette initiative de FilmExport, lancée en 2016, a apporté des résultats significatifs pour la promotion du cinéma marocain à l'échelle internationale. En tant que plateforme unique au Maroc, elle a joué un rôle crucial en offrant une visibilité accrue aux productions nationales sur les marchés mondiaux du cinéma. En intégrant les films marocains dans son catalogue et en participant à des événements majeurs tels que Le Discop, Le MICA, l'Asian Film Market, la Berlinale, Cannes, Londres et le TIFF, FilmExport a ouvert de nouvelles opportunités de diffusion et de vente pour les réalisateurs et producteurs marocains. En agissant comme un intermédiaire confiant, elle a facilité la communication entre les détenteurs de droits et les acheteurs de droits audiovisuels, créant ainsi un environnement propice à la promotion et à la commercialisation des productions marocaines. De plus, en adoptant une stratégie de communication numérique via son site web et les réseaux sociaux, FilmExport a renforcé sa présence et son impact, permettant une diffusion plus large et une plus grande accessibilité aux œuvres cinématographiques marocaines. En somme, cette initiative a contribué de manière significative à renforcer la réputation et la visibilité du cinéma marocain à l'échelle internationale, ouvrant ainsi de nouvelles perspectives pour son développement futur.

Title EN: Policies and Measures that Support the Development of Digital Creativity and Competencies
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Digital environment
Agency Implementation: 1. Ministry of Communication and Information Technology 2. Ministry of Manpower 3. National Agency for Professional Certification 4. Ministry of Education, Culture, Research, and Technology
Main Feature: In the past four years, policies and measures that support the development of digital creativity and competencies include: 1. Law 20 of 2003 on the National Education System (Sistem Pendidikan Nasional) (Law on Sisdiknas); 2. Law 13 of 2003 on Manpower (Law on Manpower); 3. Draft Law on Amendments to Law 20 of 2003 on the National Education System (Sistem Pendidikan Nasional) (Draft Law on Sisdiknas);  4. Draft Law on Amendments to Law 13 of 2003 on Manpower (Draft Law on Manpower); 5. 2020-2024 Digital Literacy Road Map; 6. Indonesian National Work Competency Standards (Standar  Kompetensi Kerja Nasional Indonesia, SKKNI);  7. Indonesian Digital Literacy Index; dan 8. National Digital Literacy Movement (Gerakan Nasional Literasi Digital, GNLD).   Law on Sisdiknas and Law on Manpower (see Goal 1, Policies and Measures for Education and Training Programs in Culture and Creative Economy Sectors) underlie education and training in Indonesia, including those related to the development of digital creativity and competencies, both through formal or non-formal education. Specifically, the Law on Sisdiknas requires mastery of digital competencies as part of the curriculum at all levels of education to respond to (1) regional and national development demands, (2) demands from work, (3) developments in science, technology, and arts; and (4) the dynamics of global development. In recent developments, stakeholders have identified a real need to update the Law on Sisdiknas and Law on Manpower to be more responsive to current developments and all their challenges and opportunities. Although the Draft Law on Sisdiknas and Draft Law on Manpower has been registered with the National Legislation Program, neither has been prioritized for completion in 2024.  Furthermore, the 2020-2024 Digital Literacy Road Map was prepared by the Ministry of Communication and Informatics, Siberkreasi, and Deloitte in 2020. This road map guides formulating a digital literacy curriculum into four competency areas: digital skills, digital culture, digital ethics, and digital security. These four competency areas offer various indicators and sub-indicators that can be used to improve the digital literacy competency of Indonesian society through multiple programs aimed at different target groups. One of the products of this roadmap is the Indonesian Digital Literacy Index, an annual research conducted since 2020.  Meanwhile, there is another measure, namely GNLD, which the Ministry of Communication and Informatics developed in collaboration with 140 partners to provide digital literacy in 514 cities/regencies. The digital literacy program has several programs that all Indonesian people can participate in, such as the Siberkreasi Digitally Competent and the Siberkreasi Empowered Inclusive Class for people in disadvantaged, frontier, and outermost areas (3T), people with disabilities, and older people. This digital literacy program also holds classes that can be attended and watched online on the Siberkerasi YouTube and social media channels.  Finally, among the many SKKNI (see Goal 1, Policies and Measures for Education and Training Programs in Culture and Creative Economy Sectors) that have been established, only one supports the development of digital creativity and competencies, namely SKKNI 173 of 2020 on Animation (SKKNI Animation). The SKKNI Animation, the reference for animation programs for schools and universities, is a new version of the one established in 2014.   In general, policies and measures that support the development of digital creativity and competencies are aimed at contributing to achieving the following agenda(s) of the National Strategy for Culture: 1. Utilize objects of culture advancement to improve people’s welfare (Agenda 4); and 2. Strengthen the role of the government as a facilitator of culture advancement (Agenda 7).
Results: SKKNI: The List of SKKNI related to Culture and Creative Economy per Main Group in the Annexes section provides a complete list with document links.  Indonesian Digital Literacy Index: In 2022, Indonesia's digital literacy level was still at 3.54 out of 5.00, or a medium level. In general, the Digital Culture pillar in the 2022 National Digital Literacy Index received the highest index score (3.84), while in 2021, it received a score of 3.90.  GNLD: Since 2017, as many as 24,640,451 people have participated in improving digital literacy.
Recommandations: GNLD: Evaluations carried out by Agustina (2021) from the KOMPAS Research and Development Division resulted in several conclusions/recommendations, as follows. Digital media users in Indonesia are still learning to use digital devices but lack the information management skills needed to become positive content creators. The public must be forced to improve their digital literacy competencies immediately. Developing digital literacy must continue to consider the perceptions and attitudes of the targeted individual toward technology because each individual has a different speed of technology adoption. The development of digital literacy must also reach all groups, especially those who still have barriers to accessing the internet due to geographical area, socio-economic status, age, and others.  References: Agustina, S. (2021, 5 Maret). Urgensi meningkatkan literasi digital. Kompas. https://www.kompas.id/baca/riset/2021/03/05/urgensi-meningkatkan-literasi-digital/

Title EN: PREPARATION OF GUIDELINES TO INCORPORATE THE INTERCULTURAL APPROACH, AND FOR THE GENERATION OF SERVICES WITH CULTURAL RELEVANCE
Goal: Integrate Culture In Sustainable Development Frameworks
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: National sustainable development policies and plans
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: Directorate of Indigenous Policies (Ministry of Culture)
Main Feature: In 2020, the National Culture Policy - PNC (Supreme Decree No. 009-2020-MC) was approved, which defined Priority Objective 1: Strengthen the appreciation of cultural diversity, developing three guidelines: L01.01 Generate strategies to strengthening the cultural identity of citizens, with emphasis on indigenous or native and Afro-Peruvian peoples; L01.02 Develop mechanisms for the attention, prevention and punishment of racism and ethnic-racial discrimination in public and private entities and L01.03 Develop strategies for the incorporation of cultural relevance in public services. Considering this framework, and having as a background the National Policy for the Mainstreaming of the Intercultural Approach (Supreme Decree No. 003-2015-MC), the following were approved: the Guidelines for the generation of services with cultural relevance through the incorporation of the ethnic variable in public entities (Supreme Decree No. 010- 2021-MC); and the Guidelines to incorporate the intercultural approach in the provision of public services (Supreme Decree No. 001-2023-MC). The “Guidelines for the generation of services with cultural relevance through the incorporation of the ethnic variable in public entities (Supreme Decree No. 010-2021-MC)”, were approved with the objective of providing technical guidance to contribute to the generation of services with cultural relevance through the incorporation of the ethnic variable in the characterization of the population that accesses public services.  Likewise, with the purpose of providing public entities with a practical tool that allows them to generate information on the ethnic-cultural characteristics of the population that uses their public services, progressively, so that they can incorporate the intercultural approach in the design and provision of its public services for citizens and to appropriately guide public policies, the “Methodological guide for the incorporation of the ethnic variable in information records of public entities (August, 2021)” was approved and published. In addition, the “Guidelines to incorporate the intercultural approach in the provision of public services (Supreme Decree No. 001-2023-MC)”; The objective is to establish technical guidelines for the incorporation of the intercultural approach in the provision of public services based on the particular characteristics of the user citizenship, with emphasis on geographical areas where indigenous or native peoples and/or Afro-Peruvian people are located.
Results: Within the framework of the aforementioned guidelines, socialization and technical assistance actions have been carried out for 20 public entities to incorporate the intercultural approach. 47 technical assistance has been coordinated and/or provided during 2023 regarding the incorporation of the ethnic variable in the administrative records of 15 entities. 16,257 public servants were trained in the incorporation of the intercultural approach to care for indigenous peoples and Afro-Peruvian people. This is a result of the development of 2 free virtual MOOC courses called “Let's Talk about Racism” and the “ABC of Interculturality”, where 3,413 people from 25 regions of the country passed, of which 868 took the “Let's Talk about Racism” course and 2,545 about the course “ABC of Interculturality”. Regarding workshops, 12,844 people were trained through talks and workshops in all regions of the country assigned to 6 sectors. Untitled-2 (www.gob.pe) Within the framework of the coordination process with regional governments, through the Deconcentrated Directorates of Culture, proposals for ordinances have been sent to 24 regional governments; In parallel, provincial ordinances have been developed, in coordination with the DDC, in 3 provincial municipalities of Loreto and a district municipality in the Ucayali region. Within the framework of the implementation of the Social Action Strategy with Sustainability – EASS through the Itinerant Social Action Platforms (PIAS), like every year, in 2023, 41 campaigns were participated in (31 in Loreto, 6 in Ucayali and 4 in Puno), providing the following services: 1) Strengthening intercultural capacities to public servants from the sectors that participate in the PIAS; 2) Accompaniment to local authorities and indigenous leaders to improve the access of the indigenous population to public services; 3) Adequacy of the provision of public services provided in the PIAS to guarantee their cultural and linguistic relevance; 4) Dissemination to prevent the spread of COVID-19 and other diseases in indigenous or native peoples.

Title EN: Pluralist, open and quality children's content. "CNTV Infantil" cultural and educational  television.
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Media diversity
Agency Implementation: National Television Council (CNTV).
Main Feature: This measure exists since May 2000, and its goal is to contribute to the integral development of children and youth of Chile though national, puralist and quality children's programming on free-to-air television, thus its purpose is for children and youth to have access to quality national free-to-air children's television that favours their integral development. Its actions are oriented towards developing and promoting cultural and educational television, by circulating content for child audiences, presenting the diversity of cultural expressions throughout country.   In order to achieve the aforementioned goal and the purpose, CNTV Infantil produces, manages and delivers cultural and educational audiovisual programming for children and youth, which are broadcast on regional, local and community television channels through partnerships, as well as screens in spaces with attention to the public in various institutions, its web page, social networks and applications. Its programming includes series, games, as well as educational content for teachers.
Results: During 2022, audiovisual production for child audiences mainly focused on the development of series with content related to the school curriculum, that address themes on Chilean history (specifically the era of independence), the country's regonal geography, natural sciences, the human body and self-care.   At the same, series were produced which promote and educate on themes of emotional intelligence, identity, respect and animal and pet care, the environment and the promotion of sustainability. In summary, nine series were produced, of which seven are in-house productions and two are co-productions, with a total of 191 episodes. The results are audiovisual series for child audiences, which show high quality and technical craft, that cover the curriculum and cross-cutting content, demonstrating diversity of formats, territories and placing diverse children on the screen.   During 2022, for the eighth year, the measure incorporated sign language, subtitles and audio descrition in 282 series episodes, which corresponds to more than 13 hours of children's content produced for CNTV Infantil. This line of work, beginning in 2015, has added 869 episodes and more than 67 hours of inclusive children's programming for deaf or hearing-impaired children. Title EN: PLURINATIONAL COORDINATOR OF SELF-MANAGED CULTURAL SPACES
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Agency Implementation: Antonio Peredo Gonzales  EMAIL: peredo.antonio@gmail.com PHONE: 591 67240217  Carmiña Dubrek Garcia Fernandez  EMAIL: dubrekster@gmail.com PHONE: 591 77541064
Main Feature: The initiative to coordinate the Plurinational Coordinator of Self-Managed Cultural Spaces (PCSCS) took place at the end of 2018, at the initiative of the El Bunker Cultural Space, with the intention of consolidating an Articulation/Network of Independent Cultural Spaces, bringing together cultural spaces from five departments of Bolivia. In October 2019, there was a political crisis within Bolivian territory that exponentially affected the informal economic sector in general, and cultural spaces and the artistic sector in particular. Following the social upheaval in March 2020, the COVID-19 global pandemic was declared, directly affecting all activities linked to the concentration of audiences. In this context, amid lockdown, the initiative to form an articulation of Cultural Spaces emerged again to call on all independent spaces that want to save their ventures to meet.  Thus, in long sessions of Zoom, the Plurinational Coordinator of Independently Managed Cultural Spaces in Bolivia was initially born, to later be called the Plurinational Coordinator of Self-Managed Cultural Spaces (PCSCS). These virtual meetings manage to build a document called PROCESS FOR THE REACTIVATION OF SELF-MANAGED CULTURAL SPACES NATIONAL COORDINATOR OF CULTURAL SPACES, a document with an important diagnosis bringing together 71 spaces in its lists to request a fund from the Ministry of Culture that can support the spaces to survive the situation. However, the Transitional Government, by Supreme Decree 4257 dated June 4, 2020, closes the Ministry of Culture and Tourism, leaving the spaces with the letter and the document in the Ministry's single window. This situation prompted the spaces to come together and take part in a march, amid the pandemic, demanding the reopening of the Ministry. Among other actions, they actively helped in the convening of a Congress called “We are all Cultures” to address the problems of the sector in general beyond cultural spaces. Currently, the PCSCS brings together around 50 cultural spaces in seven departments and nine municipalities of the national territory. The PCSCS – La Paz region brings together 25 spaces from the municipalities of La Paz, El Alto and Copacabana, carrying out the following activities: -	Project: INDEPENDENTLY MANAGED CULTURAL SPACES IN LA PAZ - REACTIVATION PLAN. Presented to the Municipal Secretariat of Cultures of the AMGLP. As a result of this effort, a budget of Bs. 50,000 was achieved. -	Carrying out a Virtual Cultural Kermesse. This activity provided the 50,000 Bs. amount destined to become the capital of all the spaces. This amount was divided into three parts: (i) capital to carry out activities; (ii) to pay for professional services; (iii) a fund to be used for loans for the spaces. This resource thus allowed for the carrying out of five subsequent fundraising activities. -	Atracón Fest. Virtual Cultural Festival and Kermesse with Delivery. -	Joy Raffle, which had four draws in 4 District fairs in the municipality of La Paz. -	Solidarity raffle to support a fellow member of a PCSCS space -	I hired a cultural manager to prepare a project based on a document written by a commission. This is how I obtained funding for the project “Promotion of Cultural and Creative Industries in the city of La Paz” from the UNESCO Fund. -	Feast of Joy. At the national level, two funds were obtained from the Ministry of Culture. -	DISCOVER BOLIVIA WITH YOUR ARTISTS. Ministry initiative considering the PCSCS database. The spaces presented artists of Literature and Visual Arts. -	NATIONAL EXHIBITION OF BOLIVIAN AUDIOVISUALS AND WINNERS OF THE EDUARDO ABAROA AWARD IN SELF-MANAGED CULTURAL SPACES: “World Day of Audiovisual Heritage 2023”, as PCSCS a project was presented to the Ministry of Cultures, obtaining financing for audiovisual artists and the participating spaces. The following actions are currently being developed: -	Management of Legal Entity. -	Capacity building, organizing open workshops for both PCSCS members and the cultural arts sector. These have a minimal cost, an amount that covers the payment to the person who facilitates, generates income for the spaces that collaborate and increases the financial capital of the PCSCS. -	PCSCS is developing a strategy to position the idea that arts and culture are fundamental to strengthening human talent in society. At the same time, these actions are intended to broaden the reach of the public, allowing more people to learn about and connect with the proposals of cultural spaces, both in La Paz society in particular and at the national level in general.
Results: -	There is an instance of agglomeration of self-managed cultural spaces. -	There is an organizational structure at the national level. -	The PCSCS La Paz regional has its own financial fund that allows it to support members of the spaces who may be going through a challenging situation. This fund also allows it to have a counterpart to face future projects. -	Cultural spaces constitute important articulating hinges for the dynamism of the artistic cultural ecosystem.

Title EN: Policies and Measures that Ensure Recognition and Protection of Artistic Freedom
Goal: Promote Human Rights And Fundamental Freedoms
SDG: SDG 5 - Achieve gender equality and empower all women and girls,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels
Area of Monitoring: Artistic freedom
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: 1. Ministry of Law and Human Rights  2. National Commission on Human Rights  3. National Commission on Violence against Women  4. National Commission for Disability  5. Ministry of Education, Culture, Research, and Technology
Main Feature: In the past four years, policies and measures that ensure recognition and protection of artistic freedom include: 1. Law 39 of 1999 on Human Rights (Law on Human Rights);  2. Law 11 of 2005 on the Ratification of the International Covenant on Economic, Social, and Cultural Rights;  3. Law 12 of 2005 on the Ratification of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights;  4. Law 19 of 2011 on the Ratification of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities;  5. Law 35 of 2014 on Amendments to Law 23 of 2002 on Child Protection (Law on Child Protection);  6. Law 8 of 2016 on People with Disabilities (Law on Persons with Disabilities);  7. Law 5 of 2017 on Culture Advancement (Law on Culture Advancement);  8. Draft Law on Amendments to Law 39 of 1999 on Human Rights (Draft Law on Human Rights);  9. Draft Law on Third Amendments to Law 23 of 2002 on Child Protection (Draft Law on Child Protection);  10. Draft Law on Indigenous People;  11. Draft Law on Empowerment of Orphans and Abandoned Children by the State (Draft Law on Orphans and Abandoned Children);  12. Government Regulation 87 of 2021 on the Implementation Regulation of Law 5 of 2017 on Culture Advancement;  13. Presidential Decree 36 of 1990 on the Ratification of the Convention on the Rights of the Child;  14. Norms and Regulations Standard 5 on the Right to Freedom of Opinion and Expression;  15. ASEAN Human Rights Declaration;   16. Culture Development Index (Indeks Pembangunan Kebudayaan, IPK);  17. Human Rights Commission Complaints Data Service Portal; and   18. Disabilities Cultural Week.  Most of these policies and measures were reported in 2020 the QPR and are still valid/ongoing at the time of drafting this report, namely (1) Law on Human Rights; (2) Law 11 on 2005 on the Ratification of the International Covenant on Economic, Social, and Cultural Rights; (3) Law 12 of 2005 on the Ratification of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights; (4) Law 19 of 2011 on the Ratification of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities; (5) Law on Persons with Disabilities; (6) Law on Culture Advancement (see Goal 1, Specific Policies that Regulate Culture and/or Creative Economy Sectors); (7) IPK (see Goal 1, Policies and Measures on Information Systems and Cultural Statistics Used in Policy Development); and (8) Disabilities Cultural Week. In recent developments, stakeholders have identified a real need to update the Law on Human Rights to be more responsive to current developments and all its challenges and opportunities. Even though it has been registered in the National Legislation Program (Prolegnas), the Draft Law on Human Rights is not yet one of the priorities for completion in 2024.  As additional information for the Disabilities Cultural Week, this program is organized by the Provincial Government of DI Yogyakarta to provide space for people with disabilities to participate in cultural life. The Disabilities Cultural Week was first held in 2019 as a development of the Disabilities Jamboree, which was held the previous year. This program is implemented every year, even during the pandemic. The 2020 and 2021 Disabilities Cultural Week was held online, while the 2022 and 2023 editions were again held in person in Bantul and Prambanan, respectively. Apart from being a space for expression for artists with disabilities, it is hoped that Disabilities Cultural Week can become a vehicle for the public to understand better the special needs of people with disabilities, especially regarding cultural rights.  Several international legal instruments relating to guarantees of artistic freedom, which have not yet been reported to be followed by Indonesia, are (1) the ASEAN Human Rights Declaration and (2) Presidential Decree 36 of 1990 on the Ratification of the Convention on the Rights of the Child. The ASEAN Human Rights Declaration was drafted and signed by Indonesia in 2012 in Phnom Penh, Cambodia. The Declaration includes (1) general principles; (2) civil and political rights; (3) economic, social, and cultural rights; (4) the right to development; (5) the right to peace; and (6) cooperation in promoting and protecting human rights. Meanwhile, as a form of guarantee of protecting artistic freedom for children, Indonesia has ratified the Convention on the Rights of the Child with the issuance of Presidential Decree 36 of 1990, followed by the issuance of the Law on Child Protection. The Law on Child Protection was considered for further refinement when drafting this report. The Draft Law on Child Protection itself has been registered in Prolegnas but has not been prioritized for completion in 2024.  Two other draft laws aimed at protecting the rights of vulnerable groups, including artistic freedom, have been registered in Prolegnas: the Draft Law on Indigenous People and the Draft Law on Orphans and Abandoned Children. The Draft Law on Indigenous People is a priority to be completed in 2024, and at the time of drafting this report, it had entered the harmonization stage.  To ensure that all laws and regulations in Indonesia do not conflict with the guarantee of protecting artistic freedom as regulated in the 1945 Constitution, in 2021, Komnas HAM issued the Norms and Regulations Standard 5 on the Right to Freedom of Opinion and Expression. The standard states that the fundamental rights to artistic freedom include (1) the right to work without censorship or intimidation; (2) the right to receive support, distribution channels, and compensation for the work; (3) the right to freedom of movement; (4) the right to freedom of association; (5) the right to protection of social and economic rights; and (6) the right to participate in cultural life. Furthermore, Komnas HAM has developed a complaint service to monitor human rights enforcement, including those related to violations of artistic freedom. The public can access all cases reported to the Komnas HAM complaints service via the Human Rights Commission Complaints Data Service Portal.  In general, policies and measures that ensure recognition and protection of artistic freedom are aimed at contributing to achieving the following agenda(s) of the National Strategy for Culture: 1. Provide space for the diversity of cultural expressions and encourage cultural interaction to strengthen the inclusiveness of culture (Agenda 1); and  2. Strengthen the role of the government as a facilitator of culture advancement (Agenda 7).

Provisional People's Consultative Assembly Decree XXV/MPRS/1966 on the Dissolution of the Indonesian Communist Party, the Declaration of Prohibited Organizations throughout the Territory of the Republic of Indonesia for the Indonesian Communist Party, and the Prohibition of Any Activities to Spread or Develop Communist/Marxist-Leninist Ideology or Teachings; b. Law 44 of 2008 on Pornography; c. Law 32 of 2002 on Broadcasting; and d. Law 33 of 2009 on Film.  References: Gumay, H., Handika, R., Lazarus, E., & Ninditya, R. (2020). Title EN: PNA - National Plan for the Arts
Goal: Integrate Culture In Sustainable Development Frameworks
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: National sustainable development policies and plans
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: PNA - National Plan for the Arts
Main Feature: The National Plan for the Arts (NPA) is an initiative of the Portuguese governmental areas of Culture and Education created for the 2019-2029 timeframe. It is a task force working with local governments, higher education institutions, schools, artists, cultural and arts organisations, private entities and civil society, with the aim of giving a central place to arts and heritage in our daily lives – especially for children and young citizens. The mission of the NPA is to promote social transformations through the educational power of arts and heritage in the lives of citizens.  The NPA Strategy/Manifesto for the first five years (2019-2024): •	favors a systemic approach to society, assuming the specificities of each territory and opening it to global cultures and universality. •	proposes a transdisciplinary approach, recognizing that arts and heritage are essential for all disciplines, not only for artistic expressions. •	assumes schools as cultural centers and cultural institutions as educational territories. The paradigm that this strategy proposes is Cultural Democracy: for all, with the participation of each one.  In 2021, taking advantage of the moment in which Portugal assumed the Presidency of the Council of the European Union, an intense networking was carried out between NPA and the representatives of the EU Member States and various European networks and organizations involved in the design of Culture and Education policies, giving rise to the “Porto Santo Charter”.  The Porto Santo Charter is a document about the relevance of Arts and Culture in the promotion of democracy. The Porto Santo Charter presents principles and recommendations for applying and developing a working paradigm for cultural democracy in Europe. It is addressed to European policy makers at European institutions, national, regional and local levels; to cultural and educational organizations and institutions; and to European citizens to take responsibility for its common cultural landscape. In order to develop a cultural citizenship that promotes democracy, the Charter presents several interconnected recommendations addressed to the different agents of the cultural ecosystem, at its different scales, and thought in a systemic way.
Results: PCE - Projeto Cultural Escola (School Cultural Project) – PCE is a territorialized measure, integrated into the educational project and the school's activity plan. It is established based upon a problem that the educational community seeks to resolve, in a dimension of active citizenship and social transformation having arts and heritage as a strategy, on the assumption that cultural manifestations constitute the necessary mediation for personal and collective recognition and to reinforce the sense of belonging to the community, based on the notion of participated cultural experience.  The PCE questions how arts, culture and heritage can help solve the challenges that schools encounter in their relationship with the territories in which they operate. Through the problematization methodology combined with the creative process, the PCE promotes the arts in the curriculum, fruition, experimentation and artistic participation, critical thinking, creativity, multiple languages and expressions, inter and transdisciplinary knowledge. These projects focus on the themes of the National Citizenship Education Strategy, namely human rights, active citizenship and democratic participation, cultural diversity, environmental sustainability, gender equality, inclusion. The systemic approach that the PNA pursues in the PCE is structuring and sustainable, it operates not only at the school but at the level of the territory, cultural organizations, artists and creators, cultural and educational agents, and the municipal cultural and educational entities themselves. More than 300 schools, across the country, are engaged in this initiative.  Academia PNA (NPA Academy) – training program, for teachers, in arts and heritage pedagogy, promoting and facilitating the transversality of languages and contents, as well as the diversity of ways of teaching and learning. It also supports the way of teaching the contents listed in the National Citizenship Education Strategy, which are aligned with the sustainable development goals of the 2030 Agenda. Training actions are designed by artists and educators with support from the NPA. This is an accredited training in digital/webinar and in-person format, ensuring: - access to NPA measures throughout the national territory, including low-density territories. - combating inequalities and school failure and dropouts. Training is carried out in partnership with School Association Training Centers/other partners such as museums and cultural facilities. The objectives of the PNA Academy are: i) to promote the transversality of languages and content and the diversity of ways of teaching and learning ii) to train agents who collaborate with the Plan for pedagogy through the arts, citizenship and heritage, in a context of autonomy, curricular flexibility and inclusion iii) focus on the student, on lifelong learning, on preparing for the exercise of responsible and participatory citizenship. Exploring training-enjoyment modalities, it promotes cultural enjoyment and the recognition of strategies and creative processes as educational processes, thus enabling teachers to be trained through more active, critical and creative teaching and students to be involved in cultural activities, either in school context or non-school contexts.  In the 2021/2022 academic year, near 3750 trainees were involved in more than 700 training hours, distributed across 44 courses/workshops and short-term actions.  Mochila Cultural (Cultural Bag) – running throughout the school year, approximately monthly, the “Cultural Bag” is a program of cultural enjoyment and learning essential to the development of students in an informal or non-formal context, which was integrated into the learning recovery plan. Includes concerts, guided tours, cinema, theatre and dance performances. In the context of the Covid 19 pandemics, “Mochila Cultural” gained an online streaming platform, which continues, simultaneously reaching the hole country's school network. These events are participatory and inclusive, including live conversations with those involved in the works presented, in an interaction between children and young people with the creators, mediators and other participants in the debates. This measure aims to: i) diversify the presence of arts, heritage and culture at school, in dialogue with the different subjects of the curriculum, promoting the opening of schools to artists and cultural mediators and encouraging students to go on study visits to artistic cultural institutions and heritage, as a pedagogical strategy and underlining the premise: culture is curriculum; ii) ensure that students from all education cycles have the opportunity to experience, enjoy and participate in professional artistic and cultural productions, each academic year, throughout their school career, thus acquiring skills defined in the students' profile upon leaving compulsory education; iii) contribute to the creation of cultural audiences; iv) develop students’ critical and creative thinking; v) frame the arts in the curricular domains and in the Citizenship and Development component within the scope of the National Education for Citizenship Strategy. vi) Provide the demystification of the creative process and cultural professions and direct contact with professionals.  Recursos pedagógicos (Pedagogical resources) - NPA makes available a very large number of online resources, available to all and specially addressed to the country's school network.
Recommandations: In 2021, the Plan officially extended its strategy to Higher Education. The Plan co-conceived and organized a European Charter on Cultural Citizenship - the Porto Santo Charter. By the end of 2023, the NAP collaborates with more than 50% of the country's school groups and with the respective territories, entities and communities of the cultural Km2. - 494 school groupings or non-grouped schools throughout the country (464 schools in mainland Portugal, 25 in the autonomous regions - 22 schools in the Azores and 3 schools in Madeira - and 5 Portuguese schools abroad) are working with the PNA; this structuring of School Cultural Projects involves creating solid bridges with local cultural and artistic institutions and associations, working in conjunction with local municipalities and agents, with a view to consolidating school cultural projects, showing that schools are Cultural Hubs. Another of the measures implemented by the PNA, the Resident Artist at School, allowed 92 resident artists to be present during this 2022/23 school year (in partnership with the National Plan for Promoting Educational Success, City Councils, Regional Directorates of Culture, the Organization of Ibero-American States and other partners) - in addition to the resident artists in partnership with the National Odyssey program of the D. Maria National Theatre. In the previous three academic years, 105 artist residencies were held in schools. PNA in numbers as of December 2023: 131,000 students; 21,000 teachers; 197 resident artists; More than 350 digital resources; 208 municipalities (> 65%); 40 protocols.

Title EN: Policies and Measures on Information Systems and Cultural Statistics Used in Policy Development
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Agency Implementation: 1. Ministry of Education, Culture, Research, and Technology   2. Indonesian Central Bureau of Statistics
Main Feature: In the past four years, policies and measures on information systems and cultural statistics used in policy development include: 1. Law 16 of 1997 on Statistics (Law on Statistics); 2. Law 14 of 2008 on Open Public Information (Keterbukaan Informasi Publik) (Law on KIP); 3. Draft Law on Amendments to Law 16 of 1997 on Statistics (Draft Law on Statistics); 4. Draft Law on the Integration of Development Data (Draft Law on the Integration of Development Data); 5. Presidential Regulation 39 of 2019 on One Indonesian Data (Satu Data Indonesia); 6. Draft Ministry of Education, Culture, Research, and Technology Regulation on the Integrated Culture Data Collection System and Protection of Culture Advancement Objects; 7. Culture Development Index (Indeks Pembangunan Kebudayaan, IPK);  8. Special Allocated Funds for Culture Information System (Sistem Informasi Dana Alokasi Khusus Kebudayaan, SIDAKBUD);  9. Indonesian Bookkeeping Information System; 10. Main Data for Culture;  11. Main Data for Linguistics and Literature; 12. Social Cultural Statistics; and 13. Tourism and Creative Economy Manpower Statistics.  IPK, Draft Ministry of Education, Culture, Research, and Technology Regulation on the Integrated Culture Data Collection System and Protection of Culture Advancement Objects, and Main Data for Culture were reported in the 2020 QPR and are still valid/ongoing while drafting this report.  In the latest developments, the Integrated Cultural Data Collection System (Sistem Pendataan Kebudayaan Terpadu, SPKT) platform is still being developed while waiting for the completion of the drafting of the Minister of Education, Culture, Research and Technology Regulation on the Integrated Cultural Data Collection System and Protection of Objects for the Promotion of Culture. The Main Data for Culture and the Main Data for Linguistics and Literature will be part of the SPKT. Later, SPKT will become part of the Satu Data Indonesia policy. The Satu Data Indonesia policy was essentially designed to ensure the validity and reliability of officially shared data and information and encourage their visibility and utility.  The Main Data for Linguistics and Literature itself was launched in 2019. Although both main data sets are the responsibility of Kemendikbudristek, the Main Data for Linguistics and Literature is managed by the Language Development and Nurturing Agency. In contrast, the Directorate General of Culture manages the Main Data for Culture. The Main Data for Linguistics and Literature focuses on storing and presenting statistical data about references, language, and literature. Language categories include (1) language links; (2) distribution of regional languages ​​by province; (3) language registration; (4) language research; (5) Indonesian Language Proficiency Unit; (6) Indonesian for Foreign Speakers (Bahasa Indonesia untuk Pembicara Asing, BIPA); (7) Network of BIPA Program Organizing Institutions; (8) controlling language use; (9) linguist; and (10) language ambassador. On the other hand, the literary category includes (1) literary links, (2) registration of oral literature, (3) manuscript registration; (4) registration of printed literature; (5) literary author; (6) literary works; (7) literary dissemination/publisher media; (8) literary prizes/competitions; (9) literary institutions; (10) literary symptoms; (11) literary research; and (12) literary community.  Two fundamental policies related to the provision of data and information trends that have not been reported in the 2016 and 2020 QPRs are the Law on Statistics and the Law on KIP. Law on Statistics is intended to organize statistics that guarantee the avoidance of duplication, easy access by data users, legal certainty for statistical activities, and protection for respondents. This law regulates the National Statistics System where: (1) BPS maintains basic statistics; (2) sectoral statistics are carried out by government agencies according to the scope of their duties and functions, independently or jointly with BPS; and (3) the community maintains special statistics, whether it be institutions, organizations, individuals, or other elements of society independently or together with BPS.  In recent developments, stakeholders have identified a real need to update the Law on Statistics to be more responsive to current developments and all its challenges and opportunities. In the National Legislation Program (Prolegnas), the Draft Law on Statistics is one of the priorities for completion in 2024. At the time of drafting this report, it has already entered the drafting stage. The Draft Law on the Integration of Development Data is another relevant draft legislation that provides data and information trends about media diversity registered in the Prolegnas. However, unlike the Draft Law on Statistics, the Draft Law on the Integration of Development Data is not yet a priority for completion in 2024.  Meanwhile, the Law on KIP guarantees citizens' rights to know public policy plans, programs, decision-making processes, and the reasons for making a public decision and encourages public participation. Requiring public bodies to post public data and information on websites or reports that can be widely accessed encourages using this data to support more participatory initiatives and programs.  As for information systems, there are several that can be reported. One of them is SIDAKBUD, an application launched by the Directorate General of Culture, Kemendikbudristek, to support electronic-based planning, implementation, and monitoring of the Special Allocated Funds for Culture (see Goal 3, Policies and Measures for Cultural Regeneration), especially for Operational Assistance Funds for Organizing Museums and Cultural Parks. This application resulted from the collaboration between Kemendikbudristek and the Ministry of Finance. The other information system is SIBI. For more detailed information, see Goal 2, Policies and Measures to Support the Development of the Publishing Industry.  Then, there is the latest published 2021 Socio-Cultural Statistics based on data from the 2021 National Socio-Economic Survey, both from the Core and Socio-Cultural and Education Module. Four main aspects were analyzed through this survey: access to information, sports, social interaction, and participation in culture advancement objects. To measure participation in culture advancement objects, the following are the general indicators used: 1. The percentage of the population aged five years and above who watched art performances/exhibitions during the last three months based on attendance (live, indirectly, or never). 2. The percentage of the population aged five years and above who watched art performances/exhibitions during the last three months based on the type of performance/exhibition (film, music/audio arts, fine arts, literary arts, Indonesian cultural dancing arts, theater/puppetry arts, or others). 3. The percentage of the population aged five years and above involved in art performances/exhibitions during the last three months (involved or not involved). 4. The percentage of the population aged five years and above who have been involved in art performances/exhibitions in the last three months based on source of income (yes, as main income; yes, as additional income; or no). 5. The percentage of the population aged five years and above who have visited historical/cultural heritage sites in Indonesia during the last year (have visited live, have visited indirectly, have visited directly and indirectly, or never). 6. The percentage of the population aged five years and above who have visited historical/cultural heritage sites in Indonesia during the last year is based on area type (urban, rural, or both). 7. The percentage of the population aged five years and above who know fairy tales/folk tales in Indonesia based on area type (urban, rural, or both). 8. The percentage of the population aged five years and above is based on the language most often used at home and socially outside the home (Indonesian, traditional language, or foreign language). 9. The percentage of the population aged five years and above who participated in traditional sports activities during the last year (participated or never). 10. The percentage of the population aged five years and above who played folk games during the last year (played or never). 11. The percentage of households producing/selling and/or buying/using traditional products during the last three months (producing/selling and/or buying/using). 12. The percentage of households that purchased/used traditional products during the last three months based on traditional product type (traditional crafts, regional/traditional clothing, traditional health care methods, traditional medicine, traditional household equipment, and/or traditional rite equipment). 13. The percentage of households that participated in traditional ceremonies during the last year (organized and attended, organized only, attended only, or did not organize and did not attend). 14. The percentage of households that attended traditional ceremonies during the past year is based on the type of traditional ceremony (birth, circumcision, marriage, death, religious ceremonies, harvest, and/or others).  The collected statistical data were analyzed at the national and provincial levels based on demographic characteristics: (1) gender (male or female); (2) age group (children 5-17, students 7-18, youth 16-30, productive 45-59, or seniors 60 and over); (3) highest level of education completed (no/never attended school, not completed elementary school, elementary school/equivalent, middle school/equivalent, high school/equivalent, or college); (4) disability status (disabled or non-disabled); (5) area type (urban or rural); and (6) expenditure group (bottom 40%, middle 40%, or top 20%).   Lastly, the 2018-2022 Tourism and Creative Economy Manpower Statistics is a publication from Kemenparekraf and BPS that presents data from analysis of the 2018-2022 National Work Force Survey carried out by BPS. For creative economy workers, the general indicators used include the following. 1. The total number of creative economy workers. 2. Number and percentage of the creative economy workforce by subsector (architecture; design; film, animation, and video; photography; crafts; culinary; music; fashion; application and game developers; publishing; advertising; television and radio; performing arts; or fine arts). 3. The percentage of creative economy workers to the total working population. 4. The percentage of the population working in the creative economy sector by age group category, 2018-2021 (15-24, 25-40, 41-59, or 60 and above). 5. The percentage of the population working in the creative economy sector by gender category, 2020-2021. 6. The percentage of the population working in the creative economy sector according to education level, 2020-2021 (junior high school or below, high school or equivalent, or diploma or above). 7. The percentage of the population working in the creative economy sector according to employment status, 2018-2021 (self-employed; self-employed with support of temporary/unpaid workers; self-employed with the backing of permanent/paid workers; labor/workers/employees; casual workers; or family/unpaid workers). 8. Recommandations: IPK: An evaluation carried out internally in 2023 by Kemendikbudristek on the 2022 IPK resulted in the following conclusions.  1.At the provincial level, 32 provinces have a "fair" IPK with scores ranging from 40 to 60 points. Only two provinces achieved a "good" IPK score, namely DI Yogyakarta and Bali, with scores of around 66 points. 2. Based on the dimensions, the highest national IPK score was recorded in the Education dimension, 72.53 points or "good." Meanwhile, the Cultural Economy dimension had the lowest achievement, 26.88 points or "medium."  Social Cultural Statistics: BPS (2021) evaluated the statistical results of several indicators related to participation in culture advancement objects, which resulted in several conclusions/recommendations.  1. Before the pandemic, 34.38% of the population watched live art performances/exhibitions. This percentage decreased by more than half to 11.32% after the pandemic. Some viewers seem to prefer to watch indirectly. However, quite a few people have stopped watching, thus increasing the percentage of the population who have never watched an art performance/exhibition in 2021 to almost double from 2018.  2. Compared to other types of art, film is one of the most popular types in society. This can be seen from the high percentage of people aged five years and above who watched films directly or indirectly, reaching 63.61%. The second most popular type of art is music/sound art, with a percentage of 47.85%, while other types of art are less than 10 percent each. To increase public interest, strategies and innovations are needed for art performances/exhibitions other than films.  3. The profession of an artist is still of little interest to the public. Only 0.49% of the population aged five years and above were involved in art performances/exhibitions during the last three months of 2021. Of this number, 7.18% use their involvement in art performances/exhibitions as their main source of income.  4. If we look at age groups, the highest percentage of people aged five years and above involved in art performances/exhibitions during the last three months of 2021 were in the 45-59 age group, representing around 14.10%. This age group is generally the productive age group, and they are typically the family's breadwinners. This needs to be considered by the government, especially during the pandemic, where many art performances/exhibitions were temporarily stopped, which resulted in the artists not receiving income to meet their family's daily needs.  5. Only around 3.21% of the population aged five years and above have visited historical/cultural heritage sites live, while 3.39% have done so indirectly. Even though there are already those who use virtual visiting services, such as Virtual Borobudur, Virtual Tour of the Sangiran Early Man Site Museum, and National Museum Virtual Tour, there is a significant portion of the population who have never visited historical/cultural heritage sites (93.11%). Awareness-raising regarding virtual visits should be increased so that more people know about and visit historical/cultural heritage sites.  6. Around 78.00% of people aged five years and above know fairy tales/folk tales in Indonesia. However, from deeper analysis based on disability status, it appears that there is a gap between people with disabilities and non-disabled people. The percentage of people with disabilities aged five years and over who know fairy tales/folk tales tends to be lower (52.88%) than non-disabled people (78.60%). This occurs in urban areas (58.25% compared to 84.34%) and in rural areas (47.01% compared to 70.87%). Strategies and innovations are needed so that more people with disabilities know fairy tales/folk tales; this could be done, for example, by making braille books or other disability-friendly media about fairy tales/folk tales.  7. The types of traditional products most frequently purchased/used by the public are traditional household equipment (52.40%), traditional medicine (49.74%), and traditional health care methods (36.63%). Today's society likely prefers to use traditional medicine and reduces the use of chemical drugs. Traditional medicine may also save money and time compared to seeking treatment at a health facility.  Tourism and Creative Economy Manpower Statistics:  An evaluation carried out by Kemenparekraf (2021) on the statistical results of several indicators for creative economy workers resulted in the following conclusions/recommendations.  1. The number of creative economy workers has increased, with an average annual growth of 5.29% and a share of 16.71% in 2021.  2. When viewed by the subsector, culinary absorbs the most workers (56.86%) while design absorbs the least (0.15%).  3. Most creative economy workers are in the 41-59 age group, have low education, are labor/employees, engage in informal activities, work in the category of production workers, transport equipment operators, and unskilled workers, and work long and excessive hours.  4. Concepts and definitions must be reviewed to identify tourism and creative economy workers, especially for sectors that fall between the main categories of tourism and non-tourism sectors and between creative economy and non-creative economy sectors. 5. It is necessary to review the sub-sectors under the creative economy sector, especially the culinary sub-sector. 6. It is necessary to consider disseminating the Interior Design, Visual Communication Design, and Product Design subsectors, which could not be presented because the relative standard error (RSE) value is still above 25%. 7. Comparing with global statistics is necessary to understand Indonesia's position in the tourism and creative economy sectors better. 8. Studying tourism and creative economy phenomena is necessary to support the presentation of tourism and creative economy statistics. 9. A dedicated survey of the tourism and creative economy workforce is necessary to obtain more accurate data. The results can also be used as a correction factor for the indicators that have been produced. 10. It is necessary to present current tourism and the creative economy sector issues in publications.
