Title EN: Policies and Measures that Decentralize Responsibilities for Policy Development
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Agency Implementation: 1. Ministry of Home Affairs   2. Ministry of Education, Culture, Research, and Technology
Main Feature: In the past four years, policies and measures that decentralize responsibilities for policy development include: 1. Law 23 of 2014 on Regional Government (Law on Regional Government); 2. Draft Law on Third Amendments to Law 23 of 2014 on Regional Government (Draft Law on Regional Government); 3. Minister of Education and Culture Regulation 2 of 2021 on Second Amendments to Minister of Education and Culture Regulation 5 of 2019 on the Technical Guidelines for the Use of Special Non-Physical Allocation Funds for Operational Assistance to Museums and Cultural Parks; 4. Minister of Education, Culture, Research, and Technology Regulation 1 of 2022 on the Procedures for Monitoring and Evaluation of the Implementation of Regional Culture White Papers;  5. Minister of Education, Culture, Research, and Technology Regulation 6 of 2023 on Amendments to the Minister of Education and Culture Regulation 45 of 2018 on the Guidelines to Form Regional Culture White Papers; and 6. Special Allocated Funds for Culture.  Law on Regional Government and Special Allocated Funds for Culture were reported in the 2020 QPR and are still valid when drafting this report.  In addition, the Law on Regional Government segregates affairs among the Government, provincial governments, and city/regency governments. Government affairs in the field of culture fall into the category of non-basic service mandatory affairs. Thus, the Central Government, provincial governments, and city/regency governments are all obliged to organize cultural affairs. On the other hand, government affairs in the field of creative economy fall into the category of optional affairs. Thus, only the Central Government is obliged to organize creative economy affairs. Provincial governments and city/regency governments may organize creative economy affairs according to the potential of their respective regions. One example of regional government measures to carry out cultural and creative economy affairs is the establishment of regional apparatus organizations and enacting local regulations related to these two affairs. In recent developments, stakeholders have identified the need to amend the Law on Regional Government to be more updated to respond to present challenges and opportunities. However, at the time of drafting this report, although it has been registered in the National Legislation Program, the Draft Law on Regional Government is yet to be prioritized for completion in 2024.   Regarding the Special Allocated Funds for Culture, this program from Kemendikbudristek is intended to assist regional governments in optimizing the implementation of culture advancement programs in their respective regions. In recent developments since 2020, local governments could no longer utilize the Special Allocated Funds for Culture for physical development. Through the Minister of Education and Culture Regulation 2 of 2021 on Second Amendments to Minister of Education and Culture Regulation 5 of 2019 on the Technical Guidelines for the Use of Special Non-Physical Allocation Funds for Operational Assistance to Museums and Cultural Parks, the available Special Allocated Funds for Culture can only be used by local governments for program implementation in museums and cultural parks. Furthermore, to optimize the planning, implementation, and monitoring of the Special Allocated Funds for Culture, Kemendikbudristek and the Ministry of Finance launched the Special Allocated Funds for Culture Information System (see Goal 1, Policies and Measures on Information Systems and Cultural Statistics Used in Policy Development).   In the 2020 QPR, it was reported that all planning for culture advancement is carried out with a bottom-up approach from the city/regency, provincial, to the national level. Each regional government must prepare a Regional Cultural White Paper (Pokok Pikiran Kebudayaan Daerah, PPKD) by involving the community, which is regulated through the Minister of Education and Culture Regulation 45 of 2018 on Guidelines for Preparing Regional Cultural White Papers. Five years later, the regulation was updated following the issuance of Minister of Education, Culture, Research, and Technology Regulation 6 of 2023 on Amendments to the Minister of Education and Culture Regulation 45 of 2018 on the Guidelines to Form Regional Culture White Papers. The PPKD preparation guidelines were updated to simplify the PPKD preparation process and to open access to broader community involvement.  In addition to obligations to prepare the PPKD, each regional government is also obliged to conduct monitoring and evaluation once a year on implementing the prepared PPKD. Monitoring and evaluation are to be carried out to ensure that the prepared PPKD is by the technical guidelines and the community’s cultural conditions. The obligation to monitor and evaluate PPKD is regulated through the Minister of Education, Culture, Research, and Technology Regulation 1 of 2022 on the Procedures for Monitoring and Evaluation of the Implementation of Regional Culture White Papers. Monitoring and evaluation of PPKD implementation is carried out in stages. The implementation of PPKD by city/regency governments will be monitored and evaluated by the provincial governments. Meanwhile, the implementation of PPKD by provincial governments will be monitored and evaluated by Kemendikbudristek.   In general, policies and measures that decentralize responsibilities for policy development are aimed at contributing to achieving the following agenda(s) of the National Strategy for Culture: 1. Institutional reform and culture budgeting to support the culture advancement agenda (Agenda 6); and 2. Strengthen the role of the government as a facilitator of culture advancement (Agenda 7).
Results: Overall, at least 41 provincial regulations on culture have been issued. These regulations include (1) 22 general policies related to culture advancement; (2) 9 policies related to cultural institutions or special areas for culture; (3) 6 policies related to cultural financial affairs; and (4) 4 policies related to other matters. The List of Provincial Government Regulations related to Culture in the Annexes section provides a complete list with document links.
Recommandations: Based on the internal evaluation conducted in 2022 by the Directorate General of Culture, Kemendikbudristek, on the PPKD in 38 provinces, the following are the conclusions/recommendations.  1. The PPKD document, as a planning document for culture advancement in the region, will not serve much nor have any implications if it is not embodied in regional development planning documents. For this reason, the Minister of Education, Culture, Research, and Technology Regulation 1 of 2022 on the Procedures for Monitoring and Evaluation of the Implementation of Regional Culture White Papers was enacted as a mechanism that can be accounted for, both empirically and juridically, as well as momentum and tool to see the extent to which PPKD documents are in line with regional development planning documents.  2. Out of the 34 provinces in Indonesia (excluding the four expanded provinces), only 22 provinces have conducted monitoring and evaluation on PPKD implementation in 2022. This is relatively good progress for the first year of implementation of the regulation. Still, future improvement is required to ensure all provinces will monitor and evaluate yearly. The 12 provinces that did not carry out monitoring and evaluation of PPKD implementation in 2022 were Bangka Belitung Islands, Banten, West Nusa Tenggara, East Nusa Tenggara, Central Kalimantan, South Kalimantan, North Sulawesi, Central Sulawesi, Gorontalo, Maluku, West Papua, and Papua.  3. Six provinces received a perfect score of A: Riau, Central Java, Yogyakarta, East Kalimantan, and South Sulawesi. Meanwhile, six other provinces scored slightly below perfect (A-): West Sumatra, Bengkulu, West Java, Bali, North Kalimantan, and West Sulawesi.  4. On the conformity of provincial PPKD preparation against the guidelines, an average score of 37.59 was obtained for all provinces. In contrast, an average score of 64.94 was obtained for provinces monitoring and evaluating PPKD implementation. The criterion that received the lowest scores was related to the structure of the provincial PPKD drafting team.  5. On the synchronization of the provincial PPKD with regional planning documents, i.e., the Regional Medium-term Development Plan (Rencana Pembangunan Jangka Menengah Daerah, RPJMD) and the Regional Government Work Plan (Rencana Kerja Pemerintah Daerah, RKPD), an average score of 42.76 was obtained for all provinces, and an average score of 73.86 for provinces that conducted monitoring and evaluation of PPKD implementation. The criterion on synchronization with the RPJMD generally has a lower score than synchronization with the RKPD.  6. On the achievement of the implementation of provincial PPKD recommendations with regional planning documents (RPJMD and RKPD), an average score of 44.23 was obtained for all provinces and an average score of 76.39 for provinces that carried out monitoring and evaluation of PPKD implementation.  7. The highest final score for monitoring and evaluation of implementing provincial PPKD in 2022 is 92.06 out of a scale of 100.  The highest score was obtained by two provinces, namely South Sumatra and South Sulawesi, due to the maximum scores (100) achieved on the synchronization of the provincial PPKD with regional planning documents and the achievement of the implementation of provincial PPKD recommendations with regional planning documents.  8. Two provinces, North Sumatra and Southeast Sulawesi, have not yet stipulated their PPKD document through a Governor Decree; hence, the final score for monitoring and evaluating the implementation of PPKD in 2022 is minimal. However, the efforts made by these two provinces in monitoring and evaluating the implementation of PPKD are appreciated, and they continue to be encouraged to stipulate their PPKD document formally.

Title EN: Policies and Measures that Demand Media Accountability
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Media diversity
Cultural Domain: Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: 1. Press Council of Indonesia 2. Ministry of Communication and Information Technology 3. Indonesian Broadcasting Commision
Main Feature: In the past four years, policies and measures that demand media accountability include: 1. Law 40 of 1999 on the Press (Law on the Press); 2. Law 32 of 2002 on Broadcasting (Law on Broadcasting); 3. Law 6 of 2023 on the Stipulation of Government Regulation in Lieu of Law 2 of 2022 on Job Creation into Law (Law on Job Creation); 4. Draf Law on Amendments to Law 32 of 2002 on Broadcasting (Draft Law on Broadcasting); 5. Government Regulation 18 of 2014 on the Film Censorship Board (Lembaga Sensor Film) (LSF); 6. Presidential Regulation 32 of 2024 on the Responsibility of Digital Platform Companies to Support Quality Journalism (PR on Publishers Right); 7. Minister of Education and Culture Regulation 14 of 2019 on the Guidelines and Criteria for Censorship, Age Classification of Viewers, and Withdrawal of Films and Film Advertisements from Distribution; 8. Press Council Regulation 1/Peraturan-DP/VIII/2015 on Journalist Competency Test Participants; 9. Press Council Regulation 4/Peraturan-DP/XII/2018 on Journalist Competency Standards; 10. Press Council Regulation 1/Peraturan-DP/I/2023 on the Data Collection of Press Companies; 11. Indonesian Broadcasting Commission Regulation 1/P/KPI/03/2012 on the Guidelines for Broadcasting Behavior (Guidelines for Broadcasting Behavior); 12. Indonesian Broadcasting Commission Regulation 2/P/KPI/03/2012 on the Standards for Broadcast Programs (Standards for Broadcast Programs); 13. Indonesian Broadcasting Commission Regulation 07/P/KPI/2020 on the Guidelines for Annual Evaluation of  14.Broadcast Program Requirements for Private Broadcasting Institutions; 15.Indonesian Broadcasting Commission Regulation 2 of 2023 on the Recommendation for Revocation of Broadcasting License for Failure to Broadcast; Indonesian Broadcasting Commission Regulation 4 of 2023 on the Supervision of General Election Campaign Reporting, Broadcasting, and Advertisements at Broadcasting Institutions; 16. Journalist Competency Test; 17. Indonesian Journalism School (Sekolah Jurnalisme Indonesia, SJI); and 18. Television Broadcast Program Quality Index (Indeks Kualitas Program Siaran Televisi, IKPSTV).  All policies and measures that have been reported in the 2020 QPR, namely: (1) Law on Broadcasting (which underlies the establishment of KPI); (2) LSF; (3) Minister of Education and Culture Regulation 14 of 2019 on the Guidelines and Criteria for Censorship, Age Classification of Viewers, and Withdrawal of Films and Film Advertisements from Distribution; (4) Guidelines for Broadcasting Behavior; and (5) IKPSTV, are still valid/ongoing at the time of drafting this report.  In recent developments, stakeholders have identified a real need to update the Law on Broadcasting to be more responsive to current developments and all its challenges and opportunities. The Draft Law on Broadcasting has been prioritized in the National Legislation Program to be completed in 2024. At the time of drafting this report, it has already entered the drafting stage. As an additional note, while waiting for the completion of the Draft Law on Broadcasting, several regulations in the Law on Broadcasting have been changed with the enactment of the Law on Job Creation (see Goal 1, Policies and Measures that Encourage Job Creation and Entrepreneurship in Culture and Creative Economy Sectors).  As regulated by the Law on Broadcasting, KPI is the leading government institution that demands accountability for broadcast media. In the past four years, KPI has produced two books on the latest IKPSTV research: Research on the 2021 Television Broadcast Program Quality Index (Period 1 and Period 2) and Report on the 2022 Television Broadcast Program Quality Index. Unlike previous years, the 2022 IKPSTV survey was carried out simultaneously by gathering a team of informants who specifically discussed specific broadcast programs. This encourages efficiency and effectiveness so that the index results can be more comprehensive and objective. IKPSTV is assessed based on the Guidelines for Broadcasting Behavior and the Standards for Broadcast Programs. These two policies are considered one package, better known as the Guidelines for Broadcasting Behavior and Standards for Broadcast Programs.  In demanding accountability for broadcast media, KPI has also issued several technical regulations, such as (1) Indonesian Broadcasting Commission Regulation 07/P/KPI/2020 on the Guidelines for Annual Evaluation of Broadcast Program Requirements for Private Broadcasting Institutions; (2) Indonesian Broadcasting Commission Regulation 2 of 2023 on the Recommendation for Revocation of Broadcasting License for Failure to Broadcast; and (3) Indonesian Broadcasting Commission Regulation 4 of 2023 on the Supervision of General Election Campaign Reporting, Broadcasting, and Advertisements at Broadcasting Institutions.  Based on the provisions in the Indonesian Broadcasting Commission Regulation 07/P/KPI/2020 on the Guidelines for Annual Evaluation of Broadcast Program Requirements for Private Broadcasting Institutions, KPI uses the annual evaluation results as evaluation material before extending the broadcasting operating license. At the time of drafting this report, the results of the yearly evaluation of broadcast program requirements for private broadcasting institutions had been recapitulated for nine years for television broadcasting and four years for radio broadcasting.  Then, for the Indonesian Broadcasting Commission Regulation 2 of 2023 on the Recommendation for Revocation of Broadcasting License for Failure to Broadcast, it is regulated that private broadcasting institutions, community broadcasting institutions, and subscription broadcasting institutions that do not broadcast for more than three months cumulatively without notification based on legally accepted reasons are subject to administrative sanctions. The accumulation can be consecutive or non-consecutive within one broadcasting operation permit period. The calculation of broadcast time per day for broadcasting institutions is based on KPI supervision and/or monitoring reports.  Meanwhile, Indonesian Broadcasting Commission Regulation 4 of 2023 on the Supervision of General Election Campaign Reporting, Broadcasting, and Advertisements at Broadcasting Institutions mandates KPI to supervise (1) reporting, (2) broadcasting in the form of a monologue, (3) dialogue involving the voice and/or image of the viewer or listener's voice; (4) election participant debates; (5) opinion polls; and (6) election campaign advertisements carried out by broadcasting institutions. Supervision occurs during the election campaign and the calm, voting, and vote-counting periods.  On the other hand, for the press media, as regulated in the Law on the Press (see Goal 1, Policies and Measures that Support Media Freedom), the central government institution that demands accountability is the Press Council. Referring to Press Council Regulation 1/Peraturan-DP/I/2023 on the Data Collection of Press Companies, one of the primary forms of media accountability carried out by the Press Council is performing administrative and factual verification of press companies. The Press Council, in collaboration with journalist competency testing institutions, also holds the Journalist Competency Test throughout provinces for free. This activity aims to strengthen the competence of journalists as the core of press companies in print, electronic, and digital media to meet the standards stipulated in Press Council Regulation 4/Peraturan-DP/X/2018 on Journalist Competency Standards. Participants who can take this competency test must meet the provisions in Press Council Regulation 1/Peraturan-DP/VIII/2015 on Journalist Competency Test Participants. Participants who pass the Journalist Competency Test will receive junior, intermediate, or senior-level journalist certification.  To support the performance of the Press Council in guaranteeing the quality of journalists, the Indonesian Journalists Association opened SJI in 2023, which has been held mobile from one province to another. Classes are not held in one location but can be held remotely in all areas that require training. One of SJI's main focuses is building journalistic skills in the newsroom or editorial room.  Finally, the PR on Publishers Rights is one of the new policies closely related to demands for media accountability. This PR aims to regulate the responsibilities of digital platform companies to support quality journalism so that journalistic news is respected and valued fairly and transparently. This PR regulates global digital platforms such as Google, Instagram, Facebook, and others to provide balanced compensation for displaying news content from local and national media. The scope of this PR includes (1) regulation of digital platform companies, (2) collaboration between digital platform companies and press companies, (3) establishment of the committee by the Press Council, and (4) funding needed to carry out committee duties and functions. The committee in question is the Independent Publishers Rights Commission, which was being prepared to regulate the resolution of press disputes between press companies and digital platform companies at the time of drafting this report.  In general, policies and measures that demand media accountability are aimed at contributing to achieving the following agenda(s) of the National Strategy for Culture: 1. Provide space for the diversity of cultural expressions and encourage cultural interaction to strengthen the inclusiveness of culture (Agenda 1);  2. Protect and develop values, expressions, and practices of traditional culture to enrich national culture (Agenda 2); and 3. Strengthen the role of the government as a facilitator of culture advancement (Agenda 7).
Results: Press Council Regulation 1/Peraturan DP/I/2023 on the Data Collection of Press Companies:  As of February 21, 2024, the Press Council has verified 1,819 media in Indonesia, including digital media from 989 companies.  Journalist Competency Test: A total of 27,704 journalists have been certified as either junior (muda), intermediate (madya), or senior (utama).
Recommandations: The Press Council's 2003 internal evaluation of media accountability resulted in the following conclusions/recommendations. 1. The Press Council must continue to verify media as stated in Press Council Regulation 1/Regulation DP/I/2023 on the Data Collection of Press Companies. 2. Journalists must take the Journalist Competency Test through one of the 24 test institutions approved by the Press Council.  Law 32 of 2002 on Broadcasting: Evaluation carried out internally by KPI (2024) resulted in several recommendations. 1. Strengthening the internal KPI institutions, consisting of the Central KPI and Regional KPIs, to optimize monitoring broadcast content, the number of which has multiplied since the implementation of Analog Switch-Off. 2. Building a sense of justice for the broadcasting ecosystem through proposals for monitoring content on digital platforms. 3. Proposing a rating audit to avoid having a single interpretation of the quality of broadcast programs on television.  Komisi Penyiaran Indonesia (KPI, 2024, 28 Mei). Title EN: Policies and Measures that Encourage Job Creation and Entrepreneurship in Culture and Creative Economy Sectors
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: 1. Ministry of Tourism and Creative Economy/Tourism and Creative Economy Agency (Kemenparekraf) 2. Indonesian Film Agency (Badan Perfilman Indonesia, BPI) 3. Revolving Funds Management Institution (Lembaga Pengelola Dana Bergulir, LPDB)
Main Feature: In the past four years, policies and measures that encourage job creation and entrepreneurship in culture and creative economy sectors include: 1. Law 10 of 2009 on Tourism (Law on Tourism);  2. Law 6 of 2023 on the Stipulation of Government Regulation in Lieu of Law 2 of 2022 on Job Creation into Law (Law on Job Creation);  3. Draft Law on Amendments to Law 10 of 2009 on Tourism (Draft Law on Tourism);  4. Draft Law on National Entrepreneurship;  5. AKATARA Indonesian Film Market & Business Forum (AKATARA);    6. Revolving Funds for Cooperatives, Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises; and  7. Acceleration of Sharia Finance for Creative Economy and Tourism (Akselerasi Keuangan Syariah Ekonomi Kreatif and Pariwisata, AKSES).  AKATARA and Revolving Funds for Cooperatives, Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises have been reported in the 2020 QPR and are still ongoing at the time of this report.   One policy that has not been reported in the 2016 and 2020 QPRs but is still valid at the time of the drafting of this report is the Law on Tourism. This Law regulates, among other things, the utilization of Indonesian arts and culture as a resource and development capital that increases the prosperity and welfare of the people, including job creation. This is indicated explicitly by one of the objectives of tourism, which is to minimize unemployment, and one of the principles of tourism, which is to empower local communities. Tourism development includes the tourism industry, tourism destinations, marketing, and tourism institutions, all aimed at creating jobs, including for artists and cultural practitioners. To respond to recent challenges and opportunities, stakeholders realize the need to update the law. In recent developments, the Draft Law on Tourism has become one of the priorities of the National Legislation Program (Prolegnas) to be completed in 2024 and is already at the drafting stage. In addition, Prolegnas has also listed plans for preparing another relevant regulation, namely the Draft Law on National Entrepreneurship, which has not yet been prioritized to be completed in 2024.  The Law on Job Creation is another policy considered a breakthrough in the past four years. The scope of this Law, which was developed using the omnibus method, includes (1) improvement of investment ecosystem and business activities; (2) employment; (3) ease, protection, and empowerment of cooperatives and micro, small, and medium enterprises; (4) ease of doing business; (5) research and innovation support; (6) land acquisition; (7) economic zones; (8) Central Government investment and acceleration of national strategic projects; (9) implementation of government administration; and (10) imposition of sanctions.   In the culture sector, primarily to facilitate film business people in conducting business activities, amendments, deletions, or stipulations of new regulations were made to Law 33 of 2009 on Film, including (1) business licenses related to broadcasting films through television or information technology networks are not necessarily to be granted from the Central Government; and (2) filmmaking by foreign parties to be shot in locations in Indonesia shall be carried out based on the approval from the Central Government free of charge.  Another sector closely related to the culture sector is tourism, especially regarding tourist attractions, tourism areas, and the organization of entertainment and recreation activities. Several amendments, deletions, or stipulations of new regulations were made to Law 10 of 2009 on Tourism, including the obligation of tourism entrepreneurs to (1) maintain and respect religious norms, customs, culture, and values that live in the local community; (2) provide insurance protection to tourism businesses with high-risk activities; (3) develop partnerships with local cooperatives and micro and small enterprises that promote empowerment and mutual benefit; (4) prioritize the use of local community products, domestic products, and provide opportunities for local manpower; (5) improve human resources competencies through training and education; (6) play an active role in infrastructure development efforts and community empowerment programs; and (7) preserve the natural and cultural environment.   In the context of the Convention, the broadcasting sector is also considered to have a strategic role in protecting and promoting the diversity of cultural expressions. Related to this broadcasting sector, several arrangements in the Law on Job Creation amend the provisions in Law 32 of 2OO2 on Broadcasting, including: (1) foreign nationals can serve on the management board of private broadcasting institutions but limited only to finance and engineering; (2) new definitions for private broadcasting institutions and subscription broadcasting institutions; (3) broadcasting institutions are obliged to pay business licensing fees based on broadcasting zones/regions determined by the economic level parameters of each zone/region; (4) broadcasting operations are carried out by following technological developments, including the migration of terrestrial broadcasting from analog technology to digital technology; and (5) the termination of analog broadcasting by no later than November 2, 2022.  Another strategic sector is the labor sector, in which several provisions in Law 13 of 2003 on Manpower have also been amended, including those relating to the regulation of foreign workers, namely: (1) every employer who employs foreign workers must have a plan for the use of foreign workers authorized by the Central Government, with some exceptions; (2) individual employers are prohibited from employing foreign workers; (3) foreign workers can be employed in Indonesia only for specific positions and certain times and have competencies in accordance with the position to be occupied; (4) foreign workers are prohibited from occupying positions that manage personnel; (5) foreign worker employers are required to appoint Indonesian workers as assistants to foreign workers employed for technology transfer and transfer of skills from foreign workers; and (6) foreign worker employers are required to provide education and job training for Indonesian workers in accordance with the qualifications of the positions occupied by foreign workers.  Meanwhile, AKSES is a new program initiated in 2023 by Kemenparekraf in collaboration with the Provincial Government of DKI Jakarta through the Office of Tourism and Creative Economy and LBS Urun Dana. This program aims to help micro, small, and medium enterprises engaged in the creative economy get easy financing to develop their business. The potential value of assistance is from IDR 500 million/ 30,652,75 USD to IDR 10 billion / 613,055,00 USD  for each business. Not only does the AKSES program provide easy access to investment through pitching forums, but it also provides capacity building and mentoring for Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises players so that they can continue to grow their businesses.  In general, policies and measures that encourage job creation and entrepreneurship in culture and creative economy sectors are aimed at contributing to achieving the following agenda(s) of the National Strategy for Culture: 1. Utilize objects of culture advancement to improve people’s welfare (Agenda 4); and 2. Strengthen the role of the government as a facilitator of culture advancement (Agenda 7).

Title EN: Policies and Measures that Protect the Social Rights of Artists
Goal: Promote Human Rights And Fundamental Freedoms
SDG: SDG 5 - Achieve gender equality and empower all women and girls,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels
Area of Monitoring: Artistic freedom
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: 1. Ministry of Education, Culture, Research, and Technology  2. Ministry of Tourism and Creative Economy/Tourism and Creative Economy Agency 3. Social Security Agency
Main Feature: In the past four years, policies and measures that protect the social rights of artists include: 1. Law 1 of 1970 on Occupational Safety (Law on Occupational Safety);  2. Law 21 of 2000 on Trade Unions/Labor Unions (Law on Trade/Labor Unions);  3. Law 40 of 2004 on the National Social Security System (Sistem Jaminan Sosial Nasional) (Law on Sisjamsosnas);  4. Law 24 of 2011 on the Social Security Agency (Badan Penyelenggara Jaminan Sosial) (Law on BPJS);  5. Law 6 of 2023 on the Stipulation of Government Regulation in Lieu of Law 2 of 2022 on Job Creation into Law (Law on Job Creation);  6. Draft Law Amendments to Law 1 of 1970 on Occupational Safety (Draft Law on Occupational Safety);  7. Draft Law on Amendments to Law 21 of 2000 on Trade Unions/Labor Unions (Draft Law on Trade/Labor Unions);  8. Draft Law on Amendments to Law 40 of 2004 tentang the National Social Security System (Sistem Jaminan Sosial Nasional) (Draft Law on Sisjamsosnas);  9. Draft Law on Amendments to Law 24 of 2011 on the Social Security Agency (Badan Penyelenggara Jaminan Sosial) (Draft Law on BPJS);  10. Minister of Tourism and Creative Economy 11 of 2022 on the 2020-2024 Ministry of Tourism and Creative Economy/Tourism and Creative Economy Agency Strategic Plan;   11. National Health Insurance Program;   12. National Work Accident and Death Insurance and Old Age Protection Programs;   13. Social Security Program for members of the Indonesian Musicians Union Federation (Federasi Serikat Musisi Indonesia);   14. Social Security Program for Senior Musicians;  15. Appreciation Program for Cultural Practitioners;  16. Indonesian Cultural Awards;  17. Bali Arts Awards; and  18. Night of Melayu Jambi Majesty (Malam Keagungan Melayu Jambi).   One of the policies reported in the 2020 QPR, the Head of the Creative Economy Agency Regulation 8 of 2017 on the 2015-2019 Creative Economy Agency Strategic Plan, has expired and was last amended by the enactment of the Minister of Tourism and Creative Economy 11 of 2022 on the 2020-2024 Ministry of Tourism and Creative Economy/Tourism and Creative Economy Agency Strategic Plan.  Furthermore, there are several fundamental policies related to protecting the social rights of artists that have not been reported in the 2020 QPR, namely the Law on Occupational Safety, the Law on Trade/Labor Unions, the Law on Sisjamsosnas, and the Law on BPJS. The Law on Occupational Safety regulates work safety in all workplaces within the legal jurisdiction of the Republic of Indonesia. The work safety in question includes goods, labor, and general safety. Meanwhile, the Law on Trade/Labor Unions guarantees the rights of workers/laborers to form and develop trade/labor unions that are free, open, independent, democratic, and responsible. The union in question is a means of fighting for, protecting, and defending the interests and welfare of workers/laborers and their families and realizing harmonious, dynamic, and just industrial relations.  Then, there is the Law on Sisjamsosnas and the Law on BPJS, which also contribute to protecting the social rights of artists by establishing a national system and implementing government institutions. Following enacting the Law on Job Creation (see Goal 1, Policies and Measures that Encourage Job Creation and Entrepreneurship in Culture and Creative Economy Sectors), several regulations in the Law on Sisjamsosnas and the Law on BPJS were amended. One of the social security measures under the Law on Job Creation is the National Health Insurance Program for all Indonesian citizens, including artists and other cultural actors, which BPJS for Health organizes. Then, specifically for workers, including arts and culture workers and creative workers, they can be protected by the National Work Accident and Death Insurance and Old Age Security Programs organized by BPJS for Manpower.  Furthermore, Kemendikbudristek, Kemenparekraf, and BPJS for Manpower continue to collaborate with various organizations that oversee arts and culture workers and creative workers to increase the distribution of social security services for them, including: 1. BPJS for Manpower, in collaboration with the Indonesian Musicians Union Federation (Federasi Serikat Musisi Indonesia, FESMI), launched a program for FESMI members. This program was then expanded in partnership with the Anugerah Musik Indonesia Foundation (AMI) to accommodate the social security needs of senior musicians.  2. BPJS for Manpower collaborated with the Jakarta Arts Council to provide social security facilities for artists and cultural arts workers in the DKI Jakarta area.  3. BPJS for Manpower, in collaboration with the Association of Indonesian Comedy Artists (Persatuan Seniman Komedi Indonesia, PaSKI), carried out awareness-raising efforts to increase comedy artists' participation in the manpower social security program.  4. Kemendikbudristek will facilitate arts and culture workers' obtaining BPJS for Manpower services. The Directorate of Personnel Development and Cultural Institutions will disseminate data collection forms for artists and arts and cultural workers through a network of arts councils spread across various provinces and cities/regencies. Artists who have been registered will later be curated and then registered with BPJS for Manpower and assisted in paying their contributions.  In recent developments, stakeholders have identified a real need from the field to update the Law on Occupational Safety, Law on Trade/Labor Unions, Law on Sisjamsosnas, and the Law on BPJS to be more responsive to current developments and all their challenges and opportunities. Even though the Draft Law on Occupational Safety, Draft Law on Trade/Labor Unions, Draft Law on Sisjamsosnas, and the Darft Law on BPJS have all been registered in the National Legislation Program, none of them are yet a priority for completion in 2024.   Especially during the COVID-19 pandemic, Kemendikbudristek and Kemenparekraf held an Appreciation Program for Cultural Practitioners, which provided social assistance to arts and creative workers whose livelihoods were disrupted due to the impact of the pandemic. Apart from that, the Central Government also has the Indonesian Cultural Award event as an appreciation for arts and cultural practitioners who have made significant contributions to culture advancement. This award has nine categories, including (1) Bintang Mahaputera; (2) Parama Dharma Cultural Star; (3) Cultural Satyalancana; (4) Traditional Arts Maestro; (5) Conservation; (6) Pioneer and/or Reformer; (7) Foreign Institutions and Individuals; (8) Children; and (9) Media.  Several local governments also have similar programs to give awards to arts and cultural practitioners who have contributed to their area. For example, the Bali Province has the Bali Jani Nugraha award for artists/literature/poets/ book writers throughout Bali, the Adi Sewaka Nugraha for artists serving the arts throughout Bali, and the Dharma Kusuma for cultural figures/scientists throughout Bali. Furthermore, the Jambi Province has the Night of Melayu Jambi Majesty event, in which awards are presented to Melayu Jambi cultural maestros.  In general, policies and measures that protect the social rights of artists are aimed at contributing to achieving the National Strategy for Culture, specifically to strengthen the role of the government as a facilitator of culture advancement (Agenda 7).
Results: Appreciation Program for Cultural Practitioners: The government assisted 59 thousand arts and creative workers.  Bali Jani Nugraha Award: 2020: 10 recipients. 2021: 10 recipients. 2022: 10 recipients. 2023: 10 recipients.  Adi Sewaka Nugraha Award: 2021: 6 recipients. 2022: 9 recipients. 2023: 10 recipients.  Dharma Kusuma Award: 2021: 4 recipients. 2022: 4 recipients. 2023: 4 recipients.
Financial Ressources: Appreciation Program for Cultural Practitioners: The total assistance is IDR 59 billion/3.595.589,80 USD.
