Main Feature: The inception of this concept in a multi-party format was a collaborative effort that commenced in 2019, bolstered by the support of the United Nations Women's Organization (UN Women). To ensure transparency, a working group was formed, and the draft document was shared for feedback with our esteemed international partners, donors, and local organizations. The consultation stage involved the participation of relevant sectoral parliamentary committees and Ministries, underscoring the importance of their insights in shaping this concept.  In 2022, a new state concept of gender equality was adopted in a multi-party format. Thus, an important step was taken in the establishment of equality policy and the fight against discrimination. The document represents a unified vision of the State to eliminate all forms of discrimination based on gender and ensure gender equality in the civil, political, economic, social, and cultural spheres, both in public and private relations.  The concept defined the main directions and measures for achieving gender equality. According to the concept, art, culture, and sports are identified as the ninth priority out of 22 existing priorities.  In addition, to ensure gender equality, the concept contributes to: Creating legal and regulatory norms and strategies in art, culture, and sports using the principles of gender mainstreaming, as well as considering gender needs, is at the stage of planning or implementation of programs and events.  Additionally, according to the concept, the State ensures the integration of the principles of gender equality in the cultural policy documents and the evaluation of the gender impact in developing political initiatives and programs.

Title EN: South African Literary Awards
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Agency Implementation: Writes Associates
Main Feature: South African Literary Awards was founded in 2005 by the wRite associates in collaboration with the then-national Department of Arts and Culture (DAC), now the Department of Sport, Arts and Culture (DSAC). The main aim of the South African Literary Awards (SALA) is to pay tribute to South African writers who have distinguished themselves as groundbreaking producers and creators of literature content, while it celebrates literary excellence in the depiction and sharing of South Africa’s histories, value systems, philosophies and art as inscribed and preserved in all official languages of South Africa.  The awards also aim to become the most prestigious and respected literary accolades in South African literature.  Awarding our literary stalwarts while they are still alive is a profound statement to the winners and the nation at large. The awards honour South Africa’s living literary practitioners, legends and, where appropriate, others posthumously irrespective of age, language, colour, gender, disability status, sexuality and other demographics. Since 2005, the number of awards has multiplied, there are now sixteen (16) categories, recognising a variety of literary forms. The categories are as follows: •	Novels Award •	Poetry Award •	Nadine Gordimer Short Stories Award •	Literary Journalism Award •	Creative Non-Fiction Award •	Children’s Literature •	Youth Literature Award •	Literary Translation Award •	Lifetime Achievement Award •	Posthumous Award •	Chairperson’s Award  •	Local Poet Laureate Award •	Regional/Provincial Poet Laureate Prize (from all the provinces except the Western Cape and Limpopo) •	First-time Published Author Award •	K. Sello Duiker Memorial Literary Award •	National Poet Laureate Prize (not open for submissions)
Results: The award has bestowed honor to over three hundred authors and writers Awards Conferred. SALA has played a significant role in encouraging and motivating writers to raise the bar in literary endeavours. From 2019 to date, SALA has proudly honoured one hundred and twenty-six authors. Below is the number of winners per year: 2019 to 2023 YEAR	NUMBER OF WINNERS PER YEAR 2019	18 2020	15 2021	26 2022	33 2023	34  SALA has also given birth to the following legacy programmes: •	The Miriam Tlali Reading & Book Club: a programme named after the literary veteran and first black South African woman to publish a novel in English, Ms Miriam Tlali, who is a recipient of the SALA inaugural 2005 Lifetime Achievement Literary Award. This programme was launched in June 2009 in order to explore the literary jewels that South Africa is in possession of. Its primary goal is to cultivate a reading and writing culture in the country. •	The National Creative Writing Skills Development Programme: is aimed at creating a platform for literary engagements and for young and old unpublished writers to showcase their work, while it introduces South African literature and legendary writers to the youth and community at large. The programme will respond to the challenges faced by our country with regard to the lack of appreciation of reading and writing, embracing indigenous languages, publishing, distribution and marketing of literary works and the involvement of the youth in literary engagements domestically and internationally. •	Africa Century International African Writers Conference: This programme was established in 2012 as a part of the legacy programmes of the SALA Awards. The inaugural International African Writers Day Lecture was delivered by former President Thabo Mbeki, followed by Dr Mustapha Sidiki Kaloko, AU Commissioner of Social Affairs at the African Union Commission (2013). The 3rd lecture was delivered by Honourable Samia Yaba Nkrumah, Chairperson and Leader of the Convention Peoples Party and Executive Director of The Kwame Nkrumah Pan African Centre, Ghana. The fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, through to the 11th Lectures were delivered by Arts and Culture Minister, HE Nathi Mthethwa, SALA Advisory Board Chairperson, Prof Zodwa Motsa, Prof Micere Mugo, Prof Kwesi Prah, Prof Mandla Makhanya, National Poet Laureate, Prof Mongane Wally Serote, Prof Puleng LenkaBula, Dr Gcina Mhlophe and Mr Ibrahima Aya, respectively.
Recommandations: The hosting of the awards has been evaluated over the years and significant achievements have been noted as well as challenges. The programme has encouraged more authors and writers to enter the space, recognised excellence especially young and upcoming writers, opened the doors for new talent in the sector. The main challenge has always been inadequate funding of the programme and its inability to adequately support and recognise everyone countrywide. There is a high need and demand for acquisition and diversification of funding sources and resources to ensure that more writers are recognised and supported. Private public sector collaboration is required to expand the scope of the awards and reach to grass root levels.  Following the evaluation of the programme the following recommendations where advanced and need to be taken forward:  •	Need for more resource allocation on the project.  •	Increase methods and tactics for making the project more attractive to current and prospective partners. •	Make the project more appealing to the prospective beneficiaries and sponsors. It can be deduced from the above that given the ever challenging and changing environment in the literary space, establishing, maintaining and continually improving a literary arts institution that is all-encompassing for South Africa is highly recommended. The South African Literary Awards and Africa Century International African Writers Conference are bold step towards preserving and celebrating our literary heritage, the country will in the coming years continue to implement the programme to encourage creativity and promote cultural expression.

Title EN: Soutien à l’industrie cinématographique nationale
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Agency Implementation: Ministère de la Jeunesse, de la Culture, et de la Communication-Département de la Communication
Main Feature: La politique du Centre Cinématographique Marocain, en matière de soutien au cinéma, date de 1980, par la création d'un Fonds de soutien pour la promotion de la production et de l'exploitation cinématographiques. Depuis lors, cet engagement n'a cessé d'évoluer, tant au niveau de la règlementation qu’au niveau des ressources financières ou des filières bénéficiaires. Ainsi, le Fonds de soutien à la production cinématographique (1980), devient en 1987, le Fonds d'aide à la production et à l'exploitation cinématographique. Si celui-ci est plus richement doté, il devient, en revanche, sélectif sur les projets de films. Dans les deux cas, les bénéficiaires ne sont pas tenus de rembourser les fonds alloués. En 2003, le système évolue encore et devient une avance sur recettes, mais avec des fonds alloués plus conséquents. En 2009, ces fonds augmentent encore et la production nationale bénéficie d'un montant annuel de 60 millions de dirhams. Depuis la publication du décret n° 2.12.325 du 17 août 2012 qui fixe les conditions et les procédures d’aide à la production cinématographique, à la numérisation, la rénovation et la création de salles de cinéma et à l’organisation des festivals de cinéma, deux autres fonds ont été créés, en plus du «fonds d’aide à la production des œuvres cinématographiques ». Il s’agit «du fonds de soutien à la numérisation, la rénovation et la création des salles de cinéma », et « du fonds de soutien à l’organisation des festivals cinématographiques».  Ces trois fonds, gérés par le Centre Cinématographique Marocain (CCM), sont financés directement par « le fonds pour la promotion du paysage audiovisuel national », et représentent des programmes de promotion de l’industrie cinématographique.  Les conditions et les critères d’octroi de tous les types de soutien et leurs modalités de versement sont fixés par arrêtés conjoints du Ministre chargé de la Communication et du ministre chargé des Finances. Ainsi, 60 millions de dirhams sont alloués annuellement à la production, 7 millions de dirhams à la numérisation des salles de cinéma et 27,5 millions à l'organisation de festivals et manifestations cinématographiques. Enfin, en janvier 2015, 15 millions de dirhams supplémentaires sont alloués à la production de films documentaires sur la culture sahraouie et hassani. L'Etat, à travers le Centre Cinématographique Marocain, soutient donc le cinéma national avec prés de 110 millions de dirhams par an (environ 10 millions de dollars). Grâce à ces mécanismes de soutien, 90% du parc de salles sont numérisés, une vingtaine de longs métrages est produit et une cinquantaine de festivals et autres manifestations cinématographiques sont aidés tous les ans. En 2018, un amendement est introduit sur le décret de 2012, afin d’instituer un nouveau soutien financier attribué à la production étrangère au Maroc d’œuvres audiovisuelles et cinématographiques. Il s’agit d’une subvention dont le montant est fixé à 20% de la totalité des dépenses effectuées au Maroc et éligibles au soutien. En 2022, le décret de 2012 a encore une fois été amendé dans le sens de porter le soutien accordé à la production étrangère d'œuvres audiovisuelles et cinématographiques au Maroc à 30% dans le but de renforcer les capacités du Maroc en matière d’attraction de productions étrangères. En matière de réglementation du secteur du cinéma, le Centre Cinématographique Marocain est un acteur clé. Il a été réorganisé en vertu de la loi n° 70.17 promulguée par le Dahir n°1-20-07 du 6 mars 2020, qui a définit ses missions ainsi que ses organes d’administration et de gestion. Ce texte vise à renforcer le rôle du Centre Cinématographique Marocain en vue de la création d’une véritable industrie cinématographique répondant aux aspirations de tous les acteurs du secteur et à consolider les principes de la bonne gouvernance, de l’égalité des chances, de la compétitivité, du pluralisme et de l’ouverture sur les cultures, à même de promouvoir le secteur cinématographique pour en faire un levier de développement. Dans la même perspective, le Centre Cinématographique Marocain a  déjà entamé le processus de refonte de l'arsenal juridique de l’industrie cinématographique marocaine, notamment mettre à jour et adapter la législation existante pour mieux répondre aux besoins des productions étrangères ainsi que le réajustement des cahiers de charges qui vont être aligner aux exigences avec les normes internationales tout en préservant les intérêts et les spécificités du Maroc.
Results: Au cours des dernières années, l’impact du soutien de l’Etat est perceptible à l’aune des résultats du secteur, les chiffres de 2023 témoignent de l'intensification des efforts et des ressources consacrés à cette industrie. En effet, la production nationale annuelle avoisine 130 productions nationales, toute catégorie confondue, longs-métrages et courts métrages, de fiction et de documentaire, dont une soixantaine ont bénéficié du soutien financier du CCM de l’ordre 7,35 millions de Dollars.  Parallèlement, le soutien à la numérisation, la rénovation et la création de salles de cinéma a permis une nette amélioration de l'infrastructure cinématographique et un meilleur accès du public à des projections de qualité.  Ainsi le parc des salles de cinéma a atteint 81 écrans avec une nette augmentation de la fréquentation des salles générant des recettes de 8.9 millions de dollars. En 2023, 10 salles ont bénéficié d’un soutien de l’ordre de 2,85 millions de Dollars, dont 2,4 millions de dollars alloués à la création de nouvelles salles avec une répartition étendue à travers toutes les régions du Maroc. De plus, l'organisation de festivals et de manifestations cinématographiques a connu une expansion remarquable. En effet en 2023, 80 festivals et manifestations cinématographiques nationaux sont organisés, dont 67 sont subventionnés par le fonds du soutien à l’organisation des festivals cinématographiques, de l’ordre de 3.1 millions de Dollars avec des dates devenues incontournables dans l’agenda des professionnels nationaux et internationaux et ce, à l’image du Festival National du Film de Tanger et le Festival International du Film de Marrakech. L'attraction de productions étrangères a également été un point fort de cette évolution. Le nombre de productions internationales tournées au Maroc a augmenté, ce qui est un indicateur clé de la reconnaissance internationale croissante du pays en tant que destination de tournage attractive. En 2023, le Maroc a accueilli le tournage de 116 projets, toute catégorie confondue, avec un montant investi au Maroc de l’ordre de 114,7 millions de Dollars. Cette évolution est soutenue par le programme de soutien accordé à la production étrangère d'œuvres audiovisuelles et cinématographiques au Maroc de l’ordre de 33,6 millions de dollars, accordé à 28 projets, à raison de 30 % pour les projets dont le montant d’investissement au Maroc dépasse un million de dollars, démontrant ainsi l'engagement du Maroc à maintenir et à renforcer sa compétitivité sur la scène cinématographique mondiale. En somme, les dernières années ont été marquées par une évolution positive et soutenue de la politique de soutien à la production cinématographique au Maroc, avec des résultats tangibles en termes de quantité et de qualité des productions, d'amélioration des infrastructures et de rayonnement international. Ainsi en 2023, le cinéma marocain a été représenté dans plus de 120 festivals et manifestations cinématographiques internationaux, la production nationale a concouru dans 87 compétitions officielles et été gratifié de 50 prix accordés à 38 longs métrages et à 12 courts métrages.
Financial Ressources: •	Festivals et manifestations cinématographiques : 33 MDH •	Production cinématographique : 73,5 MDH •	Production étrangère au Maroc : 336,38 MDH •	Salles de cinéma : 26,5 MDH
Recommandations: Les différends fonds de soutien, sont périodiquement audités par l'Inspection Générale des Finances (IGF) et par la cour des comptes. Les recommandations qui en écoulent sont prises en comptes par le Centre Cinématographique Marocain pour l’amélioration de la gestion de ces fonds.

Title EN: Soutien de projets de transformation des entreprises culturelles
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: Office fédéral de la culture OFC et services cantonaux de la culture
Main Feature: Avec les projets de transformation, un nouvel instrument de soutien aux acteurs du secteur culturel a été créé suite à la pandémie de COVID-19. Les projets de transformation avaient pour objectif d'aider les entreprises culturelles à s'adapter aux conditions modifiées par la pandémie de COVID-19. Les projets éligibles étaient, premièrement, ceux qui avaient pour objet une « réorientation structurelle des entreprises culturelles » et, deuxièmement, ceux qui visaient à « reconquérir des publics/conquérir de nouveaux segments de public ». Entre l'automne 2021 et l'automne 2023, la Confédération et les cantons ont accordé plus de 110 millions de dollars américains pour la mise en œuvre de tels projets - plus de 1400 projets ont ainsi été soutenus dans toute la Suisse.   Les cantons ont traité environ 2500 demandes pour des projets de transformation et, avec 1444 projets soutenus, ont approuvé près de 60 % des demandes. La diversité des projets soutenus en termes de domaine culturel, de type de projet et de taille de projet est grande. En moyenne, un projet s'est vu attribuer environ 77 504 dollars américains. 90 % des projets de transformation ont été réalisés par des organisations à but non lucratif ou plutôt à but non lucratif, c'est-à-dire par des organisations culturelles d'utilité publique, des fédérations, des fondations ou des associations.
Results: Les projets de transformation ont eu des effets positifs en permettant aux organisations soutenues d'acquérir de nouvelles compétences et de réfléchir fondamentalement à leur orientation et à leur développement. Les effets positifs sur les organisations soutenues sont des sources de revenus supplémentaires, l'augmentation de la notoriété et l'optimisation des processus. En outre, les projets ont conduit à une plus grande mise en réseau et à un travail plus transdisciplinaire. En ce qui concerne l'infrastructure et la numérisation, le secteur culturel est mieux placé qu'avant la pandémie grâce aux projets de transformation.

Main Feature: Visa For Music - Africa middle east music meeting - est la première plateforme professionnelle de la musique du Maroc, d'Afrique et du Moyen-Orient dont la principale mission est de favoriser la constitution d’un marché de la musique de ses régions afin d’offrir une visibilité optimale et un environnement propice à la créativité et à la professionnalisation du secteur culturel et artistique. Le marché réunit chaque année les professionnels de la filière : artistes, organismes professionnels, agents, maisons de disque, institutions culturelles et fondations, médias et édition, managers, formateurs… Il est également un moyen de dynamiser les industries culturelles et créatives des régions concernées afin de stimuler leurs économies.Visa For Music s’affirme pour l’Afrique et le Moyen Orient comme le marché international atypique et incontournable des musiques du monde et l’espace interprofessionnel de la filière musicale au Maroc et pour les pays du Sud.Cette plateforme met la lumière sur la création musicale actuelle et permet aux artistes et aux professionnels de la musique du monde de se rencontrer pour échanger et développer des projets futurs. Visa For Music rassemble et fédère les compétences et les capacités sociales, institutionnelles et économiques autour de thématiques d’importance pour le développement régional.
Results: La mission principale de Visa For Music est de faire découvrir de nouveaux talents de la région Afrique/Moyen-Orient, et de leur offrir une vitrine auprès des professionnels pour s’exporter sur les marchés du monde entier. Les résultats attendus de Visa For Music sont principalement : Positionnement du Maroc en tant que hub artistique ; Promotion des musiques d’Afrique et du Moyen-Orient à travers le monde ; Encouragement de la mobilité artistique entre les pays africains et ceux du Moyen-Orient ; Développement de la scène musicale de la région ; Amélioration de la condition des artistes des pays du Sud ; Renforcement de la diplomatie culturelle et la visibilité du Maroc ; Renforcement des rapports Nord-Sud et Sud-Sud dans le secteur culturel.
Financial Ressources: Signature d’une convention entre le Département de la Culture et l'Association ATLAS AZAWAN pour une durée de 3 ans d'un montant de 150 000 Dollars américains.
Recommandations: Evaluation interne et auprès des participants marocains et étrangers.Les organisateurs de Visa for music ont pu mesurer les retombées de l’événement pour les artistes participants, de manière qualitative ou quantitative. Pour la première, il s’agit principalement des retombées presse positives ou des prix reçus. Pour la seconde, il s’agit pour l’essentiel du nombre de dates obtenues pour les artistes et des revenus induits (cachets perçus) qui sont le résultat direct de leur passage aux deux premières éditions de Visa For Music.Visa s’est installé dans le paysage des plateformes du marché de la musique, les résultats obtenus en terme de participation et de dates retenues pour les artistes sont très encourageants. Par ailleurs la dimension africaine et moyen-orientale s’est révélée très porteuse ce qui prélude de la pérennisation de cet événement.

Title EN: Specific Policies that Regulate Culture and/or Creative Economy Sectors
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Agency Implementation: 1. Ministry of Education, Culture, Research and Technology 2. Ministry of Tourism and Creative Economy
Main Feature: In the past four years, specific policies that regulate culture and/or creative economy sectors include: 1. Law 5 of 2017 on Culture Advancement (Law on Culture Advancement);   2. Law 13 of 2018 on the Handover and Storage of Printed Works and Recorded Works (Law on the Handover and Storage of Printed Works and Recorded Works);  3. Law 24 of 2019 on Creative Economy (Law on Creative Economy);  4. Government Regulation 55 of 2021 on the Implementation Regulation of Law 13 of 2018 on the Handover and Storage of Printed Works and Recorded Works (GR on Handover and Storage of Printed Works and Recorded Works Implementation);  5. Government Regulation 87 of 2021 on the Implementation Regulation of Law 5 of 2017 on Culture Advancement (GR on Culture Advancement Implementation);  6. Government Regulation 24 of 2022 on the Implementation Regulation of Law 24 of 2019 on Creative Economy (GR on Creative Economy Implementation);  7. Draft Minister of Education, Culture, Research, and Technology Regulation on the Integrated Culture Data Collection System and Protection of Culture Advancement Objects;   8. Draft Minister of Education, Culture, Research, and Technology Regulation on the Development of Culture Advancement Objects; and   9. Draft Minister of Education, Culture, Research, and Technology on Permits to Utilize Culture Advancement Objects for Commercial Purposes for Large Industries and Foreign Parties.   The following policies, Law on Culture Advancement, Law on Creative Economy, and Law on the Handover and Storage of Printed Works and Recorded Works, have been reported in the 2020 QPR and are still valid by the time of drafting this report. As explained in the 2020 QPR, the Law on Culture Advancement is the foundation for Indonesian government policies and programs in the cultural sector. The Law has had a derivative regulation in recent developments, namely the GR on Culture Advancement Implementation. Basically, this GR stipulates (1) the Culture Advancement Master Plan, (2) the Integrated Culture Data Collection System, (3) protection, (4) development, (5) utilization, (6) capacity building, and (7) awards.   Furthermore, Kemendikbudristek is in the process of drafting several ministerial regulations to serve as technical guidelines for the implementation of culture advancement efforts. Some of the ministerial regulations that are being drafted include (1) Draft Minister of Education, Culture, Research, and Technology Regulation on the Integrated Culture Data Collection System and Protection of Culture Advancement Objects; (2) Draft Minister of Education, Culture, Research, and Technology Regulation on the Development of Culture Advancement Objects; and (3) Draft Minister of Education, Culture, Research, and Technology on Permits to Utilize Culture Advancement Objects for Commercial Purposes for Large Industries and Foreign Parties.  On the other hand, the 2020 QPR also reported the Law on Creative Economy as the primary reference for Indonesian government policies and programs in the creative economy sector. The Law has had a derivative regulation in recent developments, namely the GR on Creative Economy Implementation. The scope of this GR includes (1) financing of the creative economy; (2) facilitation of the development of marketing systems for intellectual property-based creative economy products; (3) creative economy infrastructure; (4) incentives for creative economy actors; (5) responsibilities of the central government and/or local government and community participation in the development of the creative economy; and (6) settlement of financial disputes.  Meanwhile, the Law on the Handover and Storage of Printed Works and Recorded Works is the primary reference for government policies and programs related to the inventory of all printed and recorded works published in Indonesia. In recent developments, the Law has had a derivative regulation, namely the GR on Handover and Storage of Printed Works and Recorded Works Implementation. The scope of this GR includes (1) implementation of the legal deposit of printed and recorded materials; (2) management of the results of the legal deposit of printed and recorded materials; (3) public participation; (4) awarding; and (5) procedures for imposing administrative sanctions.  In general, specific policies that regulate culture and/or creative economy sectors are aimed at contributing to achieving the following agenda(s) of the National Strategy for Culture:  1. Provide space for the diversity of cultural expressions and encourage cultural interaction to strengthen the inclusiveness of culture (Agenda 1);  2. Protect and develop values, expressions, and practices of traditional culture to enrich national culture (Agenda 2);  3. Develop and utilize cultural resources to strengthen the position of Indonesia internationally (Agenda 3);  4. Utilize objects of culture advancement to improve people’s welfare (Agenda 4);  5. Culture advancement that protects biodiversity and strengthens ecosystems (Agenda 5);  6. Institutional reform and culture budgeting to support the culture advancement agenda (Agenda 6); and  7. Strengthen the role of the government as a facilitator of culture advancement (Agenda 7).
Recommandations: Law on Culture Advancement: An evaluation conducted by Gumay (2021) from Koalisi Seni on drafting regulations for implementing the Law on Culture Advancement resulted in the following conclusions/recommendations. 1. Four years after the Law on Culture Advancement was enacted, most implementing regulations were not drafted. The Law on Culture Advancement has 17 articles stipulating the formation of derivative regulations. As of 2021, the Central Government has only been able to complete three of its obligations. In fact, the Law on Culture Advancement stipulates that the preparation of implementing regulations must be completed no later than two years after the regulation is enacted.  2. It is recommended that the government finalize the Draft GR on the Implementation Regulation of Law on Culture Advancement immediately.   References: Gumay, H. (2021, 23 April). Title EN: Standardization of Cultural Profession and Institutions
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Agency Implementation: Ministry of Culture and Sport
Main Feature: The Ministry of Culture and Sport, in collaboration with the Institute of Ethiopian Standards and relevant bodies, including film producers' associations, has established new standards for cinematography, cinema houses, theatre houses, and public libraries. These standards are designed to ensure the quality and consistency of services across these sectors. Objectives: Establish Minimum Standards: The standards set the minimum acceptable criteria for each profession and institution. This aims to enhance the quality of services and ensure standardized practices throughout Ethiopia.  Categorization: Standards are categorized into three levels based on the expected service quality and operational requirements. This tiered approach helps to address varying needs and expectations for different types of institutions and services.  Economic and Social Impact: By implementing these standards, the initiative seeks to elevate the economic and social importance of cultural institutions. Standardization is expected to boost the cultural sector’s role in society and its contribution to the economy.  Documentation and Governance: The standards will also serve as a framework for documenting and governing cultural practices. This includes providing a structured platform for experimental and scientific works and serving as a valuable resource for researchers.  Promotion of the Arts: The standards are intended to celebrate and promote the arts, ensuring that they are represented and valued in accordance with established guidelines.  Expected Benefits: Improved quality and consistency in cultural institutions. Enhanced capacity for experimental and scientific research in the arts. Better compliance with legal and regulatory frameworks governing cultural practices.
Results: The adoption of new standards for cinematography, cinema houses, theatre houses, and public libraries represents a significant step towards enhancing the quality and consistency of these cultural and public service sectors. These standards are expected to have the following impacts:  Improvement of Existing and New Services: The established standards are designed to elevate the quality of both existing and newly constructed services. By setting clear criteria and benchmarks, these standards ensure that services meet a consistent level of excellence, leading to better user experiences and operational efficiency.  Encouragement of Sector Participation: The standards create favorable conditions for both private and government entities interested in engaging with the cultural and public service sectors. Clear guidelines and expectations facilitate investment and involvement, providing a structured framework for collaboration and development.  Enhanced Sector Development: By standardizing practices, the initiative supports the growth and modernization of the cinematography, cinema, theatre, and library sectors. This can lead to increased opportunities for innovation and improvement, attracting more stakeholders and fostering a dynamic cultural environment.  Quality Assurance: The implementation of these standards assures that services are delivered with a high degree of quality and consistency, which can improve overall public trust and satisfaction in these institutions.  The new standards are poised to enhance the quality of services across these sectors, foster greater involvement from various stakeholders, and drive sector development and modernization.

Title EN: Stara mestna elektrarna – Elektro Ljubljana / The Old Power Station
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Partnering with civil society
Agency Implementation: Bunker, Ljubljana
Main Feature: Stara mestna elektrarna – Elektro Ljubljana / The Old Power Station is a space for contemporary perfroming arts. The construction of the Old Power Station began in 1898 and it was the first power plant in Ljubljana, which provided the city with electricity until the end of World War II. It was revived in 1980s, when it was first occupied by artists. Today, the use of the Old Power Station facility represents a unique case of coexistence between vivid artistic creativity and business activities (it also hosts Elektro Ljubljana’s distribution management centre). As one of the few preserved examples of industrial architecture in Slovenia, it is protected as a cultural and technical monument. The Old Power Station is owned by the company Elektro Ljubljana, but was renovated into a cultural centre for contemporary performing arts in 2004 with the help of the Ministry of Culture of Slovenia. Since then it is managed and programmed by the CSO Bunker and is now buzzing with activities: several groups use it as their rehearsal venue; it is a place for different workshops, which range from cultural management to dance techniques, while in the evening, the power station is a venue for various contemporary performances and other multimedia events.  The programme in the Old Power Station is a combination of international performances, under the framework of various festivals, as well as a selection of interesting Slovene contemporary artists. The underlying motive of all events in The Old Power Station is the desire to explore and move the boundaries of the aesthetic and the expected, as well as the desire for engagement in the local and global environment.  Each year, the Old Power Station besides the rehearsals, educational and creative programmes hosts about 130 or more public events, presented by Slovene and international independent artists, nongovernmental artistic organisations and producers, and by various (international) festivals, each bearing their own artistic mission, among which the City of Women Festival (presenting the international women creators and performers), Klovnbuf Festival (presenting the art of new circus), Ment festival (an international festival of music), CoFestival (contemporary dance festival), Gibanica (contemporary dance) and Trigger (contemporary theatre and other performative practices) platforms, Bobri festival (festival for young audiences) or Animateka festival (international festival of animated films).  The Old Power Station yearly hosts about 300 artists creating in various formats of performing arts, varying from contemporary circus to devised theatre, from contemporary dance to improvisation, from lecture performances to installations, from music to multimedia and even film and animation.  The Old Power Stations also hosts artistic residencies, offering international artists a space to work for a longer period of time, mostly during the summer, before the Mladi Festival starts buzzing with preparation. This way, every year a number of artists spend a few weeks in Ljubljana, creating their work and making some presentation for the local audiences. For over a decade, Bunker, along with the Old Power Station, has been involved in international projects that seek greener methods of artistic production. These projects connect artistic interests and practices with themes such as environmental change, multispecies landscapes, and the interconnectedness of humans and nature. At the Old Power Station, we strive to implement green transition ideas. Fifteen years ago, we stopped gifting cut flowers, switched from plastic to glass or paper cups, continually reduce waste, use only ecological cleaning agents, and reuse and recycle all materials.
Results: In the 20 years since the Old Power Stations was established as a performing arts centre, it has hosted more than 2600 public events and numerous rehearsals, creation processes and educational processes. It is a space where a big majority of contemporary performing artists from Slovenia already created or presented their work. But The Old Power Station is not only a presentation and creation place, but strives to build relations and connections with the people leaving in Tabor neighbourhood where it is located. There is a lot of energy put into the activities of the Old Power Station which connect to the local inhabitants and all the neighbouring organisations in this specific part of the city – other cultural organisations (CSOs working in culture, that are based in Metelkova City district, the Museums quarter, where three museums are based nearby, the Sports Society Tabor, two primary schools and one Highschool, a gallery and a performing arts space in the vicinity, the City Cinema and others). The Old Power Station also invites local inhabitants to join various activities that are presented in its space through the festivals it is hosting (workshops, discussions, participation in the performances ...). Throughout the years a real community got established around the Old Power Station, which functions as a hub, but also has also managed, especially through Mladi Levi Festival, which happens there every end of August, to develop a temporary community, which through different, more open, caring, more democratic means weaves together a utopia that the society in large could perhaps one day become – open, soft, democratic, creative.

Goal: Achieve A Balanced Flow Of Cultural Goods And Services And Increase The Mobility Of Artists And Cultural Professionals
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 10 - Reduce inequality within and among countries,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development

Agency Implementation: Unlimited A.C.M
Main Feature: The Stellar Program, established in 2019 by UAE Unlimited, is an ongoing educational initiative designed to support emerging artists in the United Arab Emirates. The program spans 6-8 months and includes mentorship sessions, guest artist tutorship, and practical workshops aimed at enhancing the artists' education beyond traditional art school curricula. The program is divided into three main sections, running concurrently with the planning and production of the exhibition. Each year, a guest artist provides mentorship, guiding the artists through proposal development, production planning, and the execution of their final artwork. Offering insights into art theory, criticism, and practice, providing feedback and advice on the artists' concepts and techniques. Additionally, four day-long workshops cover key skills such as artwork photography, media relations, art writing, and art business, led by leading arts professionals from the UAE. The Stellar Program is led by engaging tutors, advisors, and artists, equipping participants with the tools and techniques to excel in their professional artistic careers.
Results: Through comprehensive mentorship, intensive sessions with established artists, and practical workshops, participants have gained invaluable knowledge and skills. These initiatives have enhanced the artists' understanding of contemporary art, improved their technical abilities, and prepared them for successful careers. The program has fostered a supportive and dynamic artistic community, promoting cultural production and artistic excellence in the UAE. Through these efforts, UAE Unlimited has reinforced its commitment to nurturing emerging talent and contributing to the broader cultural development goals of the region. The Stellar Program continues to be implemented, ensuring ongoing support and development for the UAE's emerging artists.

Title EN: Strategic Partnership and Cooperation Agreement Between the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland and Georgia
Goal: Achieve A Balanced Flow Of Cultural Goods And Services And Increase The Mobility Of Artists And Cultural Professionals
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 10 - Reduce inequality within and among countries,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Treaties and agreements
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: The Ministry of Economy and Sustainable Development of Georgia
Main Feature: The Strategic Partnership and Cooperation Agreement between the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland and Georgia (from now on, the Agreement) was signed on October 21, 2019, and entered into force on December 31, 2020. The Agreement preserves most of the commitments between the Parties established under the Deep and Comprehensive Free Trade Area Agreement between Georgia and the European Union that entered into force on September 1, 2014. The Agreement comprises 8 Titles and Annexes and 2 Protocols, which form an integral part of the Agreement. Under Title IV, which covers trade and trade-related matters, the UK and Georgia established a free trade area, eliminating all tariffs on goods with some exceptions provided in the Annexes and liberalizing trade in services in accordance with the chapter on Establishment, Trade in Services and Electronic Commerce. Along with others, the Agreement also covers a Chapter on Intellectual Property Rights. Chapter on Establishment, Trade in Services and Electronic Commerce opens up exciting opportunities for cultural services in Georgia. The commitments made by the Parties in specific sectors, such as Printing and Publishing, Audiovisual services, Entertainment services, News agency services, Libraries, archives, museums and other cultural services, fully liberalize establishing commercial presence and cross-border trade in those services. This paves the way for the growth and development of our cultural industries.   Terms and conditions regarding the movement of natural persons are also prescribed under the Chapter on Establishment, Trade in Services and Electronic Commerce, where the mobility of artists and cultural professionals can be concerned. Natural persons here are categorized as Key personnel, Graduate trainees, Business sellers, Contractual service suppliers, and Independent professionals.   Chapter on Intellectual Property Rights complements and further specifies the rights and obligations between the Parties under the TRIPS Agreement and other international IP agreements. It covers copyright and related rights, trademarks, geographical indications, designs and patents.
Results: All import tariffs on goods have been completely eliminated for trade in goods.

Title EN: Strengthening and expanding the activities of the National Culture Fund of the Ministry of Culture
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Agency Implementation: National Culture Fund / Ministry of Culture
Main Feature: The National Culture Fund was established by the Law for the Protection and Development of Culture and started functioning in November 2000. Its main objective is to support at а national level the creation, development and dissemination of Bulgarian culture and art in the country and abroad. The priorities of the National Culture Fund are also in line with the criteria of the Culture and Audiovisual Chapter of the Treaty of Accession of Bulgaria to the European Union. Between 2016 and 2019, the Fund's activities and budget have increased significantly. New programmes were developed and launched to support and promote cultural diversity. (Quote the budget (especially for 2022 when it was seriously increased)
Results: The governing body of the National Culture Fund is the Governing Board, chaired by the Minister of Culture. The members of the Board are cultural activists, representatives of artistic unions, representatives of various ministries. The resources of the Fund shall be raised from financial support defined in the Law on the State Budget of the Republic of Bulgaria for the respective budget year and other sources of funding mentioned in Article 30 of the Law on the Protection and Development of Culture. The funds are mainly allocated to creative projects aimed at developing the cultural sector. Funding for creative projects shall be carried out following the announcement of competitions under a programme drawn up in advance and approved by the Management Board.  At the beginning of each year, the Board of the National Culture Fund formulates the priority areas for financial support. Transparency and competitiveness are key principles in the work of the National Culture Fund. Individual artists, private, municipal and public cultural organisations are entitled to participate in competitions on an equal footing. After the close of the competitive session, applications are evaluated by an expert committee (where necessary) and a technical committee. The expert committee proposes to the Governing Board which applications should be funded and the Governing Board takes the final decision.  As a subsidiary budget authorising officer to the Minister of Culture, it has intensive communication with the Ministry of Culture, the Ministry of Finance, the Council of Ministers, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Tourism, the National Audit Office, the National Social Security Institute, the National Revenue Agency, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Interior, the state cultural institutes, the Bulgarian cultural institutes abroad, NGO partners in the implementation of individual programmes, other NGOs in the field of culture, and representatives of the business sector.  The National Culture Fund programmes will be described in more detail in the sections of the report corresponding to their objectives.

Recognizing the significance of interdisciplinary coordination in achieving gender equality, this plan is aligned with the Law on Ensuring Gender Equality (2011.02.02) and the 2022 "Interdisciplinary Strategic Plan for Gender Equality 2022-2031" developed by the National Gender Committee. It outlines a gender strategy specific to the cultural sector to ensure its effective implementation.
Results: In cases where one gender predominates among employees of state and budgetary organisations in the cultural sector, a gender balance of 40:60 is ensured, with the following conditions implemented: 1,607 individuals are employed in the Ministry of Culture and its 47 budgetary institutions, comprising 56.3% women and 43.7% men. Across 5,665 organisations active in 92 areas of 12 branches of cultural and creative industry, a workforce of 33,931 people includes 45.5% women and 54.5% men.

Title EN: Strengthen the role of culture in international cooperation
Goal: Integrate Culture In Sustainable Development Frameworks
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: International cooperation for sustainable development
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: Ministry of Culture, and all implementing partners in the UAE
Main Feature: In the UAE, strengthening the role of culture in international cooperation involves a multifaceted approach that integrates cultural diplomacy, collaborative initiatives, and strategic partnerships. The UAE actively engages in cultural exchanges and agreements with countries around the world, fostering mutual understanding and showcasing its rich cultural heritage on the global stage. Through hosting and participating in international cultural events, such as book fairs and art exhibitions, and entering into cultural memoranda of understanding, the UAE enhances its global cultural footprint. Additionally, the country utilizes its extensive network of cultural institutions and creative industries to support cross-cultural dialogue and collaborations. below an example of the UAE participation in international platforms: � Participation in G20 meetings: The Ministry of Culture represented the UAE in the G20 Culture Working Group meetings, marking the country's third consecutive participation as an independent guest country in the G20 process. The meetings, held online, focused on four key areas: cultural diversity and social inclusion; the intersection of culture with the digital environment and copyright; the role of the creative economy in sustainable development; and the preservation and promotion of cultural heritage. Under the theme "Building a Just World and a Sustainable Planet," discussions highlighted the UAE's unwavering commitment to culture as a driver of development, innovation, and social cohesion. Emphasizing the rich cultural diversity within the UAE, which encompasses over 200 nationalities, the Ministry showcased how deeply ingrained cultural inclusivity is in the nation�s societal framework. The G20 2024 process will see the UAE�s third consecutive participation as a stand-alone Guest Country at the G20. � Launch The Group of Friends of Culture-Based Climate Action (GFCBCA): The Group of Friends of Culture-Based Climate Action (GFCBCA) at the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) was officially announced by its co-chairs, Salem bin Khalid Al Qassimi, UAE Minister of Culture, and Margareth Menezes, Minister of Culture of Brazil. This new coalition, comprising 33 countries and UN agencies, advocates for recognizing the integral role of culture in climate change policies. It aims to generate political momentum for effective, cohesive, and coordinated global action, formally acknowledging the significance of culture and heritage in climate initiatives. The unveiling of the Emirates Declaration on Culture-Based Climate Action also took place at the meeting. The declaration emphasizes that today�s challenges are not only financial, technical, and scientific but cultural as well. It asserts that addressing climate change and achieving the Paris Agreement�s goals necessitate inclusivity and collaboration across all sectors, notably culture. The declaration further stresses the need to fully realize the Paris Agreement�s long-term objectives, including mitigation, adaptation, loss and damage, and climate-resilient sustainable development, by focusing on cultural heritage, arts, and creative industries as catalysts for transformative climate action. It also highlights the urgent need for cultural sectors, including institutions and heritage sites, to adapt and evolve in response to climate change. � Partnership with UNESCO to Build historical monuments in Iraq: In collaboration with UNESCO and the Government of Iraq, the UAE has supported the Revive the Spirit of Mosul initiative, which aims to reconstruct three of Mosul�s key historical landmarks destroyed by terrorism: the Al-Nuri Mosque with its Al-Hadba Minaret, the Al-Tahera Church, and the AlSaa'a Church. Launched in 2018, this significant project, backed by the UAE with a contribution of $50.4 million, is scheduled for completion in 2024.
Results: The efforts to strengthen the role of culture in international cooperation have produced significant outcomes. Enhanced global collaboration has been achieved, with countries increasingly partnering on cultural projects and initiatives. The UAE�s active participation in international forums, such as the G20 Culture Working Group, has bolstered its role in cultural diplomacy, influencing global cultural policies and showcasing its cultural values. This commitment reflects a broader focus on promoting cultural diversity and social inclusion, which is now more evident in global cultural practices and policies. Furthermore, integrating culture into sustainable development goals has gained traction, emphasizing culture�s critical role in achieving sustainability. Overall, these efforts have led to strengthened strategies for protecting cultural heritage, demonstrating the increasing recognition of culture�s importance in fostering international cooperation and development.
Recommandations: The UAE will continue international cooperation with the aim of ensuring sustainable development for all.

Main Feature: The outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic and the rapid spread of infections led to considerable restrictions for health policy reasons, which severely affected the cultural industries in Austria. Due to the temporary loss of their business basis, the numerous providers of cultural goods and services were confronted with considerable losses in turnover and consequently liquidity problems, which jeopardised their existence. The study quantitatively analysed and classified the economic significance of the cultural sector in the Austrian economy as a whole. Secondly, the study discussed the economic consequences of the COVID-19 crisis for the cultural industries in Austria and made a first attempt to quantify them (despite considerable gaps in the data). The study quantifies the contribution of the expanded cultural sector to the Austrian gross domestic product at slightly less than 3 percent. The direct and indirect value-added effects of the cultural sector are estimated at around EUR 9.8 billion, providing for some 150,000 jobs (employed and self-employed). The economic damage in connection with the COVID-19 crisis is estimated to amount to EUR 1.5 to 2 billion and is distributed differently among the subsectors of the culture sector. The study was carried out in spring 2020.
Results: On the one hand, the study revealed quick and easy-to-implement aid measures, but on the other hand also showed the need for permanent improvements to these measures, especially with regard to their accuracy. Together with the data collected, it provided an important basis for cultural policy during the COVID-19 crisis. In the longer term, however, the study also highlighted the need to improve the database as a basis for evidence-based cultural policy that is able to map both the non-economic and economic dimensions of the cultural sector.

Title EN: Study on Social and Creative Condition of Artists (2021)
Goal: Promote Human Rights And Fundamental Freedoms
SDG: SDG 5 - Achieve gender equality and empower all women and girls,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels
Area of Monitoring: Artistic freedom
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: The study was conducted on the initiative of the Lithuanian Council for Culture. The study was conducted by the National Association of Cultural and Creative Industries and the Institute of Future Society.
Main Feature: Study on Social and Creative Condition of Artists, conducted in 2021, represents an assessment of the socio-economic and creative condition of artists and the effectiveness of state interventions aimed at the improvement of this condition, commissioned by the Lithuanian Council for Culture. The aim of this study is to evaluate the field of Lithuanian artists, socio-economic and creative conditions determining the creative expression of artists. It is the first comprehensive attempt to assess the situation of artists in terms of demographic, social, financial and other data. Objectives of the study: -	To define the concept of artist that will be used in the study. -	To systematize social security and tax relief measures applicable to artists, legal  acts regulating the activities of artists, financial and other interventions (LCC and others) applied to promote the creative work of artists. -	To analyse how the socio-economic and creative state of artists is affected by state interventions.  -	To compare state interventions in Lithuania and other countries. -	To systematize statistical data identifying the activities of artists and,  based on them, to analyse the structure of the field of Lithuanian artists. -	To develop a methodology for artists’ surveys and compile an artists’ questionnaire. -	To carry out a representative survey of the country’s artists taking into account  the distribution of the country’s artists (according to the statistical data). -	To analyse the socio-economic situation of artists based on survey results, available statistical data and other sources. -	To determine the impact of state interventions on the condition of the  artists and their effectiveness. -	To compile an indicator of the condition of artists for long-term observation, to present its forecasts in 2023 and 2026, and to compare the condition of the Lithuanian artists with the situation inother countries.   The survey was based on several sources, with data mainly up to the beginning of 2020, i.e. before the first quarantine: people with the status of artists, members of artists' unions, data from the Lithuanian Council for Culture and the Lithuanian Film Centre on artists who have received grants over the past few years, as well as information from the State Tax Inspectorate on people with the status of beneficiaries. Other criteria include the need to be professionals who create regularly or have a relevant education.  The results of the data showed that there are about 7000 artists in Lithuania. Most of the artists are concentrated in bigger cities of Lithuania – Vilnius, Kaunas and Klaipėda. Overall, the districts of these three cities account for about 73% of Lithuanian artists. Vilnius district has the highest concentration of artists, with 53% of artists.   According to the data survey, the largest number of artists (over 1 500) are aged 55-64, while the largest communities are those of artists (painters), architects and musicians, with around 1700, 1 100, and 900 artists respectively working in these fields. Female and male creators are roughly evenly split (52 percent of female artists and 48 percent of male artists, accordingly).  The results of the survey showed that in 2019, the average monthly salary of the artist was 772 Eur. Only every fifth of the artists can make a living purely from creative activities – their main profession.   In addition, 70 percent of the artists are members of the artists’ union, 64 percent are members of other associations. Only 37% of artists have beneficiary status, while 73% have a status of an artist. 73 percent of the artists are self-employed, 25 percent employed in a state/municipal cultural organization.  Summarizing the answers of artists about their social situation, it can be said that their activities were evaluated as significant and having an impact on society and the development of the cultural field but underestimated by the society and policy makers. Although their profession gives artists great satisfaction, and 76 percent of Lithuanian artists would choose this profession again, this profession does not bring sufficient income to artists, they face income instability and must look for additional sources of income.  Lithuanian artists work an average of 54 hours a week, which is significantly more than the standard working week (40 hours). Artists devote this working time to creative, partly creative and non-creative work.   Considering the number of hours worked, in 2019 the average salary of creators accounted for 67 percent of the national average salary (in 2019 the average salary constituted 822 EUR).  IArtists are active in seeking funding for the implementation of their activities, actively participate in competitions announced by Lithuanian foundations or organizations. It helps artists to fund the creative process, but it also provides additional organizational (administrative) burden filling out applications and fulfilling the official requirements for project implementation that an artist has to do in order to fulfill the main function of his profession – to do creative work. ̵Data of artists’ survey shows that only one in five artists use funding opportunities from international funds.  Most artists are not involved in long-term employment relationships with governmental or non-governmental cultural organizations, but they regularly collaborate with other artists on a project basis. It is evident that artists value creative collaboration with colleagues or professionals in other fields but lack closer collaboration with cultural organizations in the dissemination of their work.  57.23 percent of the surveyed creators agree that professional development activities are necessary in their profession.   Respondents to the survey of artists positively assess the guarantees provided by the status of an artist, more than half of the respondents mentioned that they have a positive impact on their personal well-being, over 70 percent – that they have a positive impact on the general condition of artists in the country.   In Lithuania, the most active participants in grant competitions applied to the Lithuanian Council for Culture are artists aged 25-34, for whom these grants are important at the beginning of their creative career, to create a portfolio not only from the received commissions but also from personal initiatives. Also, young artists are more inclined to work independently, and receiving an individual grant provides an opportunity to pursue independent creative work.  Based on the evaluation of state interventions and a survey of the country’s artists, a comprehensive assessment of the state of the country’s artists was carried out. As the condition of artists consists of many components, it is analysed by forming a complex indicator of the condition of artists, which consists of data from 59 indicators reflecting the condition of artists. This assessment made it possible to identify the weakest and strongest components of the condition of the artists.  The study ends with conclusions on the current social and creative status of Lithuanian artists, the effectiveness of applied state interventions, as well as recommendations on how to perfect state interventions to improve artists’ social and creative status, provide creators with a dignified reward, create conditions for long-term systematic monitoring of artists and for collecting and analysing data about them.
Results: The results of the study have led to recommendations, including: - to increase the prestige of (national and municipal) prizes and awards through publicity campaigns aimed not only at artistic communities, but also at the wider public. - to initiate research on the needs of the art labour market and to form quotas for admission to higher education institutions. - to improve the communication of the guarantees provided by the status of the artist by making the information clearer and more comprehensible and by reminding the artists periodically.  - to promote the dissemination of professional creative work at the national and international level, it is recommended that the state funding system pays more attention to the representatives of professions related to the creation and dissemination of creative work. - it is recommended to promote sponsorship and patronage. Also, as private sponsorship can be linked to beneficiary status, it is recommended to encourage artists to acquire it and to communicate more to the public about the possibilities to support artists in this way. - investments in cultural education in a broad sense would help to establish the artist’s profession, they would feel more valued by the society, and in the long run the increased demand for culture would also affect the income of artists. - improving the social and creative status of artists must become one of the state’s goals in the context of national policy and, of course, one of the priority goals in cultural policy, linking goals to objectives and implementation indicators, creating a monitoring system. - increased financial interventions in the field of culture need to be based on evidence of the importance and impact of the field of culture on society. - it is recommended to pay more attention to interdisciplinary cooperation of artists, as well as cooperation with science and technology, to get involved in European and global projects promoting artistic, scientific and technological cooperation. ̵ - it is recommended to encourage greater cooperation between the state and its cultural organizations with NGOs, businesses and private entities that support the arts and culture through their interventions for artists, so that interventions are as diverse and effective as possible and have a greater overall impact on the social and creative condition of artists. The researchers concluded that cultural policy is oriented towards the consumption of culture, with public monitoring of cultural consumption dominating and no monitoring of the status of artists.  “Artist” in this survey was understood as a person who regularly carries out creative activity: has an education in the field of art and/or creates or recreates works of art, and/or considers artistic creative work to be an essential part of his/her life, and/or receives income from this activity, and/or contributes to the development of the arts and culture and/or seeks recognition as an artist.
Financial Ressources: Approx. USD 33 000 (EUR 29 000) was allocated for the implementation of the survey.

Title EN: Sultanate of Oman Pavilion at the Venice International Art Biennale 2022-2023
Goal: Achieve A Balanced Flow Of Cultural Goods And Services And Increase The Mobility Of Artists And Cultural Professionals
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 10 - Reduce inequality within and among countries,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Mobility of artists and cultural professionals
Agency Implementation: Ministry of Culture, Sports and Youth
Main Feature: The Sultanate of Oman participated with its national pavilion for the first time in the fifty-ninth Venice International Art Gallery, which was held from April 22 to November 27, 2022. In this edition, the Sultanate of Oman has had its own separate pavilion in a unique location in pursuit of further global reach and influence, with a total area of 300 square meters, located near the historic Piazza St. Mark, the beating heart of Venice. This allowed the participating artists to exhibit the artworks independently and contributed to enhancing the artistic visibility. The National Pavilion of the Sultanate of Oman at the Venice International Art Biennale was also honoured by the official inauguration of His Highness Sayyid Dhi Yazan bin Haitham Al Said, Minister of Culture, Sports, and Youth.  By participating in the Venice Biennale Italy and a series of accompanying national programs, the Sultanate of Oman aims to introduce Omani culture at the local and international levels. The inaugural national exhibition of the Sultanate of Oman Pavilion, titled "Written Fates", brought together selected works by three generations of Omani artists whose activity spans five decades of modern and contemporary visual art in the Sultanate of Oman. These artists are Anwar Sonia, pioneer of modern Omani art since the seventies of the last century, and one of the founders of the Youth Studio, an important educational institution, and artist Hassan Mir, founder of the experimental art movement whose exhibitions from the late nineties gained an international following and influenced another generation of artists and artists. Originally a student of Sonia and Hassan Mir, Bodour Al Riyamiya has focused her current art practice on photography and video installation. Radhika Khimji, one of the artists best known for making art through textile installation, construction and personal narratives, as well as a member of Hassan Mir's circle group, and finally the late artist Riyaa Al Rawahia, one of the artists of the contemporary generation and self-taught, will exhibit a collection of her final works.   Each of the five artists selected to represent the Sultanate of Oman at the fifty-ninth International Art Exhibition at the Venice Biennale has made significant and distinct contributions to their communities and has energized the contemporary art movement in the Sultanate of Oman over the past fifty years. They have also inspired a new generation, and their involvement in Venice and community engagement in the Sultanate of Oman has provided opportunities for the younger generation to experience the wider world of contemporary art in Venice that will play an important role in the development of the future of contemporary Omani art. The Venice Art Biennale, with its value and the size of the international audiences it has attracted, was a unique opportunity to celebrate the common language of creativity and highlight emerging Omani voices. The artwork at the National Pavilion of the Sultanate of Oman presented creative content according to a philosophical concept linked to nature and what it can offer to humans under the slogan of the Venice Biennale for this edition "The Milk of Dreams", inspired by a children's book from the fifties by the surrealist artist Leonora Carrington. Exploring the dynamic and intergenerational dialogue of the Omani art movement over the past fifty years, the exhibition exemplified the breadth of Oman's cultural history and unique visual arts traditions on a global scale.  The participation of the Sultanate of Oman comes as an affirmation of the importance of the arts in shaping cultural awareness and civilizational and intellectual communication between peoples and societies and seeking to confirm the existing balance between local culture, integration and external openness, and to enable and promote cultural production based on renewal, creativity and innovation. Coinciding with the participation of the Sultanate of Oman in this event, training programs were announced for the Biennial. Furthermore, the program was available to Omani youth interested in partnering with educational institutions. The event provided them with a space to engage in dialogue with international artists and trainees, exchange experiences, develop their information and provide them with in-depth knowledge about the history of Omani art. This selected group of trainees worked alongside the participating artists in the Omani Pavilion. The exhibition is one of the most important international cultural and artistic festivals that play an active role in achieving many cultural gains, as various countries of the world participated in it through the permanent pavilions that it has established, or that have been erected around the city in various art venues, museums and exhibitions.  Coinciding with the Sultanate of Oman’s participation in this international event, training programs were announced before and during the Biennial. The program was open to young Omanis aged 21 years and above who had an interest or background in visual arts, international history and relations or represented Oman on the global stage. The training began with the training program in Muscat in partnership with local educational institutions for 20 students, which enabled the trainees to engage with a wide range of audiences and provided them with a deep knowledge of the history of Omani art.
Results: What results have been achieved so far through the implementation of the policy/measure?  •	The pavilion attracted approximately 2,000 visitors every day throughout the exhibition.  •	Launching a training program for (20) students from different arts disciplines in the Sultanate of Oman.  •	Inauguration of postage stamps for the Sultanate of Oman pavilion at the Venice International Art Biennale 2022.  •	Preparing doctoral theses for Omani Fine artists in this field.
Recommandations: •	Continue to document the journey of Omani contemporary arts by highlighting Omani artworks at the international level.  •	Continue to support the participation of artists in international forums.  •	Continue to facilitate the mobility of artists and their works.  •	Participation in the 60th Venice Biennale 2024.  •	Continue to support the international arts sector and create capacity for investment in culture.
