Title EN: COVID-19 Cultural Recovery Programme – supporting cultural and media sectors
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Agency Implementation: Manatū Taonga Ministry for Culture and Heritage
Main Feature: As part of the COVID-19 Recovery Budget, the Government made a landmark investment to help ensure the cultural sector survived, adapted and thrived. In May 2020, the Arts and Culture COVID Recovery Programme was announced. This included more than 25 initiatives designed to deliver short-term relief as well as longer-term support for the sector. Key initiatives announced as part of that package in 2020 are included below.  Arts Creative New Zealand received an initial NZD$25 million to support the creative sector through its Emergency Response Package. In early 2023, it received a further NZD $12 million to help meet increased funding demand and NZD $16 million to ensure arts institutions could retain their critical infrastructure, retain staff and stay open. A further NZD $10 million was given to Creative New Zealand for festival grants. These supported established festivals to continue to deliver their programmes celebrating the life experiences, stories, cultures and regional identities of New Zealanders. The Creative Arts and Recovery and Employment Fund (2021-2024) was adopted during COVID-19 to increase access to and participation in the cultural sector, and to create employment and skill development opportunities. This reflected the impact of the economy on creative practitioners and the support they needed to maintain their careers during COVID. Music New Music Fund The New Music Fund boosted New Zealand On Air’s New Music programmes by NZD $7.178 million over two years to support the production of new music. The New Music Fund was delivered by New Zealand On Air and the NZ Music Commission. NZ Music Month and Outward Sound Make Good funds A total of NZD$1.4 million was available for both the NZ Music Month Make Good Fund and the Outward Sound Make Good Fund. These funds helped 60 New Zealand artists and music businesses recoup lost income and costs incurred due to COVID-19 cancellations in 2020. Music Venue Infrastructure Fund This fund provided NZD$3 million to upgrade music venues across Aotearoa to ensure safe environments for audiences, workers and artists. The fund supported 85 venues in 26 towns and cities. Grants were up to NZD$50,000 per venue. Aotearoa Music Touring Programme The Aotearoa Music Touring Programme provided $5 million over two years for New Zealand artists to perform original live music on tour in Aotearoa. Seventy-six artists and businesses were awarded funding to tour Aotearoa. Heritage Heritage New Zealand Pouhere Taonga received NZD$11.3 million over four years to address existing cost pressures and enable it to continue its vision of heritage being valued, respected and preserved for present and future generations. This included NZD$250,000 towards investigating the seismic upgrade and refurbishment of Turnbull House. The Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa received NZD$18 million to remain open to the public and continue to connect treasured collections and taonga to New Zealanders. The Antarctic Heritage Trust received NZD$1.4 million to continue its heritage conservation work in Antarctica and continue to inspire young explorers in New Zealand. The Waitangi National Trust received NZD$4 million to ensure the Waitangi Treaty Grounds remained open to the public. Museum Hardship Fund The Museum Hardship Fund made NZD$4 million available through multiple funding rounds over three years. Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa National Service Te Paerangi administered the contestable grants. The fund was open to any non-profit, community-run or volunteer museums, whare taonga or galleries of small to medium size, or whānau and hapū through the relevant iwi organisation. Screen Screen Production Recovery Fund The Screen Production Recovery Fund was available to productions, which had already received funded from the New Zealand Film Commission or New Zealand On Air, that were affected by COVID-19 restrictions. The initial funding was NZD$23.4 million, with an additional NZD$17.2 million made available in response to the impacts of the Delta and Omicron variants in 2021 and 2022. The funding was extended to 31 January 2023 to maximise production activity and minimise the impacts of any further COVID-19 outbreaks. Te Puna Kairangi Premium Productions for International Audiences Fund The Government made NZD$50 million available for the New Zealand screen sector to tell our stories to international audiences. Funding was delivered by Te Tumu Whakaata Taonga New Zealand Film Commission, Irirangi Te Motu New Zealand On Air and Te Māngai Pāho. The Fund was developed in partnership with Manatū Taonga Ministry for Culture and Heritage. Pasifika Festivals Initiative  Pasifika festivals received NZD$12 million in 2020 over three years to recover from the impacts of COVID-19, remain viable, stage their festivals, and build capability (including work towards the establishment of a national peak body). Creative New Zealand administered this initiative. Manatū Taonga Ministry for Culture and Heritage developed and co-designed the initiative with Creative New Zealand, the Ministry for Pacific Peoples and a festivals working group based on Kaupapa Pasifika and Teu Le Va cultural concepts. Mātauranga Māori Te Matatini received NZD$2.43 million to help with its 2020/2021 kapa haka (traditional Māori dances accompanied by singing or chanting) programme during the COVID-19 pandemic. This included NZD$2 million to support the national 2021 Te Matatini Herenga Waka Herenga Tangata Festival, and NZD$430,000 to reimburse rohe (regions) for unrecoverable costs associated with 2020 competitions which were affected by COVID-19.   Specific funds Mātauranga Māori Te Awe Kōtuku programme The Mātauranga Māori Te Awe Kōtuku programme provided NZD$24.5 million over three years to fund diverse initiatives that support iwi, hapū, whānau and Māori communities to safeguard at-risk mātauranga. The agencies involved in Mātauranga Māori Te Awe Kōtuku were: •	Creative New Zealand Arts Council of New Zealand Toi Aotearoa •	Heritage New Zealand Pouhere Taonga •	Manatū Taonga Ministry for Culture and Heritage •	Ngā Taonga Sound & Vision •	Te Matatini •	Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa  •	Te Tari Taiwhenua Department of Internal Affairs.  The programme was first announced in May 2020 as part of the Arts and Culture COVID-19 Recovery Programme. The funding for the programme has now ended but many of the initiatives will continue to be delivered until 2024.  The pandemic brought into sharp focus significant existing risks to mātauranga Māori (indigenous knowledge systems), which is central to Māori cultural identity and wellbeing, and of vital importance for Aotearoa New Zealand. This mātauranga is, in many cases, held by a small number of knowledge holders and arts practitioners – often kaumātua – who are particularly vulnerable to COVID-19. Among the initiatives funded through Mātauranga Māori Te Awe Kōtuku were wānanga and training programmes to support iwi, hapū and marae to gather their kōrero tuku iho, protect their taonga and revitalise their mātauranga by passing it on to the next generation. There were also initiatives that increased access to mātauranga and taonga in national heritage collections. The programme included contestable funding, which supported projects that protected and revitalised mātauranga Māori, including the NZD$9.2 million Mātauranga Māori Marae Ora Fund – a contestable fund that supported marae communities directly with projects that protect and revitalise mātauranga and taonga on marae. Ngā Kaiwhakaoho Ahurea — Cultural Activators Pilot The Cultural Activators Pilot provided NZD$1.44 million in funding over a year to eight organisations to host and support cultural activators in their local communities. With the funding, established cultural sector practitioners collaborated with their communities to tell their stories, build their creative skills and connect them with opportunities in the wider cultural sector. Ngā Puninga Toi ā-Ahurea me ngā Kaupapa — Cultural Installations and Events Cultural Installations and Events was designed to create opportunities for employment and skill development for cultural practitioners and to allow more people to participate in our cultural sector. Funding was for free events held in spaces that people find easy to access and discover and where they go regularly. Examples are community hubs, shopping malls, parks, beaches, marae, churches, reserves or along a waterfront.  73 installations and events received a total of NZD$1.2 million. Cultural Sector Innovation Fund The Cultural Sector Innovation Fund was designed to support innovative projects that: •	improved the sustainability and resilience of the sector •	provided commercial opportunities •	improved access and participation. As well as meeting one or more of these outcomes, the fund had a focus on innovative projects that would safeguard mātauranga Maori.  The fund was delivered through a new approach to arts funding: a nationwide event series called Te Urungi: Innovating Aotearoa. The Government delivered 17 Te Urungi events across New Zealand, receiving 529 applications for funding. 185 projects received a total of NZD$32.7 million. Te Tahua Whakamarohi i te Rāngai Ahurea — Cultural Sector Regeneration Fund The Cultural Sector Regeneration Fund was designed to support the arts, culture and heritage sectors to recover from the impacts of COVID-19 and thrive by funding projects that built skills and knowledge, and that provided access to advice, services, tools and resources. It supported strategic, sector-led initiatives, that would have lasting benefits for arts, culture and heritage in Aotearoa New Zealand.  Funding was available to cultural sector leadership organisations to build the capability of the cultural sector practitioners, organisations and/or businesses they represent and support. This included iwi, hapū and marae organisations. 39 organisations received a total of NZD$5.9 million. NZD$28.3 million was awarded to 86 initiatives that had the strongest potential to contribute to the fund outcomes of: •	improved sustainability and resilience of the arts, culture and heritage sectors •	improved safeguarding of mātauranga Māori and support of toi Māori (Māori arts) •	improved access and participation in arts, culture and heritage sectors •	increased use of arts, culture and heritage as a tool to improve wellbeing •	increased employment and skill development opportunities.  Media sector support The Ministry for Culture and Heritage worked with the media sector to develop a NZD$50 million sector support package. The support package focused on reducing costs and easing cashflow pressure for a range of media organisations. Transmission fee waiver The Ministry funded the costs of transmission fees payable to Kordia TV/FM, Radio New Zealand AM and for iwi radio stations. This initiative immediately reduced operating costs for a range of organisations across the sector. 123 applicants received a total of NZD$19.82 million. Government news subscriptions The Ministry funded advance news subscriptions or memberships for 32 government departments and four departmental agencies in 2020/21.Nine applicants received a total of NZD$1.55 million. Publications grant The Ministry targeted NZD$4 million for magazines and community newspapers that did not receive significant relief from the media support package. Funding summary: 335 publications received over NZD$12,000. Emergency response funding The Government provided extra funding support for the arts and culture sector in September 2021 in response to the Delta outbreak. In early 2022, it provided more support in response to the Omicron variant and the shift to the ‘Red’ traffic light setting. These packages helped address the immediate relief needs and provide confidence for the sector. They were delivered using a mixture of cultural agency support and Manatū Taonga initiatives. Cultural agency support During the Delta outbreak, the Government provided NZD$10 million to cultural agencies to enable them to support at-risk organisations, key infrastructure, artists and projects as follows: •	Creative New Zealand received NZD$5 million to support at-risk organisations, including festivals and community arts organisations, and to provide employment and continuity of practice for creative practitioners. •	The New Zealand Music Commission received NZD$3 million for the continued operation of key music infrastructure, support to artists, venues and key support sectors. •	Museum of New Zealand Te Papa Tongarewa/Museums Aotearoa received NZD$1 million to increase the Museums Hardship Fund and work with the museum sector on its sustainability and viability. •	The New Zealand Film Commission received NZD$1 million for further relief to productions in extraordinary circumstances and to avoid abandonment where the Screen Production Recovery Fund or indemnity had not been sufficient to manage the costs of the restrictions given the extent of the lockdown.  Arts and Culture Event Support Scheme The Arts and Culture Event Support Scheme was designed to help organisers of arts and cultural events have confidence to commit to and deliver events while Government COVID-19 restrictions were in place. It also gave reassurance for artists and crew they would get paid if their events could not go ahead as planned. The scheme was open from December 2021 to January 2023 and made payments of $32.1 million across 464 events. Cultural Sector Emergency Relief Fund The Cultural Sector Emergency Relief Fund was split into two funding streams, one for organisations and the other for self-employed individuals. Funding for organisations supported cultural organisations, including sole traders, at clear risk of no longer operating viably. At the time of closing on 26 May 2022, 65 organisations had received support exceeding NZD$3.2 million. Funding for self-employed individuals comprised a one-off grant of NZD$5,000 to self-employed people working in arts, culture or heritage whose income was directly affected by a move to ‘Red’ under the COVID-19 Protection Framework. At the time of closing on 26 May 2022, a total of NZD$6.495 million had been awarded to 1,299 eligible applicants.

Title EN: Création d’un fonds de relance culture (FRC)
Goal: Promote Human Rights And Fundamental Freedoms
SDG: SDG 5 - Achieve gender equality and empower all women and girls,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels
Area of Monitoring: Artistic freedom
Cultural Domain: Performing Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: Le ministère des affaires culturelles (MAC)
Main Feature: Dans l’objectif de limiter les répercussions de la pandémie COVID-19 sur les opérateurs culturels, et en vertu de la croyance en la valeur du secteur culturel comme moteur essentiel de l’économie, le Ministère des Affaires Culturelles (MAC) en coordination avec le ministère des Finances et dans le cadre d’une stratégie gouvernementale visant à mettre en place des mesures d’urgence afin d’atténuer les répercussions de la pandémie, a lancé en 2020 la création d’un Fonds de Relance Culture (FRC). Il s’agit d’un compte de concours crée par arrêté du ministre des finances en date du 25 Mars 2020 autorisant la collecte des donations (provenant de diverses composantes de la société : particuliers, secteur public et privé, OSC.) pour pouvoir servir des aides ponctuelles aux artistes, créateurs, intellectuels, freelances, institutions et opérateurs œuvrant dans divers domaines de l'activité culturelle. Ce fonds d’urgence dont l’action s’inscrit également dans la durée est conçu aussi pour accompagner de manière pérenne la relance économique et sociale du secteur culturel fortement touché par la pandémie. En effet, et selon une évaluation interne de l’impact économique de la fermeture des espaces culturels, de l’annulation et du report des activités culturelles dues au COVID-19, plus de 700 activités et/ou festivals ont été annulés ou reportés, en plus de l’arrêt des activités habituelles des différents opérateurs culturels sur le territoire national à cause de la crise. Cette situation a touché l’ensemble des disciplines artistiques induisant ainsi une partie des professionnels de la culture dans une grande précarité. L’un des objectifs immédiats de ce fonds est donc d’assurer la stabilité sociale et économique de ces acteurs de manière exceptionnelle durant la crise en leur aidant à maintenir leur vitalité culturelle et économique tout en leur permettant de faire face aux difficultés engendrées par l’annulation des diverses performances et manifestations culturelles anticipant ainsi les éventuels dommages financiers et sociaux. Plus largement la création de ce fonds est à replacer dans une action ministérielle à plus long terme ayant pour but de fournir des bases solides pour le développement du secteur culturel en accompagnant de manière structurante les projets et les entreprises culturelles en Tunisie. Une attention particulière a été accordée à la gouvernance (notamment par le renforcement du principe de la transparence en mettant le plus grand nombre de données à la disposition des usagers via la conception d’une base de données ouverte dédiée à cette fin) et à la transformation digitale qui, dans le contexte de la crise sanitaire, s’est avérée comme l’une des alternatives viables permettant d’assurer la continuité de l’offre culturelle en situation de crise tout en participant activement à la circulation du produit culturel tunisien dans le pays et à l’international. Ce fonds vise donc également à financer et accompagner le développement de services culturels et artistiques en ligne et la numérisation des processus de production et de distribution des contenus culturels. Les financements sont accordés selon des critères bien définis et en fonction des besoins des individus et des institutions touchées. Ils sont orientés vers une relance structurante des institutions leur permettant d’être plus résilientes, plus digitales et plus durables. Le bénéficiaire peut être une personne physique (artiste, intermittent, Freelancer, entrepreneur …) avec un projet professionnel formalisé dans les disciplines suivantes : Arts du spectacle (Danse et théâtre) Musique, Production cinématographique ou bien une entreprise professionnelle, une association ou un organisme (théâtre, espace culturel, salle de cinéma…). Les types de financements : -	Soutien pour la dignité des professionnels du secteur de la culture : -	Accompagnement à la stabilité économique des opérateurs culturels : Dans le cas des fermetures d’espaces culturels : contribution à un certain pourcentage des charges des structures impactées par les mesures restrictives dues à la crise du COVID-19. Main Feature: Creative Europe is the European Commission's flagship programme that supports  the culture, creative and audiovisual sectors. The Creative Europe Programme 2021-2027 invests in actions that reinforce cultural diversity and respond to the needs and challenges of the cultural and creative sectors.   The Programme is structured around three strands:   •	The CULTURE strand covers cultural and creative sector initiatives such as those promoting cross-border cooperation, platforms, networking, and literary translations. •	The MEDIA strand strand supports and promotes Europe's audiovisual sector by supporting the competitiveness of the European audiovisual industry and promoting cultural diversity. •	The CROSS-SECTORAL strand aims to exploit the potential for collaboration between the two sectors and address the common challenges they face.   The Programme is complementary to actions at national level in the field of culture and the audiovisual sector, reflecting the policy priorities the EU is following in the cultural and creative field.   Creative Europe is open to cultural and creative organisations from EU Member States, as well as, under certain conditions, to some non-EU Member States, such as EEA/EFTA countries (Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway) as well as currently Armenia, Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Georgia, Kosovo, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Serbia, Tunisia and Ukraine. Participation in the MEDIA programme is subject to alignment with Directive 2010/13/EU, as amended by Directive (EU) 2018/1808 (Audiovisual Media Services Directive – AVMSD).  A list of participating countries can be found here: list-3rd-country-participation_crea_en.pdf (europa.eu)
Results: The current Creative Europe Programme (2021-2027) was launched on 26 May 2021. As of July 2024, the current Programme has supported 2 722 projects, involving 4 041 cultural and creative organisations, redistributing EUR 895 million in grants.  The MEDIA sub-programme in particular has effectively supported cultural and linguistic diversity by promoting a genre called 'European cinema', by creating an appetite for diverse 'European' content and by supporting the distribution of films that would otherwise have found it more difficult to travel and be screened.  Every year, MEDIA supports the distribution of over 400 films, reaching cross-border audiences of about 65 million per year.  MEDIA also supports the development of about 400 new films per year, equivalent to 25% of Europe's production.
Financial Ressources: Aprox. USD 2.70 [EUR 2.44 billion]

Main Feature: Creative and Cultural Innovation Expertise is one of the national ESF+ themes. ESF+ (European Social Fund Plus) is a financial instrument of the European Union that promotes employment, social cohesion and economic wellbeing.   During the period 2021–2027, the theme will fund projects that strengthen the creative industries and the creative economy, as well as expertise within the arts and culture sectors. Funded projects should, for example, aim to increase employment or expertise in the creative industries. Funding decisions are made by the ELY Centre for Häme.   The aim of the Creative and cultural innovation expertise theme is closer cooperation with business life, educational institutions and research actors, to ensure that the renewal of competence meets the rapidly changing competence needs arising from the change in the business and working world’s and the operating environment. The national coordination project facilitates mutual cooperation between projects in the same theme, implements communications and compiles and disseminates best practices.      The theme’s funding will be used to implement pilot and development projects that will strengthen creative sectors and the creative economy as a diversifier of the economic structure and strengthen arts and cultural competence. The implementation of pilot and development projects will take cross-cutting global changes in the operating environment, such as digitalisation, development of the data economy, climate change and demographic changes into account. Changes in the operating environment caused by the Covid-19 pandemic will also be taken into account.      The objective of the Creative sectors and creative economy as diversifiers of the industrial structure section is to strengthen business competence in the creative sectors, in areas such as marketing, sales, product and service development, digital competence, IPR competence, management, internationalisation and procurement competence as well as the competence of immigrants. The aim is to strengthen joint multidisciplinary operating models for creative competence in the creative and other fields.      The aim of Strengthening competence in the arts and cultural sector is to develop competence in producing new arts and cultural services, such as digital services and services that are in line with sustainable development and services that take different population groups into account. The aim is to strengthen the competence of organisers and producers of arts and cultural services also in the development of the quality, effectiveness and availability of services, and to improve customer understanding, equal participation, marketing and communication as well as the strengthening of well-being and vitality.

Main Feature: Creative Europe Desk Ireland Through the Creative Europe Programme, the European Commission provides operating grants on a co-funding basis with national institutions to a network of information offices, called Creative Europe Desks, across Europe to promote the Creative Europe Programme 2021 – 2027 and assist applicants in accessing funding. Screen Ireland is Ireland’s National Coordinator for the Creative Europe Desk Ireland. Screen Ireland partners with a number of national agencies to co-fund and host three Creative Europe Desk Ireland information offices serving the cultural and creative sectors in Ireland.  The remit of the Desk is to promote the Programme at local, regional and national level and provide expert advice and assistance to the Irish cultural, creative and audio-visual sectors in order to facilitate Irish participation in the Programme. The Desk gives expert advice on how to access Creative Europe funding, working closely with the companies and organisations in the respective sectors to ensure that they submit high quality funding applications. The Desk collaborates with key sectoral stakeholders and national agencies across the film, TV and culture sectors in order to give specialised advice, target potential applicants, expand our reach and facilitate greater participation in the Programme. Each year, the Desk organises events and networking opportunities to encourage the sectors to engage on a European level and partner with national agencies such as Screen Producers Ireland, The Heritage Council, and Media Literacy Ireland to deliver them.  An important part of the work of the Desk is to encourage cross-border cooperation within the cultural and creative sectors. The Desk also works closely with the Creative Europe Desk of 41 Desks in order to encourage pan-European partnerships and at coproduction events at festivals and online matchmaking sessions for the relevant funding calls.  Culture Moves Europe The Culture programme for Creative Europe launched Culture Moves Europe as a permanent action for mobility for artists and residency hosts in 2021 with €21million across the 2021-2027 programme. Irish participation resulted in 34 successful applications out of 1800 across 2022 and 2023.  Diversity and Inclusion are pillars of funding with top ups available to support costs for disability and to support family costs.     Creative Europe Cooperation Projects  The Cooperation Projects support and promotes Irish participation for artists and organisations in transnational collaborative projects within the EU. The Culture Desk in Ireland works directly with the sector to advise and assist on accessing and developing applications to Cooperation Projects. Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture

Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Agency Implementation: Department for Culture, Media and Sport
Main Feature: The Creative Industries Policy and Evidence Centre (PEC) works to support the growth of the UK’s creative industries through the production of independent and authoritative evidence and policy advice, including the Good Work review.      Over the next five years, Creative PEC will introduce ‘State of the Nations’ reporting in each of four high-level priority thematic areas led by the four organisations that make up the research consortium. They have a Global Creative Economy Council network of leading policy and creative economy practitioners convened by The British Council, as well as a Research Fellows network and Industry Champions programme.
Results: The arts, culture and heritage ‘State of the Nations’ report from May 2024 has presented the latest evidence on the audiences and workforces for the arts, culture and heritage sectors in the UK. It offers a supplementary online interactive map to allow policymakers to dive deeper into the data and analysis. Establishing a clear set of baseline data that will be monitored over several years will allow policymakers to identify and reflect on the effectiveness of any interventions or programmes that they introduce.
Financial Ressources: $14.26m in AHRC funding for 5 years from 2023.
Recommandations: The 2024 ‘State of the Nations’ report has highlighted that cultural employment is not dispersed evenly around the UK. For example, London is still the central hub for arts, culture and heritage workers. As the analysis of engagement shows, the types of cultural activity that tend to achieve a proportionally higher share of overall arts funding have been attracting highly unequal audiences. The report has also demonstrated that participation in culture has been largely even between disabled people and people who are not disabled, and that all occupations in the arts, culture and heritage sectors have had larger fractions of LGBTQ+ people than the general workforce.    It also identifies the good practice currently being seen in policy development, where many interventions have been designing alternatives to overcome structural barriers in relation to equality, diversity and inclusion across the arts, culture and heritage sectors. In the wider policy landscape, it identifies an increasing focus on culture: including the Department for Culture, Media and Sport’s creative industries sector vision aiming for more jobs, gross value added growth, sustainable careers and contributions to local places; the [former] Department for Levelling Up, Housing and Communities’ (now known as the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government) plans for culture to play a substantive role in regenerating towns and cities; devolved governments aim for culture to underpin sustainable growth and community development; and arts policies’ focus on broadening audiences and workforces.

Area of Monitoring: National sustainable development policies and plans

Main Feature: México Creativo views the economy as a relational action between individuals and their natural environment, resulting in the exchange of material or immaterial resources, processes, and experiences. These exchanges hold value, encompassing social, symbolic, and expressive dimensions.  In this model, the cultural and creative economy serves as the bedrock of a thriving society. It must prioritize people, respect for nature, the diverse local expressions, and adherence to cultural rights. As such, the México Creativo proposal advocates for cultural and creative practices grounded in sustainability, equity, and inclusivity.  The initiative articulates its actions through three core principles: 1.	Cooperativism: This involves collectivizing productive processes—from inputs to profits—and fostering interdisciplinary creative collaboration. 2.	Care: Emphasizing gender equity, social justice, and the actual exercise of rights. 3.	Regeneration: Focused on transmitting knowledge and ideas related to material, intangible, and natural heritage at the local level.  Through these approaches, we cultivate cultural and creative ecosystems and value chains, empowering individuals and communities to shape their own development processes.
Results: Comprehensive Initiatives for Cultural and Creative Advancement in Mexico.  - The Open Training Program: Creative Node has spearheaded multiple training initiatives aimed at equipping professionals in the creative and cultural sector with essential tools and knowledge. The program’s objective is to empower individuals to carry out their work more effectively, addressing critical topics relevant to the sector. Delivered in podcast format, complemented by infographics and manuals, the program ensures accessibility to a wide audience.  Experts from diverse backgrounds have simplified discussions on various subjects, including digital rights, video and photography production techniques, digital storytelling, management of cultural heritage, and collective rights.  - Additionally, the Creative Observatory (Research) was established to map and characterize the Cultural and Creative Ecosystem, including Value Chains (productive-creative processes). Collaborations with sectoral partners and state entities facilitated this endeavor.  - Lastly, Cooperation Actions were undertaken to create and sustain public cultural spaces. Recognizing the importance of cooperation, these efforts enhance learning processes and promote access to culture and the arts. Notably, the Creative Mexico Forum, held virtually from October 19 to 23, 2020, featured 23 dialogues, six keynote conferences, and over 100 national and international speakers discussing the intersection of creativity and social impact. The forum aimed to foster dialogue among key players in the creative economy, including national and international stakeholders, artists, private sector representatives, and government officials from the federal Ministry of Culture and state cultural secretariats and institutes. Their collaborative proposal focused on cultural and economic recovery, integrating creative industries while addressing the challenges posed by the COVID-19 pandemic

Main Feature: Creative People and Places (CPP) is an Arts Council England programme which focuses on parts of the country where involvement in creativity and culture is significantly below the national average. Launched in 2012, it funds partners in local areas to empower residents to decide what kind of creative activity they want to experience on their doorstep. Projects must be delivered by a consortia which include at least one arts or cultural organisation and one community and/or volunteer-led grassroots organisation that is not an arts organisation. Where there is only a professional community organisation and no grassroots group, consortia have to show how they will enable grassroots groups to shape the programme.
Results: In the past 12 years of the programme, Arts Council England have invested £108m in 41 projects that span across 55 local authorities and have involved over 230 partners. The projects have delivered 8,800 arts and culture experiences, and engaged 25,453 volunteers. 57% of participants are from the lowest engaged audience segments, and 92% are from low to medium engagement segments.    The next CCP Portfolio will run from 2026 to 2029.
Financial Ressources: Currently ACE have invested $50.28m in 38 projects across England for 2022-25, with the opportunity to extend projects to 31 March 2026.
Recommandations: Arts Council England specify that projects must be evaluated against three core research questions. Are more people from places of least engagement experiencing and inspired by creativity and culture and what are the most effective ways to achieve this? What approaches enable us to deliver on our aspiration for excellence, both in the process of community engagement and the creative and cultural experiences on offer? What else are we learning that facilitates better public engagement in creativity and culture?

The diverse range of workshops and activities has catered to various interests and developmental needs, promoting cultural awareness and appreciation among the participants. The diverse program, which includes activities like yoga, art exhibitions, and visits to the Dubai Iconic landmarks, has been praised for its ability to cater to the cognitive, cultural, and physical development of children. This comprehensive approach ensures that children receive a well-rounded experience that supports their overall growth. The activities are conducted under the supervision of experts and artists, ensuring a safe and supportive environment for children to explore their talents and interests. The professional guidance provided during workshops has been highlighted as a key factor in the success of the initiative. By integrating activities that celebrate cultural heritage and traditions, the program has effectively raised awareness among children about the importance of cultural diversity and preservation. This aligns with Dubai Culture’s broader goals of fostering a deeper appreciation for cultural and artistic heritage. Main Feature: The Cultural Exchange Program, launched on 10/06/2023, aims to promote the dissemination and cultural exchange of activities, social technologies and innovative actions that address themes from different areas of knowledge and that integrate and articulate cultural production chains to other themes, such as health, human rights, science, technology, environment, racial equality, social inclusion, territories, work, among others. Through a public notice, the Program selects cultural agents to receive financial support with a view to compensating travel, participation and stay expenses for these agents, to present their own work, at events, festivals, business fairs and other cultural activities, in Brazil and abroad, that promote the exchange and dissemination of transversal themes and expressions that, due to their seasonality, peculiarity, transversality or originality, do not have a clearly defined institutional locus within the scope of the Ministry of Culture. The notice is aimed at cultural agents, individuals, collectives and groups without their own legal personality who may be beneficiaries of the granting of cultural exchange scholarships, which are compensatory in nature. The program also adopts strategies aimed at affirmative actions through quotas and bonuses. Quotas are reserved for black, indigenous and disabled people (PCD), with a minimum of 20% black people or groups with a self-declared majority (half or more) of black people; minimum of 10% of indigenous people or groups with a self-declared majority (half or more) of indigenous people; and a minimum of 5% of people with disabilities (PWD) or groups with a majority (half or more) of PWD. Black, indigenous and disabled people (or groups in which such people are the majority) will compete simultaneously in quotas and broad competition. Bonuses aim to prioritize proposals that address themes from different areas of knowledge and that integrate and articulate cultural production chains, whether by territorial or thematic focus, such as culture and health, culture and human rights, culture and technology, culture and environment, culture and equality racial, cultural and social inclusion, among others and have less possibility of development with their own resources. Thus, bonuses are awarded for proposals developed by women or by groups with a majority of women (cis or trans); Urban Culture proposal; proposals originating from peripheral locations or directed towards them; and, proposals developed by elderly people or groups with a majority of elderly people.
Results: In 2023, the Exchange Program selected 71 applications, through which 223 cultural agents had their trips financed to participate, mainly, in 30 cultural festivals held in different countries. In addition to the festivals, participation in 11 cultural meetings, 9 artistic exhibitions, 5 symposiums, 4 business fairs and 12 other artistic events was also made possible.

Results: The Swedish Arts Council’s report Crisis and restart support to culture 2022 due to the Covid –19 pandemic concluded that results from regular grant allocation and crisis support reporting, as well as dialogue with the culture sector in 2022 and 2023, show that crisis support not only mitigated difficulties but also facilitated development, including cultural production and accessibility methods. Recommandations: The Swedish National Audit Office examined the economic support measures in the form of grants that the government has directed to sports and culture in response to the COVID-19 pandemic between March 2021 and June 2021. The overall conclusion of the review, from 2022, was that both the government and the grant-giving organisations designed and distributed the reviewed crisis support in a mostly appropriate and effective manner. They demonstrated the ability to act swiftly and persistently during an extended crisis, where support decisions were made in stages. However, the review also highlights transparency gaps in grant distribution, and the focus on quickly reaching cultural support recipients has sometimes come at the expense of precision. https://www.regeringen.se/contentassets/4654bf7079ed437a9d59dd385c445d86/riksrevisionens-rapport-om-statens-krisstod-till-idrott-och-kultur-under-coronapandemin-skr.-202122283.pdf  A government inquiry  from 2021, From Crisis to Strength – Restart for Culture, concluded that the pandemic has negatively impacted the cultural sector in Sweden, with effects likely to persist for years. Unemployment in the cultural field increased during the pandemic, and many professionals considered leaving the sector. Recent graduates and young artists faced limited job opportunities. Nonprofit cultural organisations experienced reduced engagement. Long-term skill loss and decreased diversity were also identified risks. There was also uncertainty about audience behaviour post-pandemic. Performing arts and music organisations faced planning challenges due to cancelled events.  The inquiry therefore recommended additional public support to the culture sector for at least a couple of years after the end of the pandemic. https://www.regeringen.se/contentassets/c96ef2e953fd481ebb68d41b980a1d0a/fran-kris-till-kraft.-aterstart-for-kulturen-sou-202177.pdf

Title EN: Cultura 4.0
Goal: Integrate Culture In Sustainable Development Frameworks
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: National sustainable development policies and plans
Agency Implementation: Ministry of Culture
Main Feature: The National Recovery and Resilience Plan of the Ministry of Culture restructures the key elements of the Italian cultural heritage to encourage the emergence of new services, to improve attractiveness, accessibility (physical and digital) safety, environmental sustainability and social participation. The measures are based on a multi-level governance model and provide for strong cooperation between public actors. The Ministry of Culture program organizes measures in three macro areas:  Cultural heritage for the next generation (Resources: 1.1 billion €). The project offers the possibility to create a digital heritage of culture to encourage the use of information and the development of services by the cultural and creative sector. This measure improves the accessibility of cultural sites and environmental sustainability, in terms of energy efficiency of museums, cinemas and public and private theatres.  Regeneration of small cultural sites, religious and rural cultural heritage (Resources: 2.72 billion €). The Italian tourist flows are catalyzed by some attractors, therefore the intensive use of the most requested cultural places risks to wear them out and impoverish them in the long term, putting their preservation and sustainability at risk. At the same time other places of great artistic and cultural value remain outside the tourist flows. To disrupt this dynamic, the interventions in support of tourism and culture will not be focused only on large cities: an intervention line will be dedicated to supporting the development of tourism and culture in rural and peripheral areas. Title EN: CULTURAL AND CREATIVE INDUSTRIES MARKET - MICC 3600 2018
Goal: Achieve A Balanced Flow Of Cultural Goods And Services And Increase The Mobility Of Artists And Cultural Professionals
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 10 - Reduce inequality within and among countries,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Flow of cultural goods and services
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: MUNICIPAL AUTONOMOUS GOVERNMENT OF LA PAZ/SECRETARY OF CULTURES AND TOURISM
Main Feature: In 2018, the first Cultural and Creative Industries Market of La Paz (MICC 3600) was created with the idea of replicating it every two years. It consisted of a platform for linking and training that allows the different providers to interact at a local, national and international level with those seeking artistic and cultural products and services.  It became a space where the different cultural actors of the municipality of La Paz have the possibility of offering their cultural projects either through the sale or exchange of the same, in traditional market systems, as well as incorporating elements of their own identity and following their own economic logics or models (market identity logics, barter, social responsibility).  The MICC 3600 included cultural workers from 9 creative sectors: Music, Theatre, Dance, Audiovisual, Video Games, Fashion, Graphic Design, Product Design and Social Cultural Projects.  It consisted of the development of 5 main spaces and/or activities:  Business Roundtables: 5 sessions of short meetings, totalling 1,500 peoples between applicants and offerors, had a maximum effective duration of 12 minutes, plus 3 minutes for changing appointments or tables, giving a total of 15 minutes per appointment. Each applicant could receive up to 10 offerors per session, either in the morning or in the afternoon. Artistic exhibitions (showcases): 51 artistic exhibitions, in music, performing arts (theater and dance) and fashion design, were presentations of between 15 and 30 minutes depending on the sector, to give applicants the opportunity to witness live demonstrations of artistic products. Exhibition stands: 12 thematic stands displayed the diversity of cultural and creative offerings to provide a space for those who, for various reasons, were unable to attend the networking sessions and thus promote cultural democracy. This allowed the articulation of the different sectors in a common space, generating intersectoral networks. Training space: Spaces were created for the transmission of knowledge and the exchange of experiences, where the presence of the different producers, managers, programmers, trainers and journalists who visited our country was mainly used in order to learn about experiences from other regions and thus articulate our experiences. Cultural Tambo: Exhibition space for small samples of street and itinerant fairs, articulating artisans from different projects that work within the concept of community and collaborative culture with their own logics of identity.  Priority was given to the Ibero-American markets and, above all, to those of neighbouring countries when inviting bidders, as a logical and natural form of circulation. For the selection of bidders, three forms of selection were established:  Project incubators. The best projects participating in the incubators were invited to participate in the first Cultural and Creative Industries Market of La Paz MICC 3600. Open call. Aimed at Bolivian citizens and foreign residents, as well as foreigners with co-production projects (with Bolivian participation), whose proposals were evaluated by an internal and external committee to form part of MICC 3600. Direct invitation. Since the quotas established in the different areas were not filled through the two processes mentioned above, incubators and public call, they were filled through direct invitations.  The selected projects underwent preparatory training through two talks, for their participation in MICC 3600.
Results: MICC 3600 allowed those with previous experiences to broaden their outlook and network of contacts, and for others to open new windows to begin to connect and circulate at a national and international level, to generate resources that boost the cultural economy of the municipality and the country, and to position La Paz as a cultural city and international benchmark. Among the main quantitative results are: •	Participation of 90 applicants from 35 cities in 15 countries (Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, Spain, France, Guatemala, Mexico, Panama, Paraguay, Peru, Poland and Uruguay). •	Competition of 196 bidders from the 6 sectors: Performing Arts, Musical Arts, Audiovisual Arts, Video Games, Design and Fashion, and Social Cultural Projects. •	Participation of more than 1000 cultural workers from the 5 main spaces or activities. •	Development of 5 spaces: networking sessions and artistic displays (showcases) that are the heart of every cultural market, exhibition windows, training space through forums, seminars and talks and a cultural dairy farm. •	1,500 meetings held between programmers and suppliers. •	15 talks and thematic meetings in the areas of Performing Arts, Musical Arts, Audiovisual Arts, Video Games, Design and Fashion, and Social Cultural Projects. •	More than 30 business intentions in the field of cultural and creative economies.
Financial Ressources: $us. 127,700 (2018 management)
Recommandations: A survey to collect data and assess the perception of MICC 3600 was sent to applicants and suppliers to obtain statistics and opinions that will allow us to evaluate the development of MICC 3600, how to plan new action plans, and to follow up on projects that may arise as a direct result of this first experience. Among the most important conclusions are:  It allowed them to expand their outlook and network of contacts, and for others, to open new windows to begin to connect and circulate at a national and international level, for the generation of resources that boost the cultural economy of the municipality and the country and position La Paz as a cultural city and international reference. The objective of showing La Paz as a new meeting point and opportunity for the professionalization and professional development of artists and cultural workers was achieved, with the confidence that concrete results will be achieved in the short and medium term. It managed to train many managers, producers and artists in the development of a cultural market, so that they now seek to participate in other regional markets and hope that the experience can be repeated so that they can participate with greater knowledge. Policies must be promoted to allow the links achieved in MICC 3600 to have a scenario in which they can develop efficiently. This can be achieved through a greater push for competitive funds (FOCUART), the implementation of municipal tax incentives for private companies and the implementation of management for the generation of bank credit plans for the artistic sector.

Title EN: Cultural Bridge
Goal: Achieve A Balanced Flow Of Cultural Goods And Services And Increase The Mobility Of Artists And Cultural Professionals
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 10 - Reduce inequality within and among countries,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Mobility of artists and cultural professionals
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: Arts Council England; Arts Council of Northern Ireland; British Council; Creative Scotland; Wales Arts International
Main Feature: The programme aims to enable social change through the medium of diverse art forms and community arts practices. It promotes cross-border cooperation between the UK nations (Wales, Scotland, Northern Ireland, and England) and German cultural institutions in various disciplines and participative methods.    Cultural Bridge celebrates bilateral partnerships between the UK and Germany through the collaboration of all UK arts councils and leading German cultural institutions. The programme aims to act as a platform of exchange, enabling others to discuss social issues, strengthen the exchange between the UK and GER, and foster artistic collaboration and cultural democracy.    Cultural Bridge partnerships explore a wide range of themes and artforms, from prison theatre, youth led and disability work, climate change, migrant activism, feminism, rural arts, environment-based art and more.
Results: Cultural Bridge has so far supported 35 partnerships through 42 awards, across three rounds of funding since its pilot year in 2021 and has recently announced two further years of funding until 2027.    Round 2 (2023-2024) of the Cultural Bridge project has provided funding for 15 partnerships, involving: 335 artists, 186 cultural professionals and over 1,000 community participants. Building on learning from the pilot year, Round 2 of Cultural Bridge split the funded partnerships into two ‘Tiers’. Tier 1 was for new partnerships to explore and understand each other’s contexts and practice (11 grants of up to £10k awarded). Tier 2 was for those with existing relationships to deepen their exchange and focus on tangible outputs for their organisations and communities (4 grants of up to £30k awarded).
Financial Ressources: here is a total of $463,204.80 available in the 2025 - 2026 funding round.
Recommandations: The main outcomes of Round 2 (2023-2045) include the following: a deeper understanding of mutual contexts (of which, a slow and steady approach is necessary), a flexible and trusting approach was welcomed, expected and unexpected collaborations were built over time, partners intend to develop their work together.      The following emerging impacts were drawn. Firstly, the Cultural Bridge programme is enabling the development of meaningful and mutual relationships between organisations and practitioners between the UK and Germany that would not be happening otherwise. The programme is having a greater impact than is generally expected when grants are awarded. The programme is enabling the development of long-term relationships based on shared aims and values (i.e., not just in response to a funding opportunity). Partners are celebrating the visibility, recognition and profile that participating in Cultural Bridge has brought them. Partners have also reported that Cultural Bridge has improved their ability to tell their stories and provided a vital opportunity to share their practice and its value.      A number of key learnings were established. Given the locally specific context of much of the work and the additional attempts to understand the impact of regional and national policy on ways of working, combining a hyper-local focus and international relevance is challenging for some partners. Some partners reported that they would have appreciated extra time or resources for admin and evaluation activities. Some partners reported that changes in travel costs and conversion rates meant they had to significantly reallocate budgets and plans.

Main Feature: *Cultural domain covered by the policy/measure: Cultural and creative sectors  Main aims: Taking stock of the cultural infrastructure of Schleswig-Holstein and raising/restoring the visibility of cultural provision and cultural players in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic.  Target groups: Cultural institutions, artists, cultural initiatives, cultural stakeholder groups, the governing authorities of elements of cultural infrastructure and adjacent areas, extending to businesses in the creative industries, regional networks and educational institutions, and cultural-policy decision-makers          Expected results: •	Investigating cultural development in Schleswig-Holstein and drawing up a network analysis of cultural collaborations on the basis of surveys  •	Creating a sound foundation of data that will make it easier to safeguard, strengthen and develop cultural infrastructure in close cooperation with municipalities  •	Developing specific goals and measures to strengthen the cultural sector in Schleswig-Holstein over the long term •	Reinforcing appreciation of the value of art and culture in all their dimensions, both in the political sphere and among the general public •	Spotlighting important issues for the development of culture (particularly participation and digitalisation) before, during and after the COVID-19 pandemic
Results: •	753 questionnaires fully completed  •	The most important collaborative relationships between cultural players and across sectors investigated •	Goals and measures reflected on and discussed in two perspective-sharing workshops with the Land cultural scene in September and October 2021, the outcomes feeding into the 2017-2021 Land cultural affairs report and the new Guidelines for Cultural Policy (Kulturpolitische Leitlinien) of the Schleswig-Holstein Land government
Recommandations: The municipalities and districts of Schleswig-Holstein are connected by many ties between their cultural players. There are hubs, or areas where activity is concentrated, which are generally located in and around the Land capital. There are four regional clusters in which particularly intensive contact is maintained between the different districts. Of all the cooperative partners recorded, international ties account for 7%. Almost one in three of those international partners is based in Denmark. The survey revealed significant needs in the face of the challenge of digital transformation, chief among them being more staff, time and money. There is a need for technology – for exhibitions, for example, or digital tools such as video-conferencing technology. Poor internet connections hamper one in six of those questioned in their activities. Only a very small group are critical of the digital transition. What is needed in future is innovative and, above all, widely accessible cultural provision (diversity, integration, accessibility for people with disabilities, low thresholds to participation, synergies generated by collaborating on event organisation). Interdisciplinary or cross-portfolio work is a shared concern, as is the wish for cultural occupation of public, unconventional and disused spaces.

Title EN: Cultural dimension of sustainable development – Working group of EU Member States’ experts and Report from the European Commission after MONDIACULT 2022

Main Feature: Cultural courage for change emerged as a Leitmotiv when the members of the European Union Open Method of Coordination expert group on the cultural dimension of sustainable development started developing its conclusions in early 2022: it is all about transformation. There is a need to rethink the relationship between humans and nature, to fuel our cultural imagination for a liveable, sustainable future. Serious commitment and action are urgently required.  The report ‘Stormy times. Nature and humans : cultural courage for change : 11 messages for and from Europe’ delivers 11 messages for action for and from Europe, each pointing to a specific area of action.   These messages for action are: 1.	Embrace Earth Overshoot Day 2.	Join the moonshot Project 2025 3.	Co-create sustainability transformation pathays 4.	Invest in scientific knowledge digests 5.	Governments to inform each other through voluntary national reviews 6.	Make the cultural carbon footprint lighter 7.	Enlarge access to change opportunities 8.	Empower for democracy, human rights and artistic freedom 9.	Connect with the next generation of change-makers 10.	Provoke change in human behaviours and promote sustainable lifestyles 11. Assess and measure impact.
Results: At the EU level, the group of EU Member States’ experts report was followed by a subsequent report from the European Commission on the “cultural dimension of sustainable development in EU actions”. The report showcases EU programmes and initiatives in fields ranging from cohesion policy, employment and social affairs, education, international and neighborhood policies, the digital economy and research actions, industrial policies and the civil protection, to climate, environmental and green deal related initiatives. The report also highlights cross-cutting priorities such as the New European Bauhaus and projects and actions in development, such as those related to the European Year of Skills 2023 The recognition of culture’s role at the heart of SDGs was as well integrated in the first ever European Union Vountary Review on the implementation of sustainable development in 2023.  Furthermore, the new EU Work Plan for Culture 2023-2026 made clear that the interplay between culture and sustainable development is a key priority for the EU in the field of culture. Under its actions, it also launched a new group of EU Member States’ experts on “Stimulating the Green Transition of Culture and Creative Sectors with a view to the energy crisis”, whose report with recommendations will be published in 2025. With the aim of sharing information on greening relevant to cultural and creative sectors in Europe and beyond, a specific “greening” section has been created on the CreativesUnite platform via the FLIP-project, to which contributions can be made. Another important achievement which gave visibility and further impact to the work undertaken during 2022 was the setting up of a Voices of Culture Expert group of civil society representatives from cultural and creative organisations, which published its report in September 2023 on “Culture & Creative Sectors & Industries driving Green Transition and facing the Energy Crisis”.

Agency Implementation: Ministry of Cultures, Arts and Heritage (MINCAP).
Main Feature: The Ministry of Cultures, Arts and Heritage has been working on a deeper gender approach in all the categories during the latest open calls for the Culture Fund, the main public instrument for funding culture in Chile. Specifically, in the 2023 call, the participation conditions for women in the projects, improved.  Within the measures that considered this broader criteria associated with gender, where women could, for example, take on roles from which they have been historically excluded, and the modification to the concept of 'curriculum', given that many times women are hindered from developing a career in a sustained manner and at the same pace as men.  In turn, for the 2024 call for projects, the focus on caregiving takes on special relevance by establishing conditions necessary for equitable participation, for example, among people who apply for the 'Chile Crea' Scholarship, where they can include costs associated with the right to caregiving of their own children or children under guardianship, from early childhood through to the last stage of primary education (up to 8th grade/year 9).  In the Fund for Books, at least 50% of the resources available in the fund, was destined for female gender applicants, both in the Metropolitan and other regions of Chile. En general terms, for the 2024 call for projects, the gender quota was mantained in all the aforementioned categories, and are included in the new 'Talleres de Creación Literaria' (Literary Creation Workshops) sub-category of the Book Fund.  Additionally, gender equality is maintained in the selection of the specialist committees, who evaluate the projects. Lastly, and in accordance with the monitoring framework of the 2005 Convention, this action reports on the indicator on 'measures and policies that promote gender equality in the culture and media sectors'.
Results: With regard to the promotion of the participation of women in the Chile Crea Scholarship, the amount of $113,637,795, equal to 4.8% of the resources awarded in the Chile Crea Scholarship, correspond to costs destined towards caregiving.  Regarding gender quotas within the distribution of resources, for the 2023 call for projects, 505 of the total budget, equalling $18,049,016,599, went to projects whose applicant was female, and 50%, equalling $17,926,248,590, to projects whose applicant was male. With regard to the distribution within the project teams, of the total benefitted projects, 48.2% are women and 51.8% are men.  Regarding the selected projects' personnel costs, by gender, of the total resources directly awarded to the selected recipient all the categries and sub-categories of the contest, 57.2% equalling $2,021,674,102, corresponds to female applicants, and 42.8% equalling $1,510,353,998 corresponds to male applicants.  Furthermore, regarding gender parity within the specialist committees, women's participation in project teams increased from 52.2% in the 2022 call for projects, to 54.2% in the 2023 call. Moreover, the resources destined towards funding the work of women in the project teams went from 55% in 2022 to 58% in 2023.  Lastly, guidelines for incorporating a gender perspective in the project planning and design were published, and beginning with the 2024 call, for the first time all the funds included, within the Single Application Forms (FUP) a mandatory checkbox which obliges the project applicant to comlpy with the 'recomendations for violence-free working environments' (free translation), which is available on the culture fund website.

Title EN: Decoding Resilience and Erased Gazes - Artistic production within BePart European Project
Goal: Promote Human Rights And Fundamental Freedoms
SDG: SDG 5 - Achieve gender equality and empower all women and girls,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels
Area of Monitoring: Gender equality
Agency Implementation: City of Women, Association for the Promotion of Women in Culture
Main Feature: From collaborative art-making and sharing to decentralized governance models involving local citizens, marginalized groups of artists and policy-makers, BePart fostered new approaches and structures for the co-creation and mobility of art through collaborations of co-creating publics, artists, researchers and organisations. Within the project we have engaged, trained and offered support to artists with migratory background or involved members of migrant communities in artistic production.  Erazed Gazes: In 1992, soon after Slovenia broke away from Yugoslavia, the administrative bodies of the Republic of Slovenia arbitrarily and illegally erased more than 25.000 people from the register of permanent residents. Because of this administrative genocide, the Erased became foreigners within their own country. They lost the right to work and went without health insurance. Many were deported or forced to leave Slovenia. To protest the injustices caused by the Erasure, the Artistic collective of the Politics of Touch project created the Erased Gazes memorial canvas. The members of the collective, including women from many parts of the world who today call Ljubljana, Logatec and Zagreb their home, created the canvas in mixed-media at the Politics of Touch workshops, devised and run by Selma Banich. The workshops took place between July and December 2022 in Slovenia and Croatia.  Decoding Resilience: The cycle of events was created as part of the European BePart project. The exhibition as the final destination of a performative journey devised by Samar Zughool, Behnaz Aliesfahanipour, Safa Saad and Sammar Al Kerawe. Samar, Behnaz and Sammar were cleaning passersbys' shoes at various locations in Slovenia, conversing with their owners while Safa took the role of an observer. During shoe cleaning, they navigated the power dynamics by conversing on expectations from those who have the status of a foreigner or are otherwise confronted with the role of being a foreigner in this country. After cleaning, the artists accepted voluntary contributions and photographed the cleaned shoes. Later, the four artists transformed the shoe photographs into images and sketches, filled with statements and comments from their owners.  The artists decoded social communication through street performances by navigating power dynamics and connecting them to a broader aspect of international politics and geopolitics within the context of contemporary times. From a shoe in Koper to a shoe in the British Museum in London, the process of decoding was mostly focused on decoloniality. In addition to the exhibition, the artists hosted workshops in the format of a public performative journey named Embodying Decoloniality. Embodying Decoloniality is a public performative journey that uses performing arts and dance therapy techniques to navigate and unpack emancipatory communication. The workshop were inspired by the novel “A Tree Like Rain” by Samar Habib and is part of the SAMA public performative journeys and Community arts series.
Results: •	Higher visibility of women facing intersectional discrimination; •	Raised visibility of artists with migratory backgrounds; •	Integration of marginalized groups of women in contemporary artistic production;  •	Establishment of platform for intercultural dialogue; •	Training and production support for disadvantaged group of artists facing intersectional discrimination; •	Integration of female and gender non-conforming asylum seekers; •	International circulation of artists and art works.

Title EN: Dawn Raids Historical Account
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Partnering with civil society
Agency Implementation: Manatū Taonga Ministry for Culture and Heritage  Ministry for Pacific Peoples Creative New Zealand
Main Feature: From the 1950s to 1970s, migration from the Pacific to Aotearoa was encouraged to support New Zealand’s manufacturing and primary production sectors. New Zealand’s economy then suffered a downturn from the early 1970s and Pacific peoples were specifically targeted due to perceptions they were causing job shortages and other social harms. Between 1974 and 1976, rigorous enforcement of immigration policies was applied with officials conducting targeted raids on the homes of Pacific families, often early in the morning or late at night, giving rise to the term the “Dawn Raids”. Implementing Government’s Commitment to Deliver a Dawn Raids Historical Account: This package of initiatives provides funding to deliver the Government’s commitment to provide reconciliation for communities impacted by the Dawn Raids of the 1970s and greater public understanding of the Dawn Raids.  The package of initiatives includes Teu le Vā Community Fund for community-led multimedia history projects, Vaka of Stories: a Ministry for Pacific Peoples-led tour to record/collate survivors’ stories in an official Dawn Raids Historical Account Report, a fund for Pacific artists and historians to complete professional arts and history projects, and an Online Pacific histories platform: Creation of a historical preservation platform and education resources with the initial focus on Dawn Raids.
Results: The Teu le Vā community funding has been allocated and projects completed. The Vaka of Stories has been completed.   Initiatives currently still underway include: •	The creation of an official Dawn Raids Historical Account Report •	A fund for Pacific artists and historians to complete professional arts and history projects has been allocated, projects are due at the end of 2024 •	The Online Pacific histories platform, a first iteration of which is due to go live in 2024.
Financial Ressources: USD$8.563 million ($13.646NZD million) over four years

Title EN: Declaration for Culture (Mondiacult 2022)
Goal: Integrate Culture In Sustainable Development Frameworks
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: International cooperation for sustainable development
Agency Implementation: Manatū Taonga Ministry for Culture New Zealand National Commission for UNESCO
Main Feature: A Declaration of Culture was adopted by 150 member states (including New Zealand) at the UNESCO World Conference on Cultural Policies and Sustainable Development held from 28-30 September 2022, at Mexico City (Mondiacult 2022).  The Conference hosted by the Government of Mexico, is the third World Conference on Cultural Policies since it was first held in Mexico in 1982. Convened by UNESCO, the conference provided an opportunity for continuous reflection by ministers of culture on cultural policies to outline immediate and future priorities (as UNESCO enters the remaining decade of action for the implementation of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals Agenda 2030), and the impact of the global COVID pandemic.  The Declaration is an affirmation of common priorities and vision of UNESCO country members for the future of cultural policies. The Declaration is non-binding and addresses global challenges such as the threat of climate change, illicit trafficking of cultural property, and the impact of increased armed conflict on cultural diversity and cultural heritage. The Declaration emphasises the need for increased recognition of the immense value and power of culture in the development of peoples and nations; and expresses the call, in solidarity, by countries on the UN Secretary General to firmly anchor culture as a global public good and to integrate it as a specific goal in its own right in the 2030 Agenda for sustainable development. Member states also called for UNESCO for more frequent multi-lateral opportunities, such as, from 2025 onwards, an establishment of a World Forum on Cultural Policies to be held by UNESCO every four years.
Results: UNESCO has announced the convening of the next Mondiacult World Forum on Cultural Policies and Sustainable Development for 2025 in Barcelona, Spain.

Title EN: Emergency Agenda
Goal: Promote Human Rights And Fundamental Freedoms
SDG: SDG 5 - Achieve gender equality and empower all women and girls,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels
Area of Monitoring: Artistic freedom
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: Center for the Analysis of Freedom and Authoritarianism - LAUT
Main Feature: The Center for the Analysis of Freedom and Authoritarianism - LAUT is an independent and non-partisan interdisciplinary research institution, committed to producing and disseminating knowledge about the quality of the Rule of Law and democracy. LAUT aims to monitor the various manifestations of authoritarianism and repression of freedoms, in order to support the mobilization of civil society and the defense of freedoms. The research center is maintained with donations from private sources and from national and international foundations and third sector organizations. These resources are invested in carrying out research, disseminating its results and promoting training programs on manifestations of authoritarianism and repression of freedoms, in addition to maintaining the necessary infrastructure for this. The Emergency Agenda seeks to identify the various risks to freedom and democracy in the current Brazilian context, showing the relationships between the ways in which these risks appear. The aim of the project is to build an archive to inform medium and long-term analyses. Recalling that the restriction of artistic freedom is expressly prohibited in the Federal Constitution, and that “censorship consists of any organized action to interrupt the free flow of information protected by the right to freedom of expression”, the Emergency Agenda presents as its main purpose to enrich understanding what Brazil was experiencing in the period from 2019 to 2022. Although it was updated weekly, the Emergency Agenda did not intend to compose an exhaustive database that covered acts of all actors at different levels of the federation (federal, state, municipal) or state spheres (Executive, Judiciary and Legislative ), on a wide range of topics. I wanted to bring together, in any case, a diverse and significant picture.
Results: In the period from 2019 to 2022, 80 results were reported on the Emergency Agenda platform, that is, 80 cases that involved acts of censorship of artistic freedom in the country. Those responsible for these censorship initiatives include: the Governors of the States of Rio de Janeiro, Rio Grande do Sul, Rondônia and São Paulo; the City Halls of Fortaleza and São Paulo; the Military Police of the Federal District and the States of Minas Gerais, Pernambuco and São Paulo; National Film Agency; Brazilian Export and Investment Promotion Agency (Apex Brasil); the Brazilian Armed Forces (Army and Navy); and the then President of the Republic.
