Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Agency Implementation: Art Jameel Dubai Alserkal Avenue The Cultural Foundation Salama Foundation Louvre Abu Dhab Manarat Al Saadiya Abu Dhabi Department of Culture and Tourism Dubai Design District others
Main Feature: The UAE fully understands the value of cultural spaces for the development of cultural talent, cultural products and businesses, and the communal benefits of culture. Many impactful cultural spaces exist in the UAE, and they range from galleries, centers, to creative clusters. Some of the notable spaces in the UAE include the following: Alserkal Avenue: Alserkal Avenue is a renowned cultural district of contemporary art galleries, non-profit organizations, and homegrown businesses in the Emirate of Dubai. Alserkal Avenue is a vibrant community of visual and performing arts organizations, designers, and artisanal spaces that have become an essential platform for the development of the creative industries in the United Arab Emirates. Alserkal develops year-round programming dedicated to fostering arts and culture education and engagement. The annual program is thematically developed to focus on a particular issue, bringing artists and professionals from different fields together to examine a concept through talks, screenings, workshops, Quoz Arts Fest, Art Week at Alserkal Avenue, Social Saturdays, November in Alserkal Avenue, Ramadan at Alserkal Avenue and Road Trips.   Manarat Al Saadiyat: Manarat Al Saadiyat is a modern art space in Abu Dhabi. It introduces people to the transformative power of the arts by providing casual, drop-in spaces for the community to work alongside a team of talented teaching artists. Art Studio, based at Manarat Al Saadiyat, has dedicated spaces for all ages to work both collaboratively and individually. Art Studio also offers arts education programs which continually adapt and respond to the needs of the community as well as dedicated outreach programs such as helping teenagers develop their art portfolios or proposing hands-on classes for people of determination (persons with disabilities) to continue to thrive. Furthermore, Photography Studio, launched in 2018 in Manarat Al Saadiyat, is committed to developing and enhancing the professional growth of talent. The Studio encourages the participation of local, regional, and international photographers through its community-driven exhibitions. It also develops and promotes a year-round calendar of activities and programs hosting specialized workshops and courses conducted by professional photographers.  The Cultural Foundation: In Abu Dhabi, the Cultural Foundation launched a cutting-edge visual arts program of exhibitions that focus on contemporary and modern art from the United Arab Emirates, the region and internationally. As part of the Foundation’s mission to foster and promote creativity, spaces have been dedicated to host community exhibitions, children’s exhibitions and art residencies. The Cultural Foundation launched a world-class, contemporary and home-grown performing arts program in its newly renovated 900-seat theatre. It has transformed its library to become the Abu Dhabi Children’s Library. This state-of-art facility offers innovative hands-on learning programs for children and families. Educational platforms at the Cultural Foundation include: Al Marsam Al Hor offers a dynamic variety of classes and workshops that focus on a wide array of artistic disciplines. The studio welcomes teens and adults of all skill levels to drop in and use the space or register for a weekly art class.  Bait Al Khatt is a new space within the Cultural Foundation dedicated to the intricate art of traditional Arabic calligraphy and is led by renowned artist and calligrapher Mohammed Mandi. It offers an ongoing program that takes both a theoretical and practical approach, with a view towards enhancing the development of Arabic calligraphy within the United Arab Emirates.  Art Residency is part a dedicated studio spaces for a comprehensive art residency program to support and advance professional artists, who are nationals or residents of the United Arab Emirates to produce and exhibit work with unparalleled visibility and endorsement.  Performing Arts Program: The program is a contemporary, popular, and home-grown program that includes music, dance and theatre. It has hosted an artistic program dedicated to families and young people, with a mix of classical and contemporary productions featuring local, regional, and international artists in its new theatre and outdoor amphitheatre in the heart of the city. It has also dedicated the second Tuesday of every month to present Emirati theatre productions as part of its ongoing mission to support artists from the United Arab Emirates.    421: A unique arts and cultural space in Abu Dhabi designed to meet the growing demand for more creative community spaces for people to meet, work, collaborate with others, and participate in social and cultural events. 421 is a home-grown arts and design center dedicated to showcasing and nurturing creative production from across the region. Working in collaboration with local, regional and international entities, 421 seeks to aid the development of the UAE’s creative ecosystem through learning, research and commissions. 421 hosts a range of public programs and learning opportunities that support creative practices, artistic exchange and stimulate critical discourse. These include short courses, events, exhibitions, and workshops which provide opportunities for children, students, educators, artists and creative professionals to develop their creative practices and inspire innovation. Among its programs are: Online programing: featuring a series of video lessons, podcasts, book readings, community talks and curatorial tours, enabling audiences to remotely engage with regional narratives in art and design.  Jameel Art Centre: In 2018, the UAE welcomed Jameel Arts Center, an independent arts institution dedicated to engaging communities through its exhibitions and programming. Learning is at the heart of its initiatives and central to the organization’s thinking and collaborations. A diverse spectrum of engaging opportunities is dedicated and adapted for children, students, educators, and professionals, including creative workshops, talks, pilot projects and tailor-made resources.   Jameel Library: The Library is part of Art Jameel Center and is an open contemporary arts research center dedicated to cultural histories of the Gulf and its neighboring regions. The arts library’s collection focuses on making accessible the knowledge of arts and culture; enabling the construction of multiple narratives; and making visible the fluidity of these ideas. Key content subjects include exhibition histories; pedagogy and alternative arts education projects; contemporary discourse and theory from and about the region; plus, selected artists’ monographs and mapped journeys of practice and influence. The library is an active and dynamic learning platform, home to public programs, reading groups, curated bibliographies, symposia, and interventions, free and open to all. The library also supports homegrown research and promotes knowledge exchange; provides spaces to less established practitioners and develops emerging practitioners’ practices and nurtures them. In5: Launched in 2017, in5, a design innovation center supports the design and fashion talent landscape, offering students, entrepreneurs, and startups an opportunity to transform their disruptive ideas into commercial successes. In addition to industry specialized training and workshops, in5 also provides members with dynamic co-working spaces, offices and community areas that are designed to inspire creativity. It is open to everyone from the fields of visual art, fashion, architecture, and product design.  Tashkeel: An arts facility established in Dubai, provides a nurturing environment for the growth of contemporary art and design practice rooted in the UAE. Through multi-disciplinary studios, workspaces, and galleries, it enables creative practice, experimentation and dialogue among practitioners and the wider community. Operating on an open membership model, Tashkeel’s annual program of training, residencies, workshops, talks, exhibitions, international collaborations, and publications aims to further practitioner development, public engagement, lifelong learning and the creative and cultural industries. Makers Space: The makerspace is an open-access and do-it-yourself workshop/fabrication studio. It is a community-based space where creative entrepreneurs, artists, makers, teachers, and students come together to learn and work. The workshop provides access to a set of high-quality machines and tools and provides all the training required to use the equipment and build new skills. Makerspace provides access to both professional equipment and software. It includes laser cutters, plastics and electronics labs, a machines shop, a wood shop, a metalworking shop, textiles department, welding stations and much more. Members of the makerspace have open access to design software, featuring the Autodesk Design Suite. Big project areas with large worktables are available for completing projects and working with others. The community of members and staff provide inspiration and support for creating projects. Comprehensive instruction and coaching are provided by expert staff members.   NYUAD Arts Center: Showcasing music, theater, dance, film, poetry, family programs, and interdisciplinary performances that defy definition, The Arts Center at NYU Abu Dhabi presents distinguished professional artists from around the world alongside student, faculty, and community productions. As a place that both presents and develops work, The Arts Center is a vibrant laboratory for performance that fosters a dynamic relationship between the arts, scholarship, and the community. Located on the NYU Abu Dhabi campus, The Arts Center presents the University with compelling programming that connects to the curriculum, using the arts to illuminate and enliven the scholarly pursuits of students and faculty. The Arts Center creates a dynamic space for research and investigation, encouraging the active pursuit of knowledge for audiences as well as visiting artists. Excellence, collaboration, creativity, accessibility, innovation, respect, and understanding are The Arts Center’s core values, striving to be a beacon on the international arts landscape, firmly rooted in the region but with a global reach. Cinema Akil: Cinema Akil is an independent cinema platform opened in 2018 that brings quality films from across the world to the audiences in the UAE. Showcasing directors and filmmakers across the decades, Cinema Akil aims to create awareness and interest in film and the cinematic arts.  Louvre Abu Dhabi:  Created by an exceptional agreement between the governments of Abu Dhabi and France signed in 2007, Louvre Abu Dhabi was designed by Jean Nouvel and opened on Saadiyat Island in November 2017. Louvre Abu Dhabi galleries tell a chronological history of human creativity that explores the shared ideas and issues that have defined our common humanity from pre-history to the present. Featuring a global selection of masterpieces drawn from its growing permanent collection, Louvre Abu Dhabi displays are also regularly updated with a rolling roster of world-class loans from their international partners. Louvre Abu Dhabi also presented a variety of cultural programming, from musical performances to creative workshops, as well as film screenings, curatorial conferences, and panel discussions. All programming aims to complement the works on show in permanent display and temporary exhibitions and serve to entertain and educate the museum’s visitors as well as the wider Abu Dhabi community. Louvre Abu Dhabi is supported by the expertise of Agency France-Museums, and prestigious partner French institutions in addition to the Musée du Louvre, which has committed to sharing its name and values with Abu Dhabi through this remarkable and innovative project. Sharjah Art Foundation: Located in Sharjah’s historic Art and Heritage Areas, Sharjah Art Foundation activities and events take place throughout the year and include exhibitions featuring the work of Arab and international artists, performances, music, film screenings and artist talks as well as extensive art education programs for children, adults and families. The Foundation hosts the annual March Meeting and every two years presents the Sharjah Biennial. Bastakiya: The traditional style of life that was prevalent in Dubai from the mid-19th century till the 1970s is reflected at Al-Fahidi Historical Neighborhood (commonly referred to as Bastakiya), where buildings with high air towers (Barajeel), built with traditional building materials such as stone, gypsum, teak, sandal wood, fronds and palm wood are aligned side by side, separated by alleys, pathways and public squares, which give the district a natural and beautiful diversity. The buildings of the district are currently used in incubating several varied cultural and artistic activities (both public and private) ranging from art exhibits, specialized museums, cultural and artistic societies, ateliers to cultural centers (such as Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Center for Cultural Understanding). The district also hosts a number of seasonal cultural and artistic events such as Sikka Art Fair, Artists-in-Residence Program, Heritage Week, National Day Events and religious celebrations. Dubai Design District (D3): D3 is a design cluster in Dubai developed through careful consultation with the design community in order to provide a creative ecosystem to engage, inspire and enable emerging talent, and educate the next generation about the power and importance of all forms of design. D3 offers work permits, hosts offices of cultural businesses and serves as a space for innovative cultural festivals and fairs that allow artists and companies to showcase their latest products and inventions and allows cultural businesses to find customers and investors. As a sincere gesture of support for the creative community, the Ministry of Culture has relocated its Dubai offices to D3 to ensure continuous dialogue and support to the creative community.
Results: Many of the spaces in the UAE have brought about positive change and growth to the cultural and creative sector in the UAE. Each of the institutions individually contribute to the creation of a vibrant creative ecosystem, and their impact collectively has been even greater, reshaping a more active and effective narrative for the UAE’s creative sector. Below we highlight some statistics, as follows: •	Alserkal Avenue is home to a community of over 70 contemporary art galleries, visual and performing arts organizations, designers, home-grown and entrepreneur-led businesses, and community spaces. As one of the region’s foremost destinations for contemporary art, and home to Dubai’s risk-takers, makers and wide-ranging creative communities, the Avenue provides cultural experiences for local, regional and international audiences through its extensive year-round programming. •	The Art Jameel Center has distinguished itself by hosting numerous exhibitions that showcase both contemporary and traditional art, emphasizing the work of regional and international artists. Its programs are designed to foster dialogue and collaboration within the art community through artist residencies, workshops, and public talks. Visitor statistics reveal the impact of these initiatives: during 2020-2021, the center experienced reduced attendance due to COVID-19, with many events moving to virtual formats or operating with limited in-person participation. However, from 2021-2022, visitor numbers began to rise gradually as the center resumed in-person events and exhibitions, benefiting from eased pandemic restrictions. By 2022-2023, there was a noticeable increase in attendance, with significant spikes during major exhibitions and cultural events, reflecting the growing interest and engagement in the center's offerings. •	Manarat Al Saadiyat, has seen notable shifts in visitor engagement and event programming from 2020 to 2024. The center experienced a significant decline in visitor numbers in 2020 due to COVID-19 restrictions, with many events transitioning to virtual formats. As restrictions eased in 2021, the center gradually increased its in-person activities, hosting a range of exhibitions and events. By 2022, visitor numbers began to rise as the center fully reopened and resumed a diverse array of programs. In 2023, there was a marked increase in attendance, reflecting the center's successful return to major exhibitions and cultural events. Looking ahead to 2024, Manarat Al Saadiyat is expected to continue attracting a growing number of visitors with an expanded calendar of exhibitions and community-focused programs. •	The Arts Center at NYU Abu Dhabi: The Arts Center’s outreach programs (Off the Stage programs) play an important role in shaping the local arts scene of Abu Dhabi and the UAE. These initiatives are committed to the educational development of youth, building artistic skills and knowledge, and addressing important civic conversations such as environmental awareness, gender issues, cultural heritage, learning disabilities, technology, and innovation. Off the Stage events are created as intimate events with small capacities, in order to maximize impact.  Cultural spaces and institutions in the UAE have worked diligently to promote awareness of modern art in our region and from the Middle East, producing public programs to educate the public on the importance of art, increased audiences to art exhibitions and appreciation for the arts.
Recommandations: The establishment of a lot of the major cultural spaces in the UAE is relatively new when compared to other countries. These spaces have already started developing a new culture and ecosystem of support for the arts and culture and businesses in the creative sector. What is required next is to elevate the ecosystem to ensure that it leads to real careers and sustainable businesses in cultural fields. Plans have been developed and are still being developed to ensure that existing spaces become effective and create real professional options for people in the UAE.

Title EN: Photo exhibition “ “Sport o Montagna: chi vince?”, - 2024
Goal: Promote Human Rights And Fundamental Freedoms
SDG: SDG 5 - Achieve gender equality and empower all women and girls,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels
Area of Monitoring: Artistic freedom
Agency Implementation: Università degli Studi di Padova - UNESCO Chair Human Rights, Democracy and Peace
Main Feature: The photo exhibition Sport or Mountain: Who Wins? focuses on the critical issues affecting mountain environments in Italy and around the world while promoting a culture of peace and nonviolence through sports and the Olympics.  Through this exhibition we aim to share educational stories and illuminate conflicts in mountain environments, as well as the human rights violations they entail. Together we explore solutions inspired by the Olympic truce, where sport overcomes tensions between nations, charting a path toward conflict resolution. Contextualizing each conflict historically and geographically, we examine how the Olympic Games can contribute to Olympic diplomacy and peace between conflicting nations. A journey through history, geography and sports to understand how to build peace.
Results: The photo exhibition and the debate around sport and environment are still being presented around the city of Padova. The theme will remain relevant as long as the Olympic game exists and allows visitors and the public to reflect on the role of sports diplomacy, sports for peace, inclusion and human rights, and sports and environmental disasters, in a narrative that is often left in the dark.

Title EN: Pilot project on automatic subtitling of television programmes
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Media diversity
Agency Implementation: Ministry of Culture
Main Feature: It is estimated that more than 200,000 people in Slovenia have a hearing impairment. In 2021-2023, the Ministry, in cooperation with RTV Slovenia - a public broadcaster - and the Faculty of Computer Science and Informatics (University of Ljubljana), carried out a pilot project for the automatic subtitling of television programmes in real time. The aim was to test language technologies (transcription of speech into text - subtitles) that enable subtitling of live television broadcasts and thus enable deaf and hard of hearing people and the elderly to watch television.
Results: The results of the project show that the subtitling of television programmes can be implemented in real time with minimal correction by the method of pronunciation repetition, thus ensuring the accessibility of television programmes and audiovisual services for people with disabilities and people with age-related hearing loss.

SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development

Main Feature: Words, that become voices and action in the field, are engines of transformation and vehicles of civil participation; they are sparks of that 'poetic justice' that enables empathy and activation. Because the road to rights is constantly under construction, and the International Declarations as well as our Constitution serve above all as a programmatic horizon that evolves thanks to everyone's commitment. While the world is an increasingly inhospitable place, looking the other way is not an option. Especially for those who do not shirk the duty to document and the need to denounce, for those who do not shy away from asking questions to seek the truth beyond propaganda, for those who want to lend their gaze, their pen and their voice to the service of those who suffer injustice and abuse. Words, stories, and culture are extraordinary tools for building bridges, for engaging in civil battles, for turning the spotlight on the new demands for recognition emerging from contemporary societies, for leading humanity into the future. The Prize is promoted by the Giangiacomo Feltrinelli Foundation and the Feltrinelli Group. An award aimed at women and the younger generations, it seeks to reward three forms of expression â" journalistic investigation, books (both fiction and non-fiction), and podcasts â" betting on the word as a vehicle for civil participation. The Prize features three categories, each dedicated to a specific form of expression and perspective on the theme of human rights protection: books, investigations and reports, and podcasts. All works will be evaluated by an international jury of excellence.
Results: The initiative has supported the works of women in the editorial and journalistic job market with a financial prize, as well as promoting their work to the great public through institutional and media communication and dissemination. At the same time, the Prize has enabled and pushed young generations to acquire new skills on content creation, specifically oriented to podcast language – addressing Secondary Schools – and literature dedicate to Kids and young people.

Title EN: Place Partnership (Arts Council England)
Goal: Integrate Culture In Sustainable Development Frameworks
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: National sustainable development policies and plans
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: Arts Council England
Main Feature: National Lottery Project Grants (NLPG) has a dedicated Place Partnerships dedicated funding strand which focuses on funding consortia-delivered projects which make a long-term difference to the cultural and/or creative life of their local community.    A Place Partnership project is a strategic place-based intervention that is intended to make a long term difference to the cultural and/or creative life of the local community and makes a clear step change in provision in that place. It must be informed by robust needs analysis, respond to relevant local strategies and be led by a consortium of partners who are relevant to delivering the project.
Results: In the period of 2022-2024 the Arts Council invested nearly £15m in 40 of these projects.     One example of the Place Partnership project includes a collaboration between Music promoters, the local library service and the local Music Education Partnership. They came together to establish a music touring circuit across a network of branch libraries including a talent and skills development programme and responds to a need identified and in the local cultural strategy.   Another example includes the new cultural strategy for a rural district, which has identified the lack of cultural activity in a number of their market towns as a barrier to them retaining and attracting younger residents. The local authority in partnership with a number of key employers in the district want to work with local and regional arts organisations to test, develop and commission a range of new cultural activities alongside a sophisticated audience engagement plan in order to shape their new cultural offer.
Financial Ressources: In the period of 2022-2024 the Arts Council invested nearly $19.29m.

Title EN: Plateforme numérique "FenArt"
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Digital environment
Agency Implementation: Ministère de la Culture et des Arts Conseil National des Arts et des Lettres
Main Feature: Le Ministère de la Culture et des Arts a mis en place une plateforme nationale de l'artiste dite Fen Art dédiée à simplifier la procédure de demande de la carte d'artiste.  En vertu de l’article 17 du décret présidentiel n°23-376 du 22 octobre 2023 portant statut de l’artiste, la carte d’artiste est délivrée à l’artiste, au technicien d’œuvres artistiques exerçant les métiers artistiques par le Conseil National des Arts et des Lettre (CNAL). Cette carte confirme sa qualité en lui permettant de bénéficier de tous les droits prévus par la législation et la réglementation en vigueur. Elle est également délivrée à l’artiste étranger qui répond aux conditions de séjour et d’emploi, conformément à la législation et à la réglementation en vigueur. L’artiste pourra désormais par voie électronique demander, renouveler sa carte arrivée à expiration ou en cas de perte. De plus, il aura la possibilité de consulter les différentes étapes de l’instruction de sa requête à partir de son compte ouvert sur la plateforme.   Le point fort de la plateforme réside dans ce qui suit :  •	la numérisation de toutes les étapes liées à la demande, à l'étude et à la délivrance de la carte d'artiste,  •	l’identification du nombre d'artistes et leurs métiers, dans l’objectif de connaitre leur position vis-à-vis de la protection sociale et de l’ONDA,  •	la création d’un système performant aidant à la prise de décisions et permettant de tirer profit de la base de données (plateforme numérique).
Results: Depuis le lancement de la  Plateforme Fen Art en date du 06 juin 2024, 307  demandes confirmées ont été enregistrées, tandis que1.035 autres sont en cours de confirmation finale par les Artistes demandeurs de la carte d'artiste.au total 1342 compte créer.

Title EN: Plateforme numérique "Lawhati"
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Digital environment
Agency Implementation: Agence Algérienne du Rayonnement Culturel (AARC)
Main Feature: Lawhati est une plateforme numérique algérienne gérée par l’AARC (Agence Algérienne du Rayonnement Culturel) depuis 2022. Elle est dédiée à la promotion et à la gestion des œuvres d'artistes. Elle offre un espace où les artistes peuvent exposer leurs œuvres, se connecter avec un public plus large et gérer leur carrière artistique. La plateforme héberge vingt-neuf (29) artistes et plus de trois cents (300) œuvres réparties sur six (6) catégories à savoir la peinture, le dessin, la sculpture, l’art graphique, la calligraphie et la photographie.   Lawhati permet aux artistes de créer des galeries virtuelles pour exposer leurs œuvres, où chaque artiste peut organiser ses œuvres en collections, ajouter des descriptions détaillées et des informations sur les matériaux utilisés, les dimensions, et les prix, etc.  Les artistes peuvent aussi créer un profil détaillé sur la plateforme, incluant leur biographie, leur parcours artistique, et leurs influences. Cela aide les visiteurs à mieux connaitre l'artiste et son travail, créant ainsi un lien personnel. La plateforme intègre une Marketplace où les œuvres peuvent être achetées directement. Les artistes peuvent fixer les prix de leurs œuvres, gérer les ventes et les expéditions, et recevoir des paiements de manière sécurisée. Lawhati facilite le réseautage entre artistes, galeries, collectionneurs et autres acteurs du monde de l'art. Les artistes peuvent collaborer sur des projets, échanger des idées et participer à des événements artistiques. La plateforme permet aux artistes de promouvoir leurs expositions, ateliers, et autres événements artistiques. Les utilisateurs peuvent découvrir les événements à venir, s'inscrire et partager l'information avec leurs réseaux. Avantages de Lawhati Visibilité accrue : les artistes peuvent atteindre un public plus large en ligne, augmentant leur visibilité et leurs opportunités de vente. Autonomie : les artistes ont un contrôle total sur la présentation de leurs œuvres, la proposition des prix, et la gestion des ventes. Réseau de soutien : la plateforme crée une communauté d'artistes et de passionnés d'art, facilitant les échanges et les collaborations. Accès aux ressources : les artistes ont accès à des ressources et à des formations pour les aider à évoluer professionnellement.
Results: Les principaux résultats atteints grâce à Lawhati, depuis son lancement sont :   •	Vingt-neuf (29) artistes plasticiens hébergés ; •	Plus de trois (300) œuvres exposées ; •	Six (06) domaines artistiques représentés ; •	Plus de 70326 visites ; •	Plus de 13298 utilisateurs ; •	Plus de 5,29 vues par utilisateur ; •	190174 évènements sur la plateforme Lawhati.
Recommandations: •	Compétition avec la prolifération des plateformes artistiques, Lawhati devra se démarquer en offrant des fonctionnalités uniques et une expérience utilisateur de qualité ; •	Encourager les artistes locaux à adopter et à utiliser régulièrement la plateforme ; •	Lawhati pourrait s'étendre à d'autres marchés, attirant des artistes et des collectionneurs internationaux ; •	Intégration de technologies comme la réalité augmentée pour des visites virtuelles plus immersives, et l'ajout de fonctionnalités de gestion avancée pour les artistes.

Title EN: Platform for culture and arts education for Brandenburg (Plattform Kulturelle Bildung Brandenburg) (with regional offices since 2014, continuity established for 2023 onwards)
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Agency Implementation: Brandenburg Society for Culture and History (non-profit LLC) (Brandenburgische Gesellschaft für Kultur und Geschichte gGmbH)
Main Feature: Main aims: Strengthening and professionalising culture and arts education in Land Brandenburg and fostering cultural participation and cultural diversity.   Target groups: All age groups (particularly children, adolescents, young adults), skilled workers and cultural professionals, as well as disseminators, cultural institutions and cultural players.          Expected results: - Improving educational prospects and social inclusion for educationally disadvantaged children and adolescents, people with histories of immigration and under-represented sections of society, e.g. by means of culture and arts education measures in non-school contexts; - Identifying Kulturschulen (“culture schools”) in the sphere of culture and arts education, providing them with specialist support and long-term ties;  - Qualitatively evaluating the preconditions of successful culture and education in rural areas;  - Creating opportunities for teachers and specialists, art mediators, artistic and cultural professionals and disseminators to gain qualifications, add to their training and forge ties; - Generating ties among culture and arts education providers and with other players, schools, municipal administrative authorities and potential supporters
Results: New in the 2020-2023 reporting period: - Continuity established for positions on the platform staff and project transferred to institutional support; - Digital map offerings in Brandenburg developed (since 2023); - 181 culture and arts education projects supported under the Land funding programme during the reporting period; - Quality control and quality development: project office established to qualitatively evaluate the conditions affecting the success of culture and education in rural areas; - More intensive and systematic knowledge-sharing in schools established across Brandenburg
Financial Ressources: around EUR 1.1 million (2020-2023)
Recommandations: The decentralised structure of the platform and what it offers in terms of network-building, qualifications and advice are essential to the sector in Brandenburg; key preconditions of success include flexible funding options, long-term planning prospects, networks, professionalisation, mobility, and the necessity of research and self-reflection.  Publication for project end: Zehn Jahre Kreativpotentiale – Erkenntnisse, Erfolge und Perspektiven (“10 years of creative potential – findings, achievements and outlooks”), 2020 (in German): kreativpotentiale.de/publikationen/abschlusspublikation-kreativpotentiale   Evaluation (in German): gesellschaft-kultur-geschichte.de/evaluation

Title EN: PLURINATIONAL SYSTEM FOR REGISTRATION OF BOLIVIAN ARTISTS
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: MINISTERIO DE CULTURAS, DESCOLONIZACIÓN Y DESPATRIARCALIZACIÓN (MINISTRY OF CULTURES, DECOLONIZATION AND DEPATRIARCHALIZATION)
Main Feature: The Plurinational Registry of Artists was created by national decree as an administrative tool to ensure compliance with a legal provision that establishes the exemptiom from paying Value Added Tax (IVA)(VAT), Transactions Tax (TT)(IT), and Corporate Income Tax – (AIC) IUE in all activities of production, presentation and dissemination of events, theater, dance, national music, painting, sculpture and cinema, produced by Bolivian artists. Reinforces state policies on behalf art manifestations to be considered factors of national culture promoting protection, in order to preserve their authenticity and increase their production and dissemination.  The registration process to comply with this benefit is under the responsibility of the Ministry of Cultures, Decolonization and Depatriarchalization, fulfilling the following requirements:  - Letter addressed to the Ministry of Cultures. Decolonization and Depatriarchalization. - Photocopy of Identity Card - Artistic resume supported by certificates, photographs, program notes, credits in audiovisual productions, etc. - A 3x3 digital photograph with a white background.  For the registration of artistic groups in different disciplines with the following requirements:  - Letter addressed to the Ministry of Cultures. Decolonization and Depatrarchalization that accredits the representative to carry out the registration on behalf of the group. The letter must be signed by the members or management detailing their Identity Card numbers. - Photocopy of the Identity Card of the representative and the members. - Documented artistic curriculum of the group, with a list of all its members. -A digital photograph or logo of the group.  The artists receive an official credential of registration.
Results: 17,594 individual and collective registrations have been made nationwide since 2012.  In 2021 after the pandemic, the largest number of registrations was recorded, with a total of 3,282 individual and collective artists. Since then, there has been a decrease in applications by 45% to date.  The registration percentages by department are as follows:  La Paz 26%  Cochabamba 21%  Oruro 21%  Santa Cruz 10%  Potosi 7% Tarija 6% Chuquisaca 5%  Pando 1% and Beni 1%  The following distribution is found by categories managed by the registry:  Musical Arts 63% Performing Arts 22% Visual Arts 7% Textiles 3% Audiovisual Arts 3% Literary Arts 2%  Popular Arts 1%   The artist card has had an important result in its use, mainly to facilitate the international circulation of artists as well as for procedures before administrative institutions of the State.

Title EN: PM Vishwakarma Scheme
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Agency Implementation: Ministry of Culture, Government of India
Main Feature: - Skill Development and Capacity Building: Implemented in early 2023, the scheme offers comprehensive training programs aimed at enhancing the skills of traditional artisans. These training sessions focus on modernizing traditional techniques while preserving their unique cultural elements. The initiative addresses Article 7 of the 2005 Convention, which emphasizes creating opportunities for cultural expressions to reach broader audiences. By 2024, it is expected that over 50,000 artisans will have benefitted from these training programs.  - Financial Support and Market Access: Since its inception, the PM Vishwakarma Scheme has provided financial assistance to artisans for purchasing modern tools and equipment. Additionally, it facilitates access to new domestic and international markets through organized craft fairs and online marketplaces. This financial empowerment directly supports the Convention's goal of fostering viable cultural industries. By the end of 2023, more than 10,000 artisans received financial grants, enhancing their economic sustainability.  - Preservation and Promotion of Traditional Crafts: A significant aspect of the scheme is its focus on preserving traditional crafts. The government has initiated projects to document and disseminate traditional knowledge, ensuring its transmission to future generations. These efforts align with the Convention's mandate to protect and promote diverse cultural expressions, particularly those vulnerable to globalization. By mid-2023, several crafts, including traditional weaving and pottery, have been documented and promoted through various cultural platforms.  - Social Inclusion and Gender Equality: The PM Vishwakarma Scheme places a strong emphasis on inclusivity, particularly the inclusion of marginalized communities and women. The scheme ensures equitable access to resources and opportunities, promoting gender equality and social inclusion within the cultural sector. This focus supports the Convention’s goal of fostering cultural diversity through the participation of all societal segments. By 2023, initiatives specifically targeting female artisans and marginalized groups have shown significant progress, with numerous success stories emerging from rural areas.
Results: Timeline of Activities and Key Milestones - January 2023: Official launch of the PM Vishwakarma Scheme. - February - April 2023: Initial training programs for artisans begin across various states. - June 2023: First round of financial grants disbursed to eligible artisans. - September 2023: Launch of an online marketplace for traditional crafts. - December 2023: Documentation projects for traditional crafts completed. - Ongoing: Continuous monitoring and evaluation of the scheme's impact on cultural preservation and economic viability.

Title EN: Policies Consultation with Non-Benefit Public Associations
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Partnering with civil society
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: Ministry of Culture
Main Feature: Since 2018, the Ministry of Culture has continued its robust dialogue process with Non-Benefit Public Associations to understand and address the challenges facing the cultural sector. This initiative has been part of broader reform efforts to develop policies and regulations that support cultural stakeholders. Key developments in recent years include the establishment of new forums for collaboration, such as the G20 Culture Working Group Taskforce, and enhanced efforts to protect cultural property, harness living heritage, and promote cultural and creative industries. The Ministry has also launched the National Grant Programme for Culture and Creativity in 2023, aimed at funding projects across various fields including Books and Literature, Music, Film and TV, Performing Arts and Theatre, Visual Arts and Design, Video Games, and Cultural Heritage. This program supports UAE talent through different grants, such as Creation and Production Grants, Distribution and Local Participations Grants, Capacity Development Grants, and International Travel and Mobility Grants
Results: Through the implementation of the policy/measure, significant progress has been made in strengthening the dialogue between Non-Benefit Public Associations and government bodies. Artists and cultural professionals have reported increased access to resources and opportunities for cross-border collaboration. The policy has facilitated the mobility of artists and professionals, enabling them to participate in international exchanges and expand their creative networks. Additionally, the consultation process has led to the development of more inclusive and transparent policies that better address the needs of the cultural sector, fostering a more supportive environment for artistic expression and innovation.

Title EN: Policies on Government Institutions and Other Government Working Groups Playing a Direct Role in Planning and Implementing Sustainable Culture Development
Goal: Integrate Culture In Sustainable Development Frameworks
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development

Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: 1. Ministry of Education, Culture, Research, and Technology  2. Ministry of Tourism and Creative Economy 3. Coordinating Ministry for Human Development and Cultural Affairs  4. Coordinating Ministry for Maritime and Investment Affairs
Main Feature: In the past four years, policies on government institutions and other government working groups playing a direct role in planning and implementing sustainable culture development include: 1. Presidential Regulation 65 of 2015 on the Ministry of National Development Planning (Kementerian Perencanaan Pembangunan Nasional) (PR on Kemen PPN);   2. Presidential Regulation 66 of 2015 on the National Development Planning Agency (Badan Perencanaan Pembangunan Nasional) (PR on Bappenas);  3. Presidential Regulation 96 of 2019 on the Ministry of Tourism and Creative Economy (Kementerian Pariwisata and Ekonomi Kreatif) (PR on Kemenparekraf);  4. Presidential Regulation 97 of 2019 on the Tourism and Creative Economy Agency (Badan Pariwisata and Ekonomi Kreatif) (PR on Baparekraf);  5. Presidential Regulation 92 of 2019 on the Coordinating Ministry for Maritime and Investment Affairs (Kementerian Koordinator Bidang Kemaritiman and Investasi) (PR on Kemenkomarves);  6. Presidential Regulation 35 of 2020 on the Coordinating Ministry for Human Development and Cultural Affairs (Kementerian Koordinator Bidang Pembangunan Manusia and Kebudayaan) (PR on Kemenko PMK); and  7. Several policies reported in the 2020 QPR, namely the PR on Kemenparekraf and PR on Baparekraf, are still valid when drafting this report. Meanwhile, Presidential Regulation 82 of 2019 on the Ministry of Education and Culture and Presidential Regulation 9 of 2015 on the Coordinating Ministry for Human Development and Culture have each been replaced with the PR on Kemendikbudristek (see Goal 1, Policies on Competent Government Institutions with a Budget for Cultural Affairs) and the PR on Kemenko PMK (see Goal 1, Policies on Cooperation Among Government Institutions), respectively. Provide space for the diversity of cultural expressions and encourage cultural interaction to strengthen the inclusiveness of culture (Agenda 1);  2. Protect and develop values, expressions, and practices of traditional culture to enrich national culture (Agenda 2);  3. Develop and utilize cultural resources to strengthen the position of Indonesia internationally (Agenda 3);  4. Institutional reform and culture budgeting to support the culture advancement agenda (Agenda 6); and  5. Strengthen the role of the government as a facilitator of culture advancement (Agenda 7).

Title EN: Policies and Measures for Education and Training Programs in Culture and Creative Economy Sectors
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: 1. Ministry of Education, Culture, Research, and Technology  2. Ministry of Tourism and Creative Economy/Tourism and Creative Economy Agency  3. Ministry of Manpower 4. National Professional Certification Agency  5. State Film Production Corporation
Main Feature: In the past four years, policies and measures for education and training programs in culture and creative economy sectors include: 1. Law 20 of 2003 on the National Education System (Sistem Pendidikan Nasional) (Law on Sisdiknas); 2. Law 13 of 2003 on Manpower (Law on Manpower); 3. Draft Law on Amendments to Law 20 of 2003 on the National Education System (Sistem Pendidikan Nasional) (Draft Law on Sisdiknas);  4. Draft Law on Amendments to Law 13 of 2003 on Manpower (Draft Law on Manpower); 5. Indonesian National Work Competency Standards (Standar Kompetensi Kerja Nasional Indonesia, SKKNI);  6. Second-party Professional Certification Institute for Culture (Lembaga Sertifikasi Profesi Pihak Kedua Kebudayaan, LSP-P2 for Culture); 7. Scholarships for Cultural Practitioners; 8. Arts Institutions Standardization and Certification in Bali; 9. Indonesiana Film; and 10. Indonesia Film Content Academy (IFCA).       SKKNI and LSP-P2 for Culture were reported in the 2020 QPR and are still valid/operating at the time of this report. As additional information on SKKNI, the standard setting for the culture sector is to be prepared by Kemendikbudristek, while the creative economy sector is the responsibility of Kemenparekraf. The SKKNI drafts will then be submitted to Kemenaker to be stipulated in ministerial regulations. The SKKNI for the culture and creative economy sectors that have been stipulated serve as a reference by professional certification bodies in carrying out capacity building and certification of various professions related to culture and creative economy.   Regarding the LSP-P2 for Culture, this institution organizes professional certification for non-association cultural professionals. Unlike the culture sector, the creative economy sector does not have a second-party institution since professional certification services in the creative economy sector have been organized independently by each professional association in the creative economy.  Furthermore, two policies not reported in the 2016 and 2020 QPRs support education and training in Indonesia, namely the Law on Sisdiknas and the Law on Manpower. The Law on Sisdiknas stipulates education and self-development training, while the Law on Manpower stipulates work training. The Law on Sisdiknas requires the presence of arts and culture learning materials in the curriculum of all primary and secondary education levels (grades I-XII). The explanatory section states that the primary purpose of arts and culture learning materials for education is to shape students' character into an individual with a sense of art and cultural understanding through writing, drawing/painting, singing, and dancing activities. In recent developments, stakeholders have identified the need to update the Law on Sisdiknas and the Law on Manpower to respond to present challenges and opportunities. Although both the Draft Law on Sisdiknas and the Draft Law on Manpower have been registered in the National Legislation Program (Prolegnas), they have not yet been prioritized to be completed by 2024.  Meanwhile, the Scholarships for Cultural Practitioners program, which in the 2020 QPR was reported as part of the scholarship program of the Education Fund Management Institution, has since 2022 been merged into the Dana Indonesiana program (see Goal 1, Measures that Provide Funds for CSO Capacity Development). Since becoming part of Dana Indonesiana, the Scholarships for Cultural Practitioners program has two main schemes: degree and non-degree. The degree scheme of the Scholarships for Cultural Practitioners program is intended to facilitate cultural practitioners pursuing formal education from bachelor to doctoral level. Meanwhile, the non-degree scheme of the Scholarships for Cultural Practitioners program is intended to facilitate cultural practitioners who will increase their capacity through non-formal channels such as workshops, internships, and residencies. Both schemes apply to national and international scholarships.  One of the new measures that can be reported is the Arts Institutions Standardization and Certification in Bali as a derivative of the Bali Provincial Regulation 4 of 2020 on the Strengthening and Advancement of Balinese Culture. Disbud Bali designs this standard to measure the key performance of studios, sekaa, foundations, and arts communities in Bali in terms of quality control, management, and productivity. The main objective of arts institution standardization is to assess the performance of studios, sekaa, foundations, and arts communities in conducting their activities and to evaluate the management capacity and productivity of arts institutions that require support or capacity building. Certification to art institutions is given in three categories, namely Parama Patram Budaya (advanced category), Madyama Patram Budaya (intermediate category), and Pratama Patram Budaya (beginner category).  Another new measure is Indonesiana Film, an incubation program for developing long-fiction film scenarios with strong local narratives by organizing workshops for screenwriters, producers, and directors. This program has been implemented by the Directorate of Film, Music, and Media, Kemendikbudristek, since 2020 and is still ongoing when drafting this report. Indonesiana Film runs throughout the year, and 2024 marks the 5th year of program implementation. Participants are trained to develop their stories by participating in screenwriting workshops under the guidance of national and international tutors and mentors from Indonesia and abroad.  Another new measure is IFCA. IFCA is a business unit under PFN, which, since 2023, has focused on building and developing film and multimedia talents to strengthen the film and digital industry ecosystem by producing quality films and content that have educational value and are based on Indonesian cultural values. IFCA was built as a center of excellence with three pillars: learning, research, and innovation in the film and content industry. IFCA's primary services include (1) the provision and development of solutions for learning and certification, (2) the implementation of research and innovation, and (3) providing consulting services in the film, multimedia, and digital services industry.  One of the measures reported in the 2020 QPR, the Innovative and Creative Nusantara Collaborations (IKKON), has been discontinued by Kemenparekraf since 2019.  In general, policies and measures for education and training programs in culture and creative economy sectors are aimed at contributing to achieving the following agenda(s) of the National Strategy for Culture: 1. Develop and utilize cultural resources to strengthen the position of Indonesia internationally (Agenda 3); 2. Utilize objects of culture advancement to improve people's welfare (Agenda 4); and 3. Strengthen the role of the government as a facilitator of culture advancement (Agenda 7).
Results: SKKNI: At the time of drafting this report, a minimum of 113 SKKNI were found for the culture and creative economy sectors with a division based on main groups as follows. 1. Furniture Industry: 5 7. Other Processing Industries: 3 8. Publishing Activities: 1 9. Education: 1 13. Entertainment, Arts, and Creativity Activities: 26 14. Libraries, Archives, Museums, and other Cultural Activities: 6 15. Other Sports and Recreational Activities: 4 16. Other Personal Services Activities: 28  Since 2020, the following SKKNI and the Indonesian National Qualifications Framework (KKNI) have been prepared. 2020: 1. SKKNI for the Tradition Sector 2. SKKNI for the Cultural Heritage Sector 3. SKKNI for Intangible Cultural Heritage Experts 4. SKKNI for Museums 5. SKKNI for Arts 6. SKKNI for Film and Music  2021: 1. KKNI in the Field of Traditions 2. KKNI for the Cultural Heritage Sector 3. KKNI in the Field of History 4. SKKNI for Museums 5. KKNI for Arts 6. SKKNI for Intangible Cultural Heritage Experts 7. KKNI for Intangible Cultural Heritage Experts  2022: 1. SKKNI for Museums 2. Specific Work Competency Standards for the Field of Indigenous Community Facilitators 3. SKKNI for Intangible Cultural Heritage Experts 4. SKKNI for the Tradition Sector (KKNI for Kris Sector)  2023: 1. SKKNI for Traditions (Indigenous Community Education Facilitator)  The List of SKKNI related to Culture and Creative Economy per Main Group in the Annexes section provides a complete list with document links.  LSP-P2 for Culture: Currently, LSP-P2 for Culture provides services for 46 culture sector professional certification schemes that already have SKKNI.  Arts Institutions Standardization and Certification in Bali: Since 2021, Disbud Bali has certified 598 art studios, sekaa, foundations, and communities in the Bali Province.  Indonesiana Film: Since 2020, more than 300 projects have been registered every year, and they are then filtered and selected into 8-10 projects.
Recommandations: SKKNI: The internal evaluation at the Directorate General of Culture, Kemendikbudristek, resulted in the following conclusions/recommendations.  1. In 2020, many activities were still carried out online or hybrid, making it challenging to supervise the preparation process and slowing down the preparation of SKKNI documents. For the following year, it is necessary to coordinate more intensively with the drafters.  2. In 2021, problems persisted due to the COVID-19 pandemic, where restrictions on community activities slowed down preparations. Assessment targets must be mapped to prepare the certification scheme and assessment qualifications appropriately; hence, an SKKNI Development Master Plan must be prepared.

Title EN: Policies and Measures that Support Media Freedom
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Media diversity
Cultural Domain: Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: 1. Press Council of Indonesia 2. Ministry of Communication and Information Technology 3. Attorney General's Office 4. Indonesian National Police 5. Indonesian Broadcasting Commision
Main Feature: In the past four years, policies and measures that support media freedom include: 1. Law 40 of 1999 on the Press (Law on the Press);  2. Law 32 of 2002 on Broadcasting (Law on Broadcasting); 3. Law 6 of 2023 on the Stipulation of Government Regulation in Lieu of Law 2 of 2022 on Job Creation into Law (Law on Job Creation); 4. Law 1 of 2024 on Second Amendments to Law 11 of 2008 on Electronic Information and Transactions (Informasi dan Transaksi Elektronik) (Law on ITE); 5. Draft Law on Amendments to Law 32 of 2020 on Broadcasting (Draft Law on Broadcasting); 6. Draft Law on the Radio Televisi Republik Indonesia (Draft Law on RTRI); 7. Indonesian Broadcasting Commission Regulation 1/P/KPI/03/2012 on the Guidelines for Broadcasting Behavior (Guidelines for Broadcasting Behavior); 8. Indonesian Broadcasting Commission Regulation 2/P/KPI/03/2012 on the Standards for Broadcast Programs (Standards for Broadcast Programs); 9. Palembang Charter of February 9, 2010, on the Agreement of National Press Companies; 10. Press Freedom Index (Indeks Kemerdekaan Pers, IKP); 11. National Press Day (Hari Pers Nasional, HPN); 12. Television Broadcast Program Quality Index (Indeks Kualitas Program Siaran Televisi, IKPSTV); and 13. Indonesian Media Diversity Monitoring Framework.  Several policies and measures have been reported in the 2020 QPR, namely: (1) Law on Broadcasting; (2) Draft Law on RTRI; (3) Guidelines for Broadcasting Behavior; (4) IKPSTV (see Goal 1, Policies and Measures that Demand Media Accountability); and (5) Indonesian Media Diversity Monitoring Framework, are still valid/ongoing at the time of drafting this report. Even though it has been registered in the latest developments, the Draft Law on RTRI is still not a priority for the National Legislation Program (Program Legislasi Nasional, Prolegnas) to be completed in 2024. Meanwhile, efforts to socialize the Indonesian Media Diversity Monitoring Framework will only start again in 2024 after being delayed due to the COVID-19 pandemic.  Some regulations in the Law on Broadcasting have been replaced with the Law on Job Creation (see Goal 1, Policies and Measures that Encourage Job Creation and Entrepreneurship in Culture and Creative Economy Sectors). Efforts to update it are already underway in the Prolegnas, where the Draft Law on Broadcasting has become one of the priority bills to be completed in 2024. At the time of drafting this report, it had already entered the drafting stage.  Meanwhile, another policy that has been reported in the 2020 QPR, namely Law 19 of 2016 on Amendments to Law 11 of 2008 on Electronic Information and Transactions, has been replaced with Law 1 of 2024 on Second Amendments to Law 11 of 2008 Electronic Information and Transactions. In essence, the changes stipulated are intended for defamation complainants to be wiser and more mature in their considerations before filing a complaint. However, there are still several parties who believe that these changes threaten the freedom of the press and freedom of public expression.    This second change was made even though the Central Government had made previous improvements to implement the Law through the Joint Decree of the Minister of Communication and Informatics of the Republic of Indonesia, the Attorney General of the Republic of Indonesia, and the Head of the National Police of the Republic of Indonesia Number 229 of 2021 Number 154 of 2021 Number KB/2/ VI/2021 on Implementation Guidelines for Certain Articles in Law 11 of 2008 on Electronic Information and Transactions as Amended by Law 19 of 2016 on Amendments to Law 11 of 2008 on Electronic Information and Transactions. The guidelines emphasize that for internet reporting carried out by press institutions, which is journalistic work by the provisions of the Law on the Press, a mechanism is applied by the Law on the Press as lex specialist.  One crucial policy related to broadcast media that has not been explicitly reported in the 2020 QPR but is still in effect is the Standards for Broadcast Programs. In terms of policy, the Standards for Broadcast Programs are always considered a package with the Guidelines for Broadcasting Behavior, so they are better known as the Guidelines for Broadcasting Behavior and Standards for Broadcast Programs (Pedoman Perilaku Penyiaran dan Standar Program Siaran, P3SPS). This P3SPS was reported in the 2020 QPR.  Apart from diversity in broadcasting media, efforts to protect and promote diversity of cultural expressions also require diversity in press media based on press freedom. The press is a pillar of democracy, an extension of society to channel its aspirations. In Indonesia, press freedom is guaranteed through the Law on the Press, which stipulates that (1) press freedom is a form of popular sovereignty based on the principles of democracy, justice, and the supremacy of law; (2) freedom of the press is guaranteed as a citizen's human right; and (3) to guarantee press freedom, the national press has the right to seek, obtain, and disseminate ideas and information. Even though the press has freedom in carrying out its profession, journalists are bound by a journalistic code of ethics. This is regulated in 11 articles as operational guidelines to maintain public trust and uphold integrity and professionalism. The principle of press freedom is also stated in the Palembang Charter of February 9, 2010, on the Agreement of National Press Companies signed by several press companies.  Furthermore, the Press Council has compiled a National IKP Survey to map and monitor press freedom conditions. This IKP is calculated yearly based on survey results in 34 Indonesian provinces from January to December of the previous year. Twenty indicators of press freedom are measured through three variables: physical and political environmental conditions, economic environmental conditions, and legal environmental conditions. It is hoped that this IKP can become a milestone in improving the life of the national press.  Another milestone in improving the life of the national press is the HPN, commemorated every February 9 in connection with the founding of the first journalists' organization in Indonesia, namely the Indonesian Journalists Association, in 1946. This HPN was only officially commemorated after the publication of Presidential Decree 5 of 1985 on the National Press Day. HPN is held annually alternately in provincial capitals throughout Indonesia with participation from the press, community, and government components, especially the regional government where it is held. One of HPN's regular agendas is a discussion forum between stakeholders regarding issues directly impacting press performance, including those related to various government policies. The 2022 HPN carries the theme "Digital Era Momentum Promotes Regional Potential," while the 2023 HPN carries the theme "Free Press, Dignified Democracy." For the 2024 HPN, the theme raised is "Guarding the National Leadership Transition and Maintaining the Integrity of the Nation," related to the implementation of General Election activities.  In general, policies and measures that support media freedom are aimed at contributing to achieving the following agenda(s) of the National Strategy for Culture: 1. Provide space for the diversity of cultural expressions and encourage cultural interaction to strengthen the inclusiveness of culture (Agenda 1); 2. Protect and develop values, expressions, and practices of traditional culture to enrich national culture (Agenda 2); and 3. Strengthen the role of the government as a facilitator of culture advancement (Agenda 7).
Results: IKP: 2020: 75.27 (Fairly Free) 2021: 76.02 (Fairly Free) 2022: 77.87 (Fairly Free) 2023: 71.57 (Fairly Free)  After a trend of increasing press freedom from 2020 to 2022, in 2023, it fell by 6.20 points, although it remained in the "Fairly Free" category. The decline in the 2023 IKP occurred in all three variables. In the physical and political environmental conditions variable, the indicators "Freedom from Intervention" and "Freedom from Violence" fell by around 7 points. In the economic environment condition variable, there was a decrease of 8 points in the "Independence from Strong Groups" indicator. Meanwhile, in the legal environment condition variable, there was the most significant decline (around 8-9 points) in two indicators, namely "Criminalization and Intimidation of the Press" and "Press Ethics." In general, the downward trend in these indicators indicates that during 2022, there were several acts of violence against the press, both against journalists and central and regional media. The violence that occurred could have been in the form of physical or non-physical violence, including violence through digital means, social media accounts belonging to journalists, and/or online media news sites.  IKPSTV: 2020: 3.14 (period I) and 3.21 (period II) 2021: 3.09 (period I) and 3.13 (period II) 2022: 3.20  Based on the 2022 IKPSTV of 3.20, 6 out of 8 program categories were of a quality that, at least, met KPI standards (3.00), with the highest index obtained by the Religious programs category (3.53). Meanwhile, the other five categories that were also considered quality programs are Talk Shows (3.46), Tourism and Culture (3.44), News (3.31), Variety Shows (3.20), and Children (3.18) programs. The program categories with an index considered not meeting the standards are the Infotainment (2.80) and Soap Opera (2.70) programs.
Recommandations: Evaluations carried out by the Press Council on press companies and journalists resulted in a number of conclusions/recommendations, as follows. 1. After showing an increasing trend from 2020-2022, the IKP declined in 2023. However, with a score of 71.57, press freedom in Indonesia remains in the "fairly free" category. 2. Efforts to strengthen press freedom in Indonesia need to continue year after year, even though they have yet to succeed in reaching the "free" category or a figure in the 90-100 range.  Draft Law on Broadcasting: Evaluations carried out by journalist organizations such as the Indonesian Journalists Alliance and the Indonesian Journalists Association have drawn the following conclusions. 1. KPI may resolve journalistic disputes in the broadcasting sector contrary to the function of the Press Council. 2. Disputes arising from KPI decisions can be resolved through the Court, creating a dualism between the Press Council and the Indonesian Broadcasting Commission because they can decide complaints on journalistic disputes. 3. The prohibition on exclusive broadcasting of investigative journalistic products needs to be reviewed. 4. The prohibition on creating content that contains insults and defamation has the subjective potential to silence press freedom.  Law on the Press: Evaluations carried out by DPR (2023) have produced several conclusions as follows. 1. The Law on the Press still has problems with substance and implementation, both at the central and regional levels. Its content is insufficient, and its implementation has not been effective because relevant stakeholders and lawmakers need to pay attention to substance and implementation problems when revising the Law on the Press. 2. Viewed from the substantive aspect, several provisions are no longer relevant to current conditions and must be refined by adding several things to the content material regulated in the Law on the Press. This is intended so that the provisions in the Law on the Press can strengthen press freedom and fulfill the principles of forming good legislative regulations as regulated in Law 12 of 2011 on the Formation of Legislative Regulations as last amended by Law 13 of 2022 on Second Amendments to Law 12 of 2011 on the Formation of Legislation. 3. From an implementation perspective, several problems were found in the Law on the Press, including low legal protection for journalists in carrying out journalistic activities; press entities that still do not have legal entity status; misperception regarding the verification and data collection activities carried out by the Press Council; and low commitment of law enforcement in positioning the Law on the Press as lex specialist. Then, regarding facilities and infrastructure, it was found that there were differences in views regarding the urgency of establishing Press Council representatives in the regions. In the aspect of legal culture, a fairly basic problem was also found, namely that people still tend to choose formal criminal channels (namely complaints to the police) in addition to resolving press disputes at the Press Council.  Based on these findings, DPR (2023) then submitted several recommendations. 1. Aspects of Legal Substance a. The Law on the Press needs to be re-evaluated to harmonize with the Law on Broadcasting, especially regarding exceptions to the censorship rules in the Law on Broadcasting for journalistic products broadcasted. b. It is necessary to regulate content material in the Law on Press for digital platforms that publish information content similar to journalistic works. c. The provisions of the Law on the Press regarding news, online media, journalist competence, digital platforms, and citizen journalism need to be defined. d. It needs to be formulated in the Law on the Press regarding the obligation for every journalist to take the Journalist Competency Test so that every journalist throughout Indonesia carries it out. e. Regulations regarding the rights and obligations of the foreign press in Indonesia should be added to the Law on the Press.  2. Aspects of Legal Structure  a. It is necessary to optimize legal assistance or advocacy for journalists by the Press Council. b. The state must compensate journalists who experience threats, intimidation, or attacks. c. It is necessary to increase sanctions for violence against journalists in areas of conflict, demonstrations, and other areas that are vulnerable to posing a threat. d. Cooperation between press companies, the government, and law enforcement agencies must be strengthened to create a safer environment for journalists. e. Regulations regarding the protection of journalists in carrying out their profession, such as one relating to digital security, must be expanded. f. The Law on the Press needs to include specific provisions regarding the types of press company legal entities in Indonesia to provide legal certainty and guarantee that press companies comply with these provisions. g. Concrete efforts need to be made to update and facilitate access to press company data so that it can provide optimal benefits for press people and related stakeholders. h. Further outreach regarding the essence and objectives of the verification process is necessary to overcome ignorance and misperceptions regarding verification activities. i. Increasing transparency and accountability in the verification process must be improved to build trust and better understanding between press companies and the Press Council. j. Awareness-raising must be carried out to all law enforcement officials and related parties so that law enforcement can resolve press disputes by adhering to the Law on the Press as a lex specialist.  3. Aspects of Facilities and Infrastructure It is recommended that lawmakers adapt to the Press Council's needs to make policy choices regarding whether or not Press Council representation is necessary in the regions.   4. Aspects of Legal Cultural  The government, press companies, and the Press Council need to raise public awareness more massively and regularly about press dispute resolution mechanisms, including criminal proceedings and the Press Council.  5.Aspects of Mainstreaming Pancasila Values  a. The regulatory provisions regarding the right to refuse need to be conceptualized comprehensively and refer to the Press Council's authority to determine the criteria for the right to refuse. b. There needs to be an addition to the Law on the Press explaining what matters are included in "events and opinions" as intended in Article 5, paragraph (1) of the Law on the Press. c.It should be revised by formulating schemes and procedures for community involvement in the journalistic process that runs as a form of democracy. d. The journalist recruitment and identity certification process needs to be revised. Journalists must also internalize morals and values ​​, including Pancasila values, as a foundation for carrying out journalistic activities. e. Comprehensive regulations regarding the foreign press, including institutions, structures, and systems, as well as their position in Indonesia, must be conceptualized.   Report on the 2022 IKPSTV: KPI (2022) carried out an evaluation that has produced a number of conclusions beyond reporting IKPSTV scores​​, as follows. 1. The yearly index results, especially in the 2020-2022 period, show a trend of stable quality (above the KPI standard of 3.00) for television broadcast programs. However, several aspects of television station programs still have deficiencies or notes. 2. For the first time in seven years of calculating this index, the Variety Shows program category meets quality standards with a score of 3.20. 3.
