Title EN: World Media and Information Literacy Week in Lithuanian public libraries
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture
SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Media diversity
Agency Implementation: Association of County Public Libraries
Main Feature: Media and information literacy - the essential competences (knowledge, skills and attitudes) to critically evaluate information in the media and social networks and to select reliable sources of information. Libraries are homes of information and knowledge, staffed by professional information specialists who are always happy to answer questions. Recent events such as the pandemic, Russia's aggression against Ukraine, the constant information noise, the abundance of the media and the information it contains, and the spread of disinformation have encouraged the public to take an interest in the principles of the media and the social networks, and to learn how to select, understand, interpret, analyse and critically evaluate the information they provide. In 2022 and 2023, the UNESCO-initiated World Media and Information Literacy Week took place in all Lithuanian public libraries. Lithuanian public libraries invite citizens to use the Media and Information Literacy Programme on their own and to participate in media and information literacy events in libraries. The activities involve county and municipal public libraries, the National Martynas Mažvydas Library of Lithuania, the Lithuanian Librarians' Association and associations, academic libraries and non-governmental organisations. The programme is financed by the Ministry of Culture of the Republic of Lithuania.  How to stay on top of the media, internet and social networks? How to distinguish between reliable information and lies? Lithuanian public libraries, which are already becoming media and information literacy centres, will help you answer these questions as they invite you to the World Media and Information Literacy Week. Each year, dozens of activities for adults have taken place. From an orienteering hike to an evening of stand-up comedy. A reading challenge, brain teasers, meetings with experts, discussions and lectures, games, a virtual escape room and much much more!  In addition to the events, the citizens of the country were invited to explore media and information literacy on the website: https://mirkt.bibliotekavisiems.lt/, to participate in workshops, and to watch the information videos "Get to know the media with Klaudia". Try out the board game "Populist", translated and adapted by the libraries.  A cooperation agreement is signed between the Association of County Public Libraries and the Lithuanian Medical Library for the organisation of the World Media and Information Literacy Week.  Partnerships with "Meno avilys", Vytautas Magnus University, DIGIRES digital resilience initiative continued from 2022. Patronage from the Lithuanian National Commission for UNESCO. Media4change initiative, improvisation theatre “Impro 241”, National Blood Centre, Local Community Journalists Network, organ donation association “Gyvastis”, financial literacy experts “Ifuture”, LRT TV game "Who and Why?", which asked participants questions about media and information literacy during the MIL week. Sponsorship agreements were signed with the Antanukas e-bookstore, Go3 TV, National Geographic Lietuva magazine, and the telecommunications company “Telia”.
Results: 2023 MIL week results: 74 events coordinated and organised: - 25 health literacy events; - 18 financial literacy events; - 10 audiovisual content creation training sessions with film directors; - 7 media4change workshops; - 5 meetings with journalists; - 3 events on misinformation on social networks; - 2 events on historical literacy; - 2 events on Artificial Intelligence; - 1 improvisation theatre performance; - 1 stand-up comedy evening; - 1 orienteering hike, with 42 Lithuanian libraries creating different hiking routes with tasks about MIL. 7 events were streamed and the recordings are also available after MIL Week on the Library for All Youtube channel.  Together with the events organised in libraries all over Lithuania, during the World Media and Information Literacy Week, 295 contact events were held, with the participation of 4,196 people, and 7,494 viewers took part in virtual events.  A crossword consisting of 15 questions was prepared as part of the learning programme. The crossword was published in the magazines "Her" and "Prie kavos" and sent to libraries for use during the events. The winners were awarded with TELIA reflectors and mobile phone accessories and NATIONAL GEOGRAPHIC magazines.  Created a virtual escape room on the Genial.ly platform "I am my own information architect". The virtual escape room was tested by 1,936 participants and overcome by 138 participants.   A reading challenge was organised. During the MIL Week, the participants are invited to read a book related to media and information literacy topics, register it and win prizes. 47 books were read.  A brain teaser based on the learning programme was developed and presented on several different difficulties, so that libraries can adapt it to different audiences. The challenge has been sent to public libraries all over Lithuania.   MIL Week events and related information reached 224 819 individual users on Facebook and 132 211 on Instagram. The number of followers of the Facebook account increased to 357 (824 at the end of the year), while the newly created Instagram account attracted 152 social network users.  3 press releases prepared and published, distributed in regional and national media.

Main Feature: Supporting the competitiveness of small and medium-sized enterprises, the WORTH Partnership Project is an incubator/accelerator programme in support of business partnerships between designers/creators, manufacturers/craftsmen and tech providers.  The aim is to develop new, innovative business ideas in the lifestyle industries (fashion, design furniture, interior design and home décor, as well as accessories). New products, services and business models have been tested with the active involvement of designers and other creative professionals. Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture

Area of Monitoring: Cultural and creative sectors
Agency Implementation: IPDJ - Institute of Sport and Youth
Main Feature: The "Young Creators" programme is a cultural initiative in Portugal aimed at fostering the artistic development of young creators by providing them with opportunities to publicize their work. Originating in the 1980s through the Portuguese Arts and Ideas Club (CPAI), it was initially known as the Portuguese Arts and Ideas Exhibition. In the 1990s, the programme evolved through a partnership with the Portuguese Institute of Sport and Youth (IPDJ), significantly extending its reach to young Portuguese artists. Since 2018, the Youth Foundation, in collaboration with the Secretary of State for Youth, has played a crucial role in the programme.  The programme covers more than 15 artistic categories, including architecture, comics, film, dance, equipment design, graphic design, literature, music, and more. This diverse range of fields ensures that young artists from various disciplines have the opportunity to showcase their talents. The programme also emphasizes the importance of providing young artists, who are often deprived of access to cultural circuits, with a platform to exhibit their work and gain recognition.  One of the distinctive features of the "Young Creators" programme is its international scope. It promotes international travel and participation, such as in the CPLP Biennial of Young Creators, offering young artists the chance to exhibit their work internationally and experience being curators and interlocutors. The programme culminates in the annual "Mostra Nacional de Jovens Criadores," a major cultural event where selected works are showcased. This event not only helps artists publicize their work but also provides them with valuable networking opportunities, enriching their professional and artistic development.
Results: The implementation of the "Young Creators" programme has yielded significant positive results, highlighting its impact on the national artistic scene. The 2019 edition of the programme, although delayed due to the COVID-19 pandemic, received a remarkable response with 300 projects submitted by 351 participants. This indicates a strong interest and engagement from young artists across the country.  The selection process involved a panel of esteemed judges from the national cultural sphere, who evaluated works across 15 artistic categories. Ultimately, 77 projects by 90 participants were selected for the National Young Creators Showcase, held on 5 and 6 November 2021 in Vila Nova de Gaia. This event provided a platform for the artists to exhibit their work, network, and gain recognition, reinforcing the programme’s role in fostering artistic talent.  The gender distribution of participants and selected artists shows a significant representation of female artists, with 61.5% of applicants and 57% of selected participants being female. This suggests that the programme is accessible and inclusive, encouraging diverse participation.  The programme's international component also demonstrated success through the International Day of Historic Centres on 26 March 2022, where young creators were invited to exhibit their projects. This event attracted 2343 visitors, including locals, tourists, and family members, showcasing 28 projects by 32 young creators. The positive turnout and the number of exhibited works highlight the programme’s effectiveness in promoting young talent and providing them with valuable exposure.  Overall, the "Young Creators" programme has successfully launched countless young artists, enabling them to gain notoriety in the cultural world and contribute to the national and international artistic landscape. The programme’s achievements underscore its importance in supporting and nurturing the next generation of artists in Portugal.
Recommandations: The implementation of the "Young Creators" program has been evaluated through rigorous assessments focusing on its physical execution and financial management. These evaluations consistently highlight its success in fostering cultural diversity, supporting the careers of young artists, and enhancing their prominence in the cultural sector. Since its inception, the program has received a cumulative total of 2,223 project submissions and involved 916 young creators, resulting in the showcasing of 392 works across various artistic disciplines. The program has effectively utilized a total budget of €365,000 over the evaluated period (2019-2023). Recommendations from these evaluations typically emphasize maintaining adequate funding levels, expanding outreach efforts to underrepresented regions or demographics, and enhancing promotional strategies to amplify the program's impact and reach.

SDG: SDG 4 - Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all,SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Partnering with civil society
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: General Directorate of Cultural Liasons, General Directorate of Promotion and Cultural Festivals (DGPFC), General Directorate of Popular, Indigenous and Urban Cultures.
Main Feature: The anual programs and actions merged into S268 provide subsidies to promote the development of cultural and artistic projects, promoting de diversity of cultural expressions. The program's economic support may be delivered to public institutions and specific social groups: state, municipal and delegacional governments, including state and municipal institutes in charge of local cultural policy; public academic institutions; civil society organizations; legally constituted groups dedicated to culture; community groups carrying popular culture; and Mexican cities that have been declared world heritage sites by UNESCO. The responsible units of the Ministry of Culture issue public announcements, which establish the requirements that interested parties must meet in order to be eligible for grants. The Secretariat of Culture delivers the grants and follows up on the progress reports to be submitted by the beneficiaries.
Results: Among its programs are:  •	Program to Support Municipal and Community Cultures (PACMyC), which aims to contribute to the development of cultural diversity by financing community cultural projects that stimulate local activities, creativity, self-management and research processes. For the last 4 years it has served people who are bearers of popular culture who live in rural, urban or mixed areas and who collectively have an interest in developing a community cultural project.  •	Support for the Cultural Infrastructure of States (PAICE), through which financial support is provided for cultural projects in two modalities. - Life to the cultural infrastructure. - Strengthening cultural infrastructure. For the last 4 years it has served the state and municipal governments and mayors of Mexico City, state public universities, as well as all those Civil Society Organizations that count among their constituent objects the promotion and promotion of arts and culture.  •	Support to State Institutions of Culture (AIEC), which aims to contribute to the exercise of the cultural rights of the population through greater access to cultural offerings and the expansion of their coverage, through cultural projects coordinated by State Institutions. of Culture, which, in turn, work with CSOs.  •	Support Program for Cultural an Artistic Festivals  (PROFEST),  which aims to contribute to  the enrichment of the artistic and cultural offer and facilitate access to it for the entire population, through the realization and professionalization of cultural and artistic Festivals. For the last 4 years it has served the state and municipal governments and mayors of Mexico City, as well as Civil Society Organizations.

Title EN: Green Filming
Goal: Integrate Culture In Sustainable Development Frameworks
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: National sustainable development policies and plans
Agency Implementation: Austrian Film Institute
Main Feature: Green Filming is a major concern for the Austrian Film Institute. Over the past years, Green Producing has continuously gained in importance and is now an central aspect of funding concepts (in Austria and abroad) The specific funding guidelines of the Austrian Film Institute and the Film Funding Act are the legal basis for the implementation and establishment of ecologically sustainable production. The actual quality standards for films supported by the Austrian Film Institute significantly contribute to national and European climate protection goals.  With the introduction of the Green-Bonus ÖFI+ of 5% and the already implemented criteria for Green Producing, the Austrian Film Institute has developed a Criteria Catalogue of Ecological Minimum Standards for Austrian Cinema Film Productions ÖFI/ÖFI+. The basis of this catalogue are the criteria and measures established by Guideline UZ76 Austrian Ecolabel ‘Green Producing in Film and Television’ and the “Ecological Standards for German Cinema, TV and Online/VOD Productions” coordinated with the film industry.  According to the Austrian Film Institute's 2023 activity report, a budget of EUR 3,135,013 (production) and EUR 133,568 (theatrical release) was invested in the Green Bonus 5%.
Results: The prerequisites for sustainable production have been created and established. The implementation of Green Filming is supported by the synergy model Green Filming Austria, which is led by Evergreen Prisma/LAFC and the Austrian Film Institute. The established instruments such as the film- specific CO2 calculator (Evergreen Prisma/LAFC), the training and further education of the Green Film Consultants (Evergreen Prisma Academy/LAFC) and the concrete, binding regulations for the implementation and review of the measures were developed in a forward-looking, transnational manner. This will allow in future to prepare the evaluation in figures and statistics and to gather experience from the audited Final Green Reports.
Recommandations: Conclusions n.a.

HII NI AFRIKA is Swahili for ‘This Is Africa’, fitting title for a historical display of Africa’s story through a vibrant expression of the evolution of its people, culture, values, customs and traditions that continue to be influenced by Africa’s historical and present events. This aim is to tell the African story from the mouth of Africans themselves. With your support to this initiative will make you be part of the champions of the new narratives, African stories, told by Africans themselves! The hope is that when people see the show, they will leave the theatre with an open heart that embraces the spirit of togetherness—the spirit that unifies, UBUNTU!.
Results: Hii ni Afrika Initiative have managed to produce and launch a unique masterpiece; theatre performance called Hii Ni Afrika Musical at the National Museum of Tanzania in August 2023. The performance is a kind and unique performance that brought together more than 1700 people for 2 days where, Individuals from various nationalities including Tanzania, Africa and outside Africa with more than 20 ambassadors and development partners booked and attended the performance. The show was also supported by the Guest Honor, Minister of Culture, Arts and Sports, Hon. Ambassador Pindi Chana (Mb). Also, In November 2023, Hii Ni Afrika Musical performed in front of 50 ambassadors at the National Museum with the Permanent Secretary for the Ministry of foreign affairs being the guest of honour. Title EN: Holding the Days of Belarusian Culture in various countries
Goal: Achieve A Balanced Flow Of Cultural Goods And Services And Increase The Mobility Of Artists And Cultural Professionals
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 10 - Reduce inequality within and among countries,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Mobility of artists and cultural professionals
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: Ministry of Culture of the Republic of Belarus
Main Feature: One of the important directions in the development of the international cooperation in the Republic of Belarus with other countries is holding the Days of Belarusian Culture abroad. It will promote the national cultural achievements, strengthen cultural ties, ensure the mobility of artists and creative people, export cultural products, and develop intercultural dialogue.  From November 24 to 26, 2024, the Days of Belarusian Culture were held in the Republic of Tajikistan. The opening ceremony of the literary and documentary exhibition "By the Blood of the Heart" was held. The exposition was organized by the State Museum of the History of Belarusian Literature and the Belarusian State Museum of the History of the Great Patriotic War. The Days of Belarusian Cinema have started. The screenings opened with the film "Black Castle". The audience also saw the non-fiction film "The Dream of the Champion" and the animated film "Song of Sirin". A gala concert of Belarusian art masters was held at the Tajik State Academic Opera and Ballet Theater named after Sadriddin Aini. From April 1 to 4, 2024, the Days of Culture of the Republic of Belarus were held in the Republic of Azerbaijan.  On May 24, 2024, the Days of Belarusian Culture in Vietnam opened. Following the negotiations between the Ministry of Culture of the Republic of Belarus and the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism of Vietnam, a Program of Cooperation in the Field of Culture for 2023-2025 was signed. On June 13-14, 2023, the Days of Culture of the Republic of Belarus were held in the Kyrgyz Republic. As part of the Days of Culture, the Days of Belarusian Cinema, an art exhibition of elements of the intangible cultural heritage of Belarus, and a gala concert of Belarusian artists were held. From August 16 to 20, 2022, the Days of Culture of the Republic of Belarus in the Russian Federation were held for the first time in Kazan. The Days of Culture were full of events: a concert of masters of arts of the Republic of Belarus, Days of Belarusian cinema, an exhibition of young artists from Belarus and Russia, the opening of a memorial plaque to Yanka Kupala in the museum of the classic of Belarusian literature in the village of Pechishchi, etc. A meeting with the Belarusian diaspora was organized in the House of Friendship of Peoples in Kazan together with the Federal National Cultural Autonomy of Belarusians of Russia. During the meeting, creative groups of the diaspora and artists of the Belarusian delegation performed, a presentation of Belarusian rituals, national cuisine, and the country's tourism potential took place. Negotiations were held within the framework of the Days of Culture, which resulted in agreements reached and cooperation agreements signed. In June 2022, the Days of Culture of the Republic of Belarus in the Russian Federation were held in Moscow
Results: • strengthening the position of culture in the policy of international cooperation; • the development of wider access for the international community to the cultural products, the creative initiatives and cultural processes of Belarus; • the development of cultural tourism; • the involvement of various creative associations and groups in the organization and holding of the Belarusian culture days abroad.
Financial Ressources: The data are not available
Recommandations: The results of international cooperation and the Days of Culture of Belarus abroad are annually summarized by the Ministry of Culture of the Republic of Belarus. A detailed analysis of these results allows to improve the management of the event and introduce new forms of presentation of Belarusian culture abroad. The recommendations are related to the expansion of the geography of international cooperation of the Republic of Belarus, the specification of goals and the development of cooperation between various stakeholders.

Title EN: International events for cultural exchange and artists’ mobility between Cuba and the rest of the world. Havana Biennale.

Area of Monitoring: International cooperation for sustainable development
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: National Council for the Visual Arts and Wifredo Lam Contemporary Art Centre
Main Feature: The Havana Biennial was first held in 1984 as a space for dialogue between the territories located in the so-called Third World, today recognized as the Global South. The event arose from the need to develop an alternative model that would subvert and expand the evaluative parameters established by the large metropolitan centers, which defined the type of production considered art and that condemned to live on the margins of contemporary creation. Since then, Havana has been established as a scene of mutual confrontation between the countries of that broad sociocultural and geopolitical region, whose artistic productions have been undervalued within the international art circuit. Faithful to its founding assumptions and its decolonizing will, the Havana Biennial continues to reformulate its discursive strategies and broaden its vision. In 2024 we will celebrate its 40th anniversary with the holding of its fifteenth edition, a significant date as it coincides with the 505th Under the title Shared Horizons, this new installment of the Havana event has among its objectives to carry out a self-reflective look that examines some of the themes and artists that have been key in its development. Furthermore, we are interested in creators who work outside the limits of their respective disciplines and are capable of encouraging collaborative practices that make it possible to relate all strata and facets of society and culture. It is our purpose that artists develop mediation strategies in favor of greater rapprochement between everyone and we aspire for the main stage to expand beyond the spaces traditionally dedicated to art. anniversary of the founding of the city.
Results: The Biennial is an event established as a creation process. It is the result of the common will of the Institutional System of Cuban Culture and its artists. and the fact of holding an event of such magnitude in difficult circumstances, such as those that Cuba has gone through in recent years. Throughout its history, the Biennial has stimulated horizontal communication spaces for artists from different latitudes and has established new ties for artistic collaboration; with diverse aesthetic discourses but committed to the assumptions proposed in the Convention.

Title EN: UK-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement
Goal: Achieve A Balanced Flow Of Cultural Goods And Services And Increase The Mobility Of Artists And Cultural Professionals
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 10 - Reduce inequality within and among countries,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Treaties and agreements
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: Department for Business and Trade
Main Feature: The UK-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement (FTA) entered into force 31 May 2023. Some features of the agreement pertinent to the cultural and creative sectors include:   1. Goods - The agreement eliminates tariffs on 100% of UK exports to New Zealand.   2. Intellectual Property - Through the FTA, New Zealand has committed to extend the term of copyright and rights in performances. This will align with the UK term of protection and shall be implemented within 15 years of the agreement coming into force. Owners of rights in original works, performances, and sound recordings will then enjoy remuneration for a further 20 years when their works are exploited in New Zealand.  Visual artists will also be compensated for the resale of their works as New Zealand adopts an artist’s resale right scheme and operates it on a reciprocal basis with the UK. This benefits both UK and New Zealand artists.  Both countries have also committed to protecting their respective brands and trademarks. Intellectual property rights holders, including UK small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), can make use of online electronic registration systems and online databases for registering and maintaining trade marks. This ensures registering rights is efficient. These commitments underpin the intellectual property in our world-leading innovation sectors, including provisions on patents, and test data, and our commitment to raising public awareness about the need to respect intellectual property rights.Intellectual property rights will be enforced, including through authorities having the capability to order an online service provider to block websites which infringe intellectual property rights and disclose information sufficient to identify a subscriber whose website is being used for infringement.  3. Digital creative sector - benefits form rules that ensure that data can flow freely between the UK and New Zealand whilst retaining the UK’s high standards on data protection. It will ensure that creative digital companies do not face unjustified barriers to data flows, such as minimising the costly requirements to store their data in servers in New Zealand.  Customs duties on electronic transmissions, such as software, will be prohibited. Digital creators can explore ways of increasing the value of their proprietary data whilst also using greater insights from trade with New Zealand. Doing so could help to cut costs, streamline operations or even create new revenue streams – such as through app development or marketing.  4. Architectural Services – The Professional Services and Recognition of Professional Qualifications Annex provides for a dialogue between relevant bodies in New Zealand and the UK responsible for regulating the profession of architects.   5. Business travel - Provisions enable British citizens to work more freely in NZ thanks to unprecedented new commitments that allow UK service suppliers, including architects and those working in the advertising industry, to deliver contracts.  6. Travel opportunities for young people - UK and NZ committed to a mobility dialogue outside the FTA that will consider how people-to-people links can be deepened even further.   7. Maori Trade and Economic Cooperation - the agreement contains provisions for cooperation activities to strengthen the trade relationships between UK, NZ and Maori enterprises. This will help Maori enterprises maximise the opportunities arising from the FTA, alongside NZ and UK enterprises. The chapter also recognises the importance and value of the Maori to NZ’s economy and society. In addition to the unique relationship between the UK, NZ and Maori.
Results: New Zealand has committed to extend the term of copyright and rights in performances. This will align with the UK term of protection and shall be implemented within 15 years of the agreement coming into force. Owners of rights in original works, performances, and sound recordings will then enjoy remuneration for a further 20 years when their works are exploited in New Zealand. Both countries have also committed to protecting their respective brands and trademarks.   British citizens will be able to work more freely in New Zealand thanks to unprecedented new commitments that allow UK service suppliers to deliver contracts. It will be easier for senior managers, executives and specialists to move on intra-company transfers. They will be eligible for visas to work for a period of 3 years and family members will also be able to join.  The agreement removes tariffs of up to 10% on clothing and footwear as well as leather goods, such as leather bags, of up to 5%. This will benefit UK clothing and fashion companies, in regions such as London and the North West. UK clothing exports to New Zealand amounted to £29.6 million in 2020.

Title EN: Ukraine Office - Support for Ukrainian Artists & Funding Programme for Ukraine
Goal: Promote Human Rights And Fundamental Freedoms
SDG: SDG 5 - Achieve gender equality and empower all women and girls,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels
Area of Monitoring: Artistic freedom
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: Federal Ministry for Arts, Culture, the Civil Service and Sport
Main Feature: “Office Ukraine. Shelter for Ukrainian Artists” is an initiative by the Federal Ministry for Arts, Culture, the Civil Service and Sport. It has been set up for Ukrainian artists and cultural workers in all disciplines fleeing war in Ukraine and seeking shelter in Austria. It serves as a liaison between them and the Austrian art scene.  Office Ukraine aims to connect Ukrainian artists and cultural workers with cultural institutions and initiatives as well as artists all over Austria: residencies, galleries, museums, off-spaces, design studios, film organizations, literature and music venues, funds, etc. The office assists in finding accommodation, studio places, residencies, and internships; provides information on applying to university as well as exhibition, concert, and other opportunities; and tries to help in finding jobs and grants. As a mediating platform, its aim is to connect those who offer support with Ukrainian artists in need. „Office Ukraine. Shelter for Ukrainian Artists“ is operated by independent arts institutions and has offices in Vienna (MuseumsQuartier), Graz (< rotor >), and Innsbruck (Künstlerhaus Büchsenhausen). Its foremost goal is to enable displaced artists and cultural workers to pursue their practice and to fuel artistic collaboration between artists from Ukraine and Austria on a long-term basis.  The Federal Ministry for Arts, Culture, the Civil Service and Sport provides significant financial support for the initiative. In order to give Ukrainian artists an additional perspective, the Ministry provides work grants and project funding. In total, around 2,1 Mio EUR have been provided so far.
Results: The programme is considered an example of European best practice. Around 2,000 artists (including family members) are currently supported by Office Ukraine. Numerous types of assistance have been offered, including temporary accommodation, residencies, exhibitions, concerts, study and research projects, mentoring, psychotherapy, scholarships and grants. There are collaborations with around 250 Austrian and international art institutions, including larger institutions such as Belvedere, Secession, Kunsthalle Wien, PEN Club, Ars Electronica, but also with many smaller galleries, art initiatives, off-spaces, music and art festivals.
Financial Ressources: See above

Title EN: Ukrainian Freedom Orchestra

SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 10 - Reduce inequality within and among countries,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: Mobility of artists and cultural professionals
Agency Implementation: Polish National Opera
Main Feature: In solidarity with the victims of the war in Ukraine, the Metropolitan Opera in New York and the Teatr Wielki - Polish National Opera in Warsaw decided to create the Ukrainian Freedom Orchestra, which includes leading Ukrainian instrumentalists - refugees who were forced to leave their country, Ukrainian musicians belonging to European orchestras, as well as leading musicians from Kyiv, Lviv, Kharkiv, Odessa and other parts of the country. The Ukrainian authorities granted special permission to participate in the event to men of military age, so that instead of weapons they could take up their instruments and in this extraordinary way demonstrate the power of art in the face of adversity. From July 28 to August 20, 2022, the ensemble went on tour in Europe and the United States, performing, among others, at in Great Britain, France, Germany, the Netherlands, New York and Washington, and then on August 20–September 3, 2023, a second tour: in Poland (Warsaw and Gdańsk), then in the most prestigious concert halls of Germany, Switzerland, the Netherlands and Great Britain. The orchestra was conducted by Keri-Lynn Wilson, a Canadian conductor of Ukrainian origin.
Results: The UFO concerts turned out to be a great success this time and had a wide resonance in the national and foreign media. The tangible result of organizing concert tours and promotional activities was helping artists from the country affected by the conflict, enabling them to reach a wider audience around the world, sensitizing public opinion to the problem of the neighboring country, including Ukrainian artists in the ranks of artistic groups, both in Poland and abroad.

Title EN: Une formation de base diplômante pour l’entrepreneuriat créatif dans le domaine des ICC : Le Master Professionnel en Management Entrepreneurial et Marketing des Industries Culturelles et Créatives - MEMICC

Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: L’École Supérieure des Sciences Économiques et Commerciales de Tunis « ESSECT »
Main Feature: Le Master Professionnel en Management Entrepreneurial et Marketing des Industries Culturelles et Créatives – MEMICC crée en 2023 par l’École Supérieure des Sciences Économiques et Commerciales de Tunis « ESSECT » (une « Business School », relevant de l’Université de Tunis qui représente une vraie pépinière de formations en phase avec l’art et la culture : Musique, Beaux-arts, Patrimoine, Art dramatique, etc.) s’inscrit dans le cadre d’une coopération interministérielle établie entre le Ministère des Affaires Culturelles et le Ministère de l’Enseignement Supérieur et de la Recherche Scientifique visant à miser sur les industries culturelles et créatives comme étant des industries à forte employabilité et créatrices de valeurs et répondre à un besoin avéré du contexte national et international suite à l’essor de l’économie orange.  L’objectif étant de créer une formation universitaire venant en appui au management et à la bonne gouvernance des organisations culturelles ainsi qu’à l’entrepreneuriat culturel et créatif notamment dans une ère portée par le numérique et répondant aux besoins actuels et futurs des acteurs de l’écosystème culturel et créatif. La formation MEMICC étant marquée par l’hybridité et l’interdisciplinarité offre l’opportunité de prétendre à des métiers à dimension générique managériale et entrepreneuriale avec une forte spécialisation dans les activités relevant des secteurs culturels et créatifs. Title EN: UNESCO Culture 2030 Indicators project
Goal: Integrate Culture In Sustainable Development Frameworks
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: National sustainable development policies and plans
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: Ministry of Culture and National Institute for Cultural Research and Training
Main Feature: Thematic Indicators for Culture in the 2030 Agenda (UNESCO Culture|2030 Indicators) is a conceptual framework to measure and monitor the progress of culture’s enabling contribution to the national and local implementation of the Goals and Targets of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. The framework assesses both culture’s role as a sector of activity, as well as the transversal contribution of culture across different SDGs and policy areas. The UNESCO Culture|2030 Indicators’ framework selects 30 SDG Targets across the 17 Goals and maps the selected Targets in four thematic dimensions: Environment & Resilience, Prosperity & Livelihood, Knowledge & Skills, and Inclusion & Participation. As a set of 22 thematic indicators, it supports and complements the global indicators agreed upon within the 2030 Agenda and foster linkages between different goals and targets. It seeks more specifically to » make culture visible » provide a thematic overview, » build messages and advocacy, » inform national and local policies and actions, » understand trends and build knowledge, » monitor global progress of culture in the SDGs.   At the end of 2020, Romania responded positively to the consultation launched by UNESCO in 2019 with respect to the piloting of the UNESCO Thematic Indicators for Culture in the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development in the Member States . Based on the previous experience in implementing UNESCO Culture for Development Indicators Project (CDIS), Romania, at national level through the Ministry of Culture and the National Institute for Cultural Research and Training (NICRT) and at the local level, through the City Hall of Cluj-Napoca with the Cluj Cultural Center and Babes Bolyai University – The Interdisciplinary Centre for Data Science, implemented the project in a cooperative and consultative manner, ensuring an as wide as possible involvement of relevant stakeholders.  Following the setting up of the implementation teams, a national working group formed by the stakeholders that could provide data was consolidated. No less than 17 national and local authorities and institutions provided data either directly (by nominating a contact person) or indirectly (public data sets were used from one national authority).  The project was officially launched both at national and local level in December 2021  when the kick-off workshop took place, with the participation of the implementation teams (national and local), regional expert, national and local stakeholders and UNESCO representatives. On 22 September 2022 the final workshop was organized where the results from the studies at national and local levels were presented and discussed.  The results of the project were included in the 2023 National Voluntary Review of Romania presented at the UN High Level Political Forum on Sustainable Development.  Internationally, as well, the results of this project were presented at the Mondiacult 2022 side-event - Data collection and measurement of culture towards evidence-based policies. The piloting of this project in Romania, was also featured as a good practice example with potential of replicability among EU Member States in the report Stormy Times - Nature and humans: cultural courage for change: 11 messages for and from Europe   drafted by the Commission’s expert group on the cultural dimension of sustainable development.
Results: The project allowed for the calculation of 22 indicators that measure the contribution of the culture in the context of sustainable development in Romania, both at national and local level. Following UNESCO Methodology, out of the 22 indicators, 17 were calculated at the local level and 21 at national level. Among the indicators, two were the international sustainable development indicators of the Agenda 2030, i.e. Expenditure on Heritage and Education for Sustainable Development.
Financial Ressources: 5000 USD

Title EN: Universal Periodic Review Report - Artistic Freedom in Zimbabwe
Goal: Promote Human Rights And Fundamental Freedoms
SDG: SDG 5 - Achieve gender equality and empower all women and girls,SDG 16 - Promote peaceful and inclusive societies for sustainable development, provide access to justice for all and build effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels
Area of Monitoring: Artistic freedom
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: : Nhimbe Trust   & Freemuse
Main Feature: In July 2021, Nhimbe Trust and Freemuse jointly reported on the state of artistic freedom in Zimbabwe, for consideration under the 40th session of the UPR cycle convened in January 2022. The report focused on the criminalisation of artistic expression, the censorship of artists and artworks, as well as the harassment and intimidation of cultural actors. Nhimbe Trust and Freemuse noted that these violations of Zimbabwe’s obligations arise from the existence of legislative frameworks that are utilised to silence artistic voices and other forms of democratic dissent, despite constitutional guarantees to the right to freedom of artistic expression. Legislation of particular concern highlighted in the report was the Criminal Law (Codification and Reform) Act of 2004 (which has since been amended to be the Criminal Law [Codification and Reform] Amendment Act of 2023), the Censorship and Entertainments Control Act and the Broadcasting Services Act, which cumulatively provide a mechanism for the Government of Zimbabwe to restrict various rights and freedoms which are essential for artists and cultural actors to exercise their right to artistic freedom.  Nhimbe Trust and Freemuse specifically expressed concern about the Instrumentalisation of criminal law to increase intolerance for, and impunity against, any form of political dissent that questions and challenges state authorities, contrary to democratic principles. In relation to COVID-19, the report highlighted the proliferated clampdown on artists and human rights defenders through the use of criminal law, with the pandemic used as a guide of restricting and suppressing civil and political liberties. This occurrence was qualified by Nhimbe Trust and Freemuse as an undemocratic assault on the right to freedom of assembly and association, essential foundations for the exercise of other rights and liberties in Zimbabwe, including the right to freedom of expression.  The regulation of artistic expression through censorship and broadcasting laws was another point of focus in the submission, for an analysis of how regulatory measures are arbitrarily applied to restrict freedom of artistic expression based on vaguely defined grounds of indecency, public morals and child protection. The arbitrary interpretation of these terms by regulatory and governance authorities was also cited in the report as having the consequence of silencing artistic expression, as well as limiting the breadth of work being produced. Cumulatively, vaguely defined terms and arbitrary interpretation weaken constitutional guarantees of the right to freedom of artistic expression, limiting the capacity for artists to engage in political and social discussions without consequences or censorship. Consequently, some artists, the report highlighted, subject their content to self-censorship, for avoidance of potential legal implications for creative expressions.     Making reference to how at least two artists critical of government were subjected to harassment and intimidation (including abduction, physical assault, threatened abductions and death threats) by unidentified individuals, the submission noted with concern that in both instances there was reluctance and insufficient action by law enforcement authorities to conduct investigations. These cases were spotlighted to demonstrate that there is lack of robust institutional mechanisms to address artists’ harassment and facilitate their access to justice.   The report recommended: a)	the ratification of the Optional Protocol to the International Covenant on Economic and, Social and Cultural Rights b)	the repealing of laws regulating artistic expression contrary to international human rights standards c)	the prosecution of state authorities misusing their powers to harass or intimidate artists and cultural actors d)	the establishment of measures on the sensibilisation and training of law enforcement personnel on artistic expression e)	the development of a national strategy and plan of action on the safety of artists and cultural workers  f)	government monitoring of violations to artistic freedom by both state and non-state actors, with follow-ups made on complaints and police reports, to assure conclusive investigations
Results: The report has been the subject of several trainings on artistic freedom in Zimbabwe, one of which was the 2022 national training on artistic freedom jointly facilitated by UNESCO Regional Office for Southern Africa, Nhimbe Trust and the International Labour Organisation, within the confines of UNESCO ROSA’s Regional Creatives for Development initiative. The specific session which partly focused on the report explored legal instruments relating to freedom of expression and freedom of artistic expression, for the consideration of what cases of artistic freedom violations expose about the main challenges relating to free creation and expression. Other trainings that have been facilitated have been at the initiative of partner CSOs. Broadly, all trainings based on the report have raised awareness of the need for artists to participate in policy dialogues and consultations that relate to legislation formulation and review. This awareness has been done through demonstrating that legislation regulating artistic freedom is not limited to just the Censorship Act but encompasses several other legislations regulating criminal conduct, broadcasting, cybersecurity, assembly etc.  Further, Nhimbe Trust has developed a ‘recommendations tracker’ which monitors policy and legislation developments that specifically relate to recommendations made in the UPR submission. To date, it has already been noted that government intends to review the Censorship and Entertainments Control Act, through an expression of intent already communicated to various CSOs.  To ensure that recommendations are taken up and legislative processes conform to international human rights law protections, Parliamentary Portfolio Committees have been identified as a core constituent of this process. Consultations with government functionaries are underway for the advocation of a training seminar for Parliamentarians, intended at building their capacity for evidence-based policy making and oversight, to ensure that artists and cultural actors are competently represented and can inform processes of governance through effective participation. Parliamentarians will be introduced to national laws, policies and measures that aid the governance and regulation of arts, culture and heritage in Zimbabwe, as informed by Zimbabwe’s obligations arising from international treaties and covenants. Central to this exchange will be the identification of policy gaps, for a discussion of how these can be addressed through interministerial collaborations and inter-portfolio committee collaborations. Under discussion will also be the portfolio committees’ current and upcoming legislation agenda applicable to arts and culture, for active engagement on how processes relating to legislative review / reform will be organised, to guarantee the effective participation and contribution of the constituent of artists and cultural professionals.

For this purpose, a call was carried out to finance projects from various disciplines: performing arts, audiovisual, publishing, music, advertising, design and visual arts. 52 proposals from the three application categories were selected and financially supported: generation of content based on entertainment; generation of content for training and/or training; generation of content linked to the creative industries at the service of the commercial, industrial and tourism sector. It brings together artists, producers and public and private programmers of the local scene, as well as entrepreneurs from other sectors (technology, infrastructure, academia) in the city of Treinta y Tres, where links are generated, artists and contents are promoted and proposals to promote cultural circuits are exchanged. The event includes business rounds, artistic programs, talks, debates, informal meeting spaces and fairs for companies related to culture.

Area of Monitoring: Gender equality
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: Ushanga Kenya Initiative
Main Feature: Ushanga Kenya is a national initiative that was established back in 2017. This initiative aims to create jobs and the transformation for the living standards for the pastoralist women through the commercialization of beadwork which has otherwise been a traditional activity with little economic benefit to the communities.  The initiative seeks to strengthen the business and production capacity for women and youth as well as improve the competitiveness for the bead products in the local, regional, and international markets for sustainable livelihoods, this can be achieved through the formation of cooperatives where the women join efforts to make the products more efficiently, more so the initiative seeks to protect the intellectual property of the communities practicing beadwork and preserve the bead culture by setting up channels that directly link the women to the buyers and monitoring any illegal activities taking place on behalf of the women.  By strengthening the business and production capacity for women, the Ushanga model is anchored on mobilizing women into organized cooperative groups, providing infrastructure for production, and facilitating competitive access to local, regional, and international markets through new designs, beading techniques, product finishings, and marketing.  The bottom-up economic model aims to empower indigenous pastoralist women to get the right skills in production to improve their competitiveness and inject start-up capital into the economy.
Results: Capacity building for 5,500 Women bead makers to improve productivity and quality of the products Development of  a marketing linkage platform Support of women beaders to international exhibitions (28 women exhibited at Dubai expo 2020)

Title EN: Viability of the cultural space as a separate goal in the Estonian national strategy for sustainable development
Goal: Integrate Culture In Sustainable Development Frameworks
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: National sustainable development policies and plans
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: - Ministry of Culture - Government Office
Main Feature: In addition to the 17 global sustainable development goals, Estonia also monitors the goal of the viability of the cultural space. Viability of the cultural space as a separate goal in the Estonian national strategy for sustainable development is implemented at the level of the Estonian national strategy Eesti2035 as well as at the level of different strategic plans of different sectors. Therefore, when the new policy documents (strategic plans) are elaborated or amended the compliance with this SDG should be analysed as well.    The viability of the cultural space has three sub-goals:  1) Estonian culture is well-known and easily accessible in Estonia, as well as (via translation) well-known abroad  2)  Estonian language and Estonian cultural patterns are well implemented in everyday life and in performance of the tasks of institutions in society   3)  the combination of the national heritage with the innovative means used in culture, the agility of cultural life.  The policy of integration is connected with this aim as well with a view to achieving better cohesion in the society.
Results: The results are measured via different indicators, which are part of the state level strategic planning and budget system. Some of the indicators show decreasing trend, others have been recovered after the COVID (such as visits to the theatres, cinemas and museums).
Financial Ressources: Described under goal 1 – all the measures directed to culture and sport
Recommandations: The Estonian Government submits regularly the reviews on the implementation on the implementation of the UN 2030 Agenda and these are published on the website   https://www.riigikantselei.ee/en/supporting-government-and-prime-minister/organisation-and-planning-work-government/global    According last review, Estonia has been quite successful in implementing SDG-s, including ensuring the viability of cultural space.

Title EN: VAT incentive for Digital Press
Goal: Support Sustainable Systems Of Governance For Culture

Area of Monitoring: Digital environment
Agency Implementation: State Tax Inspectorate
Main Feature: The standard VAT is 21 per cent in Lithuania, while books have a VAT incentive of 9 per cent. Since 2019, a reduced VAT rate of 5 per cent has been applied to the printed press. During the Covid-19 pandemic, the media faced a significant decline in advertising revenues, while the need for news and information increased, especially in digital format. Therefore, at the end of 2020, the Parliament of the Republic of Lithuania adopted amendments, and from 2021, reduced VAT of 5 percent is being applied to digital press.
Results: This measure was one of key measures that helped the media during the pandemic. It continued after the pandemic as the media continued to face economic and technological pressures (e.g. increased use of information in social media platforms).
Financial Ressources: There is no dedicated budget for this measure
Recommandations: In general, reduced VAT rates are consistently assessed as having a positive impact on the financial situation of the media, and reduced rates are also seen as fair and predictable (see report on Public financing of news media in the EU: Public financing of news media in the EU - Publications Office of the EU (europa.eu)

Title EN: Republic of Lithuania Law on the Cultural Policy Framework (adopted on 18 June 2024, shall enter into force on 1 January 2025)
Goal: Integrate Culture In Sustainable Development Frameworks
SDG: SDG 8 - Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all,SDG 17 - Strengthen the means of implementation and revitalize the global partnership for sustainable development
Area of Monitoring: National sustainable development policies and plans
Agency Implementation: Ministry of Culture of the Republic of Lithuania
Main Feature: On 18 June 2024 the Seimas of the Republic of Lithuania adopted the Republic of Lithuania Law on the Cultural Policy Framework (henceforth, the Law), which will come into force on 1 January, 2025.    Culture has been recognized at the highest political level as an important unifying factor that helps to ensure the cultural rights of individuals, the equal provision of cultural services throughout Lithuania, and the strengthening of interaction among state and municipal institutions, cultural organizations, and non-governmental organizations.   This Law establishes: -	the aim, objectives, and principles of the cultural policy,  -	the role of state and municipal institutions and agencies in shaping and/or implementing the cultural policy,  -	the relationship between the municipal cultural policy and the state cultural policy,  -	the system of cultural stakeholders, -	the role of national cultural establishments, non-governmental organizations, artists and artists’ organizations in the cultural policy,  -	and the development of competences among cultural stakeholders.  This Law shall not restrict the right of the residents of the Republic of Lithuania belonging to ethnic communities to foster their culture.  The Law clearly defines and establishes key concepts in the field of culture: culture, cultural and creative competences, cultural stakeholder, cultural and creative industries, cultural establishment, cultural service. It establishes the main 8 principles of cultural policy: cooperation, horizontality, diversity, respect for human creative work, access to culture, internationalization of culture, an arm’s length approach, uniqueness.  The principle of horizontality is of utmost importance, which binds all parts of the state system so that they may clearly perceive both their position and their responsibility in the development of a future Lithuanian cultural policy. It also promotes cross-sectoral, interdisciplinary cooperation and  strengthens the links between cultural policy and other state public policies: environment, economy and innovation, finance, national defence, regional development, social security, transport and communications, health care, education and science, justice, foreign policy, agriculture and other areas.  The implementation of the law is expected to have a positive impact on various target groups. For artists and other cultural actors, it creates better conditions for the sustainable development of cultural services or networks in the regions and for increasing access to cultural services.   The Law defines the role of NGOs that contribute to the achievement of the aim of the cultural policy through the following activities:  1) provision of cultural services; 2) launch of and engagement in the initiatives dedicated to preservation and reimagining of cultural heritage; 3) running of cultural education projects and activities; 4) organising and running of competence building and development trainings for cultural stakeholders; 5) collection and analysis of data and information on the state of Lithuanian culture and conducting of cultural research; 6) submission of opinions, conclusions or proposals to state and municipal institutions and agencies regarding the development and/or implementation of the cultural policy, the establishment of priorities of the cultural policy, and the improvement of legal regulation in culture sector. The distinction between state policy-making and the autonomous function of municipalities is more clearly defined for municipal authorities, with a clear expectation that municipalities should be proactive in choosing the ways and forms that best suit them, and that they should use non-governmental organisations for cultural promotion and activities where appropriate. The objectives and orientations of cultural policy in national planning documents will be based on research and data-driven needs of local communities, which should be integrated into municipalities' long-term cultural development objectives.  The law also establishes the obligation for state and municipal authorities responsible for cultural policy to ensure, through cultural actors (cultural institutions, artists and other providers of cultural services, and persons actively involved in the creation or participation in culture), that cultural services are provided evenly throughout the territory of the country, that all groups of society are able to learn about and take part in the creation of a diversity of cultures, and that they encourage the acquisition and development of cultural and creative competences.  Until 1 January 2025 the following two documents will have to be adopted by the Order of the Minister of Culture: -	municipal cultural policy guidelines  containing recommendations for monitoring the achievement of the aim and objectives of the cultural policy in municipalities, for indicators of cultural statistics to be collected, for balanced provision of high-quality cultural services. -	the procedure for financing cultural services provided by cultural stakeholders in the territory of several municipalities and (or) functional zones.
Results: Currently, by-laws are under preparation.

Cultural Domain: Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: Media Commission
Main Feature: The Press and Publication Law in Jordan is a legal framework that governs media and publishing activities within the country. Here are some key aspects typically covered by this law:  Freedom of Expression: It typically guarantees the freedom of journalists and media outlets to express opinions and report news without undue interference from the government or other entities, within the boundaries of ethical and legal considerations.  Licensing and Registration: Media outlets and publishers are often required to obtain licenses or register with government authorities to operate legally. This process may include criteria related to ownership, funding sources, and editorial policies.  Content Regulation: There are often regulations regarding what can be published or broadcasted, especially concerning national security, public morality, defamation, hate speech, and incitement to violence.  Ethical Standards: Codes of ethics for journalists and media organizations may be outlined, including guidelines for reporting accuracy, respect for privacy, and avoiding conflicts of interest.  Legal Responsibilities: The law typically defines legal liabilities for defamation, libel, and slander, outlining penalties for violations.  Ownership and Control: Regulations may address issues related to media ownership concentration, ensuring diversity of voices and preventing monopolies.  In Jordan specifically, the Press and Publication Law plays a crucial role in shaping the media landscape, balancing freedom of expression with societal and legal interests. The specifics of the law can vary over time and may be subject to amendments to adapt to evolving media technologies and social contexts.

The channel aims to promote documentary culture in the Arabic-speaking world, support its creators and producers, and foster a documentary industry. This includes the "Different Worlds" show, which was broadcast daily in 2021 from all continents of the world. Area of Monitoring: National sustainable development policies and plans
Cultural Domain: Design,Performing Arts,Media Arts,Cinema and Audiovisual Arts,Music,Publishing,Visual Arts
Agency Implementation: The Romanian Ministry of Development, Public Works and Administration and the Bulgarian Ministry of Tourism
Main Feature: The Romanian Ministry of Development, Public Works and Administration and the Bulgarian Ministry of Tourism are coordinating the Priority Area 3 “Culture, tourism and people to people contacts“(PA3)  of the European Union Strategy for Danube Region (EUSDR). The coordination project of PA3, “Recovery through CuLture, tOuriSm and peoplE-to-people contacts in the Danube Region“ - CLOSE, implemented during 2023-2027, supports the design and implementation of a Strategy pertaining to urban regeneration and rural development through culture and tourism, expanding the knowledge on the role of the fields addressed by PA3 as pillars for sustainable local development.  One objective of the CLOSE Project is to gather evidence for policy-makers to boost the revitalization of urban centers and surrounding rural areas based on existing or potential cultural and tourism endowment, to better prepare for future shocks, in recognition of the mutually reinforcing relationship between local development, culture and tourism planning. Also, the Project will provide a hands-on tools for urban regeneration interventions through the sustainable use of the cultural and tourism assets of urban areas, including the tangible heritage (e.g. historic buildings, ancient sites) and soft cultural assets (e.g. creative industries). Considering that cultural heritage and tourism activities have a significant territorial dimension, the solutions that will be developed and tested within the Project through pilot actions can be taken up and up-scaled for other EUSDR urban areas. The pilot actions that will be carried out by the Project tackle the issue of valorizing underutilized culture and tourism assets through heritage preservation and reuse, promotion of creative industries and sustainable tourism growth, while mitigating the risk of gentrifying inner-city areas and enabling social inclusion. Thus, the Project will bring together relevant actors during the consultation phase in order to craft solutions to transpose the principles and objectives of the New European Bauhaus initiative to promote the co-creation of inclusive urban areas through arts and culture.
